## Introduction

Chromium compounds have been a staple of consumerist society for over a century, with applications ranging from wood treatments to corrosion prevention.[1](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR1 "International Agency For Research on Cancer. IARC monographs on the evaluation of carcinogenic risk of chemicals to man: some inorganic and organometallic compounds (1973). 
                  http://monographs.iarc.fr/ENG/Monographs/vol1-42/mono2.pdf
                  
                
                        ") It has been documented since the 1920’s that hexavalent chromium is carcinogenic in nature, after multiple studies noted an increase in the incidence of nasal and lung cancer amongst industrial workers in direct contact with Cr6+ compounds.[2](#ref-CR2 "Pellerin, C. & Booker, S. M. Reflections on hexavalent chromium: health hazards of an industrial heavyweight. Environ. Health Perspect. 108, A402–A407 (2000)."),[3](#ref-CR3 "Gibb, H. J., Lees, P. S. J., Pinsky, P. F. & Rooney, B. C. Lung cancer among workers in chromium chemical production. Am. J. Ind. Med. 38, 115–126 (2000)."),[4](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR4 "Bidstrup, P. & Case, R. Carcinoma of the lung in workmen in the bichromates-producing industry in Great Britain. Br. J. Ind. Med. 13, 260–264 (1956).") A number of studies were collated and reported by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 1972 and 1980, which adjudicated the carcinogenic nature of chromium compounds based upon independent investigations around the world.[1](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR1 "International Agency For Research on Cancer. IARC monographs on the evaluation of carcinogenic risk of chemicals to man: some inorganic and organometallic compounds (1973). 
                  http://monographs.iarc.fr/ENG/Monographs/vol1-42/mono2.pdf
                  
                
                        "),[5](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR5 "International Agency For Research On Cancer. IARC monographs on the evaluation of the carcinogenic risk of chemicals to humans: some metals and metallic compounds (1980).") Despite the obvious dangers, it was not until 1980 that the toxic nature of hexavalent chromium was officially documented in the annual report on carcinogens established by the US Department of Health and Human Service (HHS).[6](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR6 "National Toxicology Program, U. S. First Annual Report on Carcinogens (1980). 
                  ​https://ntrl.ntis.gov/NTRL/
                  
                
                        ") Hexavalent chromium is now known to induce irreversible health damage including nose, throat, eye and skin irritation, but most notably, significantly increases an individual’s risk of lung cancer.[3](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR3 "Gibb, H. J., Lees, P. S. J., Pinsky, P. F. & Rooney, B. C. Lung cancer among workers in chromium chemical production. Am. J. Ind. Med. 38, 115–126 (2000)."),[4](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR4 "Bidstrup, P. & Case, R. Carcinoma of the lung in workmen in the bichromates-producing industry in Great Britain. Br. J. Ind. Med. 13, 260–264 (1956)."),[7](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR7 "MONOGRAPHS, I. Evaluation of carcinogenic risks to humans—chromium, nickel and welding (1990). ​
                  http://monographs.iarc.fr/ENG/Monographs/vol49/mono49.pdf
                  
                
                        ") In addition, chromates have also been documented to induce genotoxicity on aquatic and botanic life through soil and water contamination, owing to poor waste management and disposal maintenance.[8](#ref-CR8 "Oliveira, H. Chromium as an environmental pollutant: insights on induced plant toxicity. J. Bot. 2012, 1–8 (2012)."),[9](#ref-CR9 "Das, A. P. & Mishra, S. Hexavalent chromium (VI): environment pollution and health hazard. J. Environ. Res. Dev. 2, 386–392 (2008)."),[10](#ref-CR10 "Jacobs, J. & Testa, S. Chromium (VI) handbook 1–22 (2005)."),[11](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR11 "Bartlett, R. & James, B. Behavior of chromium in soils: III. Oxidation. J. Environ. Qual. 8, 31 (1979).")

In response the Registration, Evaluation, Authorization and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH) was developed in 2006. REACH is a European (E.U.) legislation that obligates companies to identify, manage and register the risks associated with listed dangerous substances when production or consumption levels exceed 1 ton per year.[12](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR12 "The European Parliament and the Council. Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 18 December 2006 concerning the Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH), Establishing a European Chemicals Agency, amending Directive 199 (2006)..") Consequently, chromium compound usage is now restricted unless granted exclusive authorization from the European Chemical Agency (ECHA).[12](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR12 "The European Parliament and the Council. Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 18 December 2006 concerning the Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH), Establishing a European Chemicals Agency, amending Directive 199 (2006)..") Although companies continue to use hexavalent chromium in numerous industrial formulations, the present period of so-called “respite” has a non-negligible economic impact on companies, as the total cost associated with this authorization is estimated at €1.5 M.[13](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR13 "The European Commission. Regulations: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2015/864 of 4 June 2015 Amending Regulation (EC) No 340/2008 on the fees and charges payable to the European Chemicals Agency pursuant to Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 of the European Parliament (2015).​ 
                  http://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2015/864/oj
                  
                
                        ") Furthermore, this authorization is only valid for a limited time, with an imminent sunset date set for January 2019.[14](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR14 "European Commission. Commission Regulation (EU) No 143/2011 of 17 February 2011 amending Annex XIV to Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 of the European Parliament and of the Council on the Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (‘REACH’). Off. J. Eur. Union L244/6–L244/9 (2014).") In the wake of legislative shift, albeit no global legislative shift to date, many metal finishing industries are now compelled to seek safe, environmentally friendly alternatives to chromate compounds.

Although extensive research has been underway since the 1980s to date, hexavalent chromium remains the benchmark corrosion preventative compound in essentially all industries. For instance, corrosion protection of metallic components in aeronautical applications continues to rely on hexavalent chromium compounds. In one example that confronts the present industrial status quo, it was stated that environmental and health concerns drove the use of a non-chromated (i.e., non Cr6+ containing) primer on the F-22 aircraft (produced by Lockheed Marin), resulting in inadequate corrosion protection.[15](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR15 "Edwards, J. E. Defense Management: DOD needs to monitor and assess corrective actions resulting from its corrosion study of the F-35 Joint Strike Fighter. 84, (2010).") Thereafter the F-22 program switched to a chromated primer. Interestingly, the F-35 (Joint Strike Fighter) under present day development has also opted to use a non-chromated primer that has—interestingly—never been tested on an aircraft in a corrosive operating environment (albeit that the F-35 program cost is estimated at US$1.508 trillion.[16](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR16 "F-35 Lightning II. F-35 Lightning II program fact sheet selected acquisition report (SAR) 2015 Cost Data. (2017).") This is just one scenario that highlights the implications of inevitable eradication of chromates from the market, and the lack of viable (demonstrated) substitutes incites the need for unorthodox approaches and for revision of previously disregarded alternatives, in the hope of creating a future that promises engineering quality whilst also ensuring user safety and social responsibility.

## Hexavalent chromium: retrospective view

Hexavalent chromium-based coatings are defined by an exceptional versatility, which also includes remarkable corrosion protection and cost-effectiveness.[17](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR17 "Kendig, M. W. & Buchheit, R. G. Corrosion inhibition of aluminum and aluminum alloys by soluble chromates, chromate coatings, and chromate-free coatings. Corrosion 59, 379–400 (2003).") The remarkable corrosion resistance of chromates is persistent over a very wide range of pH and electrolyte concentrations;[18](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR18 "Kendig, M. W. & Buchheit, R. G. Corrosion inhibition of aluminum and aluminum alloys by soluble chromates, chromate coatings, and chromate-free coatings. Corrosion 59, 379–400 (2003)."),[19](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR19 "Frankel, G. S. & Mccreery, R. L. Inhibition of Al alloy corrosion by chromates. Electrochem. Soc. Interface 10, 34–38 (2001).") a feature unable to be matched by alternative inhibiting compounds to date, most having finite operating pH and minimum concentration requirements.[20](#ref-CR20 "Ralston, K. D., Chrisanti, S., Young, T. L. & Buchheit, R. G. Corrosion inhibition of aluminum alloy 2024-T3 by aqueous vanadium species. J. Electrochem. Soc. 155, C350 (2008)."),[21](#ref-CR21 "Guan, H. & Buchheit, R. G. Corrosion protection of aluminum alloy 2024-T3 by vanadate conversion coatings. Corrosion 60, 284–296 (2004)."),[22](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR22 "Iannuzzi, M. & Frankel, G. S. Mechanisms of corrosion inhibition of AA2024-T3 by vanadates. Corros. Sci. 49, 2371–2391 (2007).") The mechanism of corrosion inhibition from chromates, irrespective of chromates being known utilized for many decades prior, is something that has really only been understood in more contemporary times.[19](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR19 "Frankel, G. S. & Mccreery, R. L. Inhibition of Al alloy corrosion by chromates. Electrochem. Soc. Interface 10, 34–38 (2001)."),[23](#ref-CR23 "Ramsey, J. D. & McCreery, R. L. In situ Raman microscopy of chromate effects on corrosion pits in aluminum alloy. J. Electrochem. Soc. 146, 4076 (1999)."),[24](#ref-CR24 "Xia, L. & McCreery, R. Chemistry of a chromate conversion coating on aluminum alloy AA2024‐T3 probed by vibrational spectroscopy. J. Electrochem. Soc. 145, 3083–3089 (1998)."),[25](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR25 "Ilevbare, G. O., Scully, J. R., Yuan, J. & Kelly, R. G. Inhibition of pitting corrosion on aluminum alloy 2024-T3: effect of soluble chromate additions vs chromate conversion coating. Corrosion 56, 227–242 (2000).") Unlike most inhibiting compounds, chromates are both anodic and cathodic inhibitors, meaning that they can restrict the rate of metal dissolution,[19](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR19 "Frankel, G. S. & Mccreery, R. L. Inhibition of Al alloy corrosion by chromates. Electrochem. Soc. Interface 10, 34–38 (2001)."),[26](#ref-CR26 "Hurley, B. L. & McCreery, R. L. Raman spectroscopy of monolayers formed from chromate corrosion inhibitor on copper surfaces. J. Electrochem. Soc. 150, B367 (2003)."),[27](#ref-CR27 "Zhao, J., Frankel, G. & McCreery, R. L. Corrosion protection of untreated AA-2024-T3 in chloride solution by a chromate conversion coating monitored with Raman spectroscopy. J. Electrochem. Soc. 145, 2258–2264 (1998)."),[28](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR28 "Zin, I., Howard, R., Badger, S., Scantlebury, J. & Lyon, S. The mode of action of chromate inhibitor in epoxy primer on galvanized steel. Prog. Org. Coat. 33, 203–210 (1998).") and simultaneously reduce the rate of reduction reactions (both oxygen reduction and water reduction)[19](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR19 "Frankel, G. S. & Mccreery, R. L. Inhibition of Al alloy corrosion by chromates. Electrochem. Soc. Interface 10, 34–38 (2001)."),[26](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR26 "Hurley, B. L. & McCreery, R. L. Raman spectroscopy of monolayers formed from chromate corrosion inhibitor on copper surfaces. J. Electrochem. Soc. 150, B367 (2003)."),[27](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR27 "Zhao, J., Frankel, G. & McCreery, R. L. Corrosion protection of untreated AA-2024-T3 in chloride solution by a chromate conversion coating monitored with Raman spectroscopy. J. Electrochem. Soc. 145, 2258–2264 (1998)."),[29](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR29 "Baghni, I. M., Lyon, S. B. & Ding, B. The effect of strontium and chromate ions on the inhibition of zinc. Surf. Coat. Technol. 185, 194–198 (2004).") in many environments (Fig. [1](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#Fig1)).

**Fig. 1**

![Fig. 1](//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41529-018-0034-5/MediaObjects/41529_2018_34_Fig1_HTML.jpg)

[Full size image](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5/figures/1)

Compilation of several polarization tests illustrating the cathodic and anodic inhibition of chromates on: **a** AA2024-T3 in 1 M NaCl exposed to 10−3 M and 10−4 M Na2Cr2O7 (adapted with permission from ref. [19](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR19 "Frankel, G. S. & Mccreery, R. L. Inhibition of Al alloy corrosion by chromates. Electrochem. Soc. Interface 10, 34–38 (2001).") copyright Electrochemical Society 2001), **b** 2205 duplex stainless steel in 1 M NaCl and Na2CrO4 varying from 0 to 0.5 M[124](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR124 "Luo, H., Dong, C. F., Cheng, X. Q., Xiao, K. & Li, X. G. Electrochemical behavior of 2205 duplex stainless steel in NaCl solution with different chromate contents. J. Mater. Eng. Perform. 21, 1283–1291 (2012).") (adapted with permission from ref. [124](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR124 "Luo, H., Dong, C. F., Cheng, X. Q., Xiao, K. & Li, X. G. Electrochemical behavior of 2205 duplex stainless steel in NaCl solution with different chromate contents. J. Mater. Eng. Perform. 21, 1283–1291 (2012).") copyright Springer 2012) and finally **c** Zinc in acid rain solution exposed to 0, 10, and 50 ppm of SrCrO4 (adapted with permission from ref. [29](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR29 "Baghni, I. M., Lyon, S. B. & Ding, B. The effect of strontium and chromate ions on the inhibition of zinc. Surf. Coat. Technol. 185, 194–198 (2004).") copyright Elsevier 2004)

The ability to function as potent corrosion inhibitors in a wide range of pH conditions, has also meant that chromates have been (widely and successfully) implemented into corrosion protection primers and coatings. For example, when a morphological failure in a chromated coating or primer occurs, the chromate ion (CrO42−) leaches into the electrolyte (and to so called “active sites”) and undergoes cathodic reduction (coupled to anodic metal dissolution) to form a protective chromium oxide (Cr2O3) film (Fig. [2](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#Fig2)).[30](#ref-CR30 "Ketchum, S. J. & Brown, S. R. Chromate conversion coatings of aluminum Alloys. Met. Finish. 74, 37–41 (1975)."),[31](#ref-CR31 "Hagans, P. L. & Haas, C. M. in Surface Engineering: Dip, Barrier, and Chemical Conversion Coatings, Vol. 5 (eds Cotell, C. M., Sprague, J. A. & Smidt, F. A. Jr.,) 405–411 (ASM International, 1994)."),[32](#ref-CR32 "Scholes, F. et al. Chromate leaching from inhibited primers part I. Characterisation of leaching. Prog. Org. Coat. 56, 23–32 (2006)."),[33](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR33 "Hawkins, J. K. et al. An investigation of chromate inhibitors on aluminium using fluorescence detection of X-ray absorption. Corros. Sci. 27, 391–399 (1987).")

**Fig. 2**

![Fig. 2](//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41529-018-0034-5/MediaObjects/41529_2018_34_Fig2_HTML.jpg)

[Full size image](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5/figures/2)

Schematic illustrations of the different inhibition scenarios associated with Cr(VI) compounds in: **a** aqueous solution, or when a morphological defect occurs **b** in the presence of a Sr–Cr-based primer, or **c** a Cr(VI) conversion coating, with a particular emphasis on the self-healing and barrier properties

The Cr2O3 film can serve as a barrier to corrosion, given its relative insolubility in aqueous environments that span the environmental pH spectrum, and its adherence to the underlying metal.[18](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR18 "Kendig, M. W. & Buchheit, R. G. Corrosion inhibition of aluminum and aluminum alloys by soluble chromates, chromate coatings, and chromate-free coatings. Corrosion 59, 379–400 (2003).") A similar “universal” anti-corrosion compound is yet to be identified for implementation in coatings and primers, such that the need for chromate replacements spans many industries and forms of corrosion protection deployment. The need for chromate replacements in primers is a field in which only minor advances have been occurring and will be an area where significant translation will be required in the near term.

In light of the performance and simplicity of chromates for corrosion protection, it is clear that replacements are not only needed, but will also ideally be required to meet acceptable anti-corrosion performance (which is now industrially expected and will also be demanded by consumers who have become accustomed to specific durability or warranties), and cost expectations as previously met by hexavalent chromium.

## Trivalent chromium: the unsuccessful alternative

The substitution of the hexavalent chromium with the less toxic trivalent chromium, was initiated in the early 1990s for chemical conversion coatings on Al alloys.[34](#ref-CR34 "Cho, K., Shankar Rao, V. & Kwon, H. Microstructure and electrochemical characterization of trivalent chromium based conversion coating on zinc. Electrochim. Acta 52, 4449–4456 (2007)."),[35](#ref-CR35 "Qi, J. T. et al. Trivalent chromium conversion coating formation on aluminium. Surf. Coat. Technol. 280, 317–329 (2015)."),[36](#ref-CR36 "Li, L., Desouza, A. L. & Swain, G. M. Effect of deoxidation pretreatment on the corrosion inhibition provided by a trivalent chromium process (TCP) conversion coating on AA2024-T3. J. Electrochem. Soc. 161, 246–253 (2014)."),[37](#ref-CR37 "Pearlstein, F. & Agarwala, V. S. Trivalent chromium solutions for applying chemical conversion coatings to aluminum alloys or for sealing anodized aluminum. Plat. Surf. Finish. 81, 50–56 (1994)."),[38](#ref-CR38 "Whitman, B. W., Li, L. & Swain, G. M. Anti-corrosion properties of a TCP pretreatment conversion coating on aluminum alloy 2024-T3 during moist SO2 atmospheric testing: effects of galvanic coupling. J. Electrochem. Soc. 164, 135–147 (2017)."),[39](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR39 "Li, L. & Swain, M. G. Formation and structure of trivalent chromium process coatings on aluminum alloys 6061 and 7075. Corrosion 69, 1205–1216 (2013).") The trivalent conversion coating (TCC) typically contains fluoride salts (NaF), trivalent chromium salts (Cr(OH)3 or Cr2(SO4)3) and hexafluorozirconate (ZrF62−).[40](#ref-CR40 "Qi, J. Trivalent chromium conversion coatings on Al and Al-Cu alloys. (University of Manchester, 2015).
                   ​https://www.escholar.manchester.ac.uk/jrul/item/?pid=uk-ac-man-scw:277523
                  
                
                        "),[41](#ref-CR41 "Qi, J. et al. An optimized trivalent chromium conversion coating process for AA2024-T351 alloy. J. Electrochem. Soc. 164, 390–395 (2017)."),[42](#ref-CR42 "Guo, Y. & Frankel, G. S. Active corrosion inhibition of AA2024-T3 by trivalent chrome process treatment. Corrosion 68, 1–10 (2012)."),[43](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR43 "Guo, Y. & Frankel, G. S. Characterization of trivalent chromium process coating on AA2024-T3. Surf. Coat. Technol. 206, 3895–3902 (2012).") Surface film formation takes place in an acidic environment where the co-precipitation of hydrated zirconia and trivalent chromium hydroxides occurs, hence providing high barrier properties.[40](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR40 "Qi, J. Trivalent chromium conversion coatings on Al and Al-Cu alloys. (University of Manchester, 2015).
                   ​https://www.escholar.manchester.ac.uk/jrul/item/?pid=uk-ac-man-scw:277523
                  
                
                        ") However, due to the absence of hexavalent chromium within the coating, a significant decrease in the so-called self-healing properties associated with trivalent chromium protection strategies was noted.[37](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR37 "Pearlstein, F. & Agarwala, V. S. Trivalent chromium solutions for applying chemical conversion coatings to aluminum alloys or for sealing anodized aluminum. Plat. Surf. Finish. 81, 50–56 (1994).")

Perhaps, most critically however, recent work has indicated that during the coating growth in the case of trivalent conversion coating for alloys, trivalent chromium may be oxidized by hydrogen peroxide (generated by oxygen reduction or deliberately added to the coating environment), forming hexavalent chromium. In fact, it was argued that the fluorides species present in the bath (usually added to accelerate film growth and native oxide dissolution) were promoting hydrogen peroxide formation, subsequently oxidizing Cr3+ species to Cr6+.[35](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR35 "Qi, J. T. et al. Trivalent chromium conversion coating formation on aluminium. Surf. Coat. Technol. 280, 317–329 (2015)."),[39](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR39 "Li, L. & Swain, M. G. Formation and structure of trivalent chromium process coatings on aluminum alloys 6061 and 7075. Corrosion 69, 1205–1216 (2013)."),[44](#ref-CR44 "Li, L., Kim, D. Y. & Swain, G. M. Transient formation of chromate in trivalent chromium process (TCP) coatings on AA2024 as probed by Raman spectroscopy. J. Electrochem. Soc. 159, C326–C333 (2012)."),[45](#ref-CR45 "Qi, J. et al. Organic systems that are used to impart corrosion protection to metal systems include organic inhibitors, hybrid sol–gel and polymer-based coatings.[61](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR61 "Zheludkevich, M. Herein, instead of a deep focusing on the mechanisms involved, we briefly cover the main aspect of these technologies.

Organic-based coatings traditionally used to protect metal systems such as Al alloys comprise of multiple layers (i.e., primer and top coat).[96](/articles/s41529-018-0034-5#ref-CR96 "Bierwagen, G. args.summary:
This is a review article published in npj Materials Degradation (volume 2, article 12, 2018) by Gharbi, Thomas, Smith, Birbilis et al., titled "Chromate replacement: what does the future hold?" The article reviews the origins of chromium replacement motivations, legislative actions aimed at reducing chromium compound use, and critically evaluates alternative corrosion prevention technologies developed since the 1980s.

Key content:
- Hexavalent chromium (Cr6+) compounds have been widely used for corrosion prevention since the second industrial revolution, but are documented carcinogens (linked to lung, nasal cancer since the 1920s; officially documented by the US HHS in 1980). Cr6+ also induces genotoxicity in aquatic and botanic life via soil/water contamination.
- REACH (Registration, Evaluation, Authorization and Restriction of Chemicals) legislation was developed in 2006, restricting chromium compound use in the EU unless authorized by the European Chemical Agency (ECHA). Authorization costs are estimated at €1.5M, with a sunset date of January 2019.
- Chromates remain the benchmark corrosion inhibitor due to their versatility, acting as both anodic and cathodic inhibitors over wide pH ranges, forming protective Cr2O3 films via self-healing mechanisms. No equally effective universal alternative has been identified.
- Aeronautical case study: F-22 aircraft switched to non-chromated primer (for environmental/health reasons), resulting in inadequate corrosion protection, and reverted to chromated primer. The F-35 program also uses non-chromated primer that has never been tested on an aircraft in a corrosive environment (program cost est. US$1.508 trillion).
- Trivalent chromium (Cr3+) conversion coatings (TCC), introduced early 1990s for Al alloys, are the most common Cr6+ replacement to date (commercialized by Henkel's Alodine T 5900 RTU, Socomore's Socosurf TCS). However, they show significantly reduced self-healing properties, and recent studies show Cr3+ may be oxidized to Cr6+ during coating growth via hydrogen peroxide (promoted by fluoride species). There are also emerging concerns about Cr3+ genotoxicity among tannery workers.
- Alternative technologies reviewed:
  1. Rare-earth-based coatings (cerium, lanthanum) - inhibit cathodic reactions but dissolve in acidic environments; supply threatened by China's near-monopolization of rare-earth market (Ce price fluctuated from US$4.35/kg to US$100/kg between 2001-2012).
  2. Vanadate-based coatings - inhibit oxygen reduction but carcinogenicity of vanadium compounds makes this alternative no longer viable.
  3. Lithium-containing coatings - Li salts intercalate into Al hydroxide matrix, forming Al-Li layered double hydroxide (LDH), providing promising corrosion resistance and self-healing properties; passed 168-hour salt spray test; not yet industrialized but shows promise comparable to hexavalent chromium.
  4. Organic coatings and nanocomposites (graphene-based) - improve barrier properties but graphene costs exceed AUD$130/kg, limiting viability.
- Smart coatings with controlled inhibitor release (responsive to pH, moisture, light) are emerging as a design direction.

## Abstract

Major vibrational spectroscopy studies have focused on the preparation of chromium coatings via chemical processes (conversion coatings), and few studies have focused on electrochemical processes (electrodeposition). Initially, the chemical precursors were hexavalent chromium salts, but these compounds are now replaced by less toxic trivalent ions. There is a profound understanding of the process when vibrational spectroscopy is used in combination with other techniques. This is the case for chromium(VI) conversion coatings, and the results of several techniques, such as synchrotron infrared microspectroscopy, have made it possible to understand the structure of the two-layer coating and the chemical composition of each layer. Vibrational spectroscopy confirmed the mechanism for coating formation, in which ferricyanide was a redox mediator. In addition, vibrational spectroscopy was effective in determining the mechanism of corrosion resistance of the coatings. Conversely, there are very few studies on the electrodeposition of trivalent chromium ions, and the mechanics of electrodeposition are unknown. To simplify the use of spectroscopy, spectra of potassium dichromate and chromium(III) sulfate are presented as references for coating studies, and a compilation of and vibrational modes is provided to facilitate band assignment. Our review highlights that spectroscopic techniques have been insufficiently applied in this field; however, the results of vibrational spectroscopy accelerate the transition to safer Cr(III) technology.

## 1. Introduction

In the nineteenth century, three patents were filed on trivalent chromium baths; however, the massive use of chromium coatings emerged in the 1930s. During these historical time periods, the quality of the coatings obtained from Cr(III) baths was lower than that of the Cr(VI) coatings [[1](#B1-analytica-06-00047)]. Therefore, industrial production during the 20th century was based on Cr(VI) baths, but at the beginning of the 21st century, interest in Cr(III) baths resumed on the basis of their lower toxicity. Currently, there is a systematic abandonment of Cr(VI) baths in favor of Cr(III) baths, but the success of these new coatings depends on understanding precisely the underlying mechanisms of protection offered by hexavalent chromium. Consequently, studies involving vibrational spectroscopy of hexavalent baths have also been revised.

The coatings can be formed by electrodeposition of a chromium bath with trivalent chromium or by conversion coatings, which are formed through a chemical reaction between a metal substrate and a solution containing trivalent chromium. Studies of the electrodeposition of chromium from Cr(VI) baths were reviewed by Dubpernell [[1](#B1-analytica-06-00047)] and Mandich et al. [[2](#B2-analytica-06-00047)], and studies of chromate(VI) conversion coatings were reviewed by Prakash and Balaraju [[3](#B3-analytica-06-00047)]. The processes involving Cr(VI) provide excellent corrosion protection but have the disadvantage that Cr(VI) is highly toxic. Studies of the electrodeposition of coatings from Cr(III) baths have been reviewed by several authors [[4](#B4-analytica-06-00047),[5](#B5-analytica-06-00047),[6](#B6-analytica-06-00047)]. Hesamedini [[7](#B7-analytica-06-00047)] reviewed 105 studies of Cr(III)-based conversion coatings and analyzed how the studies answered fundamental questions.

In the aerospace industry, chromium conversion coatings have been used because of their outstanding performance in the corrosion protection of aluminum alloys. Becker [[8](#B8-analytica-06-00047)] presented a comprehensive overview of new promising technologies in terms of corrosion inhibition. In the case of chromium coatings, the formation of Cr(VI) from Cr(III) is an intense drawback, and future research should focus on eliminating Cr(VI) formation. On the other hand, chromium electrodeposition comprises 2 categories according to the thickness of the Cr layer: (1) a decorative coating with a thickness of less than 0.8 μm, which provides acceptable resistance to corrosion, and (2) a functional coating with a thickness greater than 0.8 μm, which provides hardness and high corrosion resistance [[2](#B2-analytica-06-00047)].

There are more publications based on vibrational spectroscopies for the characterization of coating surfaces [[9](#B9-analytica-06-00047),[10](#B10-analytica-06-00047),[11](#B11-analytica-06-00047),[12](#B12-analytica-06-00047),[13](#B13-analytica-06-00047),[14](#B14-analytica-06-00047),[15](#B15-analytica-06-00047),[16](#B16-analytica-06-00047),[17](#B17-analytica-06-00047),[18](#B18-analytica-06-00047),[19](#B19-analytica-06-00047),[20](#B20-analytica-06-00047),[21](#B21-analytica-06-00047),[22](#B22-analytica-06-00047),[23](#B23-analytica-06-00047),[24](#B24-analytica-06-00047),[25](#B25-analytica-06-00047),[26](#B26-analytica-06-00047),[27](#B27-analytica-06-00047),[28](#B28-analytica-06-00047),[29](#B29-analytica-06-00047),[30](#B30-analytica-06-00047),[31](#B31-analytica-06-00047),[32](#B32-analytica-06-00047),[33](#B33-analytica-06-00047),[34](#B34-analytica-06-00047),[35](#B35-analytica-06-00047),[36](#B36-analytica-06-00047),[37](#B37-analytica-06-00047),[38](#B38-analytica-06-00047),[39](#B39-analytica-06-00047),[40](#B40-analytica-06-00047),[41](#B41-analytica-06-00047),[42](#B42-analytica-06-00047),[43](#B43-analytica-06-00047),[44](#B44-analytica-06-00047),[45](#B45-analytica-06-00047),[46](#B46-analytica-06-00047),[47](#B47-analytica-06-00047),[48](#B48-analytica-06-00047),[49](#B49-analytica-06-00047),[50](#B50-analytica-06-00047),[51](#B51-analytica-06-00047)], and few studies have focused on electrodeposition baths [[52](#B52-analytica-06-00047),[53](#B53-analytica-06-00047),[54](#B54-analytica-06-00047),[55](#B55-analytica-06-00047),[56](#B56-analytica-06-00047),[57](#B57-analytica-06-00047),[58](#B58-analytica-06-00047),[59](#B59-analytica-06-00047),[60](#B60-analytica-06-00047),[61](#B61-analytica-06-00047),[62](#B62-analytica-06-00047),[63](#B63-analytica-06-00047),[64](#B64-analytica-06-00047),[65](#B65-analytica-06-00047),[66](#B66-analytica-06-00047)], which implies a lack of use of vibrational spectroscopies to determine the species in solution. On the other hand, UV–visible spectroscopy is routinely used in Cr(III) bath studies; however, this technique has not allowed us to understand the mechanisms of coating formation, and our proposal is that it must be complemented with vibrational spectroscopies. Therefore, our objective is to summarize the contributions of vibrational spectroscopy to the study of chromium coatings and to demonstrate that these techniques are fundamental to understanding the coating formation process. Vibrational spectroscopy is a very effective technique for surface characterization because it clearly shows how the constituent ions of the bath are transformed into surface species. Vibrational spectroscopy studies can focus on several aspects: (1) determining the influence of surface species on the tribological, visual or other properties ([Section 2](#sec2-analytica-06-00047)); (2) identifying corrosion products on the surface ([Section 2](#sec2-analytica-06-00047)); and (3) determining the species in the solution and electrolyte/electrode interface to understand the mechanisms of formation of the coating ([Section 3](#sec3-analytica-06-00047)). The aspects (i) and (ii) are presented in the majority of studies, whereas the aspect (iii) is addressed in a few studies.

## 2. Vibrational Spectroscopy to Elucidate the Structures of the Coatings

### 2.1. Studies of Hexavalent Chromium Conversion Coatings

Between 1920 and 1985, the unfortunate results of trivalent chromium baths favored the entry of hexavalent chromium baths [[1](#B1-analytica-06-00047)]. Hexavalent baths have few requirements and extensive lifetimes, which makes it difficult to replace them with trivalent baths, which require many conservation operations. This explains why Cr(VI) conversion baths were first studied, and these coatings were prepared from commercially named Alodine baths. This chemical treatment of surfaces involves immersing the metal piece in a solution containing chromic acid and potassium hexacyanoferrate, which reacts with the metal surface to form a thin film. The coatings have the objective of creating a layer that is highly resistant to corrosion, which is why studies have focused on determining the species on the surface and the evolution of the passive layer immersed in corrosion media.

Ahern et al. [[9](#B9-analytica-06-00047)] compared the sensitivity of 3 Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) techniques to characterize chromium-phosphate conversion coatings on aluminum: (1) attenuated total reflectance (ATR), (2) diffuse reflectance infrared spectroscopy (DRIFTS), and (3) reflection absorption infrared spectroscopy (RAIRS). This study and other studies [[10](#B10-analytica-06-00047),[11](#B11-analytica-06-00047)] revealed that these techniques have very low sensitivity to chromium species. Nonetheless, IR specular reflectance detected the presence of deposited in stainless steel [[12](#B12-analytica-06-00047)]. The bands observed via infrared spectroscopy in several studies [[11](#B11-analytica-06-00047),[12](#B12-analytica-06-00047),[13](#B13-analytica-06-00047),[14](#B14-analytica-06-00047),[15](#B15-analytica-06-00047),[16](#B16-analytica-06-00047),[20](#B20-analytica-06-00047),[26](#B26-analytica-06-00047),[27](#B27-analytica-06-00047)] are listed in [Table 1](#table_body_display_analytica-06-00047-t001). In the IR spectra, there is a band of C-N, and the bands of water are related to the hydration of the films. In addition, the wavenumbers of the aluminum oxide bands were reported by Ahern [[9](#B9-analytica-06-00047)] and Campestrini [[16](#B16-analytica-06-00047)]. Chromating has also been applied to hot-dipped galvanized steels to improve the protective action of metallic zinc coatings.

Chromium phosphate conversion coatings on aluminum were studied by Schram et al. [[18](#B18-analytica-06-00047)]. In the RAIRS spectra, several bands of chromium phosphate were observed, and a band at 758 cm−1 was assigned to chromium oxide. The Raman spectra of this coating revealed that aluminum oxide was a minor component of the surface. The combination of vibrational and ellipsometry techniques results in a two-layer optical model in which the upper layer can be attributed to the chromium phosphate film. Schram and Terryn [[19](#B19-analytica-06-00047)] selected the infrared spectroscopic ellipsometry (IRSE) technique to analyze chromium phosphate conversion films. This technique involves directing infrared light onto the sample surface at various angles of incidence and analyzing the reflected light. This technique allows for a comprehensive characterization of a film, which is essentially composed of chromium phosphate () with a lower concentration of aluminum oxide. The IRSE technique measures the thickness of the films, which varies from approximately 20 nm to a few micrometers. Chidambaram [[20](#B20-analytica-06-00047)] analyzed aluminum alloys AA2024-T3 via two different FTIR techniques employing a synchrotron source: (1) grazing angle infrared spectroscopy (GAIRS) and (2) the RAIRS technique. This type of electromagnetic radiation is produced when charged particles accelerate to high speeds, and the radiation is in the range of far-infrared wavelengths [[21](#B21-analytica-06-00047)]. The grazing incidence was highly sensitive, and the chromium on the surface was aligned perpendicular to the surface, whereas approximately half of the bonds of Cr(III) were oriented in that direction. The thickness of the coating (approximately 400 nm) was calculated via theoretical expressions. A new band of Cr(III) was observed at 606 cm−1 and was tentatively assigned to oxide . Vasquez et al. [[22](#B22-analytica-06-00047),[23](#B23-analytica-06-00047)] analyzed coatings on the aluminum–copper alloy AA2024-T3 via synchrotron radiation. The synchrotron infrared microspectroscopy (SIRMS) measurements were performed on a small spot (less than 5 μm) in reflection mode. This technique was complemented by extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) and X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) techniques. Infrared radiation was used to map the distribution of chromate oxides (820 cm−1) and cyano species (2100 cm−1) on the surface. Additionally, wavenumbers at approximately 3300 cm−1 were analyzed to determine the hydration state of the film. The coating formed on the AA2024-T3 alloy had a topographically heterogeneous composition and was formed by a mixed oxide. Moreover, a lower aluminum content in the film decreases the thickness of the coating. In addition, the surface was monitored for 24 h after deposition of the coating. A slight decrease in the Cr(VI)/Cr(III) ratio was observed in the mixed oxide, and there was no significant change in hydration. Vasquez and Halada [[23](#B23-analytica-06-00047)] confirmed that ferricyanide is a mediator that oxidizes aluminum in the mechanism of coating formation ([Figure 1](#fig_body_display_analytica-06-00047-f001)). A thinner coating was formed, only when ferricyanide was absorbed by the Cu-enriched particles. When damage occurred in the coating, the Cr(VI) located on the thicker film mitigated corrosion [[23](#B23-analytica-06-00047)]; that is, the Cr(VI) present on the coating provided a repair mechanism by migrating to active sites and Chidambaram [[24](#B24-analytica-06-00047)] studied this process via SIRMS. The coating contains a Cr(VI)/Cr(III) mixed oxide, but several lateral and depth heterogeneities are associated with the microstructural features. Repassivation occurred when Cr(VI) ions slowly migrated from the protected surface to the scratch. In addition, a band corresponding to the Al(III)-Cr(VI) film (797 cm−1) appeared in the pits, and secondary ion mass spectra revealed an adjacent film of . These two-layer film processes are referred to as bipolar models of repassivation. The Al(III)–Cr(VI) complex formed within the scratch, predominantly along the edges, where the chromium concentration was relatively high [[24](#B24-analytica-06-00047)].

The studies are focused on pitting corrosion and passivation in chloride media. The Raman spectra confirm the effectiveness of passivation because chromate accumulates at pits, and this compound forms a barrier that inhibits further reactions on the surface. Vibrational spectroscopies could effectively evaluate the influence of environmental conditions and other unresolved issues, but more studies are necessary on this topic. [Table A1](#table_body_display_analytica-06-00047-t0A1) ([Appendix A](#app1-analytica-06-00047)) offers further insights into the chromium protection mechanism, which has been investigated for several techniques, exceeding the scope of [Section 2.1](#sec2dot1-analytica-06-00047).

Between 1998 and 2012, hexavalent chromium coatings were systematically studied via Raman spectroscopy [[13](#B13-analytica-06-00047),[14](#B14-analytica-06-00047),[25](#B25-analytica-06-00047),[26](#B26-analytica-06-00047),[27](#B27-analytica-06-00047)]. These studies highlight the great potential of vibrational spectroscopy, since the mechanism of coating formation has been clarified [[14](#B14-analytica-06-00047),[25](#B25-analytica-06-00047)]. Zhao et al. [[26](#B26-analytica-06-00047)] reported the spectra of pure oxides , , and Cr(VI) coatings, and the Raman bands of the coatings were close to those of the pure elements but significantly broadened. The spectrum of the coating displayed a band at 852 cm−1 when the spatial resolution was 15 μm. In another series of experiments, the laser was focused across a light area of approximately 50 μm in diameter, and a mapping surface was obtained. After 48 h of exposure to 0.1 M NaCl, the pit corrosion zone had a diameter of approximately 100 μm, and the band corresponding to Cr(VI) was observed at 839 cm−1. The Raman spectra were plotted in a Cartesian coordinate system, where the x-axis represents the wavenumber, the y-axis represents the distance from a central point, and the z-axis represents the signal intensity [[25](#B25-analytica-06-00047)]. This graph significantly assists in identifying the distributions on the surfaces of the different phases present. A protective film was detected, and a low concentration of Cr(VI) in the film or a lack of chromium did not ensure good corrosion protection. This study demonstrates how vibrational spectroscopy is very effective in determining the conditions under which a highly corrosion-resistant coating is formed. In these studies [[13](#B13-analytica-06-00047),[26](#B26-analytica-06-00047)], mixed oxide Cr(VI)/Cr(III) bands were observed, and the wavenumbers are listed in [Table 1](#table_body_display_analytica-06-00047-t001). In the study of McGovern [[25](#B25-analytica-06-00047)], the formation of chromium conversion coatings on aluminum alloys was monitored via a single band at 860 cm−1. Raman spectroscopy revealed that the reduction of Cr(VI) to Cr(III) during coating formation is dependent upon redox mediation by ferricyanide. [Figure 1](#fig_body_display_analytica-06-00047-f001) shows a scheme of the mechanism proposed on the basis of Raman spectroscopy; Cr(VI) ions react with hexacyanoferrate(II) ions, forming Cr(III) and hexacyanoferrate(III) ions, which subsequently undergo redox mediation, and the latter reacts with aluminum metal to form a passive layer in aluminum [[14](#B14-analytica-06-00047),[25](#B25-analytica-06-00047)]. Hurley [[27](#B27-analytica-06-00047)] attributed a broad band between 535 and 665 cm−1 to a Cr(III) species with contributions from α-CrOOH. [Table A1](#table_body_display_analytica-06-00047-t0A1) ([Appendix A](#app1-analytica-06-00047)) provides further readings and summarizes this section.

### 2.2. Studies of Trivalent Chromium Conversion Coatings

Owing to the high toxicity of Cr(VI), it began to be replaced by the trivalent chromium process. Cr(III) coatings on aluminum alloys were studied from 2004 to 2023 via infrared [[28](#B28-analytica-06-00047),[29](#B29-analytica-06-00047)] and Raman spectroscopy [[29](#B29-analytica-06-00047),[30](#B30-analytica-06-00047),[31](#B31-analytica-06-00047),[32](#B32-analytica-06-00047),[33](#B33-analytica-06-00047),[34](#B34-analytica-06-00047),[35](#B35-analytica-06-00047),[36](#B36-analytica-06-00047),[37](#B37-analytica-06-00047),[38](#B38-analytica-06-00047),[39](#B39-analytica-06-00047),[40](#B40-analytica-06-00047)]. [Table 2](#table_body_display_analytica-06-00047-t002) lists the Raman bands observed in studies of chromate(III) conversion coatings.

Zhang [[28](#B28-analytica-06-00047)] investigated the compositions of conversion coatings on steel via FTIR and Auger electron spectroscopy. The Cr(III) coatings contained a mixture of zinc oxides and Cr(III) oxides. The main constituents of trivalent chromium conversion baths are Cr(III) and fluoro-zirconate salts [[30](#B30-analytica-06-00047),[31](#B31-analytica-06-00047),[32](#B32-analytica-06-00047),[33](#B33-analytica-06-00047),[34](#B34-analytica-06-00047),[35](#B35-analytica-06-00047),[36](#B36-analytica-06-00047),[37](#B37-analytica-06-00047),[38](#B38-analytica-06-00047),[39](#B39-analytica-06-00047),[40](#B40-analytica-06-00047)], and no IR or Raman spectra of these solutions have been reported. On the other hand, the surfaces were well characterized via vibrational spectroscopy, and [Table 2](#table_body_display_analytica-06-00047-t002) lists the Cr(III) oxide and hydroxide bands observed in the studies [[13](#B13-analytica-06-00047),[29](#B29-analytica-06-00047),[30](#B30-analytica-06-00047),[32](#B32-analytica-06-00047),[34](#B34-analytica-06-00047),[35](#B35-analytica-06-00047),[39](#B39-analytica-06-00047),[42](#B42-analytica-06-00047),[43](#B43-analytica-06-00047),[44](#B44-analytica-06-00047)]. The first Raman study of the trivalent coating process revealed a band at 547 cm−1 assigned to the oxide Cr(III) [[29](#B29-analytica-06-00047)], but the band position shifted between 520 and 580 cm−1 depending on the state of hydration of the oxide [[30](#B30-analytica-06-00047)]. Previous studies [[29](#B29-analytica-06-00047),[30](#B30-analytica-06-00047),[31](#B31-analytica-06-00047),[32](#B32-analytica-06-00047),[33](#B33-analytica-06-00047)] revealed the formation mechanism of the coating on an Al alloy from a bath, which contains , and a Cr(III) sulfate salt.

In the first step, the anions assisted in the dissolution of the native oxide layer of , and simultaneously, the oxygen reduction reaction and hydrogen discharge accompanied the dissolution of the alloy. In the second step, as a consequence of these reactions, the interfacial pH increases, and and precipitate. The trivalent chromium conversion coating consists of two main layers [[32](#B32-analytica-06-00047)]: (1) the outer layer of a mixture of aluminum hydroxide and oxide (438, 804 and 945 cm−1) [[32](#B32-analytica-06-00047),[34](#B34-analytica-06-00047),[35](#B35-analytica-06-00047)], zirconium oxide (233 and 470 cm−1) [[32](#B32-analytica-06-00047)], chromium hydroxide species and species [[32](#B32-analytica-06-00047)]; (2) the inner layer, which has a high content of aluminum, with the presence of oxide and fluoride species. The products of reactions (1) and (2) form a two-layer coating, and the combination of Raman and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) allows a detailed description of the formation of these two-layers on an Al alloy [[32](#B32-analytica-06-00047)] or an AZ91D magnesium alloy [[39](#B39-analytica-06-00047),[40](#B40-analytica-06-00047)].

The main components of the coating were , , and . Industrial experience has noted that Cr(VI) electrodeposition can be performed only in the presence of [[2](#B2-analytica-06-00047)]. However, there are no studies that use vibrational spectroscopy to characterize sulfate baths used in the electrodeposition of Cr(VI). Other Cr(VI) coatings have been explored for elaborate cathodes for the production of sodium chlorate. In 2016, Hedenstedt et al. “Traditional electrochemical methods” are usually based on measuring the current required to establish the experimental potential of a working electrode. These techniques suggest general models similar to schema reactions (5)–(7). In contrast, the combination of electrochemical methods and vibrational spectroscopy results in an understanding of the structural features at the molecular level, and it is possible to elaborate on the scheme of reactions (8) and (9).

Two processes are noted: first, amorphous is formed in the coating, and second, the phase transformation of amorphous produces crystalline [[44](#B44-analytica-06-00047)]. ### 2.4. Studies of Coatings Formed from Electrodeposited Trivalent Chromium Baths

Cr(III) electrodeposition is an essential process in several industries and needs improvement. There are approximately 880 articles focused on evaluating the quality of Cr(III) coatings, and in some cases, the quality of these coatings is acceptable. However, few studies have reported vibrational spectroscopy results [[45](#B45-analytica-06-00047),[46](#B46-analytica-06-00047),[47](#B47-analytica-06-00047),[48](#B48-analytica-06-00047),[49](#B49-analytica-06-00047),[50](#B50-analytica-06-00047),[51](#B51-analytica-06-00047)], which limits a deeper understanding of the coating formation process.

Mardanifar et al. [[45](#B45-analytica-06-00047)] evaluated the effects of heat treatment temperature on the characteristics of cobalt chromium coatings. FTIR spectra of the surfaces of the deposited oxides were obtained at several temperatures. Mardanifar et al. [[45](#B45-analytica-06-00047)] suggested that the surface is composed of oxide on the basis of bands at 589 and 882 cm−1; however, in our opinion, this claim needs to be revised, and the bands corresponding to water (1623 cm−1) and hydroxyl groups (1680 cm−1) observed in the spectra indicate that Cr(III) was hydrated (bond in [Table 2](#table_body_display_analytica-06-00047-t002)). In addition, the Raman spectra obtained by Zhao et al. [[26](#B26-analytica-06-00047)] of pure did not display a band at 882 cm−1, and consequently, in the study [[45](#B45-analytica-06-00047)], the coating contained some Cr(VI). The band observed at 420 cm−1 is related to the formation of an oxide . Kus [[46](#B46-analytica-06-00047)] electrodeposited Cr(III) via a pulse current and recorded the FTIR spectra of the coating over time. The evaporation of water was detected by the changes in the bands corresponding to water (1620 cm−1) and hydroxyl groups (3100 cm−1). Kus [[46](#B46-analytica-06-00047)] reported a band at 1430 cm−1, which was attributed to a native oxide formed due to exposure to air; however, this band has not been reported in other studies. Zhou [[47](#B47-analytica-06-00047)] prepared a Cr/SiC coating on a ferronickel alloy via pulse electrodeposition. Raman and XPS revealed that the coating mainly included a small amount of SiC and the oxide (551 cm−1 bond in [Table 2](#table_body_display_analytica-06-00047-t002)). Kajita et al. [[48](#B48-analytica-06-00047)] recorded the Raman spectrum of Cr(III) electrodeposited on . The authors attributed the band at 850 cm−1 to chromium-oxo compounds (), which implies that the band is related to a vibrational mode of . In addition, a band at 848 cm−1 ([Table 2](#table_body_display_analytica-06-00047-t002)) was ascribed to amorphous in the mixed oxide Cr(III)/Cr(VI) [[44](#B44-analytica-06-00047)]. In our opinion, these 2 claims need to be revised, and it is likely that the spot area of the laser focused in the area that contains Cr(III) and Cr(VI) species. Consequently, bands cannot be directly related to specific species. These bands may be related to dehydrated Cr(VI) oxide ( in [Table 1](#table_body_display_analytica-06-00047-t001)). Huang et al. [[49](#B49-analytica-06-00047)] analyzed the carbon in a coating by monitoring the Raman band of sp3 carbon at several temperatures (approximately 1330 cm−1). The hardness increases with the precipitation of the diamond structure on the surface. Prabhakar et al. [[50](#B50-analytica-06-00047)] evaluated a coating with an outer layer composed of oxygen and chromium () and an inner layer containing chromium, oxygen and carbon (). The thickness of the outer layer was between 1.5 nm and 12 nm, and the thickness of the inner layer was approximately 10 nm. In the outer layer, a Raman band appears at 551 cm−1 ( bond and Eg symmetry in [Table 2](#table_body_display_analytica-06-00047-t002)); conversely, in the inner phase, this band disappears, probably due to the formation of new bonds . In addition, Raman spectroscopy and XPS revealed the presence of unsaturated carbon () and aliphatic carbon ().

Survilienė [[51](#B51-analytica-06-00047)] recorded the IR spectra of coatings formed from a formate-urea bath, a formate–urea bath containing hydroxylaminophosphate and a formate–urea bath containing hydrazine. This is a scientific review article published in Analytica (MDPI journal, 2025, Volume 6, Issue 4, article 47) titled "Review of Vibrational Spectroscopy Studies of Coatings Based on Hexavalent or Trivalent Chromium Baths" by Julio C. Avalos, Eugenia Aldeco-Pérez, Julieta Torres-González, Raul Garcia-Garcia, and German Orozco (corresponding author). The paper was submitted September 29, 2025, revised November 8, 2025, accepted November 10, 2025, and published November 14, 2025, with DOI: 10.3390/analytica6040047.

The review examines the application of vibrational spectroscopy (Raman and infrared/FTIR) to study chromium coatings, comparing hexavalent (Cr(VI)) and trivalent (Cr(III)) chromium baths used for both conversion coatings (chemical processes) and electrodeposition (electrochemical processes). Key historical context: three trivalent chromium bath patents were filed in the 19th century, but industrial production during the 20th century was based on Cr(VI) baths due to superior quality; at the beginning of the 21st century, interest in Cr(III) resumed due to lower toxicity, with systematic abandonment of Cr(VI) baths underway.

Main findings across four sections:

1. Hexavalent chromium conversion coatings: Studied extensively (especially on aluminum alloys like AA2024-T3) using FTIR techniques (ATR, DRIFTS, RAIRS, GAIRS, IRSE) and Raman spectroscopy. Synchrotron infrared microspectroscopy (SIRMS) enabled mapping of chromate oxides (820 cm⁻¹) and cyano species (2100 cm⁻¹) with <5 μm spatial resolution. The two-layer coating structure was understood, and ferricyanide was confirmed as a redox mediator in coating formation. Cr(VI) provides a self-repair mechanism by migrating to damaged/active sites (bipolar repassivation model). Chromium phosphate conversion coatings on aluminum were characterized, with film thicknesses from ~20 nm to a few micrometers.

2. Trivalent chromium conversion coatings: Studied from 2004-2023. Coatings form in two steps: (1) fluoride anions dissolve the native Al₂O₃ oxide layer; (2) interfacial pH increases causing hydroxide/oxide precipitation. The coating has two layers: an outer layer of aluminum hydroxide/oxide, zirconium oxide, and chromium hydroxide; and an inner layer rich in aluminum with oxide and fluoride species. Cr(VI) species are formed on the surface even from Cr(III)-only baths due to oxidation by hydrogen peroxide (produced by oxygen reduction). The presence of Cu(II) or Fe(II) ions suppresses Cr(VI) formation. The Raman band of Cr(VI) is approximately 3 orders of magnitude larger than Cr(III), making detection of small Cr(VI) amounts challenging.

3. Electrodeposited hexavalent chromium coatings: The mechanisms of Cr(VI) electrodeposition remain unidentified, with unclear intermediates. Vibrational spectroscopy revealed that amorphous Cr₂O₃ forms first, followed by phase transformation to crystalline Cr₂O₃. Raman laser heating causes in-situ formation of Cr₂O₃. The characteristic band at ~550-552 cm⁻¹ corresponds to the A1g vibrational mode involving Cr-O stretching in octahedrally O-coordinated Cr(III).

4. Electrodeposited trivalent chromium coatings: Approximately 880 articles evaluate Cr(III) coating quality, but very few use vibrational spectroscopy. Studies examined heat treatment effects on cobalt-chromium coatings, pulse current electrodeposition, Cr/SiC composite coatings on ferronickel alloy, and carbon analysis in coatings (sp3 carbon band ~1330 cm⁻¹). Several band assignments in the literature are questioned by the authors, who suggest revisions.

The review notes that very few studies have focused on vibrational spectroscopy of dissolved species in chromium baths—only 2 studies report Raman bands of commercial Cr(VI) conversion coating baths and only 1 electrodeposition bath study exists. Reference spectra of potassium dichromate and chromium(III) sulfate are presented as standards, and a compilation of vibrational modes is provided to facilitate band assignment. The authors conclude that spectroscopic techniques have been insufficiently applied in this field, but vibrational spectroscopy results accelerate the transition to safer Cr(III) technology.

# What Is Chromate Conversion Coating? Benefits And Applications Explained

by [Julie Sims](https://www.valencesurfacetech.com/the-news/author/juliesims/ "Posts by Julie Sims") | Sep 9, 2024

[Get A Quote](https://www.valencesurfacetech.com/get-a-quote-from-valence-old/)

## ***Key Takeaways***

* *Chromate conversion coating is a versatile process that improves the corrosion resistance, paint adhesion, and aesthetics of metal components.*
* *It is used across various industries, including aerospace, automotive, military, and construction, where the protection and durability of metal parts are crucial.*
* *Choosing the right chromate conversion coating requires careful consideration of factors such as the base metal, desired level of protection, environmental concerns, and aesthetic requirements.*

Chromate conversion coating, known for its exceptional corrosion resistance properties and ability to improve paint adhesion, is crucial in protecting and enhancing metal surfaces, especially aluminum and its alloys. Given the stringent requirements of the aerospace, defense, and space industries, understanding the benefits and applications of chromate conversion coating becomes essential for companies seeking top-of-the-line surface finishing options. 

This article will discuss the benefits and applications of chromate conversion coating, exploring how this technology can significantly extend the lifespan of metal components and optimize their performance. Whether you’re involved in the aerospace, automotive, or manufacturing industries, understanding the advantages and practical uses of this coating can help you make informed decisions for your projects.

## **What Is Chromate Conversion Coating?**

Chromate conversion coating is a chemical treatment applied to metal surfaces, primarily zinc-plated or aluminum components, to enhance their corrosion resistance and improve adhesion for subsequent coatings. This treatment forms a protective layer on the metal that provides excellent resistance to oxidation and corrosion while also offering a range of finishes, from clear to various colors. Chromate conversion coatings are commonly used in industries such as automotive, aerospace, and electronics to protect metal parts and extend their service life.

In the context of Valence Surface Technologies’ mission to offer [integrated solutions](https://www.valencesurfacetech.com/services/) in aerospace surface finishing, chromate conversion coating represents a critical step in preparing and protecting metal surfaces. Valence is the most trusted partner in aerospace surface finishing through expert coating application, providing a foundation for the high-performance, corrosion-resistant components essential to the aviation, defense, and space industries.

[Contact us today](https://www.valencesurfacetech.com/contact-valence-surface-technologies/) to learn how we can support your surface finishing needs and contribute to the success of your projects.

## **How Does Chromate Conversion Coating Work?**

Chromate conversion coating is a chemical process that transforms the surface of a metal (typically aluminum, but also applicable to zinc, magnesium, and their alloys) to create a protective layer. This conversion coating is achieved through the application of chromate solution, which contains hexavalent chromium, a compound known for its excellent corrosion resistance and ability to promote adhesion for subsequent coatings.

The process begins with thoroughly cleaning the metal surface to remove any impurities, oils, or existing oxides that may interfere with the coating’s effectiveness. Following cleaning, the metal is immersed in or sprayed with a chromate solution. As the solution interacts with the metal, it reacts chemically to form a passivation layer that is thin, protective, and tightly adherent to the underlying metal. This layer is composed mainly of chromium oxide.

The conversion coating process operates at a molecular level, where the chromate compounds in the solution undergo a redox reaction with the metal surface. This reaction consumes the metal’s surface layer, replacing it with a new compound layer—chromium oxide. The specifics of the coating characteristics can be controlled through variations in the chromate solution composition, concentration, temperature, and the time the metal is exposed to the solution.

As the chromium oxide layer forms, it effectively seals the metal from the environment, significantly reducing its oxidation rate. This protective barrier is highly resistant to corrosion. It provides an exemplary base for adherence to additional coatings or paint, without compromising the metal’s conductivity—a paramount feature for aerospace applications.

## **Common Metals Used With Chromate Conversion Coating**

The versatility of chromate conversion coating sees it applied to a diverse range of metals, each benefiting from its unique protective properties:

### **Aluminum**

Aluminum is the primary metal used in chromate conversion coatings, particularly in aerospace. Its lightweight nature and high strength make aluminum an ideal choice for aircraft and defense equipment.

The chromate conversion coating on aluminum enhances its natural corrosion resistance while providing a conductive surface essential for ensuring electrical continuity across components. This treatment is especially beneficial for aluminum alloys susceptible to corrosion, significantly extending their usable life in challenging environments.

### **Magnesium**

Another metal that benefits from chromate conversion coating is magnesium. Known for being even lighter than aluminum, magnesium is utilized in applications where weight reduction is critical without compromising structural integrity. However, magnesium is highly reactive and susceptible to corrosion.

Chromate conversion coatings offer a solution by creating a protective barrier that shields the magnesium surface from corrosive elements, thereby improving the longevity and reliability of magnesium-based components.

### **Zinc**

The aerospace and defense industries often use zinc for its excellent corrosion protection. When coated with a chromate conversion layer, zinc’s resistance to corrosion is significantly enhanced, making it an ideal choice for protective coatings on fasteners, brackets, and other small components that require long-lasting durability in harsh conditions. The chromate coating on zinc also provides a good base for paint, ensuring adhesion and extending the paint job’s life.

### **Cadmium**

Despite being less commonly used due to environmental and health considerations, cadmium is occasionally treated with chromate conversion coatings in specific aerospace applications. Cadmium-coated parts exhibit exceptional corrosion resistance, especially in marine environments.

The chromate conversion coating further enhances this property while deterring the surface from becoming a potential source of galvanic corrosion when in contact with dissimilar metals.

## **Key Benefits Of Chromate Conversion Coating For Metal Protection**

Below are some of the key advantages chromate conversion coating offers for metal protection:

### **Enhanced Corrosion Resistance**

One of the primary benefits of chromate conversion coating is its exceptional ability to protect metals against corrosion. This is particularly crucial in the aerospace, defense, and space industries, where metal parts are frequently exposed to harsh environmental conditions. By forming a protective layer that effectively seals the metal surface, chromate conversion coatings significantly reduce the risk of corrosion, thereby extending the life of the components.

### **Improved Adhesion for Additional Coatings**

Chromate conversion coatings protect metal surfaces and prepare them for subsequent finishing processes. The coating creates an ideal surface for the adhesion of paints, primers, and other coatings. This improved adhesion is vital for aerospace components, ensuring that subsequent layers of protection adhere properly and deliver their intended protective properties.

### **Electrical Conductivity**

Unlike many other protective coatings that can insulate electrical components, chromate conversion coatings maintain the electrical conductivity of the metal surfaces to which they are applied. This feature is essential for aerospace applications where electrical grounding or conductivity must be preserved while protecting the components from environmental damage.

### **Minimal Dimensional Impact**

The process involves applying a thin film that does not significantly alter the dimensions of the component. This is particularly important in the aerospace industry, where precision and adherence to strict dimensional specifications are mandatory. Chromate conversion coating ensures that parts meet their dimensional requirements without compromising their fit and functionality in the assembly.

### **Cost-Effectiveness and Efficiency**

In addition to its protective benefits, chromate conversion coating is a cost-effective surface treatment solution. Its application process is relatively simple and efficient, making it an attractive option for companies looking to protect metal components without incurring excessive costs or delays in production timelines.

## **Comparing Chromate Conversion Coating To Other Metal Treatments**

While chromate conversion coating has long been lauded for its corrosion resistance and affordability, the search for alternative metal treatment options is ongoing, driven by environmental concerns and evolving performance demands.

* **Anodizing**, primarily used on aluminum, presents a robust alternative. This electrochemical process increases the thickness of the naturally occurring oxide layer, enhancing corrosion and wear resistance beyond what chromate conversion coating offers. However, the superior performance comes at a higher cost.
* **Powder coating**, a dry coating method, provides a durable and aesthetically versatile finish, making it popular for applications with visual appeal. While offering decent corrosion resistance, it may not match the longevity of chromate conversion or anodizing, especially in harsh environments.
* **Electroplating**, depositing a thin metal layer onto a substrate using an electric current, delivers excellent corrosion resistance and can be tailored to specific performance needs. However, this process can be costly and unsuitable for all applications due to its workpiece geometry and size limitations.
* **Other emerging alternatives** include trivalent chromium conversion coating, which uses a less toxic form of chromium, and organic coatings, which are environmentally friendly but may not provide the same level of durability.

The optimal choice hinges on a careful evaluation of several factors:

* **Application:** The intended use of the treated metal, including environmental exposure, plays a crucial role.
* **Desired properties:** Corrosion resistance, wear resistance, aesthetics, and electrical conductivity are key considerations.
* **Budget:** Cost differences between treatments can significantly impact overall project feasibility.
* **Environmental impact:** The environmental footprint of each process, including waste disposal and potential hazards, is increasingly important.

Ultimately, selecting the best metal treatment requires a holistic approach that balances performance, cost, and environmental considerations. As technology evolves, new alternatives to chromate conversion coating are continually emerging, offering a wider range of options for specific applications.

## **Military Uses Of Chromate Conversion Coating: Durability And Functionality**

Chromate conversion coating has found widespread application in the military due to its exceptional durability and functionality. Its ability to provide corrosion protection, enhance paint adhesion, and improve electrical conductivity is crucial for critical military equipment.

### **Key Military Applications**

* **Aircraft Components:** Chromate coatings are applied to various aircraft components, including fasteners, fittings, and structural elements. They protect against corrosion, ensuring the structural integrity of the aircraft in harsh environments.
* **Weapons Systems:** Chromate coatings are used on weapon components to prevent rust and corrosion, maintaining reliability and functionality.
* **Military Vehicles:** Chromate coatings are applied to various parts of military vehicles, such as body panels, chassis components, and suspension systems. They protect against the elements and improve the vehicles’ overall durability.
* **Electronic Equipment:** Chromate coatings are used on electronic components within military equipment, such as circuit boards and connectors. They protect against corrosion, ensuring the reliable operation of sensitive electronics.

### **Benefits for Military Use**

* **Corrosion Resistance:** Chromate coatings provide excellent protection against corrosion, even in harsh conditions like saltwater environments and extreme temperatures.
* **Durability:** The coatings enhance the durability of military equipment, ensuring that it can withstand the rigors of combat and field operations.
* **Paint Adhesion:** Chromate coatings promote better adhesion of paints and other coatings, providing a more durable and aesthetically pleasing finish.
* **Electrical Conductivity:** Depending on the type of chromate coating, it can maintain or improve the electrical conductivity of metal components, which is essential for many military applications.

Chromate conversion coating is a valuable technology for the military. It offers durability, functionality, and protection for critical equipment. Its ability to withstand harsh conditions and enhance the performance of various components makes it an essential tool for ensuring military readiness.

## **Applications Of Chromate Conversion Coating In The Aerospace Industry**

Chromate conversion coating is a chemical process that is extensively utilized in the aerospace industry due to its effective corrosion resistance, paint adhesion, and electrical conductivity properties. This process forms a protective layer on metal surfaces, making it indispensable for components exposed to harsh environmental conditions.

### **Enhanced Corrosion Resistance**

The primary application of chromate conversion coating in the aerospace sector is to enhance the corrosion resistance of aircraft components. This is crucial as aerospace parts are regularly subjected to extreme atmospheric conditions, including high levels of humidity and variations in temperature, which can lead to corrosion if not adequately protected. The chromate conversion coating acts as a sacrificial layer, protecting the base metal from corrosive elements.

### **Improved Paint Adhesion**

Another significant application of chromate conversion coating in aerospace is as a pre-treatment for painted surfaces. It provides an excellent foundation that improves paint adherence to metal surfaces, ensuring a longer-lasting finish. This is especially important in the aerospace industry, where the quality of paintwork is not only a matter of aesthetics but also impacts the longevity and maintenance costs of aircraft.

### **Electrical Conductivity**

Chromate conversion coating is vital for maintaining electrical conductivity in components where necessary. Unlike other protective coatings that might insulate electrical components, chromate conversion coatings maintain a conductive surface. This property is essential for grounding electrical components in aircraft to prevent electrostatic accumulation that could lead to electrical failures or hazards.

### **Lightweight and Eco-Friendly**

In an industry always looking to reduce weight for fuel efficiency, chromate conversion coatings offer a lightweight solution compared to alternative metal treatments. Moreover, advancements in chromate coating technologies have led to more environmentally friendly options, aligning with Valence Surface Technologies’ commitment to sustainability and innovation in aerospace surface finishing solutions.

## **Choosing The Right Chromate Conversion Coating: Factors To Consider**

Here are key factors to examine when choosing the right chromate conversion coating for your project:

### **Material Compatibility**

Compatibility with the base metal is paramount. Chromate conversion coatings are primarily used on aluminum and its alloys, enhancing corrosion resistance without compromising the metal’s conductivity.

However, the specific alloy and its properties can influence the coating’s effectiveness and adhesion. Consulting with a finishing expert like Valence can help ascertain the best coating formulation for your material.

### **Environmental Regulations**

Environmental compliance is increasingly crucial in material finishing processes. Chromate conversion coatings traditionally contain hexavalent chromium, which is known for its environmental and health risks. However, advancements in coating technology include trivalent chromium options, offering a safer, more environmentally friendly alternative without sacrificing performance.

Valence stays abreast of the latest regulations and technological advancements, ensuring solutions that are effective and compliant.

### **Performance Requirements**

The intended application significantly influences the type of chromate conversion coating chosen. Factors such as exposure to corrosive environments, electrical conductivity needs, and wear resistance play critical roles in the selection process.

For aerospace applications, where the balance between corrosion resistance and maintaining electrical conductivity is crucial, the specific requirements of the component or surface must be carefully evaluated.

### **Aesthetic Considerations**

While functional performance is usually the primary focus, the appearance of the coating can also be significant, especially for visible components. Chromate conversion coatings can vary in color from clear to iridescent yellow or gold, affecting the component’s final appearance. Your project’s aesthetic requirements influence the choice of coating specifications.

### **Application Method and Scale**

Applying the chromate conversion coating—whether by dipping, brushing, or spraying—can impact its uniformity and outcome, especially for complex geometries or large-scale production runs.

Additionally, considerations related to production throughput, economic efficiency, and available facilities will affect the feasibility of certain coatings over others. Valence can accommodate various application methods to suit diverse needs as a completely integrated solution provider.

## **Final Thoughts**

In the competitive landscape of aerospace, defense, and space industries, achieving superior quality in product finishing is non-negotiable. Chromate conversion coating stands out as a pivotal process in surface technologies, offering a range of benefits, from enhanced corrosion resistance to improved paint adhesion. Its versatility and efficacy in safeguarding metal surfaces underscore its value across numerous applications, making it an indispensable solution for companies aiming to ensure the longevity and durability of their components.

Our extensive experience and commitment to excellence position us as the most trusted partner in the aerospace surface finishing landscape.

Leveraging our comprehensive [service offerings](https://www.valencesurfacetech.com/services/), we are dedicated to catering to the exacting demands of the aerospace, defense, and space industries, ensuring your components receive the highest standard of care and protection available in the market.
