## Introduction

Reinforced concrete (RC) structures are widely used in various environments, such as ocean, atmosphere, soil, sewage, and nuclear power industries[1](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR1 "Vishwakarma, V. & Anandkumar, B. Molecular biological tools in concrete biodeterioration—a mini review. Environ. Technol. 40, i–xi (2019)."). Seawater is a considerably complex medium containing not only chloride ions but also various microorganisms, which can enhance the localized corrosion process of metallic materials and the localized deterioration process of concrete[2](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR2 "Olivia, M., Moheimani, N., Javaherdashti, R., Nikraz, H. R. & Borowitzka, M. A. The influence of micro algae on corrosion of steel in fly ash geopolymer concrete: a preliminary study. Adv. Mater. Res. 626, 861–866 (2013)."),[3](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR3 "Javaherdashti, R., Nikraz, H., Borowitzka, M., Moheimani, N. & Olivia, M. On the impact of algae on accelerating the biodeterioration biocorrosion of reinforced concrete a mechanistic review. Eur. J. Sci. Res. 36, 394–406 (2009)."). Chloride ion penetration leading to steel corrosion in RC structures has been discussed extensively[4](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR4 "Bastidas-Arteaga, E., Sánchez-Silva, M., Chateauneuf, A. & Silva, M. R. Coupled reliability model of biodeterioration, chloride ingress and cracking for reinforced concrete structures. Struct. Saf. 30, 110–129 (2008)."),[5](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR5 "Thoft-Christensen, P. Deterioration of concrete structures. In Proceedings of the First International Conference on Bridge Maintenance, Safety and Management 1–8 (IABMAS, 2002)."). On the other hand, microorganisms such as bacteria and algae can cause corrosion, which is known as microbiologically influenced corrosion. For instance, sulfate reducing bacteria (SRB) produce hydrogen sulfide with a very low pH value under anaerobic conditions to destroy the RC structures in sewer pipes[6](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR6 "Nica, D., Davis, J. L., Kirby, L., Zuo, G. & Roberts, D. J. Isolation and characterization of microorganisms involved in the biodeterioration of concrete in sewers. Int. Biodeterior. Biodegrad. 46, 61–68 (2000)."). Another type of corrosion-enhancing bacteria, sulfur-oxidizing bacteria, is aerobic and can co-exist with SRB[7](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR7 "Javaherdashti, R. Microbiologically Influenced Corrosion—An Engineering Insight (Springer, 2008)."). *Chlorella*, *Stichococcus*, and *Gloeocapsa* are the most commonly encountered microalgal genus found in the construction materials[1](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR1 "Vishwakarma, V. & Anandkumar, B. Molecular biological tools in concrete biodeterioration—a mini review. Environ. Technol. 40, i–xi (2019)."),[8](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR8 "Miller, A., Dionísio, A. & Macedo, M. F. A comparative study of different Portuguese lithotypes. Int. Biodeterior. Biodegrad. 57, 136–142 (2006)."). The metabolic activities of the microorganisms often lead to a decrease in the pH values in the RC environments[4](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR4 "Bastidas-Arteaga, E., Sánchez-Silva, M., Chateauneuf, A. & Silva, M. R. Coupled reliability model of biodeterioration, chloride ingress and cracking for reinforced concrete structures. Struct. Saf. 30, 110–129 (2008)."), which is approximately 12 for undeteriorated RC structures[9](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR9 "Wei, S., Sanchez, M., Trejo, D. & Gillis, C. Microbial mediated deterioration of reinforced concrete structures. Int. Biodeterior. Biodegrad. 64, 748–754 (2010)."). Clearly, the microalgae interact with the interior of the RC structures. However, the corrosion behavior of microalgae on the RC structures under alkaline conditions are yet to be reported in detail.

Carbon steel (CS) is a commonly used material in the RC structures, but it may undergo a critical integrity degradation process in marine environments. This process can cause many harmful results, such as economic and environmental impacts, serious damage of concrete support structures, and even fatal safety disasters[10](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR10 "Schmitt, G. Global Needs for Knowledge Dissemination, Research, and Development in Materials Deterioration and Corrosion Control (World Corrosion Organization, 2009)."). Adding corrosion inhibitors into the RC structures is a widely adopted approach to protect the functionality and durability of the CS[11](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR11 "Brenna, A., Bolzoni, F., Pedeferri, M. & Ormellese, M. Corrosion inhibitors for reinforced concrete structures: a study of binary mixtures. Int. J. Corros. Scale Inhib. 6, 59–69 (2017)."). The corrosion inhibitors are divided into organic, inorganic, and hybrid types, which have different action mechanisms, such as formation a passive film or precipitate, consumption of aggressive species, enhancement of hydrophobicity, etc[12](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR12 "Chen, S. et al. Trigger and response mechanisms for controlled release of corrosion inhibitors from micro/nanocontainers interpreted using endogenous and exogenous stimuli: A review. J. Mater. Sci. Technol. 125, 67–80 (2022)."). Benzotriazole (BTA), an organic corrosion inhibitor, is widely used in engineering applications because of its ability to inhibit both anodic and cathodic reactions[13](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR13 "Aramaki, K. Effects of organic inhibitors on corrosion of zinc in an aerated 0.5 M NaCl solution. Corros. Sci. 43, 1985–2000 (2001)."). BTA has been proved by many studies to have an efficient inhibition effect against steel and iron corrosion[14](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR14 "Satpati, A. K. & Ravindran, P. V. Electrochemical study of the inhibition of corrosion of stainless steel by 1,2,3-benzotriazole in acidic media. Mater. Chem. Phys. 109, 352–359 (2008)."),[15](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR15 "Yao, J. L. et al. Extending surface Raman spectroscopy to transition metals for practical applications IV. A study on corrosion inhibition of benzotriazole on bare Fe electrodes. Electrochim. Acta 48, 1263–1271 (2003)."). The benefits of applying this corrosion inhibitor include low toxicity and cost, good thermal stability, and reasonable solubility in water[16](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR16 "Custódio, J. V., Agostinho, S. M. L. & Simões, A. M. P. Electrochemistry and surface analysis of the effect of benzotriazole on the cut edge corrosion of galvanized steel. Electrochim. Acta55, 5523–5531 (2010)."). In addition to the chemical corrosion inhibitors, green corrosion inhibitors, especially biological corrosion inhibitors, are emerging as a promising and environmentally friendly option due to their cost-effective and biodegradable properties[17](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR17 "Valdez-Salas, B. et al. Azadirachta indica leaf extract as green corrosion inhibitor for reinforced concrete structures: corrosion effectiveness against commercial corrosion inhibitors and concrete integrity. Materials (Basel) 14, 3226 (2021)."). The dual role of microorganisms has been reported in recent years[18](#ref-CR18 "Alasvand Zarasvand, K., Rai, V. R. Microorganisms: induction and inhibition of corrosion in metals. Int. Biodeterior. Biodegrad. 87, 66–74 (2014)."),[19](#ref-CR19 "Herrera, L. K. & Videla, H. A. Role of iron-reducing bacteria in corrosion and protection of carbon steel. Int. Biodeterior. Biodegrad. 63, 891–895 (2009)."),[20](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR20 "Liu, H., Sharma, M., Wang, J., Cheng, Y. F. & Liu, H. Microbiologically influenced corrosion of 316L stainless steel in the presence of Chlorella vulgaris. Int. Biodeterior. Biodegrad. 129, 209–216 (2018)."). Some microalgae, such as *Spirulina platensis* and *Dunaliella salina*, have been shown to inhibit metallic corrosion[21](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR21 "Mert, B. D., Mert, M. E., Kardaş, G. & Yazıcı, B. The role of Spirulina platensis on corrosion behavior of carbon steel. Mater. Chem. Phys. 130, 697–701 (2011)."),[22](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR22 "Heakal, F.E.-T., Hefny, M. M. & El-Tawab, A. M. A. Electrochemical behavior of 304L stainless steel in high saline and sulphate solutions containing alga Dunaliella salina and β-carotene. J. Alloys Compd. 491, 636–642 (2010)."). To date, no studies have been conducted on the combined effect of corrosion inhibitors and microalgae on the corrosion process of the CS in alkaline conditions.

In this study, a laboratory investigation was carried out on the combined effect of BTA with *Chlorella* sp. on the corrosion inhibition behavior of Q235 CS specimens under alkaline artificial seawater conditions using a range of chemical and electrochemical measurements. *Chlorella* sp., a common species of marine microalgae, was selected for this study because of its reported inhibition effect against CS corrosion in f/2 medium[23](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR23 "Chen, S. et al. Effect of marine microalgae Synechococcus sp., Chlorella sp., Thalassiosira sp. on corrosion behavior of Q235 carbon steel in f/2 medium. Bioelectrochemistry 150, 108349 (2023)."). Therefore, we hypothesized that the combined inhibition effect of the microalgae and BTA on CS corrosion was superior to that of BTA alone. This study provides a new insight into CS corrosion control by combining biological and chemical approaches for future research and applications.

## Experimental

### Material preparation

The corrosion specimens in this study were cut from a Q235 CS sheet. The elemental composition (wt%) of the specimens was 0.17 C, 0.11 Si, 0.02 Mn, 0.017 P, 0.006 S, and balance Fe. The measurements were carried out using square shape specimens with a side length of 1 cm, and the rest was sealed with epoxy resin and soldered with a copper wire. Before immersion experiment, all the specimens were abraded through 200-, 400-, 600-, 800-, and 1200-grit emery paper, degreased in absolute ethanol, washed with ultrapure water, dried by air dry oven, and desiccated until use. In addition, the specimens were sterilized by an ultraviolet lamp for 30 min to ensure the absence of other bacteria.

The *Chlorella* sp. in this study was provided from Yellow Sea Fisheries Research Institute, Chinese Academy of Fishery Sciences, and cultivated in the f/2 medium[23](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR23 "Chen, S. et al. Effect of marine microalgae Synechococcus sp., Chlorella sp., Thalassiosira sp. on corrosion behavior of Q235 carbon steel in f/2 medium. Bioelectrochemistry 150, 108349 (2023)."). The inoculums were incubated in an incubator at 25 ± 1 °C under a light: dark (12:12) cycle with an irradiance of 2400 lx. All experimental devices and media used were sterilized by autoclaving at 121 °C for 30 min prior to use. The cell counts were determined using a hemocytometer under an optical microscope (Leitz Laborlux, Germany) at 400× magnification. The algal biomass was calculated by algal volume as per the previous study[24](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR24 "Chen, S. et al. Ecotoxicological effects of sulfonamides and fluoroquinolones and their removal by a green alga (Chlorella vulgaris) and a cyanobacterium (Chrysosporum ovalisporum). Environ. Pollut. 263, 114554 (2020)."). BTA was purchased from San Yao Hong Co., Ltd. (Macau, China). Ultrapure water (18.2 MΩ × cm) was obtained using a Millipore Direct-Q 3UV system (Merck, Billerica, MA, USA).

### Test solution

The immersion experiment lasted for 384 h in a 250-mL beaker filled with 100 mL corrosive solution. The corrosive solution in this study was alkaline artificial seawater, containing sterilized filtered river water and 3.5% NaCl. Its solution pH was adjusted to 10 with 0.1 mol·L−1 NaOH. The stock solution of BTA was prepared with neutral artificial seawater. To verify the hypothesis that the microalgae and BTA inhibit CS corrosion better than BTA alone, two treatment groups (algae-BTA-CS and BTA-CS), one control group (CS alone), and one blank group (algae alone) were studied. Before the immersion experiment, the microalgal cell and BTA stock solution in the algae-BTA group were magnetically stirred for 1 h under a neutral condition to ensure that the adsorption/desorption equilibrium was reached. Then, the rest of the corrosive solution was added into this system to simulate the onset of corrosion, followed by the prepared specimen into the corrosive solution. The initial concentration of BTA was set as 10 mg·L−1, and the initial biomass of the microalgae was set as 160 mg·L−1. The microalgal biomass and/or BTA concentration (3 mL) from each beaker were detected at 0, 24, 48, 72, 96, 192, 288, and 384 h. Three mL of fresh alkaline artificial seawater with and without 10 mg·L−1 BTA was replenished to the beakers in the two treatment groups and the blank group, respectively. All the experiments were performed within the incubator under the same culture condition. To simulate flow disturbances and prevent microalgal deposition, the beakers were gently shaken, and their positions were randomly changed every 24 h for uniform distribution of light. The dissolved oxygen (DO) concentration of the corrosive solution was measured with an oxygen electrode (DO-957, Leici, China). All the measurements were carried out at room temperature and repeated three times for reproducibility.

### Weight loss measurement

All the specimens were weighed by an analytical balance (ATX224R, Shimadzu, Japan) with an accuracy of 0.1 mg before and after the immersion experiment. The specimens were taken out from the corrosive solution, and the passive films were sequentially stripped with a solution of 2.5% glutaraldehyde in phosphate buffer saline (PBS) and a Clarke’s solution (20 g antimony trioxide + 50 g stannous chloride + 1000 mL 37% concentrated hydrochloric acid). The exposed specimen surfaces were cleaned in absolute ethanol, rinsed with ultrapure water, and dried by the air dry oven. The exposed specimens and passive films were used for further surface analysis.

### Electrochemical measurements

The open circuit potential (OCP), electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), and potentiodynamic polarization curves were performed in the corrosive solution using an electrochemical workstation (Gamry Interface 1000E, USA). A saturated calomel electrode (SCE) and a platinum plate served as the reference and counter electrodes, respectively. Q235 CS specimens were used as the working electrodes one at a time. The three-electrode cell system was open without aeration. The EIS measurement was obtained after immersion for 1, 24, 48, 72, 96, 192, 288, and 384 h by applying a sinusoidal voltage signal of 10 mV in a frequency range of 105 Hz to 10−2 Hz. The EIS data were analyzed by Gamry Echem Analyst software, and fitted with a suitable circuit model. After 384 h, potentiodynamic polarization curves were measured by scanning the potential from − 400 mV/SCE to + 600 mV/SCE vs. OCP at a sweep rate of 0.167 mV·s−1.

### Surface analysis

After the immersion experiment, the exposed specimens and passive films were examined using scanning electron microscope (SEM, Zeiss sigma 500, Carl Zeiss, Germany). Energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) was used for elemental analysis of the passive films, and 3-D optical profiler (S neox, Sensofar, Spain) was used to characterize the surface roughness of the exposed specimens. Before SEM observation, the exposed specimens were dried and placed in desiccators; the passive films were collected in PBS solution containing 2.5% glutaraldehyde, and then dehydrated using serial dilution of ethanol (50%, 60%, 70%, 80%, 90%, 95%, and 100%) for 10 min each. An X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo Scientific K-Alpha, Thermo Fisher Scientific, UK) analysis was also adopted to evaluate chemical compounds in the passive films, and the data were fitted by Avantage 5.948 software (Thermo Fisher Scientific, UK).

## Results

### Open circuit potential measurement

Figure [S1](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#MOESM1) shows the OCP variation of Q235 CS specimen in the control, BTA, and algae-BTA groups within 384 h. The changes of OCP in the three groups were similar, where the highest values reached at 1 h, followed by a rapid decrease within the first 72 h and a slow increase to 192 h, and remained stable until 384 h. The experimental results can be explained by the formation of passive films. Initially, the electrode surface had no protective film to hinder the corrosive solution. However, in the early stage of the CS corrosion, the microalgae began to reproduce and colonize rapidly, and a biofilm appeared on the surface of the electrode[25](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR25 "Li, Y. et al. Mitigation of microbial corrosion by Cu addition to X65 pipeline steel by Pseudomonas aeruginosa MCCC 1A00099. Arch. Microbiol. 204, 299 (2022)."),[26](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR26 "Yang, J. et al. Effect of Alcaligenes sp. and sulfate-reducing bacteria on corrosion of Q235 steel in simulated marine environment. Int. J. Electrochem. Sci. 14, 9193–9205 (2019)."). In addition, BTA could also form a polymeric film to prevent corrosion of the immersed CS specimens[27](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR27 "Akhavan, H., Izadi, M., Mohammadi, I., Shahrabi, T. & Ramezanzadeh, B. The synergistic effect of BTA-Co system on the corrosion inhibition of mild steel in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution. J. Electrochem. Soc. 165, C670–C680 (2018).").

### Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy measurement

Figures [S2](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#MOESM1) and [S3](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#MOESM1) illustrate the Nyquist and Bode diagrams of the impedance measurements for Q235 CS specimens exposed to the control, BTA, and algae-BTA groups within 384 h. Fig. [S2](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#MOESM1) suggests that the corrosion rate in the algae-BTA group was lower than that in the control and BTA groups due to the larger the diameters shown in Nyquist plots indicating the lower the corrosion rates[28](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR28 "Kalajahi, S. T., Rasekh, B., Yazdian, F., Neshati, J. & Taghavi, L. Green mitigation of microbial corrosion by copper nanoparticles doped carbon quantum dots nanohybrid. Environ. Sci. Pollut. Res. Int. 27, 40537–40551 (2020)."). However, the diameters of these three groups changed within the immersion, indicating a change in the metal/solution interface[29](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR29 "Salgar-Chaparro, S. J., Tarazona, J. & Machuca, L. L. Corrosion of carbon steel by Shewanella chilikensis DC57 under thiosulphate and nitrate reducing conditions. Front. Bioeng. Biotechnol. 10, 825776 (2022)."). Figure [S3](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#MOESM1) shows that the phase angle at middle frequencies of the algae-BTA group was higher than that of the control and BTA groups. It means that the corrosion resistance was the highest in the presence of the microalgae and BTA[30](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR30 "Chidiebere, M. A., Oguzie, E. E., Liu, L., Li, Y. & Wang, F. Corrosion inhibition of Q235 mild steel in 0.5 M H2SO4 solution by phytic acid and synergistic iodide additives. Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. 53, 7670–7679 (2014)."). Moreover, as a decisive parameter, impedance modulus at low frequency (|*Z*|0.01 Hz) was taken as it reflects the corrosion process at the metal/solution interface[31](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR31 "Milošev, I. Contemporary modes of corrosion protection and functionalization of materials. Acta Chim. Slov. 66, 511–533 (2019)."). Figure [1](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#Fig1) presents the plot of the logarithmic value of |*Z*|0.01 Hz as a function of immersion time for the three groups. It shows that the value of log |*Z*|0.01 Hz in the algae-BTA group was always significantly higher than that in the control and/or BTA groups (*p* < 0.05), except for 48 and 288 h, indicating that the algae-BTA group had the highest corrosion resistance performance[32](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR32 "Balakrishnan, A., Jena, G., Pongachira George, R. & Philip, J. Polydimethylsiloxane-graphene oxide nanocomposite coatings with improved anti-corrosion and anti-biofouling properties. Environ. Sci. Pollut. Res. Int. 28, 7404–7422 (2021)."). The microalgae and BTA may form a more compact passive film than BTA, thereby slowing down the corrosion rate and increasing the low-frequency impedance modulus.

**Fig. 1**

![Fig. 1](//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41598-024-74557-4/MediaObjects/41598_2024_74557_Fig1_HTML.png)

[Full size image](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4/figures/1)

Impedance modulus at low frequency of Q235 carbon steel specimens in the control, BTA, and algae-BTA groups within 384 h of immersion. Different letters represent significant differences (*p* < 0.05) between groups. Measurements were made in triplicate; error bars indicate the standard deviation.

To analyze the impedance data in detail, a two-time constant model was employed in this study. Figure [S4](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#MOESM1) exhibits the equivalent circuit used for fitting the impedance spectra of the CS specimens in the three groups. In this model, *R*s is the solution resistance; *Q*f and *R*f are the capacitance and resistance of the passive films, respectively; *Q*dl and *R*ct are the double layer capacitance and charge transfer resistance, respectively. The impedance of constant phase element (CPE), *Q*, is defined by the following equation[33](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR33 "Hao, Y., Sani, L. A., Ge, T. & Fang, Q. Phytic acid doped polyaniline containing epoxy coatings for corrosion protection of Q235 carbon steel. Appl. Surf. Sci. 419, 826–837 (2017)."):

$${Z}\_{\text{C}\text{P}\text{E}}=1/{{[Y}\_{0}\left(j\omega \right)}^{n}]$$

(1)

where *Y*0 and *n* are the admittance and empirical exponent of the CPE, respectively, *j* is the imaginary number, *j* = (–1)1/2, and *ω* is the angular frequency, *ω* = 2π*f*. For *n* = 1, the CPE represents an ideal capacitor (*Y*0 = *C*). For *n* = 0.5, the CPE represents a Warburg impedance (*Y*0 = *W*). For *n* = 0, the CPE represents an ideal resistor (*Y*0 = *R*). For *n* = − 1, the CPE represents an inductance (*Y*0 = *L*−1)[34](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR34 "Cui, J., Yang, Y., Li, X., Yuan, W. & Pei, Y. Toward a slow-release borate inhibitor to control mild steel corrosion in simulated recirculating water. ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces 10, 4183–4197 (2018).").

Using a CPE instead of a capacitor provides the deviation from ideal capacitive behavior. The impedance parameters calculated from the equivalent circuit are listed in Table [1](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#Tab1). The *R*ct value in the algae-BTA group were higher than that in the control and BTA groups. It suggests that the microalgae contributed to the low corrosion rate, which may be related to the lower charge transfer rate between the passive film and CS specimen surface.

### Potentiostatic polarization curves measurement

Figure [2](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#Fig2) shows potentiostatic polarization curves of Q235 CS specimens exposed to the control, BTA, and algae-BTA groups after 384 h. The polarization parameters calculated from the potentiostatic polarization curves including current density (*i*corr), corrosion potential (*E*corr), cathodic slope (*β*c), and anodic slope (*β*a) are listed in Table [2](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#Tab2). The corrosion rate (mm·y–1) of the specimens was calculated by *i*corr using the following equation[35](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR35 "Jones, D. A. Principles and Presentation of Corrotion 2nd edn. (Prentice-Hall Inc, 1996)."):

$${w}\_{corr}=\frac{3.27\times{10}^{\--3}\times{i}\_{\text{c}\text{o}\text{r}\text{r}}\times a}{n\times\rho}$$

(2)

where *w**corr*, *i*corr, *a*, *n*, and *ρ* were the corrosion rate (mm·y−1), corrosion current density (*µ*A·cm–2), relative atomic weight (Fe, *a* = 55.845 g·mol−1), number of electrons produced by the corrosion reaction (Fe2+, *n* = 2), and specimen density (CS, *ρ* = 7.85 g·cm−3), respectively.

The values of *i*corr and *w**corr* in the control and BTA groups were higher than those in the algae-BTA group. It shows that the microalgae slowed down the corrosion rate of the CS specimens, which is consistent with the EIS results.

### Surface morphology of exposed specimens and corrosion products

The surface morphology of Q235 CS specimens without passive films was examined using SEM, which is shown in Fig. [3](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#Fig3). At 192 h, clear grinding scratches on the specimens of the BTA (Fig. [3](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#Fig3)b) and algae-BTA (Fig. [3](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#Fig3)c) groups could be easily recognized. However, some corrosion pits could also be found in the control (Fig. [3](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#Fig3)a) and BTA (Fig. [3](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#Fig3)b) groups. At 384 h, the scratches disappeared, and the uniform and pitting corrosion could be observed in all groups (Fig. [3](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#Fig3)a’, b’, c’). Figure [S5](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#MOESM1) and Table [S1](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#MOESM1) show the 3-D surface morphology and surface roughness of the CS specimens after removing the passive films. As can be seen from Fig. [S5](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#MOESM1), the maximum pitting pit depths in the algae-BTA group were 5 *µ*m (Fig. [S5](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#MOESM1)c) and 16 *µ*m (Fig. [S5](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#MOESM1)c’) at 192 and 384 h, respectively, which were less than those in the control (Fig. [S5](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#MOESM1)a and [S5](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#MOESM1)a’) and BTA (Fig. [S5](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#MOESM1)b and [S5](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#MOESM1)b’) groups. It indicates that the addition of the microalgae could reduce the pitting pit depth. However, the phenomenon of uniform corrosion still existed in the algae-BTA group (Fig. [S5](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#MOESM1)c’). Moreover, by comparing the SEM and 3-D surface morphologies between 192 and 384 h, it was found that the CS corrosion of all groups became more severe with time. In Table [S1](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#MOESM1), the average surface roughness (*R*a) was the highest in the BTA group at 192 and 384 h, indicating that the inhibitor had a very short protection period for CS uniform corrosion in this study. The *R*a in the algae-BTA group at 192 h was the lowest, which means that the microalgae could slow down the corrosion rate of the CS specimens in a period of time after the onset of corrosion.

SEM morphologies and the corresponding EDS results of the passive films are shown in Fig. [S6](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#MOESM1). The EDS results show that the key elements were C, O, and Fe, the secondary elements were Na, Cl, and P, and the trace elements were K and Si in the elemental constituent of the corrosion products. Therefore, it can be concluded that the corrosion products of all groups were similar. XPS results further revealed the composition of the chemical compounds of the corrosion products. Figure [4](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#Fig4) presents the high-resolution XPS spectra of survey, Fe 2p, O 1s, and C 1s for corrosion products from different groups at 192 and 384 h. In Fig. [4](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#Fig4)a and a’, the survey spectrum of the algae-BTA group was different from that of the control and BTA groups. For example, in the algae-BTA group, the Fe content was higher than that in the other two groups, while the Na, Cl, and P contents were lower than those in the other two groups. The Fe 2p peak (Fig. [4](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#Fig4)b and b’) contains contributions from Fe2O3 at 711.71 eV, Fe(II) at 715.58 and 729.18 eV, Fe(III) at 719.58 eV, and FeCl2 at 724.88 eV[36](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR36 "Biesinger, M. C. et al. Resolving surface chemical states in XPS analysis of first row transition metals, oxides and hydroxides: Cr, Mn, Fe, Co and Ni. Appl. Surf. Sci.257, 2717–2730 (2011)."),[37](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR37 "Uhlig, I., Szargan, R., Nesbitt, H. W. & Laajalehto, K. Surface states and reactivity of pyrite and marcasite. Applied Surface Science 179, 222–229 (2001)."). The variations of the valence state and composition of Fe reflect the changes in the composition and structure of the passive films. The high content of Fe2O3 in the algae-BTA group is beneficial to the stability of the passive films and the improvement of corrosion inhibition efficiency[38](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR38 "Zhou, Y., Zuo, Y. & Lin, B. The compounded inhibition of sodium molybdate and benzotriazole on pitting corrosion of Q235 steel in NaCl + NaHCO3 solution. Mater. Chem. Phys. 192, 86–93 (2017)."). With regard to the O 1s peak (Fig. [4](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#Fig4)c and c’), it includes three basic components, that is, Fe2O3 and/or FeCO3 at 531.17 eV, Fe(OH)3 at 533.08 eV, and organic O and/or adsorbed H2O at 536.08 eV[39](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR39 "Nohira, H. et al. Characterization of ALCVD-Al2O3 and ZrO2 layer using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy. J. Non-Cryst. Solids 303, 83–87 (2002)."). The presence of FeCO3 in each group is due to the conversion of dissolved CO2 into CO32– in the corrosive solution and/or microalgal growing environment[40](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR40 "Zhao, J. & Chen, G. The synergistic inhibition effect of oleic-based imidazoline and sodium benzoate on mild steel corrosion in a CO2-saturated brine solution. Electrochim. Acta 69, 247–255 (2012)."). Compared with the BTA and algae-BTA groups, the relative amount of Fe(OH)3 in the control group was the highest, indicating that Fe(III) hydroxide mainly exists existed in the alkaline artificial seawater without inhibitors, which is consistent with the result of Wang et al.[41](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR41 "Wang, D. et al. Synergetic effect of two inhibitors for enhanced corrosion protection on the reinforcing steel in the chloride-contaminated carbonated solutions. Constr. Build. Mater. 286, 122916 (2021)."). The content of the adsorbed H2O in the control and BTA groups was much higher than that in the algae-BTA group, which means that the adsorbed H2O was responsible for accelerating the surface corrosion of the CS specimens. In addition, the peak of C 1s (Fig. [4](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#Fig4)d and d’) at 284.8, 286.51, and 288.37 eV correspond to C-C and/or C = C, C-O and/or C = O, and CO32– and/or C-N[42](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR42 "Shchukarev, A. V. & Korolkov, D. V. XPS study of group IA carbonates. Cent. Eur. J. Chem. 2, 347–362 (2004)."). It indicates that a biofilm of organic compounds produced by the microalgae and/or a BTA polymeric film existed in the algae-BTA and BTA groups.

### Weight loss measurement

The corrosion rate of Q235 CS specimens calculated by weight loss are listed in Table [S2](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#MOESM1). The corrosion rate (mm·y−1) of the specimens was assessed using the following equation[43](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR43 "Dong, Y. et al. Severe microbiologically influenced corrosion of S32654 super austenitic stainless steel by acid producing bacterium Acidithiobacillus caldus SM-1. Bioelectrochemistry 123, 34–44 (2018)."):

$${V}\_{\text{c}\text{o}\text{r}\text{r}}=\frac{8.76\times {10}^{4}\times \varDelta m}{\rho \times A\times t}$$

(3)

where *V*corr, Δ*m*, *ρ*, *A*, and *t* were the corrosion rate (mm·y−1), weight loss (g), specimen density (g·cm−3), exposed area of specimens (cm2), and immersion time (h), respectively.

The value of *V*corr in the algae-BTA group was less than that in the control and BTA groups. The result is consistent with the polarization data above.

### Microalgal biomass and BTA and DO concentrations

Figure [S7](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#MOESM1) shows the microalgal biomass and BTA concentration in different groups of corrosive solutions within 384 h. The comparison between the blank and algae-BTA groups shows that the presence of BTA and Q235 CS specimens had no significant effect on the growth of microalgal cells (Fig. [S7](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#MOESM1)a). The concentration of BTA firstly decreased within 96 h due to the consumption of the inhibitor for corrosion control, and then increased to the end of the immersion due to the addition of BTA at each sampling time point, indicating that the added BTA mass was greater than the consumed BTA mass (Fig. [S7](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#MOESM1)b).

In Table [S3](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#MOESM1), the DO concentration of the blank group was higher than that of the control, BTA, and algae-BTA groups. It suggests that the life activity of the microalgae changed the concentration of DO in the alkaline artificial seawater. However, the DO concentration of the algae-BTA group was the lowest, and the corrosion rate of this group was also the lowest. A possible explanation for this observation is that the more oxygen vacancies on the surface of the passive films had a corrosion inhibition effect, which was reported on 316 L stainless steel by Liu et al.[44](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR44 "Liu, S., Wang, Y., Zhang, D. & Wan, Y. Electrochemical behavior of 316L stainless steel in f/2 culture solutions containing Chlorella vulgaris. Int. J. Electrochem. Sci 8, 5330–5342 (2013).").

## Discussion

BTA is a heterocyclic organic compound with three nitrogen atoms in its structure. The nitrogen atoms and the π electrons in the aromatic ring are the active sites of BTA molecules. BTA molecules can form a polymeric film by a donor-acceptor reaction with the metallic surface, resulting in corrosion resistance of immersed metals[27](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR27 "Akhavan, H., Izadi, M., Mohammadi, I., Shahrabi, T. & Ramezanzadeh, B. The synergistic effect of BTA-Co system on the corrosion inhibition of mild steel in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution. J. Electrochem. Soc. 165, C670–C680 (2018)."). The structure of BTA molecules varies with pH, and is a deprotonated anionic species (BTA−) at pH > 8.6[45](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR45 "Jia, Y., Aagaard, P. & Breedveld, G. D. Sorption of triazoles to soil and iron minerals. Chemosphere 67, 250–258 (2007)."). There are several studies on corrosion prevention of steel in acidic electrolytes containing BTA[46](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR46 "Rodrigues, P. R. P., Andrade, A. H. P. D. & Agostinho, S. M. L. Benzotriazole as corrosion inhibitor for type 304 stainless steel in water–ethanol media containing 2M H2SO4. Br. Corros. J. 33, 211–213 (1998)."),[47](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR47 "Sanad, S. H. Effect of benzotriazole on acid corrosion of steel. Surf. Technol. 22, 29–37 (1984)."). However, there are only few studies on the anticorrosion performance of BTA in alkaline saline solutions[41](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR41 "Wang, D. et al. Synergetic effect of two inhibitors for enhanced corrosion protection on the reinforcing steel in the chloride-contaminated carbonated solutions. Constr. Build. Mater. 286, 122916 (2021)."),[48](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR48 "Mennucci, M. M., Banczek, E. P., Rodrigues, P. R. P. & Costa, I. Evaluation of benzotriazole as corrosion inhibitor for carbon steel in simulated pore solution. Cement Concrete Compos. 31, 418–424 (2009)."). In these studies, the corrosion inhibition mechanism of BTA has been reported as physical and chemical adsorption. The physical adsorption is due to the presence of van der Waals forces between the corrosion inhibitors and the metals[49](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR49 "Kosec, T., Milošev, I. & Pihlar, B. Benzotriazole as an inhibitor of brass corrosion in chloride solution. Appl. Surf. Sci. 253, 8863–8873 (2007)."). The chemical adsorption rises from a polymeric film formed on the steel surface due to the complexation between the Fe2+ cations with empty 3d orbitals and the central N atoms with lone-pair electrons in the BTA structure[16](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR16 "Custódio, J. V., Agostinho, S. M. L. & Simões, A. M. P. Electrochemistry and surface analysis of the effect of benzotriazole on the cut edge corrosion of galvanized steel. Electrochim. Acta55, 5523–5531 (2010)."). In this study, the reduced corrosion rate in the potentiodynamic polarization curves and weight loss measurements show that the addition of BTA inhibited the corrosion of Q235 CS specimens in comparison with the control specimens in the alkaline artificial seawater (Table [2](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#Tab2) and [S2](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#MOESM1)). XPS results demonstrate that it is mainly the presence of corrosion product film of iron oxides, hydroxides, and carbonates (Fig. [4](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#Fig4)). In addition, the alkaline environment is favorable for the transformation from 1 H-benzotriazole to 2 H-benzotriazole[50](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR50 "Qian, B., Ren, J., Song, Z. & Zhou, Y. One pot graphene-based nanocontainers as effective anticorrosion agents in epoxy-based coatings. J. Mater. Sci. 53, 14204–14216 (2018)."), which mainly exists in the form of BTA−. Moreover, the composition of the polymeric complex film was considered as [Fe*n*(BTA)*m*] and [Fe*n*(Cl)*p*(BTA)*m*] in the study of Mennucci et al.[48](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR48 "Mennucci, M. M., Banczek, E. P., Rodrigues, P. R. P. & Costa, I. Evaluation of benzotriazole as corrosion inhibitor for carbon steel in simulated pore solution. Cement Concrete Compos. 31, 418–424 (2009)."). These polymeric complexes can effectively hinder the dissolution and oxidation of iron, and are the main corrosion inhibition mechanism of BTA.

Many studies have reported the synergetic effect of two types of inhibitors on metallic corrosion inhibition[40](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR40 "Zhao, J. & Chen, G. The synergistic inhibition effect of oleic-based imidazoline and sodium benzoate on mild steel corrosion in a CO2-saturated brine solution. Electrochim. Acta 69, 247–255 (2012)."),[51](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR51 "Larabi, L., Harek, Y., Traisnel, M. & Mansri, A. Synergistic influence of poly(4-vinylpyridine) and potassium iodide on inhibition of corrosion of mild steel in 1M HCl. J. Appl. Electrochem. 34, 833–839 (2004)."),[52](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR52 "Zhang, B., He, C., Chen, X., Tian, Z. & Li, F. The synergistic effect of polyamidoamine dendrimers and sodium silicate on the corrosion of carbon steel in soft water. Corros. Sci. 90, 585–596 (2015)."). Previous studies also found an increase in corrosion inhibition efficiency of BTA in combination with other inorganic or organic chemical inhibitors[38](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR38 "Zhou, Y., Zuo, Y. & Lin, B. The compounded inhibition of sodium molybdate and benzotriazole on pitting corrosion of Q235 steel in NaCl + NaHCO3 solution. Mater. Chem. Phys. 192, 86–93 (2017)."),[53](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR53 "Liu, S. et al. Corrosion inhibition of carbon steel in tetra-n-butylammonium bromide aqueous solution by benzotriazole and Na3PO4. Corros. Sci. 51, 1356–1363 (2009)."),[54](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR54 "Rammelt, U., Koehler, S. & Reinhard, G. Synergistic effect of benzoate and benzotriazole on passivation of mild steel. Corros. Sci. 50, 1659–1663 (2008)."). However, there are limited studies on the synergistic corrosion inhibition effect of chemical and biological corrosion inhibitors. In this study, the corrosion inhibition behavior of a mixture of a microalga and BTA for Q235 CS specimens in alkaline artificial seawater and its possible mechanisms were investigated for the first time. The potentiodynamic polarization curves and weight loss measurements show that *Chlorella* sp. and BTA could reduce the corrosion rates and improve the corrosion inhibition efficiency on the CS specimens for RC structure compared with BTA alone (Table [2](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#Tab2) and [S2](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#MOESM1)). The potentiodynamic polarization curves also indicate that the BTA inhibitor and the microalgae and BTA combined inhibitors were both mixed-type inhibitors (Fig. [2](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#Fig2)). It is because the *E*corr displacement for both systems did not exceed 85 mV. However, based on the different directions of the *E*corr displacement, one can argue that the dominating corrosion inhibition mechanisms of these two systems were different: the BTA system was better at inhibiting the anodic reaction process, while the algae-BTA system was better at inhibiting the cathodic reaction process. The corrosion inhibition action of BTA has been reported to act as an anode-type inhibitor in low alkaline solutions[41](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR41 "Wang, D. et al. Synergetic effect of two inhibitors for enhanced corrosion protection on the reinforcing steel in the chloride-contaminated carbonated solutions. Constr. Build. Mater. 286, 122916 (2021)."), which is consistent with the result of its positive displacement observed in this study. The *Chlorella* sp. was a mixed-type inhibitor in the f/2 medium, which has been reported in our previous study, preferring to inhibit the cathodic reaction process[23](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR23 "Chen, S. et al. Effect of marine microalgae Synechococcus sp., Chlorella sp., Thalassiosira sp. on corrosion behavior of Q235 carbon steel in f/2 medium. Bioelectrochemistry 150, 108349 (2023)."). Combined with the results of *β*c and *β*a, it was found that the addition of the microalgae could enhanced the corrosion inhibition efficiency of BTA in both anodic and cathodic reaction processes.

The BTA– can be adsorbed in the surface region of the corrosion product film since the oxygen atoms positions of Fe2O3 can be occupied by BTA–[41](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR41 "Wang, D. et al. Synergetic effect of two inhibitors for enhanced corrosion protection on the reinforcing steel in the chloride-contaminated carbonated solutions. Constr. Build. Mater. 286, 122916 (2021)."). However, it has been reported that BTA– adsorption conditions were strict due to the requirement of satisfying the inclination of the BTA molecular plane[55](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR55 "Agafonkina, M. O., Kuznetsov, Y. I., Andreeva, N. P., Pronin, Y. E. & Kazanskii, L. P. Formation of protective layers by 5-chlorobenzotriazole and its mixture with sodium fluphenaminate on low-carbon steel from aqueous solutions. Prot. Metals Phys. Chem. Surf. 48, 773–779 (2012)."). Therefore, one can speculate that the microalgae owning to their natural adhesion properties may be able to access CS surfaces more quickly than BTA. Moreover, the interaction between the microalgae and BTA may increase the corrosion resistance of BTA, because BTA is adsorbed into the biofilm in the form of [Fe[BTA][EPS]*y*(OH)*z*]1–*y*–*z* to stabilize the layer, which may make it easier for BTA to reach the metallic surface. The amount of BTA– was sufficient due to each sampling supplement of BTA, as shown in Fig. [S7](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#MOESM1)b. Two iron complexes containing EPS in the biofilm have been reported in our previous study[23](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#ref-CR23 "Chen, S. et al. Effect of marine microalgae Synechococcus sp., Chlorella sp., Thalassiosira sp. on corrosion behavior of Q235 carbon steel in f/2 medium. Bioelectrochemistry 150, 108349 (2023)."). In addition, the corrosion product film of iron oxides, hydroxides, carbonates, and BTA-containing polymeric complex film as described above were also present in the algae-BTA group. In summary, the anticorrosion mechanisms of Q235 CS specimens in the algae-BTA group are illustrated in Fig. [5](/articles/s41598-024-74557-4#Fig5).

args.summary:
This study, published in Scientific Reports (volume 14, Article 24547, 2024), investigates the synergistic corrosion inhibition effect of Chlorella sp. microalgae combined with benzotriazole (BTA) on Q235 carbon steel (CS) in alkaline artificial seawater. This is the first study to examine the combined effect of chemical and biological corrosion inhibitors on CS corrosion under alkaline conditions.

**Methodology:**
- Q235 CS specimens (composition: 0.17 C, 0.11 Si, 0.02 Mn, 0.017 P, 0.006 S, balance Fe) were immersed for 384 hours in alkaline artificial seawater (pH 10, 3.5% NaCl).
- Four groups were studied: algae-BTA-CS (treatment), BTA-CS (treatment), CS alone (control), and algae alone (blank).
- Initial concentrations: 10 mg·L⁻¹ BTA and 160 mg·L⁻¹ microalgal biomass.
- Techniques used: weight loss measurements, open circuit potential (OCP), electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), potentiodynamic polarization curves, SEM, EDS, 3-D optical profiling, and XPS.

**Key Results:**
- The algae-BTA system demonstrated reduced corrosion rates compared to BTA alone and the control, confirming that Chlorella sp. facilitates the corrosion inhibition efficiency of BTA.
- The algae-BTA system exhibited a mixed-type corrosion inhibition effect, though it showed a preference for inhibiting cathodic reactions, while BTA alone was better at inhibiting anodic reactions.
- EIS showed the algae-BTA group consistently had the highest low-frequency impedance modulus (|Z|₀.₀₁ Hz) compared to control and BTA groups (p < 0.05), indicating superior corrosion resistance.
- Maximum pitting pit depths in the algae-BTA group were 5 µm (192 h) and 16 µm (384 h), less than in control and BTA groups.
- XPS analysis revealed the algae-BTA group had higher Fe content and higher Fe₂O₃ levels (beneficial for passive film stability), while Na, Cl, and P contents were lower than other groups.
- The presence of BTA and CS specimens had no significant effect on microalgal growth.
- DO concentration was lowest in the algae-BTA group, correlating with the lowest corrosion rate.

**Proposed Mechanism:**
The corrosion inhibition is attributed to the precipitation of iron complexes such as Fe-BTA-EPS and Fe-BTA, along with iron compounds (iron oxides, hydroxides, carbonates) on the steel surface. BTA⁻ can adsorb into the biofilm as [Fe[BTA][EPS]y(OH)z]¹⁻ʸ⁻ᶻ, stabilizing the protective layer and making it easier for BTA to reach the metallic surface. The microalgae's natural adhesion properties may allow them to access CS surfaces more quickly than BTA alone.

**Conclusion:** This study highlights a novel approach to CS corrosion control by combining biological and chemical methods, providing new insights for future research and practical applications in reinforced concrete structures in marine environments.

   Walker, Robert

2. [Halloysite tubes as nanocontainers for anticorrosion coating with benzotriazole.](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20355946)

   Abdullayev, Elshad; Price, Ronald; Shchukin, Dmitry; Lvov, Yuri

   Halloysite clay nanotubes were investigated as a tubular container for the corrosion inhibitor benzotriazole. Halloysite is a naturally occurring cylindrical clay mineral with an internal diameter in the nanometer range and a length up to several micrometers, yielding a high-aspect-ratio hollow tube structure. Halloysite may be used as an additive in paints to produce a functional composite coating material. A maximum benzotriazole loading of 5% by weight was achieved for clay tubes of 50 nm external diameters and lumen of 15 nm. Variable release rates of the corrosion inhibitor were possible in a range between 5 and 100 h, as was demonstrated by formation of stoppers at tube openings. The anticorrosive performance of the sol-gel coating and paint loaded with 2-5% of halloysite-entrapped benzotriazole was tested on copper and on 2024-aluminum alloy by direct exposure of the metal plates to corrosive media. Kinetics of the corrosion spot formation at the coating defects was analyzed by the scanning vibrating electrode technique, and an essential damping of corrosion development was demonstrated for halloysite-loaded samples.

The objectives of this research are to study the performance of benzotriazole as corrosion inhibitors. The result of XRD and EDS analysis reveal the iron sulfide (FeS) formation on corroded carbon steel surface without inhibitor. The EDS spectrum show the Nitrogen (N) bond on carbon steel surface inhibited by BTAH.« less

5. [Stability of Benzotriazole Derivatives with Free Cu, Zn, Co and Metal-Containing Enzymes: Binding and Interaction of Methylbenzotriazoles with Superoxide Dismutase and Vitamin B12](http://adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018MS%26E..305a2024A)

   Abudalo, R. A.; AbuDalo, M. A.; Hernandez, M. T.

   Benzotriazole derivatives form very strong bonds with transition metals, and are the most widely used type of industrial corrosion inhibitor. Some benzotriazole derivatives have been implicated as hormone regulators which also carry the ability to induce uncoupling responses or otherwise inhibit respiration processes in some microorganisms. However, the mechanisms associated with benzotriazole toxicity and inhibition are unknown. Using Differential Pulse Polarography, the stability constants of commercially significant corrosion inhibitors, 4-and 5-methylbenzotriazole, coordinated with free Cu (II) and Co (III), were determined to be 1015 and 108, respectively. Polarographic analyses were extended to confirm that methylbenzotriazole also binds the copper center(s) in the ubiquitous enzyme superoxide dismutase, and the Corrin site in the coenzyme cobalamin (vitamin B12). These results suggest that the metal-chelating ability of this unique class of compounds may confer inhibition to certain enzyme systems.

   Borisova, Dimitriya; Möhwald, Helmuth; Shchukin, Dmitry G

   This work presents the synthesis of monodisperse, mesoporous silica nanoparticles and their application as nanocontainers loaded with corrosion inhibitor (1H-benzotriazole (BTA)) and embedded in hybrid SiOx/ZrOx sol-gel coating for the corrosion protection of aluminum alloy. The developed porous system of mechanically stable silica nanoparticles exhibits high surface area (∼1000 m2·g(-1)), narrow pore size distribution (d∼3 nm), and large pore volume (∼1 mL·g(-1)). As a result, a sufficiently high uptake and storage of the corrosion inhibitor in the mesoporous nanocontainers was achieved. The successful embedding and homogeneous distribution of the BTA-loaded monodisperse silica nanocontainers in the passive anticorrosive SiOx/ZrOx film improve the wet corrosion resistance of the aluminum alloy AA2024 in 0.1 M sodium chloride solution. The enhanced corrosion protection of this newly developed active system in comparison to the passive sol-gel coating was observed during a simulated corrosion process by the scanning vibrating electrode technique (SVET). These results, as well as the controlled pH-dependent release of BTA from the mesoporous silica nanocontainers without additional polyelectrolyte shell, suggest an inhibitor release triggered by the corrosion process leading to a self-healing effect.

   The present paper describes different methods for storing the benzotriazole (BTA) corrosion inhibitor in the titanium dioxide nanotubes (TNT) as nanocontainers. Three methods were used, including the vacuum impregnation at ambient temperature, the vacuum impregnation at cooling temperature () and the rotary vacuum evaporation. TNT, BTA and BTA/TNT products were characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) surface area, differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) and Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy. nanotube powder was synthesized by hydrothermal treatment from the inexpensive spherical commercial precursor. The results obtained from SEM, TEM images and BET values showed the successful synthesis of TNT with a homogeneous morphology of nano size tubes and a large specific surface . The existence of BTA in TNT was demonstrated. The BTA/TNT obtained via the rotary vacuum evaporation contained a very significant amount of BTA (66.6 weight %) but BTA existed mostly outside the nanotubes.    Abu-Dalo, M. A.; O'Brien, I.; Hernandez, M. T.

   Fourteen benzotriazole derivatives were subjected to microcosm tests to study the influence of substitutions on their biodegradation potential. Methylated, nitrated, carboxylated, and propionated bezotriazoles, a heterocyclic triazole, as well as methylated benzimidazoles, were introduced to activated sludge and soil enrichment cultures as the only carbon source. Some of the enrichment cultures were derived from airport soils that had been previously contaminated with aircraft deicing fluids and subsequently enriched with the commercially significant corrosion inhibitor methylbenzotriazole. 11. [Protection of bronze artefacts through polymeric coatings based on nanocarriers filled with corrosion inhibitors](http://adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016AIPC.1736b0048D)

    de Luna, Martina Salzano; Buonocore, Giovanna; Di Carlo, Gabriella; Giuliani, Chiara; Ingo, Gabriel M.; Lavorgna, Marino

    Protective coatings based on polymers synthesized from renewable sources (chitosan or an amorphous vinyl alcohol based polymer) have been prepared for the protection of bronze artifacts from corrosion. Besides acting as an effective barrier against corrosive species present in the environment, the efficiency of the coatings has been improved by adding corrosion inhibitor compounds (benzotriazole or mercaptobenzothiazole) to the formulations. The liquid medium of the formulations has been carefully selected looking at maximizing the wettability on the bronze substrate and optimizing the solvent evaporation rate. The minimum amount of inhibitor compounds has been optimized by performing accelerated corrosion tests on coated bronze substrates. The inhibitors have been directly dissolved in the coating-forming solutions and/or introduced by means of nanocarriers, which allow to control the release kinetics. The free dissolved inhibitor molecules immediately provide a sufficient protection against corrosion. On the other hand, the inhibitor molecules contained in the nanocarriers serve as long-term reservoir, which can be activated by external corrosion-related stimuli in case of particularly severe conditions. Particular attention has been paid to other features which affect the coating performances. Specifically, the adhesion of the protective polymer layer to the bronze substrate has been assessed, as well as its permeability properties and transparency, the latter being a fundamental feature of protective coating for cultural heritages. Finally, the protective efficiency of the produced smart coatings has been assessed through accelerated corrosion tests.

13. [Toxicity of benzotriazole and benzotriazole derivatives to three aquatic species.](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11229011)

Recent studies have shown that benzotriazole derivatives are a major component of aircraft deicing fluids (ADFs) responsible for toxicity to bacteria (Microtox). Our current research compared the toxicity of benzotriazole (BT), two methylbenzotriazole (MeBT) isomers, and butylbenzotriazole (BBT). Acute toxicity assays were used to model the response of three common test organisms: Microtox bacteria (Vibrio fischeri), fathead minnow (Pimephales promelas) and water flea (Ceriodaphnia dubia). Vibrio fischeri was more sensitive than either C. dubia or P. promelas to all the test materials, while C. dubia was less sensitive than P. promelas. Benzotriazole (BTA), which is used as corrosion inhibitor in the copper CMP slurry, is the primary source for the formation of organic contaminants. The presence of BTA can degrade the electrical properties and reliability of ICs which needs to be removed by using an effective cleaning solution. In this paper, an alkaline cleaning solution was proposed. The alkaline cleaning solution studied in this work consists of a chelating agent and a nonionic surfactant. The removal of BTA was characterized by contact angle measurements and potentiodynamic polarization studies. The cleaning properties of the proposed cleaning solution on a 300 mm copper patterned wafer were also quantified, total defect counts after cleaning was studied, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) review was used to identify types of BTA to confirm the ability of cleaning solution for BTA removal.     Rossi, Luca; Queloz, Pierre; Brovelli, Alessandro; Margot, Jonas; Barry, D. A.

    The aim of this work was to evaluate low-cost and easy-to-operate engineering solutions that can be added as a polishing step to small wastewater treatment plants to reduce the micropollutant load to water bodies. The removal of five micropollutants with different physico-chemical characteristics (three pharmaceuticals: diclofenac, carbamazepine, sulfamethoxazole, one pesticide: mecoprop, and one corrosion inhibitor: benzotriazole) was studied to evaluate the feasibility of the proposed system. A deformed layer with thickness of 20 ± 5 µm was produced on mild steel surface after NS-SPD process due to accumulated strains. The NS-SPD process caused more effective adsorption of corrosion inhibitors due to the fabrication of a surface with a high density of preferential adsorption sites. However, the stability of protective layer was predominantly influenced by the effect of NS-SPD process on inhibition efficiency. The fairly good persistence of protective layer formed on the surface by SM-containing solution and also positive effect of NS-SPD process on adsorption of molybdate ions caused higher inhibition performance for sodium molybdate. However, NS-SPD process encouraged deterioration of protective layer formed on steel surface in the presence of BTA inhibitor. It was ascribed to partial coverage of surface, low stability of adsorbed layer and thus more adsorption of aggressive ions on unprotected area which was uncovered during immersion time.

Previous studies have focused primarily on ground and surface water impacts of larger volume ADAF users. The detection of triazoles in soils at low volume ADAF use airports suggests that deicing activities may have a broader environmental impact than previously considered.

By gradient elution, BTri, 4-TTri, 5-TTri, and xylyltriazole can be determined simultaneously with three benzothiazoles, but here TTri isomers coelute. The instrumental detection limit of 2 pg allows the determination of the three most important benzotriazoles from municipal wastewater and most surface waters by direct injection into the HPLC system without previous enrichment. When solid-phase extraction is employed with mean recovery rates of 95-113%, the limit of quantification for benzotriazoles range from 10 ng/L in groundwater to 25 ng/L in untreated wastewater. BTri and TTri were determined in municipal wastewater in microgram per liter concentrations. Elimination in wastewater treatment appears to be poor, and BTri and TTri can be followed through a water cycle from treated municipal wastewater through surface water to bank filtrate used for drinking water production. The mechanical properties of the surface layer were investigated using nanoindentation measurements. The electrochemical investigation showed that the thickness of the surface layer is controlled by the chemicals such as an oxidizer (hydrogen peroxide), a corrosion inhibitor (benzotriazole), a complexing agent (citric acid), and their concentrations. This is a Science.gov search results page containing sample records for the corrosion inhibitor "benzotriazole" (BTA). The page compiles 20+ research abstracts and publications from various scientific databases (ERIC, NASA ADS, PubMed, OSTI.GOV, EPA Science Inventory, NASA Technical Reports Server, etc.) covering the chemistry, applications, and environmental impacts of benzotriazole and its derivatives.

KEY RESEARCH FINDINGS ACROSS RECORDS:

**Application as Corrosion Inhibitor:**
- Benzotriazole (BTAH) is a well-known corrosion inhibitor for copper, copper-alloy, and other metal surfaces, used since the 1950s. Applications include deactivating computer hard drive surfaces, treatment of apparel hardware (zippers, buttons), and protection of antiques/cultural heritage objects.
- BTA is widely used in copper CMP (chemical mechanical polishing) slurries for semiconductor manufacturing.

**Inhibition Performance Studies:**
- BTAH achieved optimum inhibition efficiency of 93% at 5 mmol/l concentration for API 5LX65 carbon steel in 3.5% NaCl solution containing H2S at 70°C (EIS study by Solehudin & Nurdin).
- BTA adsorption on Cu(111) surface was studied via STM, RAIRS, and DFT, revealing BTAH adsorbs as anionic BTA- with Cu(BTA)2 as the majority adsorbed species forming chains (Grillo et al.).
- Methylbenzotriazoles bind strongly to transition metals; stability constants of 4- and 5-methylbenzotriazole with Cu(II) and Co(III) were determined as 10^15 and 10^8 respectively (Abudalo et al.).
- Copolymers of N-(methacryloyloxymethyl) benzotriazole (MMBT) and methyl methacrylate (MMA) at 1:1 mole ratio exhibited best protection for mild steel in 0.1 M HCl (Srikanth et al.).

**Nanocontainer/Loading Technologies:**
- Halloysite clay nanotubes achieved maximum BTA loading of 5% by weight, with variable release rates between 5-100 hours; effective on copper and 2024-aluminum alloy (Abdullayev et al.).
- Mesoporous silica nanoparticles (surface area ~1000 m²/g, pore diameter ~3 nm) loaded with BTA in SiOx/ZrOx sol-gel coatings provided active corrosion protection for AA2024 aluminum alloy with pH-dependent release and self-healing effect (Borisova et al.).
- TiO2 nanotubes stored BTA via three methods; rotary vacuum evaporation achieved 66.6 wt% BTA (mostly outside nanotubes) while vacuum impregnation stored ~8 wt% BTA mostly inside tubes (Nguyen et al.).
- Chitosan-based and vinyl alcohol-based polymer coatings with BTA or mercaptobenzothiazole were developed for bronze artifact protection (de Luna et al.).

**Environmental Fate and Toxicity:**
- Benzotriazole and derivatives are major components of aircraft deicing fluids (ADFs) and are incompletely removed in wastewater treatment. In Berlin wastewaters: 12 µg/L BTri, 2.1 µg/L 4-TTri, 1.3 µg/L 5-TTri; removal in activated sludge ranged from 37% for BTri to insignificant for 4-TTri.
- Toxicity study by Pillard et al. (2001): butylbenzotriazole (BBT) was the most toxic derivative, inducing acute toxicity at ≤3.3 mg/L; 5-methylbenzotriazole more toxic than 4-methylbenzotriazole; Vibrio fischeri most sensitive test organism.
- Sunlight photolysis of benzotriazoles yields environmental half-lives of 2.4-8 days in surface waters; 36 transformation products identified (Weidauer et al., 2016).
- Biodegradation studies showed only 5-methylbenzotriazole and carboxylated derivatives are degraded by soil/activated sludge biomass; carboxylated derivatives are more readily biodegradable than methylated counterparts (Abu-Dalo et al., 2018).
- Triazoles detected in airport soils at concentrations of 2.35-424.19 µg/kg even at low-volume deicing airports (McNeill & Cancilla).
- Ozonation with 1 mg O3/mg DOC achieved near-complete removal of benzotriazoles from wastewater (Weiss et al., 2006).

**Semiconductor/Industrial Applications:**
- Alkaline cleaning solutions with chelating agents (FA/O II) and nonionic surfactants (FA/O I) were developed for effective BTA removal during post-Cu CMP cleaning (multiple studies).
- Research on barrier slurry development without BTA and oxidizer aims to avoid post-CMP challenges including organic residue, toxicity, and particle adhesion (Xiaodong et al.).

**Other Topics Covered:** The page also includes records on green corrosion inhibitors (ginger extract achieving up to 91% inhibition efficiency, banana peel extract at 78.59%, Dioscorea hispida starch at 95.97%), a dual-use corrosion inhibitor/penetrant for neutron/X radiography (NASA patent), and the influence of near-surface severe plastic deformation on inhibitor performance.

Results revealed that, following a one-layer adsorption isotherm, the ILs predominantly exhibited anodic spontaneous physicochemical interactions with the corroding substrate. As a result, according to impedance studies, at least 84% of the acidic corrosion was mitigated using 4 mM of the ILs. Furthermore, chloride-mediated cooperative (indirect) adsorption, apart from direct surface binding, was confirmed experimentally for the first time, providing better justification for the dominant anodic performance. Utilizing quantum calculations, it was demonstrated how the data computed for standalone inhibitors can contribute to estimate the most stable adsorption configurations. In addition, the role of each functional group and atomic constituent in the adsorptive corrosion inhibition was elaborated, given different possible adsorbate-adsorbent interaction modes. Finally, a novel quantum parameter was introduced, and its potential application as an indicator for identifying superior corrosion inhibition was described. Keywords Inhibition mechanism, Acidic corrosion, Ionic liquid, Adsorption, Quantum calculation Introduction At low concentrations, corrosion inhibitors can significantly reduce the corrosivity of the fluids to which metals and alloys are exposed. A wide variety of organic chemicals have been evaluated in order to explore their inhibitory effects. Satisfactory to excellent inhibition efficiencies were copiously reported in the literature [1,2]. However, the inhibition mechanism still remained elusive, requiring further research [3]. It is generally known that the solubility, mobility, and adsorptive behavior of an organic chemical must be compatible with a metal-solution system to have significant corrosion mitigation [4,5]. Ionic liquids (ILs), zwitterions, and betaines are modern organic examples of inhibitors with a particular feature: containing charged components. This characteristic facilitates dissolution and molecular mobility, especially in common corrosive aqueous solutions, thus reducing dependency on the parameters in mechanistic studies. Among the inhibitor species, ILs with their great qualities—highly soluble in polar and non-polar solvents; negligibly volatile; non-flammable; minimally toxic; thermally, chemically, and electrochemically stable; and considerably tunable—presented prospects for less-toxic anticorrosion applications, which is vital regarding contemporary environmental concerns [6–8]. Multiple studies have scrutinized ILs as corrosion inhibitor in acidic-to-alkaline aggressive media and for different metallic substrates: aluminum [9], copper [10,11], magnesium [12,13], zinc [14], brass [15] and a broad spectrum of steel alloys [16,17]. Across the wide variety of ILs, those derived from imidazole have received the most attention in light of their easy, low-cost, and high yield synthesis [2]. In the presence of halide counter anions, the resultant imidazolium-based cations are the primary components responsible for inhibitive performance. It is important to note that the cationic moieties essentially undergo protonation during synthesis in strong acids. Hence, their chemical properties are more likely to remain unchanged in corrosive acidic media, particularly with main substituents other than –H. This issue decreases suffering caused by ambiguities usually associated with using (de)protonation-prone organic inhibitors and the dissociative adsorption processes they may come across [18–22]. Moreover, the anion-cation pairs of ILs can present synergistic inhibition performance [23]. The concept of inhibitive synergy between solution anions, acting as intermediate bridge, and organic compounds has been recognized for a long time [24,25]. According to this mechanism, I− > Br− > Cl− can enhance the adsorption (inhibition efficiency) of organic inhibitors [26]. Nonetheless, most supportive evidence on this subject has been inferred from electrochemical methods [27], and there is no direct published evidence to substantiate bonding either between organic inhibitors and pre-adsorbed anions or between the anionic and cationic moieties of ILs. It should be also emphasized that, from a mechanistic viewpoint, using ILs with the same anions to the corrosive solution (e.g., Cl− as IL anion for corrosion studies in HCl solutions) can reduce the complexity of the system under investigation and aid in unraveling inhibition processes. Given this perspective, even if they may not be the most effective in terms of inhibition efficiency [28], ILs with the specific characteristics discussed can serve as exemplar compounds for enhancing our understanding of corrosion inhibition mechanisms. This is particularly relevant because the anticorrosive performance of the ILs primarily relies on their adsorptive behavior. Conventional theory frequently proposed in the literature suggests that organic inhibitors adsorb onto metal substrates, making a protective surface film, and prevent corrosion through sharing/donating π and non-bonding electrons to the vacant orbitals of the metal [29,30]. In the majority of cases, this performance is attributed to the presence of constituents capable of doing so, that is, conjugated (double or triple) bonds, heteroatoms (N, P, O, S), and halogens (F, Cl, Br, I) [31–33]. Based on this, inhibition-oriented improvements have been sought either by chemicals containing the constituents or by incorporating the constituents into various core structures – whether as individual elements or functional groups. Ab initio atomistic simulation as an advanced computational method have enabled us to gain deeper insights into inhibition-bearing adsorption [34,35]. However, even the latest classifications still fail to establish a comprehensive correlation between electronic features and adsorption/inhibition efficacy [33,36–38]. It appears that certain aspects within this field necessitate reevaluation. Kovačević et al. [21] recommended that relevant studies should be devoted to a definite substrate, because the partially or fully occupied d- or sp-orbitals of metals may exhibit different coordination behavior toward organic adsorbates. Despite this, the nature of the metal substrate, at least as long as it belongs to the transition type studied, had no effect on the direction of total electron transfer between the adsorbents and adsorbates [39]. Note that most documented conclusions are drawn without considering the effect of adsorption configuration and that of intermediate species—Inhibitor molecules are assumed to adsorb immediately onto the surface, which may not justify a predominant anodic or cathodic inhibition mechanism [10]. In addition, the traditionally assigned fixed role (electron donation) to organic molecules and their specific constituents (N, O, etc.) has been questionable. The State-of-the-art analysis using the Bader charge concept explicated that electron withdrawal—rather than electron donation—by organic molecules occurs through adsorptive interactions with metallic substrates, contradicting conventional theory [21,37,40–45]. Radilla et al. [41] studied different adsorption sites for 2-mercaptoimidazole onto Fe(100) surface. These authors found that the nitrogen atoms of the aromatic imidazole ring can play little to significant roles in electronic exchanges of surface bonding, depending on the adsorption configuration and relaxation distance from the surface. Kokalj et al. [42] demonstrated that cysteine and penicillamine molecules, during adsorptions onto Fe(110), become negatively charged (taking electrons from the surface) while variable electronic changes for −COOH group and its atoms were observed. In another study, Lgaz et al. [43] made an attempt to compare functional group effects on quinoline derivatives, concluding that oxygen atoms might act as electron donors or acceptors, depending on the functional groups involved. Therefore, it seems that further studies are required to identify up-to-date universal principles and strengthen the link between quantum properties of inhibitors in free and adsorbed states, provided there is sufficient empirical and theoretical validation. Furthermore, there is still a growing interest in identifying which quantum parameter best discriminates inhibition efficacy. The significance of finding such a parameter lies in its capacity to shed light on the underlying inhibition mechanism and pave the way for the discovery of more sustainable inhibitors without extensive experimental trials. Many studies have used DFT-calculated adsorption energy as a criterion for identifying more effective inhibitors, often focusing on small, planar molecules and in a single parallel configuration to the surface. This approach has limitations for delivering conclusive results, because adsorption energy is not independent; factors such as adsorption configuration, or steric restrictions can crucially influence the final adsorbed configuration and associated quantum values. Some researchers have evaluated ‘net electron transfer’ for this purpose, yet the correlation with adsorption energy values remained disputable without reasonable explanation. Recently, Fu et al. [37] developed the idea - also briefly proposed by T. Le Minh Pham [44] - that a partial correlation between the d-band center and adsorption energy can be employed as a potential discriminant. It is unfortunate that the authors did not specify which substrate atoms' d-band centers were regarded for establishing the correlation, where the surface atoms revealed different electronic conditions after inhibitor adsorption. More importantly, the d-band center is essentially the first moment of the d-band density of states, which is not intrinsically unique - different distributions can result in the same d-band center. This study compares mild steel corrosion in 0.5 M HCl without and with two ILs that has not been previously synthesized and investigated as inhibitors. The large, non-planar geometries of the ILs are expected to demonstrate illustrative performance as model inhibitors. Additionally, the presence of heteroatoms (N and O) and halogens (Cl) in the studied structures offers opportunities to observe which elements can have significant effects on adsorptive corrosion inhibition. A systematic examination of inhibition efficacy is conducted using electrochemical methods and surface analysis. Experimental evidence is presented for the first time on cooperative adsorption of Cl− and the cationic moieties of the ILs. Adsorption and quantum-based modeling confirm the electrochemical findings and elucidate the factors influencing inhibition mechanism. The study also illustrates how the relative positioning of the frontier orbitals of the adsorbing inhibitors may cause the lowest adsorption energy values and contribute to atomic-level interactions. Last but not least, a new quantum parameter is introduced to find more efficient inhibitors. Experimental and theoretical investigations Synthesis of ionic liquids Imidazole (99%), 2-chlorethyl ether (99%), 1,2-bis(2-chloroethoxy)ethane (97%), ethyl acetoacetate (99%), and acetonitrile were purchased from Merck. All reagents were used as received. After synthesis, the chemical structures of the synthesized compounds were verified using 1H-NMR (500 MHz) spectra obtained by a Bruker Advance 500 instrument, Germany. Additionally, FTIR spectra were recorded and compared to the results of a similar analysis conducted on the mild steel surface, as described in section 0. Synthesis of 1,3-Bis-[2-(2-chloro-ethoxy)-ethyl]-3H-imidazol-1-ium chloride To prepare the IL, hereafter denoted as [CE1EI]Cl (Fig. 1), 0.68 g (0.01 M) of imidazole was dissolved in 50 ml of acetonitrile. Then, 2.86 g (0.02 M) of 2-chloroethyl ether was added to the solution. The mixture was heated at 80°C for 24 hours, then cooled to -10°C for 72 hours. Surface characterization As described for the electrochemical measurements (section 0), sample preparation for the following surface analyses on mild steel samples was performed. FE-SEM images were taken using a TESCAN MIRA3 LMU scanning electron microscope. Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) analysis in the range of 450 – 4000 cm–1 was conducted using spectroscopic-grade KBr and an FTIR spectrophotometer (PerkinElmer).
