This is a peer-reviewed research article published in Heliyon (2023 Nov 10;9(11):e22158, DOI: 10.1016/j.heliyon.2023.e22158, PMID: 38034666, PMCID: PMC10685366) by Kabiru Haruna, Tawfik A. Saleh, and Ahmad A. Sorour from the Interdisciplinary Research Center for Advanced Materials and Department of Chemistry at King Fahd University of Petroleum & Minerals, Dhahran, Saudi Arabia. The corresponding author is Kabiru Haruna (kabiru.haruna@kfupm.edu.sa). The article is open access under CC BY-NC-ND license.

STUDY OBJECTIVE: The study used a silver nanoparticle (AgNPs) anchored transparent tape sensor to detect 1,4-bis(2-aminoethyl)piperazine functionalized graphene oxide (AEP-GO) adsorbed on X60 carbon steel surfaces in 15% HCl solution using surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS). This represents the first time SERS was used to detect inhibitor molecules on carbon steel (a non-plasmonic material).

KEY METHODOLOGY:
- AgNPs were synthesized at room temperature by reduction of silver nitrate with hydroxylamine hydrochloride (Leopold and Lendl method).
- AgNPs sensor was fabricated using a translucent adhesive tape pressed onto an array of AgNPs in a watch glass.
- Carbon steel coupons were immersed in different AEP-GO concentrations (1, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 ppm) for 24 hours.
- SERS signals were collected using a LabRAM Horiba Raman spectrophotometer at 633 nm laser excitation, 50x objective lens, 600 gr/mm gratings, 60s acquisition, 2s accumulation.
- DFT calculations were performed using Gaussian 09 at B3LYP level with 6-31G basis sets for C, N, O, H atoms and SDD basis set for the Ag cluster (Four-Ag cluster).

KEY RESULTS:
- AgNPs absorption maximum at 456 nm with fwhm beyond 100 nm, indicating polydispersed nanoparticles with average particle size ~70 nm (predominantly spherical).
- AEP-GO showed characteristic Raman peaks at 1320 cm⁻¹ (D-band) and 1583 cm⁻¹ (G-band) typical of graphitic structures.
- Without the AgNPs sensor, no visible Raman peaks were detected on steel surfaces; with the sensor, AEP-GO peaks were visible even at the lowest concentration of 1 ppm.
- Strong linear correlation between SERS intensity and AEP-GO concentration (5-25 ppm) with R² = 0.9976.
- Limit of detection (LOD) is far below 1 ppm (signal-to-noise ratio >3 at 1 ppm), compared to 1.2 ppm reported for benzotriazole on aluminum alloy in similar SERS tape studies.
- Excellent reproducibility with less than 3% intensity fluctuation across three randomly selected spots at 25 ppm.
- DFT calculations revealed silver atoms preferentially approach the oxygen atom at the GO epoxy group (not carbonyl or hydroxyl groups) due to its lesser stability. The epoxy C-O bond distance increased from 1.443 Å (AEP-GO) to 1.488 Å (AEP-GO_Ag adduct) due to epoxy ring opening. Calculated Ag-O bond distance was 2.081 Å, and Ag-Ag bonds ranged 2.734-2.879 Å (mean 2.791 Å, close to experimental value of 2.850 Å).

CONCLUSIONS: SERS signal intensity increased with AEP-GO concentration, corroborating prior weight loss and electrochemical studies. The appearance of characteristic Raman bands confirmed inhibitor adsorption on the steel surface, blocking it from aggressive acid attack. The fabricated SERS tape sensor is versatile with no substrate material restrictions and can be used to track corrosion inhibitor dynamic adsorption regardless of metal type.

## Abstract

This study presents the synthesis of an eco-friendly and green Schiff base, namely Isatin-Cs Schiff base [corrosion inhibitor](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/materials-science/corrosion-inhibitor) for Q235 carbon steel in 1.0 M HCl corrosion solution. Fourier-transformed infrared FT-IR and 1 H NMR was utilized to characterize the prepared Isatin-Cs Schiff base corrosion inhibitor. The inhibition performance in 1.0 M HCl solution was investigated via classic weight loss at various temperatures, potentiodynamic polarization (PPD), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). Scanning electron microscopy SEM, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy XPS, and water contact angle methods are used to analyze the surface morphology of Q235 carbon steel. The polarization measurements indicate that the corrosion inhibitors act as mixed type. Moreover, the weight loss studies show that the efficiency of inhibitor increases with the concentration of inhibitor to reach a maximum efficiency of 88.4 % with 250 ppm at 25 °C. Nevertheless, increasing temperature has negative effect on the efficiency of the Isatin-Cs inhibitor. The Langmuir isotherm Unveil that Isatin-Cs adsorption on Q235 carbon steel is mediated via physi/chemi-sorption. Based on SEM and XPS analyses Isatin-Cs forms stable protective film on Q235 carbon steel. The DFT results complemented the experiments results, both observed the effectiveness of inhibitor adsorption.

## Introduction

Carbon steels are playing pivotal role in diverse of industrial such as oil, gas, marine, and automotive. This is due to the virtue of carbon steel in terms of cost-effectiveness and favourable mechanical properties, which represent an excellent attraction factor for industrial and scientific research [1,2]. Utilizing mineral acidic solutions, such as HCl, to remove unwanted scales and salt deposits in the pickling process causes corrosive attack and destruction of carbon steel structures [3]. This not only results in substantial economic losses and resource waste, but also contributes to the corrosion of metallic structures, equipment, and components. This in turn leads to raising the production costs, and also poses safety risks, and harmful environmental effects [4,5]. One of the most common techniques to protect metal from corrosive attack is using inhibitor materials [6]. Several published research works have discussed mitigating the corrosion effect on carbon steel, including determining the efficacy of different inhibitor materials [7,8]. Natural and organic extracted materials pause interesting area of research due several reason including availabilities, cost-effective, nontoxicity, and demonstrate superior efficiency when compared to counterparts derived from unnatural sources. Several naturally occurring polymers, such as carboxymethyl cellulose [9], cassava starch [10], Arabic gum [11], have been previously utilized as a green corrosion inhibitors for metals in acidic solutions. Safety concerns are the main drive toward producing non-toxicity and effective corrosion inhibitors. Although numerous anticorrosion materials were commonly used, most of them are chemically synthesized with harmful health and environmental side effects. Researchers are currently focusing on the development of cost-effective and green corrosion inhibitors with high of efficiency.

This research work focuses on developing chitosan, which can be extracted from crustacean shells such as crabs and shrimps, which are considered natural sources. Chitosan has distinct characteristics such as nontoxicity, biodegradability, biological activity, and biocompatibility making it a perfect candidate as environmentally friendly corrosion inhibitor. Previous studies also conformed this [[12], [13], [14]]. Chitosan also has anti-corrosion preparties as it was applied as surface coating material [15]. The presence of amine(-NH 2), hydroxyl -OH, and N-acetamide groups on chitosan molecules can establish hydrogen bonds internally and between different molecules, leading to decrease its water solubility and hence limiting its use [16]. Researchers from around the world have proposed various methods of chemical modification to improve the water solubility of chitosan [[17], [18], [19]]. In an early study, chitosan modified with Isatin based on Schiff base showed anti-bacterial activity [20]. However, no report is available on applying chitosan and Isatin Schiff bases as an eco-friendly inhibitor of corrosion for Q235 carbon steel in acid solutions.

In this study, we uniquely present a chemical modification of chitosan-based on Schiff base caused by its reaction with Isatin-Cs. The result modified chitosan can be applied as a green and eco-friendly corrosion inhibitor for Q235 carbon steel in 1.0 M HCl corrosion solution. Chitosan Schiff base modification can enhance the weight molecular and solubility of chitosan leading to high performance of inhibition. Classic weight loss at 25 °C, 35 °C,45 °C and 55 °C temperature, Potentiodynamic polarization, and impedance spectroscopy (EIS) are used to investigation modified chitosan Schiff base performance. Moreover, scanning electron microscopy SEM, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and contact angle techniques was applied to study the morphologies features. Also density function theory used to carried out calculations of quantum chemicals to further determination the interaction between inhibitor and metal surface [21,22].

This is a research article published in the Journal of Molecular Structure (Volume 1321, Part 1, Article 139592, dated 5 February 2025) by Elsevier, titled "Eco-friendly corrosion inhibitor of Q235 carbon steel in 1.0 M HCl by Isatin/Chitosan Schiff base." The study, authored by Mohammed Mustafa Yousif Modwi, Huixia Feng, Mohammed Kamal Hadi, Nali Chen, Jiarui Hou, Eltyib Kamal, and Kai Yang, presents the synthesis of an eco-friendly green Schiff base corrosion inhibitor (Isatin-Cs) for Q235 carbon steel in 1.0 M HCl solution.

Key methodology and results:
- The Isatin-Cs Schiff base inhibitor was characterized using FT-IR and 1H NMR.
- Inhibition performance was tested via weight loss at various temperatures (25°C, 35°C, 45°C, 55°C), potentiodynamic polarization (PPD), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS).
- Surface analysis used SEM, XPS, and water contact angle methods.
- Polarization measurements indicate the inhibitor acts as a mixed-type inhibitor.
- Weight loss studies showed maximum inhibition efficiency of 88.4% at 250 ppm concentration at 25°C.
- Increasing temperature negatively affects inhibitor efficiency.
- Langmuir isotherm revealed adsorption is mediated via physi/chemi-sorption.
- DFT calculations complemented experimental results, confirming inhibitor adsorption effectiveness.

Background context: The research addresses corrosion protection for carbon steel used in oil, gas, marine, and automotive industries. Chitosan (extracted from crustacean shells) was chemically modified with Isatin via Schiff base reaction to improve its water solubility and corrosion inhibition performance. This is noted as the first report applying chitosan-Isatin Schiff bases as eco-friendly corrosion inhibitors for Q235 carbon steel in acid solutions.

Materials used include chitosan (95% degree of deacetylation), glacial acetic acid, isatin (98% purity), sodium hydroxide, hydrochloric acid, and ethanol. The work was supported by multiple National Natural Science Foundation of China grants. The article has 61 references and has been cited by 51 subsequent works.

## Highlights

*   •Two chitosan derivatives (CS-PT, CS-PT-Bn) were synthesized as green [corrosion inhibitors](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/chemistry/corrosion-inhibitor) for carbon steel in acidic environment. 
*   •CS-PT and CS-PT-Bn exhibit high inhibitive performance with the inhibition efficiencies of 98.4% and 98.5%. 
*   •CS-PT and CS-PT-Bn molecules can adsorb on Fe surface in a parallel pattern. 
*   •The adsorption mechanism of CS-PT and CS-PT-Bn was explored by theoretical calculations. 

## Abstract

Among the biodegradable polysaccharide, chitosan is widely present in the cell membranes of bacteria and algae and in the cell walls of higher plants. As a promising biopolymer, chitosan has great potential as eco-friendly corrosion inhibitor. Herein, two synthetic chitosan derivatives (_N_-phenylthiourea chitosan (CS-PT), _N_-phenyl-O-benzylthiourea chitosan (CS-PT-Bn)) were investigated as high-efficient acidic [corrosion inhibitors](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/materials-science/corrosion-inhibitor) to deal with the corrosion issue of carbon steel. The anti-corrosion property of the chitosan derivatives was explored by electrochemical tests, surface characterization and theoretical calculations. The experimental results indicate that both CS-PT and CS-PT-Bn present high-efficient inhibition performance with the inhibition efficiency of 98.4% and 98.5% at the concentration of 100 mg/L, respectively. Their adsorption mechanism at steel/solution interface is revealed by quantum chemical calculations, molecular dynamics (MD) and GFN-xTB calculations. It is found that CS-PT and CS-PT-Bn adsorb at the steel/solution interface by forming Fe-N and Fe-S bonds. Compared to CS-PT molecule, the introduction of benzyl group endows CS-PT-Bn molecule with stronger electrostatic effect and hydrophobicity, which favors the interfacial adsorption of CS-PT-Bn molecule on carbon steel surface.

## Introduction

As one of the most common metals, carbon steel (CS) has been extensively used in the building structures, mechanical equipment, petroleum and electric industries [1], [2], [3], [4]. Unfortunately, it is prone to corrosion when being exposed to acid solutions [5], [6], [7]. Acid solutions are widely used in acid pickling, industrial cleaning, acid descaling, oil-well acidizing in oil recovery and the petrochemical processes [8], [9]. The corrosion rate of carbon steel in acid solutions is relatively high. The mitigation of acid corrosion not only reduces global economic losses, but also avoids potential safety hazard [10], [11], [12], [13]. Therefore, the inhibition of CS corrosion in acid solutions is important for its practical applications [14]. Although there are many methods to prevent the corrosion of carbon steel, such as cathodic protection, coatings and corrosion inhibitors, adding corrosion inhibitors into acid environments has been the most popular method for reducing the corrosion of CS [15], [16], [17]. Although some corrosion inhibitors have been widely used on account of their remarkable inhibition efficiency, the corrosion inhibitors with high toxicity are not in compliance with the environmental protection laws and regulations issued by the administration and government [18]. Therefore, developing the new environmentally friendly corrosion inhibitors is important to the corrosion inhibition of carbon steel.

Recently, with the increased awareness of sustainable ecosystem development, eco-friendly corrosion inhibitors have attracted widespread attentions [19], [20]. As a category of green compounds, natural polymers (e.g., chitosan [21], [22], [23], [24], [25], starch [26], guar gum [27], [28], etc.) have the potential to be high-efficient eco-friendly corrosion inhibitors with the O atoms in their molecular structures, which can act as active sites for their adsorption on CS surface [21], [29], [30], [31]. Among these natural polymers, chitosan and its derivatives have attracted more attention because they possess a large amount of –OH and –NH 2, which facilitates their adsorption on CS surface [32], [33]. However, the inhibition efficiency of chitosan is usually low in most environment. Chitosan can be chemically modified by introducing functional groups on the –OH and –NH 2 to enhance its inhibition performance [34]. Therefore, it is necessary to develop efficient eco-friendly chitosan derivatives corrosion inhibitors with biodegradability and eco-compatibility by chemical modification.

Given the limitations of experimental means in exploring the corrosion inhibition mechanism, especially in describing the bonding information of corrosion inhibitors/metal surface, theoretical calculations could acquire the information on the interaction between inhibitor molecules and metal surface at the molecular level, which facilitates the clarification of corrosion inhibition mechanism [35], [36], [37]. Currently, most theoretical calculations about corrosion inhibitors adsorptive mechanism were implemented by the force field-based molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, which provide limited information on the inhibition mechanism [38], [39], [40]. While the theoretical calculations based on GFN-xTB (Geometries, Frequencies, Noncovalent interactions eXtended Tight Binding) method could obtain detailed information on bonding, electron transfer, density of state for the adsorption of corrosion inhibitors on metal surface, which is conducive to in-depth revealing the inhibition mechanism of inhibitors.

Herein, two eco-friendly chitosan derivatives (CS-PT, CS-PT-Bn) were developed and used as corrosion inhibitors for CS in acidic environment. Their inhibitive effects were investigated by electrochemical technique and surface characterization. The electrochemical test results show that both CS-PT and CS-PT-Bn exhibit outstanding inhibition performance with a high inhibition efficiency. Furthermore, the inhibitive mechanism of CS-PT and CS-PT-Bn for CS was elucidated by GFN-xTB calculations.

This is a research article published in the Journal of Colloid and Interface Science (Volume 640, pages 1052-1067, June 15, 2023) by Elsevier. The paper, authored by Q.H. Zhang, N. Xu, Z.N. Jiang, H.F. Liu, and G.A. Zhang, investigates two synthetic chitosan derivatives—N-phenylthiourea chitosan (CS-PT) and N-phenyl-O-benzylthiourea chitosan (CS-PT-Bn)—as eco-friendly, green corrosion inhibitors for carbon steel in acidic environments.

Key findings:
- Both CS-PT and CS-PT-Bn exhibit high inhibition efficiencies of 98.4% and 98.5%, respectively, at a concentration of 100 mg/L.
- The inhibition mechanism was explored using electrochemical tests, surface characterization, quantum chemical calculations, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and GFN-xTB calculations.
- The molecules adsorb on the Fe surface in a parallel pattern by forming Fe-N and Fe-S bonds at the steel/solution interface.
- Compared to CS-PT, the introduction of a benzyl group in CS-PT-Bn provides stronger electrostatic effects and hydrophobicity, which favors interfacial adsorption on carbon steel.
- Chitosan, a biodegradable polysaccharide abundant in nature, has great potential as an eco-friendly corrosion inhibitor due to its –OH and –NH2 functional groups.
- The study addresses the need for environmentally friendly corrosion inhibitors that comply with environmental protection regulations, as traditional inhibitors often have high toxicity.
- Theoretical calculations (particularly GFN-xTB) offer advantages over conventional force-field-based MD simulations by providing detailed information on bonding, electron transfer, and density of states for inhibitor adsorption on metal surfaces.

The article is cited by 111 subsequent publications and includes 62 references. Funding was provided by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (No. 51571097) and the Scientific Research Start-up Fund for Introduced Talents of Anhui Polytechnic University (No. 2022YQQ079, No. 2022YQQ080).

The [PDP](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/chemical-engineering/potentiodynamic-polarization) results showed that both ChSB-1 and ChSB-2 inhibitors have anti-corrosion characteristics because [heteroatoms](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/chemistry/heteroatom) caused a protective layer to develop that functioned as mixed-typed inhibitors. The calculated adsorption-free energy $\Delta G_{\mathit{ads}}^{o}$ for ChSB-1 and ChSB-2, respectively, was found −36.1 and−37.1 kJ mol−1. The ChSB-1 and ChSB-2 inhibitors adsorb on carbon steel in acidic conditions through [physisorption](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/chemistry/physical-adsorption) and [chemisorption](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/materials-science/chemisorption) interactions, and their adsorption is in line with the Langmuir adsorption model. Inhibited and uninhibited metallic surfaces were subjected to surface morphological assessments using contact angle (CA), the scanning electron microscopy and the energy dispersive X-ray (SEM/EDX) analysis. The DMol 3 part of Materials Studio 7.0 software was used to perform the [quantum chemical calculations](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/chemistry/quantum-chemical-calculations) based on DFT to visualize the structural features. Studies from [quantum chemistry](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/chemistry/quantum-chemistry) suggest the possibility of surface interaction between the unoccupied orbitals of the metal surface and the inhibitors ChSB-1, ChSB-2, ChSB-1H+, and ChSB-2H+. The results clearly show that the two inhibitors work well as environmentally friendly carbon steel corrosion inhibitors in acidic medium. This could be advantageous for industrial procedures such as pickling, cleaning, acidizing oil drilling in oil wells, and using citrus to de-sediment boilers.

## Introduction

The employment of steel and its alloys for residential and industrial reasons such as electrical uses, heat conductivity, pipes, and many others significantly enhances the current generation's lifestyle and comfort [1,2]. Carbon steel is a key component in numerous industrial fields due to its great mechanical strength, ductility, and inexpensive cost [3,4]. When exposed to acidic environments, these metals deteriorate [5]. Worldwide, corrosion losses to the economy amount to over $2.5 trillion [6]. where each country loses 3–5% of its gross domestic product (GDP) due to corrosion. A resource with a good ecological profile, abundant renewable supply, and potential application as a green metal corrosion inhibitor is chitosan. To address this, inhibitors are added to the prevent metal deterioration [[7], [8], [9]]. It has been claimed that using organic inhibitors with heteroatoms, such as N, O, and S, improves inhibition efficacy by creating a chemical connection between the inhibitor's electron-rich atoms and the metal [10,11]. Strict safety and environmental protection regulations have limited the use of hazardous compounds as corrosion inhibitors [12,13]. Because of their non-toxic and biodegradable characteristics, polymers that occur naturally and related compounds [[14], [15], [16], [17]] are considered to be more promising and have been identified by numerous researchers as superior corrosion inhibitors for carbon steel [18]. Thus, the extraction of natural polymer materials from plants such as pectin [19], tannin [20], caffeine [21], gum [22], curcumin [23], pigeon pea leaf extract [24], locust bean gum [25], alkaloid [26], and chitosan [[27], [28], [29]] as environmental and green corrosion inhibitors is progressively emerging as a new trend and direction. It has been reported that chitosan, a widely accessible renewable resource with a positive ecological profile and uses in the industrial and medical sectors, is a “green inhibitor” [19,30]. Large biopolymer chitosan has more heteroatoms (hydroxyl and amine groups) than other biopolymers, which makes it easier for it to cling to metal surfaces and improves its anti-corrosion qualities [28,31]. To give chitosan more of the required properties, imine linkages are formed with the free amino groups in chitosan to make a Schiff base [32,33]. Schiff bases are used in many different fields, particularly in medicine and pharmacology, where they are useful as corrosion inhibitors and have analgesic, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, anticancer, and antioxidant properties [34]. They are also easily prepared and safe for the environment [35]. Several studies on new chitosan derivatives have been conducted in an effort to increase the inhibitory efficacy of Schiff base compounds. To date, nevertheless, scientists remain interested in enhancing the heterocycle's capacity to further inhibit metallic corrosion. The first investigation into the inhibitory effect of Schiff base, which is produced by reacting chitosan with salicylaldehyde, on mild steel in an acidic solution was conducted by Menaka et al. [36]. The 70% inhibition efficiency of the modified inhibitor. Additionally, Zhang et al. [37] increased the inhibitor molecules' adsorbed zones and covered the metal surface, which further enhanced the chitosan Schiff base and significantly increased the inhibitor's efficiency. Consequently, the goal of the current study is to produce corrosion inhibitors that are economical, ecologically benign, and have great protective potential. Thus, this work's originality lies in its ability to identify phenylethanone and chitosan based on Schiff bases as green compounds with more heteroatoms, hydroxyl groups, and amine groups that are thought to be efficient corrosion inhibitors. These compounds' polar groups and their tendency to form bonds with the metal surface-an additional benefit-likely contribute to their improved adsorption on metallic surfaces under aggressive conditions. A shielding layer is also developed by the methyl and methoxy groups attaching to the benzene rings and the imine group's abundance of π-electrons and pairs of unshared electrons interacting with the d-orbitals of any metal. Adding these moieties of functional groups to its structure is one tactic for dealing with this. From the foregoing, it is evident that Schiff bases have a special structure that includes nitrogen atoms that donate electrons, making them effective chelating compounds that prefer to chemically bind to metal surfaces. Furthermore, they can be protonated in acidic environments, which aids in their physical adsorption to the metallic substrate to form an anti-corrosion coat.

For this reason, the current study is being conducted with the goal of generating corrosion inhibitors that are affordable, ecologically benign, and have good protective potential. Using Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), the functional group of altering chitosan by two phenylethanone Schiff base derivatives (ChSB-1 and ChSB-2) was investigated. More precisely, the aim of this work was to assess the corrosion protection properties of the modified carbon steel chitosan 1 M HCl system by using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), mass loss, and PDP methodologies. At different concentrations, the behaviour of the modified chitosan ChSB-1 and ChSB-2 was investigated. In addition to analysing the adsorption type and behaviour, the corrosion prevention mechanism was also described. Density functional theory (DFT) and molecular dynamic (MD) simulation were used to screen for theoretical inhibitive performance.

Thermodynamic studies confirmed that the corrosion inhibition resulted from the adsorption of **SCH-1** and **SCH-2** molecules on the steel surface obeying Langmuir adsorption isotherms with a physicochemical adsorption nature. Studies of thermodynamics verified that the suppression of corrosion was due to the adsorption of **SCH-1** and **SCH-2** molecules on the steel surface, which followed physicochemical adsorption isotherms according to Langmuir adsorption isotherms. Potentiodynamic polarization (PDP) confirmed that **SCH-1** and **SCH-2** are mixed-type inhibitors. To better understand the inhibition and adsorption behavior of **SCH-1** and **SCH-2** molecules on the Fe(110) surface, various computational models have been applied including Mulliken population analysis, molecular electrostatic potential surface (ESP), density functional theory (DFT), natural bond orbital analysis (NBO), and molecular dynamics simulation (MDS). The theoretical finding showed that the interaction/binding energies of SCH-2 molecules are much higher than that of SCH-1 molecules. This conclusively confirms the strong adsorption of SCH-2 molecules on the metal-surface, which in turn highlights its superior inhibitory capacity. The study, authored by Ahmed A. Farag, S.M. Al-Shomar, and N.S. Abdelshafi, investigates the use of eco-friendly modified chitosan as a corrosion inhibitor for carbon steel in acidic medium (1 M HCl). Two modified chitosan Schiff base derivatives (ChSB-1 and ChSB-2) were synthesized via condensation methods. Key findings include: mass loss data showed 89.3% and 91.5% inhibition efficacy at 1 mM concentration for ChSB-1 and ChSB-2 respectively; ChSB-2 exhibited better performance due to the electron-donor methoxy (–OCH₃) substituent providing more delocalized electrons. Both inhibitors acted as mixed-type inhibitors (confirmed by potentiodynamic polarization, PDP) by forming a protective layer through heteroatoms. Adsorption free energy (ΔG°ads) values were −36.1 and −37.1 kJ mol⁻¹ for ChSB-1 and ChSB-2, respectively, indicating a combination of physisorption and chemisorption following the Langmuir adsorption model. Surface analysis was conducted using contact angle measurements and SEM/EDX. Quantum chemical calculations were performed using DFT (DMol³ module of Materials Studio 7.0) to visualize structural features and confirmed surface interactions between the metal's unoccupied orbitals and the inhibitors (ChSB-1, ChSB-2, and their protonated forms). The research was motivated by the fact that corrosion causes ~$2.5 trillion in global economic losses (3-5% of GDP per country). The inhibitors show promise for industrial applications including pickling, cleaning, acidizing oil drilling, and boiler de-sedimentation. The research received no funding, and the authors declare no competing interests.

## Abstract

There is a high demand for high performance, effective and eco-friendly corrosion inhibitors for industrial applications. Consequently, many researchers are focused on developing efficient, cost-effective materials to protect metals. In this study, an ecofriendly chitosan methionine derivative (M) was developed, synthesized, characterized, and tested for its anticorrosion properties. The ability of this compound as a corrosion inhibitor for carbon steel (CS) was confirmed through weight loss measurements (WL), potentiodynamic polarization (PDP), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) studies in a 1.0 M hydrochloric acid solution. The findings showed that the inhibitor, M, achieved a maximum inhibition efficiency of 99.8% at a concentration of 100 ppm by the PDP method. Additionally, the corrosion potential value, being less than 85 mV, supported classifying M as a mixed-type inhibitor with a cathodic tendency. The adsorption behavior of the inhibitor on the CS surface was consistent with Langmuir’s adsorption isotherm. EIS data also confirmed that increasing inhibitor concentration raised the charge transfer resistance (*R*ct), indicating improved protection. Surface examination using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) revealed the formation of a protective layer of the M molecules on the CS surface. Moreover, theoretical studies, including analyses of the highest occupied molecular orbital (EHOMO), lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (ELUMO), dipole moment (µ), were thoroughly examined. Overall, both experimental and theoretical findings demonstrate that this derivative can effectively form a protective layer and mitigate corrosion.

Acetyl thiourea chitosan has been reported as effective corrosion inhibitor for mild steel in 0.5 M H2SO4 solution[39](/articles/s41598-025-98981-2#ref-CR39 "Fekry, A. & Mohamed, R. R. Acetyl thiourea Chitosan as an eco-friendly inhibitor for mild steel in sulphuric acid medium. Electrochim. Acta. 55, 1933–1939 (2010).").

Metal corrosion occurs through electrochemical reactions at metal/solution interface, making electrochemical experiments and weight loss techniques ideal for studying corrosion. Electrochemical experiments provide authentic results in a shorter time frame. The adsorption film’s characteristic, which supports the inhibition mechanism, are explored in detail through adsorption and kinetic modeling weight losses method.

The novelty of our work lies in developing an environmentally friendly, cost-effective corrosion inhibitor with excellent protection efficiency, by synthesizing a soluble chitosan methionine derivative (M) suitable for use in acidic environments, thereby expanding its industrial application potential. This study evaluates the efficiency of the synthesized chitosan derivative (M) on carbon steel in hydrochloric acid using both electrochemical and weight loss measurements, providing comprehensive understanding of its performance across various methods. We also explore the relationship between inhibition efficiencies obtained experimentally and theoretical insights from quantum calculations, offering a deeper molecular-level analysis of its mechanism. This comprehensive approach enhances our understanding of this inhibitor’s potential for scalable industrial use.

## Experimental

### Material

All the chemicals utilized were of analytical reagent grade and were employed without additional purification. For immersion studies, commercially available carbon steel (CS) strips were sheared into dimensions of 5 cm × 2 cm × 2 mm, while for electrochemical studies, they were cut into 2 × 1 cm. The composition of the CS strips was determined to be as follows: Fe 99.3; C 0.218; Si 0.0198; Mn 0.188; P 0.0091; S 0.0246; Ni 0.0256; Al 0.0456; Cu 0.0376; Cr 0.0189; Mo 0.0089. prior to experimentation, the samples were abraded using successively finer grade emery papers, washed with absolute ethanol, rinsed with doubly distilled water, dried, weighed, and stored in desiccators for subsequent use. Analar grade hydrochloric acid (Merck) was employed to prepare the corrosive medium, with 1 M solutions being prepared using double distilled water.

### Preparation of chitosan methionine

Chitosan (1.0 g) was added to 30 ml deionized water and allowed to swell overnight. Subsequently, alpha amino gamma-methyl thiol butyric acid (methionine) (0.5 g) was slowly added while stirring. At room temperature the mixture was stirred for 24 h, and half of the solvent was then removed under the reduced pressure. Anhydrous ethanol was gradually added to the solution until no fibrous precipitate formed. Centrifuging at 3500 rpm for 5 min and the precipitate residue was washed twice with ethanol. After vacuum drying, off-white powders were obtained[40](/articles/s41598-025-98981-2#ref-CR40 "Hu, Z., Qin, Y., Guang, J. & Cai, Y. Preparation and characterization of chitosan amino acid salts. In IOP Conference Series: Materials Science and Engineering 012023 (IOP Publishing, 2019)."). The structure of chitosan M was generated using the software ChemDraw Ultra Version7.0.

### Characterization

#### Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR)

The structure of the prepared chitosan derivative M was measured by Fourier transform infrared spectrometer—Perkin–Elmer 1750, in range of 400 –4000 cm− 1. The IR image in this study was generated using the software Origin Pro Version 8.5.

#### Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR)

Bruker Advance II 400 NMR spectrometer was used to determine the 1HNMR spectra of chitosan derivative. The NMR image in this study was generated using the software MestReNova Version 14.2.1-27684.

#### Thermal analysis (TGA and DTA)

Thermal analysis of M was performed by thermo-gravimetric analyzer model TGA TA-51 at 20 °C/min in a nitrogen atmosphere. The TGA image in this study was generated using the software Sigma plot version 10.

### Corrosion analysis

The experiments were conducted in 1 M HCl solution with and without different concentrations (25–100 ppm) of the prepared Chitosan derivative M. The images in this part were generated using the software Sigma plot version 10.

#### Weight loss measurements (WL)

The weighed samples were immersed in 100 ml of 1 M HCl solution, both with and without different concentrations of M (ranging from 25 to100 ppm) at temperature ranging from 298 to 328 K. After maintaining the specified immersion time and temperature, the specimens were removed, dried in moisture-free desiccators and re-weighed using a sensitive analytical balance Model FA 2104 A (cap.: 210 g, d.: 0.1 mg). To ensure the reproducibility, the experiments were conducted in triplicate. The difference in weight before and after immersion was considered as the weight loss, which was utilized to calculate the corrosion rate.

The corrosion rates were calculated according to Eq. ([1](/articles/s41598-025-98981-2#Equ1))[5](/articles/s41598-025-98981-2#ref-CR5 "Abdel-karim, A. M., Shahen, S. & Gaber, G. 4-Aminobenzenesulfonic acid as effective corrosion inhibitor for carbon steel in hydrochloric acid. Egypt. J. Chem. 64, 825–834 (2021).") :

$$\:{C}\_{R}=\frac{\Delta W \times 534}{Atd}$$

(1)

where *C**R* is the corrosion rate (mpy), *∆W* (g), is the difference in the specimen weight before and after immersion, A is the surface area of CS specimens (cm2), t is the exposure time (*h*) and d is density of CS in g/cm3.

The degree of surface coverage (*θ*) was calculated using Eq. ([2](/articles/s41598-025-98981-2#Equ2))[41](/articles/s41598-025-98981-2#ref-CR41 "Abdel-karim, A. M., Shahen, S., Elsisi, D. M., Hyba, A. M. & El-Shamy, O. A. Experimental and theoretical studies of corrosion resistance enhancement of carbon steel in 1 M HCl by quinoxalinosulfonamide hybrid-bearing Theophylline moiety. J. Bio-and Tribo-Corros. 8, 70 (2022).")

$$\:\theta=\frac{{W}\_{o}-{W}\_{i}}{{W}\_{0}}$$

(2)

where, *W*i and *W*o are the weight losses of CS specimens in inhibited and uninhibited solutions, respectively. The inhibition efficiency *IE*% was calculated according to Eq. ([3](/articles/s41598-025-98981-2#Equ3)):[42](/articles/s41598-025-98981-2#ref-CR42 "Yadav, M. et al. Electrochemical, thermodynamic and quantum chemical studies of synthesized benzimidazole derivatives as corrosion inhibitors for N80 steel in hydrochloric acid. J. Mol. Liq. 213, 122–138 (2016).").

$$\:IE \%= \theta \times 100$$

(3)

#### Electrochemical corrosion tests

Electrochemical measurements were conducted in a conventional three-electrode glass cell using Potentiostat/ galvanostat 302 supported by Nova software Version 1.11. A carbon steel CS specimen with an exposed area of 1 cm2 served as working electrode, while silver/silver chloride electrode was used as reference electrode, and a platinum electrode as the counter electrode. The electrochemical tests were performed at room temperature (298 k) after reaching a steady-state potential.

##### Potentiodynamic polarization (PDP)

PDP studies were performed by scanning the potential in the range ± 250 mV versus open circuit potential (OPC) at a sweep rate of 1 mVs− 1. The anodic and the cathodic branches of the PDP curves were extrapolated until they intersected to determine the corrosion potential (*E**corr*), the corrosion current density (icorr), and polarization resistance (*R**p* ). the corrosion inhibition efficiency (*IE %*) was calculated using an Eq. ([4](/articles/s41598-025-98981-2#Equ4))[43](/articles/s41598-025-98981-2#ref-CR43 "Abdel-karim, A. M. et al. Abd El-Sattar, green synthesis of novel Bis structure of (Carbamothioyl) oxalamide derivatives as corrosion inhibitors for copper in 3.5% NaCl; experimental and theoretical investigation. J. Mol. Struct. 1295, 136597 (2024).").

$$\:IE\%=\frac{{I}\_{o}-{I}\_{i}}{{I}\_{0}} \times 100$$

(4)

where, Io, Ii are the current densities in absence and presence of M.

##### Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS)

EIS measurements were conducted at the open circuit potential by applying a frequency range of 100 kHz to 0.01 Hz with a10 mV amplitude. The corrosion inhibition efficiency was evaluated using the polarization resistance (*R*P)[44](/articles/s41598-025-98981-2#ref-CR44 "Hussien, H. et al. Experimental and theoretical evaluations: green synthesis of new organic compound Bis Ethanethioyl oxalamide as corrosion inhibitor for copper in 3.5% NaCl. Egypt. J. Chem. 66, 189–196 (2023).") .

$$IE\% = \frac{{{R\_1} - {R\_0}}}{{{R\_1}}} \times 100$$

(5)

### Surface studies

The influence of the corrosive attack on the CS surface was investigated using a scanning electron microscope (SEM), Quanta 250 FEG, FEI, Hillsboro, Oregon) at high vacuum chamber conditions (4.8 × 10 − 6 Torr pressure), 20 kV acceleration voltage. CS samples were prepared to the specified surface finish and then immersed in 1 M HCl solution period of 6 h, both with and without 100 ppm of M inhibitor.

## Results and discussion

The active sites on chitosan include the amine and hydroxyl groups. As a result, chitosan derivatives have been synthesized and applied to inhibit metals and alloys in in aggressive environments. One of the modifications involves the formation of chitosan derivative (M), as depicted in Fig. [1](/articles/s41598-025-98981-2#Fig1), through the reaction of an alpha amino gamma methyl thiol butyric acid (methionine) with the free amino group of chitosan, which improve chitosan’s functionality and expand its application scope.

### Weight loss measurements

#### Influence of inhibitor dosage

The weight loss experiment was conducted in 1 M HCl solution both in the absence (blank) and presence of various concentrations of M ranging from 25 to 100 ppm. The weight loss data obtained from these experiments was utilized to calculate the corrosion rate and the inhibition efficiency using Eqs. ([1](/articles/s41598-025-98981-2#Equ1)–[3](/articles/s41598-025-98981-2#Equ3)). The variation with time is illustrated in Fig. [5](/articles/s41598-025-98981-2#Fig5).

The weight loss of CS in the presence of inhibitor exhibits a linear variation with time, consistently lower than that of the blank solution. Additionally, there is an observed increase in weight loss with an increase in immersion time. This trend is accompanied by a decrease in efficiency, may be attributed to the desorption of protective layer[53](/articles/s41598-025-98981-2#ref-CR53 "Outirite, M. et al. Bentiss, ac impedance, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and density functional theory studies of 3, 5-bis (n-pyridyl)-1, 2, 4-oxadiazoles as efficient corrosion inhibitors for carbon steel surface in hydrochloric acid solution. Electrochim. Acta. 55, 1670–1681 (2010).").

The increase in the inhibitive performance of chitosan derivative M with the increase in concentration implies that higher concentrations of the inhibitor lead to more effective protection against corrosion, likely due to increased adsorption of the M molecules on the CS surface forming a more robust layer.

These findings suggest that M effectively inhibits metal corrosion across all studied concentrations. The results indicate that CS experiences significant corrosion uninhibited 1 M HCl solution. However, increasing the concentration of M considerably reduce the dissolution and corrosion rate, while also enhancing inhibition efficiency. This suggests a strong interaction between the inhibitors and metal surface[54](/articles/s41598-025-98981-2#ref-CR54 "Abakedi, O. U. & Asuquo, J. E. Corrosion Inhibition of aluminium in acidic medium by ethanol leaf extract of Azadirachta indica. J. Basic. Appl. Res. 2, 556–560 (2016)."), rendering M effective as an inhibitor for CS in 1 M HCl. The observed reduction in corrosion rate and weight loss can be attributed to the adsorption of the inhibitor compounds onto the surface of the CS, thereby blocking sites and facilitating the formation of a protective film on the surface.

The notable efficiency of compounds is attributed to the presence of adsorption sites in the organic compounds, which facilitate favorable adsorption[55](/articles/s41598-025-98981-2#ref-CR55 "El-Asri, A. et al. Understanding imidazole derivatives effect as a corrosion inhibitor for brass in nitric acid: a combined experimental and theoretical assessments. Corros. Eng. Sci. Technol. 57, 680–695 (2022)."). At the optimum inhibitor concentration of 100 ppm, a remarkable 98.84% inhibition efficiency is achieved. This high level of inhibition efficiency underscores the effectiveness of the inhibitor in mitigating corrosion.

The results existing in Table [1](/articles/s41598-025-98981-2#Tab1), indicates that regardless of immersion time, the inhibition efficiency increases as the concentration of the inhibitor increases. This trend suggests that higher concentrations of the inhibitor lead to more effective inhibition of corrosion, consistently enhancing the protection afforded to the metal surface.

#### Adsorption isotherms and thermodynamic examination

##### Thermodynamic adsorption parameters

To obtain a thorough understanding of how inhibitor molecules (M) reduce CS corrosion, researchers designed multiple adsorption isotherms. These isotherms offer valuable insights into interactions between inhibitor molecules and the active sites of the metal surface[29](/articles/s41598-025-98981-2#ref-CR29 "Menaka, R., Geethanjali, R. & Subhashini, S. Electrochemical investigation of eco-friendly Chitosan schiff base for corrosion Inhibition of mild steel in acid medium. Mater. Today: Proc. 5, 16617–16625 (2018)."). The surface coverage θ is determined using Eq. ([2](/articles/s41598-025-98981-2#Equ2)), which derives from the weight loss data observed during the experiments.

In thermodynamic studies of adsorption isotherms, the goal is to understand how inhibitor molecules interact with active centers on metal surfaces to inhibit corrosion. This process involves fitting experimental data of surface coverage (θ) into various mathematical models of adsorption. These models include Langmuir, Temkin, Freundlich, Frumkin, and Flory-Huggins isotherms, and each offering different insight into the adsorption behavior of the inhibitor molecules. Figures [7](/articles/s41598-025-98981-2#Fig7) and [8](/articles/s41598-025-98981-2#Fig8) display the different isotherm models used. For more details, the corresponding parameters adsorption equilibrium constant (*K*ads) and regression coefficient (R2) for M were calculated and listed in Table [2](/articles/s41598-025-98981-2#Tab2). The increase in *K*ads values indicates the power of the adsorption of M inhibitor molecules on the metal surface[57](/articles/s41598-025-98981-2#ref-CR57 "Geethanjali, R. & Subhashini, S. Thermodynamic characterization of metal dissolution and adsorption of Polyvinyl alcohol-grafted Poly (Acrylamide-Vinyl Sulfonate) on mild steel in hydrochloric acid. Portugaliae Electrochim. Acta. 33, 35–48 (2015).").

The best-fit model is typically identified by the highest *R*2 value obtained from the linear plots. The Langmuir isotherm emerges as the best suited, with the highest *R*2 values as shown in Fig. [7](/articles/s41598-025-98981-2#Fig7); Table [2](/articles/s41598-025-98981-2#Tab2) Therefore, it is suitable for evaluating the adsorption equilibrium constant, *K**ads*[61](/articles/s41598-025-98981-2#ref-CR61 "Abusaif, M. S. et al. Novel Water-soluble quinoxaline-2, 3-dione-6-sulfohydrazide derivatives as efficient acid corrosion inhibitors: design, characterization, experimental, and theoretical studies. J. Taiwan Inst. Chem. Eng. 153, 105207 (2023).").

This is a peer-reviewed scientific research article published in Scientific Reports (volume 15, Article 15924, 2025) by S.F. Hamza, Seham Shahen, Amal M. Abdel-karim, Ahmed A. El-Rashedy, and Amira M. Hyba, investigating an eco-friendly corrosion inhibitor called "chitosan methionine derivative (M)" for carbon steel in 1 M hydrochloric acid solution.

**Purpose/Novelty:** The study develops a cost-effective, environmentally friendly corrosion inhibitor by synthesizing a water-soluble chitosan methionine derivative to protect carbon steel in acidic environments, expanding industrial application potential. Chitosan (a natural, biodegradable biopolymer) was modified with methionine (alpha amino gamma-methyl thiol butyric acid) to improve its poor water solubility while maintaining adsorption sites.

**Methodology:** The inhibitor was synthesized by reacting 1.0 g chitosan with 0.5 g methionine in deionized water, stirred for 24 hours at room temperature, then precipitated with anhydrous ethanol and vacuum dried. Characterization was performed using FT-IR, 1H-NMR, and TGA/DTA thermal analysis. Corrosion testing employed three methods in 1 M HCl with inhibitor concentrations from 25-100 ppm: weight loss measurements (WL, at 298-328 K), potentiodynamic polarization (PDP), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). Surface studies used SEM and EDX, while theoretical analysis employed Density Functional Theory (DFT) using Gaussian 09 with B3LYP functional on 3-21G basis set.

**Key Results:**
- Maximum inhibition efficiency of 99.8% achieved at 100 ppm concentration by PDP method
- Weight loss measurements showed 98.84% inhibition efficiency at 100 ppm (optimum concentration)
- Corrosion potential value below 85 mV classified M as a mixed-type inhibitor with cathodic tendency
- Adsorption followed Langmuir's adsorption isotherm (best fit with highest R² values among Langmuir, Temkin, Freundlich, Frumkin, and Flory-Huggins models)
- Thermodynamic parameters: ΔG°ads = -9.002 kJ/mol (spontaneous physisorption via electrostatic interaction), ΔH°ads = -20.29 kJ/mol (exothermic), ΔS°ads = -0.0378 JK⁻¹mol⁻¹ (decreased disorder)
- Activation energy increased from 38.06 kJ/mol (uninhibited) to 68.61 kJ/mol with 100 ppm M, confirming physical adsorption
- EIS showed increasing inhibitor concentration raised charge transfer resistance (Rct), indicating improved protection
- Inhibition efficiency decreased with increasing temperature (298-328 K) due to desorption of protective layer
- SEM/EDX confirmed formation of a protective M layer on the carbon steel surface
- Carbon steel composition: Fe 99.3; C 0.218; Si 0.0198; Mn 0.188; P 0.0091; S 0.0246; Ni 0.0256; Al 0.0456; Cu 0.0376; Cr 0.0189; Mo 0.0089

**Characterization findings:** FT-IR confirmed formation of the conjugate via protonation (NH3+ formation at ~3375 cm⁻¹, C=O stretch at ~1569 cm⁻¹, C-S peak at 1079 cm⁻¹). 1H-NMR showed additional peaks at 1.89-2.03 ppm indicating methionine conjugation. TGA revealed three degradation stages (99.4-281°C, starting 282°C, and 543-976°C), with methionine incorporation improving thermal stability compared to pure chitosan.

**Conclusion:** Both experimental and theoretical findings demonstrate the chitosan methionine derivative effectively forms a protective layer on carbon steel and mitigates corrosion in 1 M HCl, making it a promising eco-friendly alternative to toxic organic corrosion inhibitors.

## Abstract

The corrosion inhibition of carbon-steel in 0.5 M HCl by sodium aliginate has been investigated using weight loss method, potentiodynamic polarization, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and electrochemical frequency modulation (EFM) techniques. Results obtained showed that sodium aliginate are good inhibitor and its inhibition efficiency increases with increasing sodium aliginate concentration and decrease with increase in temperature. Moreover, polarization studies clearly revealed that the presence of sodium aliginate changes the mechanism of hydrogen evolution and the metal dissolution i.e. they act as mixed type inhibitors. EIS study showed that charge transfer resistance increases with the increase of sodium aliginate concentration but the capacitance of double layer decreases. The adsorption of sodium aliginate obeys Langmuir's adsorption isotherm. The activation parameters were determined and discussed. The mechanism of adsorption had been explained on the basis of chemical structure of sodium aliginate. It was found that there is a good agreement between the different tested techniques.

4.   Langmuir adsorption isotherm best describes sodium alginate adsorption on carbon steel surfaces.
5.   Electrochemical techniques confirm consistent inhibition efficiency results across weight loss, EIS, and EFM methods.

This is an Academia.edu page for the research paper "Sodium Alginate as Corrosion Inhibitor for Carbon Steel" by Ameena Al-Bonayan (Umm Al-Qura University, Makkah, Saudi Arabia), published in the International Journal of Scientific & Engineering Research (Volume 5, Issue 4, April 2014, ISSN 2229-5518). The paper is 8 pages with 150 views.

**Abstract/Findings:** The study investigated corrosion inhibition of carbon steel in 0.5 M HCl by sodium alginate using weight loss method, potentiodynamic polarization, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), and electrochemical frequency modulation (EFM) techniques. Key findings: (1) sodium alginate is a good inhibitor, with inhibition efficiency increasing with concentration and decreasing with temperature; (2) polarization studies revealed sodium alginate acts as a mixed-type inhibitor, altering hydrogen evolution and metal dissolution mechanisms; (3) EIS showed charge transfer resistance increases with concentration while double-layer capacitance decreases; (4) adsorption follows Langmuir's adsorption isotherm; (5) good agreement was found across all tested techniques.

**Key takeaways (AI-generated):** Sodium alginate serves as a mixed-type inhibitor for carbon steel in 0.5 M HCl, primarily acting cathodically; inhibition efficiency increases with concentration and decreases with temperature; polarization studies reveal changes in hydrogen evolution and metal dissolution mechanisms; Langmuir adsorption isotherm best describes adsorption; electrochemical techniques confirm consistent inhibition efficiency results across weight loss, EIS, and EFM methods.

**FAQs (AI-generated):** Inhibition efficiency peaks at approximately 88% at lower temperatures (25°C) and declines at higher temperatures; corrosion current densities drop up to 60% with increasing concentration; Langmuir isotherm provides the best fit with correlation coefficient near unity; increasing temperature elevates corrosion rates notably above 30°C; adsorption is primarily physical (physisorption) with a ΔG°ads value of 4.19 kJ mol⁻¹ indicating weak electrostatic interactions.

**Figures (13):** Includes Langmuir adsorption isotherm plots, Arrhenius plots, polarization curves, Nyquist plots, Bode plots, equivalent circuit model, intermodulation spectra, and data tables at 30°C with various sodium alginate concentrations.

**Related papers:** The page lists numerous related studies on corrosion inhibitors, including (+)-catechin hydrate, sodium alginate grafted with polyacrylamide (efficiency increased from 64% to 86% when grafted), arabinogalactan, phenolic compounds, alizarin red (efficiency up to 96.5% at 1×10⁻² M), modified cassava starches, polysorbate compounds, sodium caprylate (77% efficiency), sodium glutarate, sodium citrate, and sodium alginate for API X60 steel in saline medium.

**References:** The paper cites 45 references covering corrosion inhibition literature, electrochemical techniques, and adsorption isotherm studies.

## Green Sodium Alginate Corrosion Inhibitor for Carbon Steel Neutral Medium (CN102140641A)

**Patent Overview:**
This Chinese patent (CN102140641A), filed by the Institute of Oceanology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) on February 18, 2011 and published August 3, 2011, describes a green (environmentally friendly) corrosion inhibitor for carbon steel in neutral media, based on sodium alginate. The inventors are 王毅 (Wang Yi) and 张盾 (Zhang Dun). The patent's legal status is listed as "Pending" (application deemed withdrawn after publication per legal events).

**Technical Composition:**
- The corrosion inhibitor is sodium alginate with the chemical composition formula (C₆H₇NaO₆)ₙ and an average molecular weight (Mw) of 20,000–100,000 (specific values: 20000, 30000, 40000, 50000, 80000, 90000, or 100000).
- Sodium alginate is a natural product extracted from brown algae and is widely used in the food industry.
- It is a copolymer composed of α-L-mannuronic acid (M unit) and β-D-guluronic acid (G unit) connected by 1,4-glycosidic bonds, made up of different GGGMMM segments.
- The α-L-mannuronic acid unit contains numerous carboxyl groups that can coordinate (complex) with metals.

**Application Method (Claim 3):**
- Steel is immersed in a neutral medium solution containing the sodium alginate inhibitor.
- Dosage: 0.06g–1.00g of inhibitor per liter of neutral medium solution (0.06g, 0.08g, 0.1g, 0.3g, 0.5g, 0.8g, or 1.0g).
- Immersion temperature: room temperature.
- Immersion time: 0.5–4 hours (0.5h, 1h, 1.5h, 2h, 2.5h, 3h, 3.5h, or 4h).
- Neutral medium solution: NaCl aqueous solution with mass concentration of 3.0–4.0%.

**Experimental Results (Embodiments):**
- Embodiment 1: 0.5g/L sodium alginate (Mw=50,000) in 3.5% NaCl, 0.5h immersion → inhibition efficiency >90% (high-efficiency corrosion inhibitor), tested via Tafel polarization curve using a three-electrode system (carbon steel working electrode, 0.196 cm² exposed area, platinum wire counter electrode, Ag/AgCl reference electrode in 3M KCl, CHI 760C electrochemical workstation, potential range -300 to 300mV vs. open circuit potential, scan rate 0.5mV/s).
- Embodiment 2: 0.06g/L sodium alginate (Mw=100,000) in 4% NaCl, 2h immersion → inhibition efficiency >80%.
- Embodiment 3: 1.00g/L sodium alginate (Mw=20,000) in 3.0% NaCl, 4h immersion → inhibition efficiency >90%.

**Advantages Claimed:**
1. Low cost.
2. Environmental friendliness — natural product from brown algae, non-toxic, harmless to environment and organisms, no post-use environmental issues; aligns with green corrosion inhibitor development trends (unlike traditional inorganic inhibitors such as chromates, nitrates, and nitrites, which have toxic side effects and poor environmental friendliness).
3. Low dosage with good results — small amounts effectively suppress metal corrosion in neutral media; high inhibition efficiency, strong continuous action ability.

**Claims (3 total):**
1. A green sodium alginate corrosion inhibitor for carbon steel neutral medium with formula (C₆H₇NaO₆)ₙ and Mw of 20,000–100,000.
2. Application of the sodium alginate corrosion inhibitor to prevent steel corrosion.
3. Application method involving immersion in neutral medium solution with specified dosage, temperature, time, and NaCl concentration.

**Background Context:**
The patent addresses the problem that metal corrosion causes serious losses across national economy and national defense. Common inhibitors (chromate, nitrate, nitrite) have toxic side effects and are being phased out due to environmental regulations. There is a growing need for efficient, environmentally friendly, cheap, and readily available green corrosion inhibitors. The patent cites four non-patent references, including works on chitosan phosphate corrosion performance in seawater (《材料保护》2009) and synergistic corrosion inhibition of carboxymethyl chitosan (《装备环境工程》2010). The patent has been cited by 7 subsequent patents (including circulating cooling water corrosion inhibitors, solar water heater heat exchange media, copper inhibitors, and rust water-based transforming agents).

# Electrochemical investigations of hydrochloric acid corrosion for carbon steel and coating effect by Poly (butyl Methacrylate)-grafted alginate/Fe3O4

Eman Alzahrani, Hala M. Abo-Dief, Faouzia Algethami

Department of Chemistry, College of Science, Taif University, P.O. Box 11099, Taif 21944, Saudi Arabia

**Received:** , **Accepted:** ,

© The Author(s) 2021

**Disclaimer:**  
This article was originally published by *Elsevier* and was migrated to Scientific Scholar after the change of Publisher.

## Abstract

This study aimed at analyzing the performance of a corrosion resistant coating made from tri-iron tetraoxide (Fe3O4) nanoparticles (NPs) and (Butyl-2-methylprop-2-enoate)-grafted alignate/Fe3O4 nanocomposite. Two methods were used to characterize the combination; Thermo Gravimetric Analysis (TGA) and the Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC). It was observed that the rate of corrosion of the carbon steel was greatly influenced by the molarities of HCl used, temperature and time of immersion. Corrosion rate was found to increase with increase in molarity of the hydrochloric acid and temperature but was inversely proportional to the time of immersion. Carbon steel was coated with the corrosion resistant combination using the hot-dip coating method. To characterize the coating, Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM), Energy dispersive X-Ray (EDX), Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) and X-Ray Diffraction (XRD) methods were used. Electrochemical studies (Tafel polarization and cyclic voltametry) showed that the optimum conditions for prevention of corrosion of the carbon steel were 150 °C and immersed time of 2 hrs. The efficiency of coating varied between the 2 combinations, with PBMA-gft-Alg/Fe3O4 nanocomposite being more effective than Fe3O4NPs coating.

1

## ***1*** Introduction

Coating to enhance mechanical strength and corrosion resistance is one of the best practical and cost effective methods for metallic components ([Gray & Luan, 2002; Lin & Dahan, 2015](#bibr70-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Protective coatings on magnesium and its alloys—a critical review")). Carbon steels typically contain less than 1.5% carbon content along with the minute presence of Mn, Si, P and S. Based on the percentage of carbon, the classification is further divided into three forms, namely low carbon steels (<0.25% C), medium carbon steels (0.25–0.70% C) and high carbon steels (0.70–1.05% C). Variation of the percentage of carbon content allows to attain different mechanical properties such as strength, ductility, hardness, *etc.* Based on the steel properties, related to carbon content, plain carbon steels are further divided into certain grades, such as grade 1008 (0.08 wt% C), which is good for forming and has good ductility; grade 1018 (0.18 wt% C), useful for general application and good for welding; grade 1030 (0.30 wt% C), which has low hardenability; grade 1045 (0.45 wt% C), which has applications in power transmission and shafting; and X-65, which is a seamless grade and weldable ([Dwivedi et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2020](#bibr50-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Carbon steel corrosion: a review of key surface properties and characterization methods")). An economic study has shown that internal coating on pipelines or other structures is more cost effective than that of bare carbon steel plus inhibitors, ([Radhamani et al., 2020](#bibr185-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Nanocomposite coatings on steel for enhancing the corrosion resistance: A review")). In a marine environment, steel corrosion is influenced by parameters such as salinity (concentration of dissolved salt), alkalinity (concentration of hydrogen ions) and hardness of sea water, ([Radhamani et al., 2020](#bibr185-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Nanocomposite coatings on steel for enhancing the corrosion resistance: A review")). Steel corrosion of is basically an electrochemical reaction which occurs in the presence of water, O2, and ions such as C−or F− ions, ([Bertolini et al., 2004; Horwood](#bibr30-j.arabjc.2021.103100)). In corrosion, electrons get transferred from metals with greater negative potential and the corrosion occurs at the point from where the electrons leave, ([Radhamani et al., 2020](#bibr185-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Nanocomposite coatings on steel for enhancing the corrosion resistance: A review")). Nano structured hydrophobic and super-hydrophobic coating of primers were explored to prevent steel corrosion, ([Morton et al., 2018; Xiang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2016](#bibr150-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Volumetric superhydrophobic coatings for offshore corrosion protection")). ([Ershad-Langroudi et al., 2017; Ledwig & Dubiel, 2017; Mora et al., 2017](#bibr60-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Mechanical properties of sol–gel prepared nanocomposite coatings in the presence of titania and alumina-derived nanoparticles")) found that in a typical nanocomposite coating, specific nanoparticles (NPs) are added to enhance the overall performance.

([Harb et al., 2020; Joshi et al., 2018](#bibr85-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Effective corrosion protection by eco-friendly self-healing PMMA-cerium oxide coatings")) used organic polymer coating or paints with epoxy resins polyurethane (PU) and acrylic are widely used to prevent corrosion. ([Cui et al., 2018; Mai & Yu, 2006; Nguyen-Tri et al., 2018](#bibr40-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Polydimethylsiloxane-titania nanocomposite coating: fabrication and corrosion resistance")) found that pristine polymer alone is insufficient in effectively preventing corrosion. ([Peng et al., 2018; Qu et al., 2013](#bibr175-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Applications of nanotechnology in oil and gas industry: Progress and perspective")) described many science disciplines influenced by nanotechnology. ([Alam et al., 2018](#bibr10-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Polymer composite hydrogels containing carbon nanomaterials—Morphology and mechanical and functional performance"); and [Guan et al., 2018](#bibr75-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Three-dimensional graphene-based polymer nanocomposites: preparation, properties and applications")) have found that organic/inorganic fillers have become prominent. ([Radhamani et al., 2020](#bibr185-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Nanocomposite coatings on steel for enhancing the corrosion resistance: A review")) showed that fillers size, shape, morphology and the weight percent greatly influence the intrinsic properties of composites. ([Morton et al., 2018; Xiang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2016](#bibr150-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Volumetric superhydrophobic coatings for offshore corrosion protection")) used nanostructured hydrophobic and super-hydrophobic coating to prevent steel corrosion and ([Radhamani et al., 2020](#bibr185-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Nanocomposite coatings on steel for enhancing the corrosion resistance: A review")) found that specific nanoparticles (NPs) must be added to enhance the overall performance of the nanocomposite coating.

([Jagtap et al., 2018](#bibr110-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Functionalized carbon nanotube reinforced polymer nanocomposite microcapsules with enhanced stiffness")) improved nanocomposites thermal resistance, corrosion resistance and mechanical properties with both a high surface area and van der Waals’ force of attraction. ([Ramezanzadeh et al., 2016](#bibr190-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Enhancement of barrier and corrosion protection performance of an epoxy coating through wet transfer of amino functionalized graphene oxide")) concluded that hybrid coatings have the potential to open up a new scope especially in epoxy-based coatings. ([Deyab, 2015](#bibr45-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Effect of carbon nano-tubes on the corrosion resistance of alkyd coating immersed in sodium chloride solution")) discussed the problems of the coating permeability and weak adhesion. ([Sanchez et al., 2011](#bibr195-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Applications of advanced hybrid organic–inorganic nanomaterials: from laboratory to market")) explored the combination of organic and inorganic coating is getting explored to make use of both their properties. ([Elmorsi & Hassanein, 1999; Nagiub et al., 2013; Yusoff et al., 2020](#bibr55-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Corrosion inhibition of copper by heterocyclic compounds")) have shown that the organic inhibition of the corrosion by dyes is mainly attributed to the formation of complex compounds between the metal-ions and the dye at the electrode surface. Their adsorption characteristics depend on several factors including the nature and number of potential adsorption sites present in the dye molecule. But, ([Oguzie et al., 2006](#bibr165-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Corrosion inhibition and adsorption behaviour of bismark brown dye on aluminium in sodium hydroxide solution")) found that adsorption of such dyes on the metal surface can distinctly alter the corrosion susceptibility, thus elucidation of the correlation between inhibitor adsorption and corrosion resistance is of immense importance.

([Ye et al., 2020](#bibr240-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "A high-efficiency corrosion inhibitor of N-doped citric acid-based carbon dots for mild steel in hydrochloric acid environment")) showed that the inhibition efficiency of three carbon dots exceeded 90% at 200 mg/L and the highest inhibitive efficiency was found for the carbon dots prepared at the reaction time of 2 h and ([Ye et al., 2020](#bibr240-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "A high-efficiency corrosion inhibitor of N-doped citric acid-based carbon dots for mild steel in hydrochloric acid environment")) found that the inhibition efficiency of carbon steel reached up to 93.93% (1 M HCl) and 88.96% (3.5 wt% NaCl) at 200 mg/L of N-CDs. ([Aslam et al., 2020](#bibr20-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Gravimetric, electrochemical, and morphological studies of an isoxazole derivative as corrosion inhibitor for mild steel in 1M HCl")) found that The inhibition efficiency of IOD for mild steel in 1 M HCl was increased by rising its concentration attaining maximum value (96.6%) at 300 ppm at 30 °C and decreases with increasing temperature from 30 °C to 60 °C. ([Ahmaeed et al., 2019](#bibr5-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Corrosion inhibition effect of sodium iodide for mild steel in 1 m hydrochloric acid: gravimetrical and electrochemical studies")) found that sodium iodide (NaI) Maximum inhibition efficiency was 96.1% at a higher level of inhibitor concentration, time and temperature in mild steel and 1 M HCl. ([Hu et al., (2017)](#bibr100-j.arabjc.2021.103100) concluded that the macromolecule DNA protected carbon steel against 1 M HCl solution with the maximum inhibition efficiency reached 91.9%. ([Haque et al., 2017](#bibr80-j.arabjc.2021.103100)) evaluated Aliquat 336 as a green and novel corrosion inhibitor for mild steel in a 1 M HCl solution with maximum inhibition efficiency of 94.6% at a very low concentration of 4.95 μM. ([Srivastava et al., 2017](#bibr205-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Amino acid based imidazolium zwitterions as novel and green corrosion inhibitors for mild steel: Experimental, DFT and MD studies")) presented AIZ-3 inhibitor with maximum inhibition efficiency (IE) of 96.08% at a concentration as low as 0.55 mM (200 ppm) in 1 M HCl.

This investigative study was aimed at analyzing the effectiveness of a corrosion resistant coating composed of iron (III) nanoparticles and nanocomposite. To characterize the combination, both TGA and DSC methods were used. The carbon steel was coated with the combination. Coating characterization was done using SEM, XRD, EDX and FT-IR. The effect of the coating on the hydrochloric acid, MG, MB and formation water corrosion is discussed using Tafel and cyclic voltammetry methods.

## ***2*** Experiment

2.1

### ***2.1*** Chemicals/Materials

98% FeSO4·7H2O (RFM 151.91), HCl, NaOH, CH3OH (methanol), C2H5OH (ethanol), C2H4 (ethene), dimethylcrylate (EDMA, 98%), sodium alignate, NaNO3 (RFM 84.99), potassium peroxydisulfate (RFM 270.31), Butyl methacrylate (BMA, 99%), formation water. Carbon steel working electrode (WE) of surface area 1 cm2 containing 99.12% iron and the rest is carbon (0.06%), silicon (0.06%), manganese (0.005%), phosphorus (0.001%), sulphur (0.012%), nickel (0.015%), chromium (0.004%), molybdenum (0.002%), vanadium (0.02%) and copper (0.02%). Platinum and calomel are used as counter electrode (CE) and reference electrode (RE) respectively. Stock solutions were prepared by dissolving suitable quantities of dyes in distilled water.

2.2

### ***2.2*** Instruments

JEOL JSM 6390 Scanning electron microscope, D8-advance CuKá1-radiation diffractometer and pH meter are used. PerkinElmer RX FT-IR X2 used to provide FT-IR spectra (collected in ATR mode). Thermo Gravimetric Analysis (TGA) Mettler. Magnetic stirrer, an oven and a blast furnace. EZstat Propotentiostat (from NuVant Systems Inc. manufacturer, USA).

2.3

### ***2.3*** Synthesis of Fe3O4 and PBMA-gft-Alg/Fe3O4

Fe3O4 was prepared as described earlier ([Alzahrani et al., 2020](#bibr15-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Poly (butyl methacrylate)-grafted alginate/Fe3O4 nanocomposite: Synthesis and its application for removal of dyes")). To obtain Fe3O4 NPs, 3.3 g of iron (II) sulphate heptahydrate. was mixed with 2 g of sodium nitrate, dissolving the mixture in 50 cm3 of distilled water then mixing the solution obtained with 20 cm3 of 2.5 M NaOH solution. The mixture was then heated to 80 °C while stirring constantly to ensure growth of the nanoparticle crystals. The reaction was allowed to proceed for 30 min before being cooled. The suspension formed was filtered and washed in distilled water to remove any unreacted chemicals. The Fe3O4 NPs, being magnetic, were separated from this mixture by use of a magnet before being dried overnight in an oven maintained at 50 °C before the coating process.

The nanocomposite were prepared as described in our previous work ([Alzahrani et al., 2020](#bibr15-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Poly (butyl methacrylate)-grafted alginate/Fe3O4 nanocomposite: Synthesis and its application for removal of dyes")). First, Ig of the Fe3O4 NPs prepared from the previous procedure was placed in 100 mL of de-ionized water and dispersed by use of a sonicator for a period of 30 min. This was followed by addition of alignate made by dissolving 2 g of the alignate in 200 mL of de-ionized water at 40 °C. 0.75 g of EDMA was mixed with 20 mL of BMA monomer at 60 °C and stirred continuously for 1hr. This was followed by addition of the Fe3O4 NPs dispersion, and 20 cm3 of KPS (with 3% concentration) solution acting as initiator. The reaction was left to proceed for further 6hrs at 60 °C to form a nanocomposite which is then mixed with excess methyl alcohol in order to stop any further polymerization. The resulting product is filtered and washed thoruoghly in distilled water followed by drying in an oven at 60 °C for 2 hrs. The resultant product is ground and sieved to obtain final product.

2.4

### ***2.4*** Measurement of corrosion resistance

To measure corrosion performance, carbon steel sealed with epoxy resin was used as a working electrode. Only the sealed area was exposed to the hydrochloric acid electrolyte. Concentration of the acid and temperature were varied at (0.001, 0.005, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1 and 0.5 M) and (25, 50, 75 and 100 °C) respectively while time was varied at (0, 15, 30, 45 and 60 min) to study the extent of corrosion. Before measurements, the electrodes were ground down to 300, 400, 600, 800, 1200 and 2000 using a series of emery papers, washed in distilled water and dried using ethanol. A potentioscan was used to draw the potentiodynamic current–potential curves. The curves obtained by linear change from − 0.6 V (stating potential) upwards in reference to SCE but within 20 mVs−1 (the required scan rate), to the end of experiment ([Keera & Deyab, 2005; Ye et al., 2021](#bibr120-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Effect of some organic surfactants on the electrochemical behaviour of carbon steel in formation water")).

The nanoparticle and nanocomposite (Fe3O4 NPs and PBMA-gft-Alg/Fe3O4) materials were coated on the carbon steel by dipping the carbon steel electrodes in molten forms of the materials (hot-dip method). The effect of varying temperatures (100, 150, 200 and 250 °C) and time (1, 2 and 3 hrs) were studied at optimum temperature of 150 °C. Characterization of the coating was achieved using FT-IR, cyclic voltammetry, EDX, X-ray diffraction, SEM, and Tafel polarization.

2.5

### ***2.5*** Assessment using formation water/dyes

Analysis of the formation water in the first test was done using the ion chromatography equipment and its chemical composition; 67,675Na+, 127 K+, 7708 Ca+2, 2449 Mg+2, 132,118Cl−, 370 SO4−2, 568 Br−, 11.8 SiO4−2 and 6.7 pH. Test solution 2 was dyes carried out on MG/MB at pH = 10. The tests used the carbon steel coated with the nanocomposite at optimum conditions. Measurement was done at high corrosive condition.

## ***3*** Results and discussions

3.1

### ***3.1*** Characterization of the materials

[Fig. 1](#fig5-j.arabjc.2021.103100) illustrates TGA curves representing Fe3O4 NPs weight loss as a result of residual water loss over temperature range between 50 °C and 650 °C in agreement with ([Hussein-Al-Ali et al., 2014](#bibr95-j.arabjc.2021.103100)). According to the TGA thermogram, the alignate had a rapid weight loss at 230 °C with rate decrement at 271 °C which became constant at 350 °C. At 510 °C the alignate became at stable state continously. The weight decrease from 230 °C to 350 °C indicated the alignate decomposition within this range of temperatures. Above 350 °C, the weight loss decreased due to the PBMA (poly Butyl methacrylate) decomposition in agreement with ([Yao et al., 2010](#bibr230-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Hydrophobic modification of sodium alginate and its application in drug controlled release")).

![TGA thermograms of Fe3O4 NPs and PBMA-gft-Alg.](/content/184/2021/14/5/img/10.1016_j.arabjc.2021.103100-fig1.png)

![]()

***Fig. 1***  TGA thermograms of Fe3O4 NPs and PBMA-gft-Alg.

[Fig. 2](#fig10-j.arabjc.2021.103100) illustrates an analysis of (Fe3O4 NPs and PBMA-gft-Alg/Fe3O4 repectively) using differential scanning calorimetry. Due to the solvent molecule elimination, the nanoparticles of Fe3O4 have a strong endothermic peak at 60 °C. Crystallization of the magnetite is responsible for the endothermic transition at 210 °C. The nano composite (PBMA-gft-Alg/Fe3O4) has even higher endothermic peak of about 115 °C.

![DSC thermograms of Fe3O4 NPs and PBMA-gft-Alg/Fe3O4.](/content/184/2021/14/5/img/10.1016_j.arabjc.2021.103100-fig2.png)

![]()

***Fig. 2***  DSC thermograms of Fe3O4 NPs and PBMA-gft-Alg/Fe3O4.

Exothermic peaks observed at 140 °C and 190 °C due to crystallization and rearrangement of the molecules. This temperature range allowed crystallization of the powder as it allows the Fe3O4 NPs to interact strongly with the PBMA-gft-Alg/Fe3O4 nano composite. Secondly, the temperature rise resulted from the re-arranging of alignate and PBMA(poly Butyl methacrylate) groups themselves. These observations largely agree with the thermogravimetric analysis ([Sneha & Sundaram, 2015](#bibr200-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Preparation and characterization of an iron oxide-hydroxyapatite nanocomposite for potential bone cancer therapy")).

#### ***3.2.2*** Effect of temperature

#### ***3.2.3*** Effect of time

#### ***3.3.7*** Effect of time

The PBMA-gft-Alg/Fe3O4 2θ Peak values observed at 17° due to the presence of amorphous PBMA. The results indicate that PBMA-gft-Alg/Fe3O4 successfully synthesized as indicated in [Fig. 14](#fig70-j.arabjc.2021.103100) ([Bashtani et al., 2018](#bibr25-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "A nanocomposite consisting of poly (methyl methacrylate), graphene oxide and Fe 3 O 4 nanoparticles as a sorbent for magnetic solid-phase extraction of aromatic amines")).
