##### ***3.3.7.5*** The potentiodynamic polarization curves

[Fig. 15](#fig75-j.arabjc.2021.103100) illustrated pre and post coating at (150 °C and 1hr, 2 hrs., 3 hrs.) with the nanocomposite and nanoparticles at zero time, acid molarity of 0.5. [Table 3](#table15-j.arabjc.2021.103100) showed the values of *E*corr, *i*corr, cathodic and anodic Tafel calculated from the curves. The curves representing that coated surfaces shift to lower current densities with greater negative potential values. The nanoparticles curve produced a lower effect compared to other coatings. [Table 3](#table15-j.arabjc.2021.103100) indicated the measured corrosion parameters curves. The data showed that the corrosion potentials and current densities inversely proportional. Also, the cathodic Tafel and polarization decreased after coating. This due to the polarization concentration reduction that reduced the metals dissolution and the electron production necessary to reduce cathodic reaction. This situation causes a buildup of O2 at the cathode leading to polarization concentration. [Fig. 15](#fig75-j.arabjc.2021.103100)b and [Table 3](#table15-j.arabjc.2021.103100), illustrated that the nanoparticles coating slope at (150 °C, and 2hrs.) is higher that related to highest polarization and corrosion resistance. [Fig. 15](#fig75-j.arabjc.2021.103100)d and [Table 3](#table15-j.arabjc.2021.103100), indicated the coating cycle slope obtained using PBMA-gft-Alg/Fe3O4 at temperature of 150 °C, and 2 hrs. is greater due to the greatest polarization and corrosion resistance ([Ibrahim & Bakdash, 2014](#bibr105-j.arabjc.2021.103100 "Zinc coatings of high hardness on steel by electrodeposition from glutamate complex baths")).

4

## ***4*** Conclusions

1. Corrosion rate largely depended on the hydrochloric acid concentration and temperature.
2. Corrosion rate directly proportional to acid concentration and temperature.
3. Coating carbon steel by the HCl reduced corrosion.
4. PBMA-gft-Alg/Fe3O4 have superior coating quality compared to Fe3O4 NPs, and MG/MB respectively.
5. Electrochemical studies showed that both PBMA-gft-Alg/Fe3O4 and Fe3O4 NPs have good inhibiting properties for steel corrosion.
6. PBMA-gft-Alg/Fe3O4 is more effective in coating compared to the Fe3O4 NPs.
7. PBMA-gft-Alg/Fe3O4 have 99.9% corrosion resistance within the formation water corrosive medium.
8. PBMA-gft-Alg/Fe3O4 have 99.9% corrosion resistance within the MG and MB corrosive medium.

This is a scientific research article published in the Arabian Journal of Chemistry (2021, Volume 14, Issue 5, DOI: 10.1016/j.arabjc.2021.103100) by Eman Alzahrani, Hala M. Abo-Dief, and Faouzia Algethami from the Department of Chemistry, College of Science, Taif University, Taif, Saudi Arabia. The article was originally published by Elsevier and migrated to Scientific Scholar.

STUDY OBJECTIVE: The study analyzed the performance of a corrosion-resistant coating for carbon steel made from tri-iron tetraoxide (Fe3O4) nanoparticles and a Poly (butyl methacrylate)-grafted alginate/Fe3O4 (PBMA-gft-Alg/Fe3O4) nanocomposite.

KEY FINDINGS:
- Corrosion rate of carbon steel increased with increasing HCl molarity (0.001-0.5 M) and temperature (25-100°C), but was inversely proportional to immersion time (0-60 min).
- The corrosion-resistant coating was applied using the hot-dip coating method.
- Optimum coating conditions were 150°C with 2 hours immersion time.
- The PBMA-gft-Alg/Fe3O4 nanocomposite was significantly more effective than Fe3O4 NPs alone.

CHARACTERIZATION METHODS: TGA and DSC for material characterization; SEM, EDX, FT-IR, and XRD for coating characterization; Tafel polarization and cyclic voltammetry for electrochemical studies.

COATING EFFICIENCY DATA (Table 2 - temperature effect at high corrosive conditions):
- Fe3O4 NPs: best efficiency at 150°C (86.7% inhibition efficiency)
- PBMA-gft-Alg/Fe3O4: best efficiency at 150°C (91.0% inhibition efficiency)

COATING EFFICIENCY DATA (Table 3 - time effect at 150°C):
- Fe3O4 NPs: 2 hrs = 98.5% IE, 3 hrs = 97.8% IE
- PBMA-gft-Alg/Fe3O4: 2 hrs = 98.6% IE, 3 hrs = 97.9% IE

CORROSION RESISTANCE IN DIFFERENT MEDIA (Table 4 - PBMA-gft-Alg/Fe3O4 coated, 150°C, 2 hrs):
- In HCl: 98.6% inhibition efficiency
- In formation water: 99.2% inhibition efficiency
- In malachite green (MG): 99.8% inhibition efficiency
- In methylene blue (MB): 99.9% inhibition efficiency

SYNTHESIS METHOD: Fe3O4 NPs were prepared by mixing 3.3g iron(II) sulphate heptahydrate with 2g sodium nitrate in 50cm3 distilled water, adding 20cm3 of 2.5M NaOH, heating to 80°C for 30 min. The nanocomposite was prepared by dispersing 1g Fe3O4 NPs in de-ionized water, adding alginate (2g in 200mL water at 40°C), EDMA (0.75g) with 20mL BMA monomer at 60°C, then KPS initiator (3%), reacting for 6 hours at 60°C.

CARBON STEEL COMPOSITION: 99.12% iron with carbon (0.06%), silicon (0.06%), manganese (0.005%), phosphorus (0.001%), sulphur (0.012%), nickel (0.015%), chromium (0.004%), molybdenum (0.002%), vanadium (0.02%), and copper (0.02%).

CHARACTERIZATION RESULTS:
- XRD confirmed pure cubic spinel structure of Fe3O4 NPs with peaks at 2θ = 30.35, 35.68, 43.35, 54.70, 57.29, 62.82, and 74.30.
- FT-IR showed Fe-O bond in Fe3O4 at 553 cm⁻¹, acrylate carboxyl group at 1,730 cm⁻¹, C-H stretching at 2,985 and 2,937 cm⁻¹.
- TGA showed alginate decomposition at 230-350°C and PBMA decomposition above 350°C.
- Formation water composition: 67,675 Na+, 127 K+, 7,708 Ca+2, 2,449 Mg+2, 132,118 Cl-, 370 SO4-2, 568 Br-, 11.8 SiO4-2, pH 6.7.

CONCLUSIONS: (1) Corrosion rate directly proportional to acid concentration and temperature; (2) coating carbon steel reduced corrosion; (3) PBMA-gft-Alg/Fe3O4 has superior coating quality compared to Fe3O4 NPs; (4) both materials show good corrosion inhibition; (5) PBMA-gft-Alg/Fe3O4 achieved up to 99.9% corrosion resistance in formation water, MG, and MB corrosive media.

The research was supported by Taif University Researchers Supporting Project number TURSP-2020/136. The authors declared no competing financial interests. No animals or humans were used in the study.

--- SOURCE 1: Combined Electrochemical, Raman Analysis and Machine Learning Assessments of the Inhibitive Properties of an 1,3,4-Oxadiazole-2-Thiol Derivative against Carbon Steel Corrosion in HCl Solution ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/1996-1944/15/6/2224

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in Materials (MDPI) journal (Materials 2022, 15(6), 2224, DOI: 10.3390/ma15062224) investigating the corrosion inhibition properties of 5-(4-pyridyl)-1,3,4-oxadiazole-2-thiol (PyODT) against carbon steel corrosion in 1.0 M HCl solution. The study was conducted by researchers from the "1 Decembrie 1918" University of Alba Iulia, the National Institute for Research and Development of Isotopic and Molecular Technologies (Cluj-Napoca), and the Technical University of Cluj-Napoca, Romania. The article was submitted December 31, 2021, revised March 10, 2022, accepted March 14, 2022, and published March 17, 2022.

Key findings and methods:
- Electrochemical methods (potentiodynamic polarization and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, EIS), Raman spectroscopy, SEM-EDX analysis, and machine learning algorithms were used to evaluate PyODT as a corrosion inhibitor.
- PyODT behaves as a mixed-type corrosion inhibitor, reaching an efficiency of about 93.1% at 5 mM concentration after 1 hour exposure to 1.0 M HCl solution. The optimum inhibitor concentration was determined to be 5 mM.
- Higher inhibitive effectiveness of approximately 97% was achieved at 24 hours immersion due to molecular adsorption and structural organization of PyODT molecules on the C-steel surface.
- Polarization measurements showed the highest inhibiting efficiency of 91.2% at 5 mM PyODT; corrosion potential shifts were less than ±85 mV, confirming mixed-type inhibition behavior.
- EIS results showed inhibition efficiencies of about 95.9% and 97.1% after 12 h and 24 h immersion, respectively, at 5 mM PyODT concentration.
- The adsorption of PyODT followed the Langmuir adsorption isotherm with an equilibrium constant K = 1.18 × 10^5 M^-1 and standard free energy of adsorption of −38.9 kJ mol^-1, indicating both physical and chemical adsorption mechanisms (physisorption and chemisorption).
- SEM-EDX analysis confirmed significantly reduced degradation of the carbon steel surface in the presence of PyODT, with N and S atoms detected in EDX spectra confirming inhibitor adsorption.
- A combination of Raman spectroscopy and machine learning algorithms (including decision trees, discriminant analysis, support vector machines, KNN, and ensemble classifiers) was demonstrated as a facile and reliable tool for early/incipient identification of corrosion sites on metallic surfaces exposed to corrosive environments.
- The study is novel in applying the Raman + machine learning approach to metallic alloys exposed to highly corrosive environments.
- The research addresses the need for environmentally friendly corrosion inhibitors, as traditional inorganic inhibitors (phosphates, chromates, vanadates) are toxic or environmentally non-compliant. 1,3,4-oxadiazole derivatives are highlighted as low-toxicity, effective organic inhibitors for steel corrosion in acidic media.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The electrochemical measurements revealed that PyODT behaves as a mixed-type corrosion inhibitor, reaching an efficiency of about 93.1% at a concentration of 5 mM, after 1 h exposure to 1.0 M HCl solution."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Combined Electrochemical, Raman Analysis and Machine Learning Assessments of the Inhibitive Properties of an 1,3,4-Oxadiazole-2-Thiol Derivative against Carbon Steel Corrosion in HCl Solution - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8950990

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in the MDPI journal "Materials" (March 2022, collection date) investigating the corrosion-inhibiting properties of 5-(4-pyridyl)-1,3,4-oxadiazole-2-thiol (PyODT) on carbon steel in 1.0 M HCl solution. The authors are Simona Varvara, Camelia Berghian-Grosan, Gianina Damian, Maria Popa, and Florin Popa.

**Study Purpose:** To investigate, for the first time, PyODT as an effective corrosion inhibitor for carbon steel in HCl solution, combining electrochemical analysis, Raman spectroscopy, and machine learning algorithms for early identification of corrosion sites.

**Methods Used:**
- Potentiodynamic polarization and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) in a three-electrode cell configuration
- SEM-EDX surface analysis
- Raman spectroscopy (JASCO NRS-3300, 785 nm laser excitation)
- Machine learning algorithms (decision trees, discriminant analysis, SVM, KNN, ensemble classifiers) applied to Raman data using MATLAB Classification Learner app
- Adsorption isotherm analysis (Langmuir, Temkin, Frumkin)

**Key Results:**
- PyODT acts as a mixed-type corrosion inhibitor with ~93.1% efficiency at 5 mM concentration after 1 hour exposure
- Higher efficiency of ~97% was achieved after 24 hours immersion due to molecular adsorption and structural organization of PyODT on the C-steel surface
- The optimum inhibitor concentration was determined to be 5 mM (from polarization: 91.2% IE; from EIS: 93.1% IE)
- Langmuir adsorption isotherm best described the adsorption behavior with K = 1.18 × 10^5 M⁻¹ and ΔG°ads = −38.9 kJ/mol, indicating a combination of physisorption and chemisorption
- EIS data showed polarization resistance (Rp) values increased with inhibitor concentration up to 5 mM (337.5 Ω·cm² vs. 23.2 Ω·cm² for blank), with inhibition efficiencies reaching ~95.9% at 12 h and ~97.1% at 24 h immersion
- SEM-EDX analysis confirmed significantly reduced surface degradation in the presence of PyODT, with N and S atoms detected in EDX spectra, indicating inhibitor adsorption; oxygen was absent in the surface film after 1 h in the inhibited solution, showing rapid barrier film formation
- Raman spectroscopy combined with machine learning proved to be a facile and reliable tool for incipient identification of corrosion sites on metallic surfaces

**Materials:**
- C-steel composition (wt%): Mn 0.6%, C 0.32%, Si 0.04%, S 0.029%, P 0.01%, balance Fe
- PyODT purchased from Alfa Aesar (97% purity)
- Test solutions prepared with 1.0 M HCl and ethanol (90:10 v/v)
- PyODT concentrations tested: 0.1 to 10 mM
- Training dataset for ML contained 47 Raman spectra across 6 classes; testing dataset contained 27 points

**Significance:** The study demonstrates that the combination of Raman spectroscopy (a non-destructive technique) with machine learning algorithms offers a promising approach for rapid, early identification of corrosion damage on metallic surfaces, particularly useful for monitoring applications where handheld/mobile Raman spectrometers can be deployed.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The electrochemical measurements revealed that PyODT behaves as a mixed-type corrosion inhibitor, reaching an efficiency of about 93.1% at a concentration of 5 mM, after 1 h exposure to 1.0 M HCl solution. Due to the molecular adsorption and structural organization of PyODT molecules on the C-steel surface, higher inhibitive effectiveness of about 97% was obtained at 24 h immersion."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Vibrational Spectroscopy in Studies of Atmospheric Corrosion ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/1996-1944/10/4/413

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article titled "Vibrational Spectroscopy in Studies of Atmospheric Corrosion" by Saman Hosseinpour (Max Planck Institute for Polymer Research, Mainz, Germany; current address: FAU Erlangen-Nürnberg) and Magnus Johnson (KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, Sweden). Published in the journal Materials, Volume 10, Issue 4, Article 413 on April 18, 2017 (DOI: 10.3390/ma10040413). The article belongs to the Special Issue "Fundamental and Research Frontier of Atmospheric Corrosion."

The review summarizes decades of work using vibrational spectroscopy—primarily infrared (IR) spectroscopy, Raman spectroscopy, and vibrational sum frequency spectroscopy (VSFS/SFG)—to identify and quantify atmospheric corrosion products. Key points covered:

1. **Technique Comparison**: IR and Raman spectroscopy have complementary strengths. Raman covers ~100–4000 cm⁻¹ while IR typically reaches down to ~600 cm⁻¹ (MCT detector cutoff) though DTGS detectors allow ~80 cm⁻¹. Confocal Raman microscopy offers spatial resolution of hundreds of nm vs ~5 μm for conventional IR microscopy, but novel nano-FTIR microscopy achieves 20 nm spatial resolution. IR absorbance is directly proportional to corrosion product amount (quantitative), whereas Raman is more qualitative. IRRAS requires no sample preparation and enables in-situ real-time measurements.

2. **IR Transmission Spectroscopy**: Used to identify FeOOH phases on steel (β-FeOOH at 450, 690, 840 cm⁻¹; γ-FeOOH at 1020 cm⁻¹; δ-FeOOH at 790, 880, 1110 cm⁻¹). Studies covered carbon steel near Qinghai salt lake (China), tropical marine climate in Panama, and pre-corroded steel in China. For copper, Cu2O was the main product in Ibero-America exposures. For aluminum alloy AA2024 and magnesium alloy AZ91D, corrosion products like [Mg1-xAlx(OH)2]x+Cl-x·mH2O, Mg(OH)2, MgCO3, and Mg2Al2(SO4)5·39H2O were identified.

3. **DRIFTS**: Applied to nickel exposed at 39 European and North American test sites, identifying sulfates, water, and hydroxides. Two sample types distinguished—non-crystalline with lower protective ability vs. more resistant, disordered products formed at longer exposures.

4. **IRRAS** (most frequently used technique): 
   - Iron: Studies by Weissenrider et al. on SO2/NO2/O3-induced corrosion; Kotenev et al. identified Fe3O4 (412 cm⁻¹), α-Fe2O3 (555, 602 cm⁻¹), and γ-Fe2O3 (652 cm⁻¹) initially, with α-Fe2O3 dominating after longer oxidation.
   - Steel: Person et al. studied Zn-Al-Mg coated, electrogalvanized, and hot-dipped galvanized steel with NaCl deposits at 80% RH and 350 ppm CO2; Kim et al. studied silane/epoxy protection of steel.
   - Copper: Extensive studies by Person et al., Kleber et al., Aastrup et al., Wadsak et al., and Gil et al. combining IRRAS with QCM and cathodic reduction. Cuprite (Cu2O) formation at ~645 cm⁻¹ follows logarithmic growth kinetics. Gil et al. demonstrated linear correlation between IRRAS absorbance, QCM mass, and cathodic reduction thickness for Cu2O under 90% RH with carboxylic acids. Field studies at Royal Palace (Stockholm), St. Vitus Cathedral (Prague), and indoor locations revealed carboxylates (formate, acetate) as main corrosion products on zinc, copper, and nickel, while silver sulfide dominated on silver.
   - Silver: PM-IRRAS proved superior to conventional IRRAS for detecting thin corrosion layers. UV light significantly enhanced basic silver carbonate (AgOHAg2CO3) formation on silver under CO2 exposure.

5. **Corrosion Inhibitors**: IRRAS characterized ultrathin organic films including fluoro-thiol SAMs on copper, benzotriazole on copper, imidazoles, and silane-based films for corrosion protection.

6. **Key advantages**: In-situ real-time measurements allow studying corrosion kinetics and minimize surface property changes that can occur in ex-situ experiments. Combining complementary techniques (SEM, XPS, QCM, cathodic reduction, AFM) provides multi-faceted understanding. Novel nano-FTIR microscopy enables corrosion studies at 20 nm spatial resolution, crucial since corrosion often occurs heterogeneously on surfaces at the nanoscale.

The article concludes that depending on the specific system, the most favorable vibrational spectroscopy technique should be chosen, and often combining IR and Raman provides complementary information.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Some of these techniques offer the valuable possibility to perform in-situ measurements in real time on ongoing corrosion processes, which allows the kinetics of formation of corrosion products to be studied, and also minimizes the risk of changing the surface properties which may occur during ex-situ experiments."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Qualitative and quantitative detection of corrosion inhibitors using surface-enhanced Raman scattering coupled with multivariate analysis ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0169433221020262

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a research article published in Applied Surface Science (Volume 568, December 1, 2021, Article 150967) by Yajie Wang, Jinke Wang, Lingwei Ma, Chenhao Ren, Dawei Zhang, Li Ma, and Mingxian Sun, describing a novel strategy for the on-site qualitative and quantitative detection of corrosion inhibitors using surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) coupled with partial least squares regression (PLSR).

The study focuses on the detection of 2-mercaptobenzothiazole (MBT) corrosion inhibitors adsorbed on AA2024 aluminium alloy surfaces. Key methodology elements include:
- Use of a transparent SERS tape (containing silver nanorods/AgNRs) as a Raman signal amplifier to enable detection on normally SERS-inactive engineering metal surfaces like aluminium alloys.
- MBT solutions prepared in 3.5 wt% NaCl at concentrations of 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, and 0.4 g/L.
- AA2024 alloys with compositions including Cu 3.94 wt%, Mg 1.46 wt%, Mn 0.85 wt%, Fe 0.45 wt%, Zn 0.10 wt%, Cr 0.05 wt%, Si 0.05 wt%, and Al balance, polished with 400-2000 grit sandpapers.
- PLSR algorithm used to establish regression relationships between SERS spectra and MBT concentrations, showing good predictive ability.

Key findings: SERS intensities grew monotonously with increasing inhibitor concentration and immersion time, indicating continuous accumulation of MBT molecules that facilitated effective corrosion inhibition. The established PLSR model successfully predicted MBT concentration on metal surfaces, including during reversible desorption processes. The regression relationship between SERS spectra (0.1-0.4 g/L MBT on AA2024) and concentrations showed satisfactory prediction performance.

The article highlights that this is the first reported quantitative analysis of corrosion inhibitors based on SERS sensing. Prior work using SERS for inhibitor monitoring focused on plasmonic materials (Ag, Au, Cu) and primarily on qualitative characterization. The combination of SERS with multivariate analysis (PLSR) offers a promising approach for sensitively detecting, quantifying, and predicting corrosion inhibitors, which helps in understanding corrosion inhibition mechanisms and promoting development of new corrosion inhibitors.

The study was funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (No. 51901015) and the Research Fund of State Key Laboratory for Marine Corrosion and Protection, Luoyang Ship Material Research Institute (LSMRI) under contract No. KFJS1902. The article has been cited by 35 subsequent publications, including work on carbon dots-based corrosion inhibitors, active corrosion protection coatings, and smart self-healing/self-reporting coatings.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In this study, a novel strategy was proposed for the on-site detection and quantitation of corrosion inhibitors by means of surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) detection and partial least squares regression (PLSR) algorithm."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Emerging surface characterization techniques for carbon steel corrosion: a critical brief review - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5378249

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific review article published in the Proceedings of the Royal Society A on March 8, 2017 (doi: 10.1098/rspa.2016.0852), authored by D Dwivedi, K Lepkova (corresponding author, k.lepkova@curtin.edu.au), and T Becker from Curtin University's Department of Chemical Engineering (Curtin Corrosion Engineering Industry Centre) and Nanochemistry Research Institute in Western Australia. The review identifies emerging surface analytical techniques suitable for analyzing thin films on metallic substrates but not yet widely applied to carbon steel corrosion or corrosion inhibitor studies.

The paper reviews ten emerging analytical techniques for carbon steel corrosion characterization:

1. **Time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (ToF-SIMS)**: A modified SIMS technique allowing capture of entire mass spectra with a single pulse, high sensitivity, and minimal sample damage. Used to study corrosion inhibitor films (e.g., quaternary ammonium compounds on iron), depth profiling of coatings (Al2O3, Ta2O5 on steel), atmospheric corrosion of Mg alloys, and biofilm corrosion. Advantages include molecular specificity, detection of almost all elements (including hydrogen for embrittlement studies), and 3D imaging capability. Limitations include complex spectra interpretation, ultra-high vacuum requirements, and surface damage in dynamic mode.

2. **X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS)**: Includes XANES and EXAFS techniques. EXAFS examines corrosion products and determines structure/bond strength; XANES provides cluster information. Used to study CO2 corrosion phases (Fe2(OH)2CO3, Fe2O2(CO3), Fe6(OH)12(CO3)), nuclear waste interactions (Tc and Re oxidation states), and in situ corrosion monitoring. Major limitation is difficulty conducting in situ studies due to high X-ray beam energy.

3. **Rutherford backscattering spectroscopy (RBS)**: Measures film thickness and provides compositional/depth profiling through energy loss of ion beams. Used to study oxide layers on iron, uranium incorporation in carbon steel corrosion layers, cerium inhibitor films, and TaN anti-corrosive coatings. Quantitative method requiring no standards but needing an expensive accelerator and smooth, thin samples.

4. **Auger electron spectroscopy (AES)**: Provides elemental and chemical state information up to ~5 nm depth, typically combined with ion milling for depth profiling. Used for studying corrosion inhibitor adsorption (triazoles, thiosemicarbazide, macrocyclic compounds), oxide film formation, grain boundary segregation, and molybdite solution polarization effects on carbon steel.

5. **Particle-induced X-ray emission (PIXE)**: Non-destructive ion beam technique detecting elements at ppm levels (Z = 11-92). Used for volatile corrosion inhibitor analysis in polymer films, elemental mapping of corroded carbon steel, and chromate depletion zone studies in protective paints.

6. **Electron probe microanalysis (EPMA)**: Micro-beam non-destructive technique for quantitative elemental analysis at 1-2 µm spot sizes. Used for rust analysis, corrosion inhibitor film distribution studies, and anti-corrosive polymer coating investigations. Cannot detect light elements (H, Li, He), limiting analysis of hydrous corrosion products.

7. **Near-edge X-ray absorption fine structure spectroscopy (NEXAFS)**: Studies adsorption processes, bond orientation of adsorbates on substrates, and π-bonding. Successfully used to investigate imidazoline inhibitor adsorption on carbon steel, showing benzene ring orientation flat on surface with C-N group oriented at 30-35°.

8. **X-ray photoemission electron microscopy (XPEEM)**: Provides sub-micrometer imaging (0.5 µm lateral resolution) and can distinguish between Fe3O4 and γ-Fe2O3 (which have identical LEED patterns). Used to study Cr diffusion in stainless steel, work function variations with grain orientation, and phase transformations affecting corrosion potentials.

The review concludes that the combined use of emerging techniques (e.g., XPS-RBS, ToF-SIMS-XPS, NEXAFS, NR) with established methods could provide novel insights into unexplained corrosion processes. Key challenges include the scarcity of literature, expensive equipment requirements, and the need for multi-technique approaches to overcome individual method limitations. The paper emphasizes that hydrophobicity alone does not ensure corrosion prevention—surface texture also plays a critical role—and understanding metal properties' effects on corrosion-protective film formation requires advanced analytical methods.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The general consensus of corrosion inhibition, involving an organic layer that is hydrophobic and thus corrosion-protective to the underlying steel, has been changed with recent evidence showing that hydrophobicity of a surface alone does not ensure the prevention of corrosion, but surface texture also plays a critical role in corrosion of carbon steel."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: A critical review on advanced surface analysis techniques used for studying the adsorption mechanisms of organic corrosion inhibitors ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2667266926000198

SUMMARY:
<summary>

The article is authored by Luntao Wang, Bingxiao Shi, Xin Guo, Xuequn Cheng, Xiaogang Li (all affiliated with an institution) and Philippe Marcus. It is open access under a Creative Commons license (CC BY 4.0) and has a DOI of 10.1016/j.corcom.2026.02.003. The article has been cited 6 times and has 22 figures and 3 tables.

--- SOURCE 7: Organic Compounds as Corrosion Inhibitors for Carbon Steel in HCl Solution: A Comprehensive Review ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8954067

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive scientific review article published in Materials (Basel) on March 9, 2022 (doi: 10.3390/ma15062023), authored by Liangyuan Chen, Dongzhu Lu, and Yanhu Zhang. The paper, "Organic Compounds as Corrosion Inhibitors for Carbon Steel in HCl Solution: A Comprehensive Review," systematically reviews organic corrosion inhibitors for carbon steel in 1.0 M HCl solution systems.

KEY FINDINGS AND CONTENT:

**Background**: Corrosion is a common industrial problem affecting metal cost and safety. Adding corrosion inhibitors is the most economical and commonly used method. Carbon steel corrosion research is most common due to its high strength, low cost, and widespread use. The 1.0 M HCl system is standard because iron oxide reacts over three times faster with HCl than with H2SO4, and corrosion rates in HCl are more than twice that in H2SO4.

**Corrosion Mechanism**: Iron corrosion in HCl involves anodic (oxidative dissolution of Fe) and cathodic (H+ reduction to H2 gas) half-reactions. Key intermediate species include [FeOH]ads and [FeClOH]ads. Iron dissolution in HCl depends more on H+ ions than Cl- ions, though at pH 0.0 to -0.6 it depends principally on chloride ion activity.

**Inhibition Mechanism**: Organic inhibitors form a thin layer on metal surfaces via substitution with water molecules. Two adsorption mechanisms:
- Physisorption: van der Waals/Coulombic forces; forms inner and outer Helmholtz planes via Cl- bridging; loosens with increasing temperature
- Chemisorption: heteroatoms (S, N, P, O) donate lone pairs to Fe d-orbitals; stronger interaction; includes retro-donation mechanism

Electron-releasing substituents (-NH2, -OH, -OCH3, -CH3) make better inhibitors than electron-withdrawing ones (-NO2, -CN, -COOH).

**Evaluation Methods** (with formulas):
1. Weight Loss (WL) - accurate but time-consuming; only for general corrosion
2. Potentiodynamic Polarization (PDP) - uses Tafel extrapolation; Ec corr >85 mV indicates anodic/cathodic type, <85 mV indicates mixed type
3. Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) - nondestructive; analyzes solution resistance (Rs), charge transfer resistance (Rct), double layer capacitance (Cdl)
4. Electrochemical Frequency Modulation (EFM) - nondestructive; gives corrosion current density and causality factors directly
5. Other methods: FTIR peak intensities, Electrochemical Noise (EN), hydrogen evolution measurements, temperature-time curves, CV measurements, PZC measurements, SVET

**Adsorption Isotherms**: Six models evaluated: Langmuir, Temkin, Freundlich, Frumkin, El-Awady, and Flory-Huggins models. Thermodynamic parameters (Kads, ΔGads, ΔHads, ΔSads) are used to distinguish physisorption vs. chemisorption.

**Inhibitor Classification**: Organic inhibitors classified into six types: drug molecules, ionic liquids, surfactants, plant extracts, polymers, and polymeric nanoparticles.

**Statistical Analysis**: Performed only on data from carbon steel/1.0 M HCl systems to compare maximum inhibition efficiency, optimum concentration, and optimum temperature across inhibitor types, helping reduce workload for selecting best-suited inhibitors (low concentration/high efficiency, nontoxic, cost-effective synthesis).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 8: Film-forming amines as corrosion inhibitors: a state-of-the-art review | npj Materials Degradation ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41529-024-00523-0

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a state-of-the-art review article published in npj Materials Degradation (Volume 8, Article 111, 2024) by Deni Jero, Nicolas Caussé, and Nadine Pébère, summarizing the use of film-forming amines (FFAs) as corrosion inhibitors for carbon steel in water/steam industrial circuits, including boilers, power plants, and pressurized water reactors in nuclear plants.

**Key content areas:**

1. **FFA Structure and Properties**: Film-forming amines have the general formula R1-[-NH-R2-]n-NH2, with R1 being an aliphatic hydrocarbon chain (8–22 carbon atoms), R2 a shorter chain (1–4 carbons), and n an integer from 0–7. Two primary commercial FFAs are octadecylamine (ODA, C18H39N) and N-oleyl-1,3-propanediamine (OLDA, C21H44N2). These molecules adsorb to metal surfaces via their polar amine group while the apolar hydrocarbon chain forms a protective layer. ODA has a pKa of 10.6 at 25°C; OLDA has two pKa values (10.6 and 8.4). Both have very limited water solubility at room temperature. Commercial formulations include ODYVAP and Cetamine® (containing OLDA), ODACON® (containing ODA), FINEAMIN, HELAMIN, and Steamate PAS.

2. **Industrial Feedback**: FFA treatments minimize general/localized corrosion, erosion-corrosion, and stress-corrosion cracking. Key reported benefits include: an 80% increase in heat transfer coefficient (Topp et al., 2012, OLDA vs. phosphate treatment); 0.3–1.1% plant efficiency increase and 10–40% reduction in heat exchanger costs (Hoenig et al., 2021); successful use in nuclear plants (first ODA injection in Russia in the 1980s, Armenia WWER-440 in 1988, Almaraz Spain Unit 1 at 1040 MWe in 2011 by AREVA GmbH, Embalse Argentina CANDU-6 in 2015). Typical FFA dosages range from 0.5 to 10 mg/kg, with a minimum 3–4 week adjustment period. Risks include overdosage (leading to precipitate formation and pipeline blocking), thermal degradation, and formation of low-molecular-weight organic acids. FFAs also impact reverse osmosis membranes and ion-exchange resins (cationic resin capacity reduced by 20%, anionic by 37%).

3. **Experimental Methods**: Industrial quantification uses methyl orange complexation or the Bengalrose method, with alternatives including paper spray mass spectrometry (PS-MS) and liquid chromatography-high-resolution mass spectrometry (LC-HRMS). Surface analysis uses the water drop test (contact angle >90° indicates hydrophobicity, though oxides also show hydrophobic behavior, making this method unreliable), electrochemical techniques (EIS, polarization curves), QCM-D, XPS, Raman/IR spectroscopy, SERS, AFM, and PM-IRRAS (detection limit below 10 nm).

4. **Concentration Effects**: Optimal inhibitor concentration is often related to the critical micellar concentration (CMC), though no consensus exists on ODA or OLDA CMC values (ranging from 3–4 mg/kg to 36 mg/kg for OLDA, and 1.35 g/L for ODA at 75°C). Studies report maximum inhibition efficiencies of 82% (Duprat et al., 500 mg/kg oleylamine mixture), 96% (Rohani-Rad et al., ODA at 0.2 mg/kg, 140°C), and 93% (Ma et al., ODA at 120 mg/kg, 40°C).

5. **Chemical Conditioning Effects**: ODA adsorption is more favorable in the presence of a protective oxide layer (formed with hydrazine); dissolved oxygen prevents effective film formation. OLDA reduced corrosion more than alkalizing amines (cyclohexylamine and ammonium hydroxide) at 140°C. ODA reduced magnetite deposition on filmed tubes by approximately 58%.

6. **Temperature Effects**: Best protection for ODA (25 mg/kg) on carbon steel was obtained at 220°C in deaerated solution at pH 9.0–9.5. ODA reduced corrosion rate by a factor of two at both 228°C and 300°C. There is a "critical temperature" between 120°C and 275°C where ODA efficiency decreases, likely due to molecular degradation. Thermal stability reports vary: ODA stable up to 560°C in vapor phase (Cao et al.), decomposing to CO2, H2, CH4, and NH3 at 450°C (IAPWS), while OLDA is stable up to 300°C. Other studies report decomposition between 85°C and 350°C depending on treatment time.

7. **Adsorption Mechanisms**: OLDA acts as a mixed inhibitor, blocking both anodic and cathodic sites without altering corrosion mechanisms. A 1981 mechanism proposed by Duprat et al. suggests chelate formation between iron oxide layers and nitrogen/oxygen atoms of the inhibitor plus hydrogen bonding, but this has not been experimentally verified. The review emphasizes that despite widespread industrial use, the fundamental mechanisms of FFA adsorption, their influence on iron oxide formation kinetics, and the structure/morphology of the layers they form remain poorly understood, primarily due to the difficulty of characterizing these thin organic layers on rough, corrodible surfaces under industrial conditions.
</summary>

Al-Amiery (University of Technology-Iraq and Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia), Wan Nor Roslam Wan Isahak (Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia), and Waleed Khalid Al-Azzawi (Al-Farahidi University, Iraq). The review covers the following key topics:

1. **Introduction**: Discusses two types of corrosion inhibitors - natural (derived from plants/minerals; eco-friendly, biodegradable, low toxicity but potentially limited effectiveness and higher cost) and synthetic (chemically manufactured; more effective, reliable, longer shelf life but more expensive and require careful selection/dosing to avoid environmental damage).

2. **Types of Corrosion**: Lists seven types including uniform corrosion, pitting corrosion, galvanic corrosion, crevice corrosion, intergranular corrosion, erosion corrosion, and stress corrosion cracking.

5. **Estimating Inhibitor Efficiency**:
   - **Potentiodynamic Polarization**: Applies a controlled potential ramp to the metal and measures current response to determine corrosion current and potential. Inhibitors classified as anodic (chromates, molybdates, phosphates), cathodic (nitrates, nitrites, amines), or mixed-type (benzotriazole, tolyltriazole, mercaptobenzothiazole). 6. **Additional sections** include adsorption isotherms, mechanisms of organic corrosion inhibitors, kinetics of corrosion modeling, computational methods, comparison studies, and future outlooks.

Key figures in the article include polarization curves for mild steel corrosion in HCl, Nyquist plots in sulfuric acid, SEM micrographs showing steel surface morphology with and without inhibitors, and Langmuir adsorption isotherm models. The review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of organic corrosion inhibitors to promote their wider use in corrosion protection across industries such as oil and gas, petrochemical, and marine applications.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: A novel high-efficient imidazoline derivative corrosion inhibitor for carbon steel in CO2-containing oilfield produced water: experimental and theoretical studies ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12335115

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in BMC Chemistry (2025 Aug 8;19(1):234, doi: 10.1186/s13065-025-01457-7) by researchers from PetroChina Southwest Oil and Gasfield Company (Chengdu, China) and Huazhong University of Science and Technology (Wuhan, China). The study develops a novel thiourea-based dimer acid imidazoline (DIMTU) corrosion inhibitor for N80 carbon steel in CO2-containing oilfield produced water.

METHODOLOGY: DIMTU was synthesized in two steps: (1) dimer acid imidazoline (DIM) was produced by reacting dimer acid with diethylenetriamine in xylene at 135°C (4h) then cyclized at 200°C (4h); (2) DIM (0.1 mol) was reacted with thiourea (0.2 mol) via deamination at 150°C for 2h, yielding 78% purified product. Characterization used FTIR and 1H NMR. Corrosion tests employed electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and polarization curves (PC) in a three-electrode cell at 60°C in CO2-saturated simulated oilfield produced water. Surface analysis used SEM and XPS. Theoretical studies included quantum chemical calculations (B3LYP/6-311G(d,p) with Gaussian 09) and GFN-xTB semiempirical calculations for adsorption on Fe(110) surface.

KEY RESULTS: DIMTU achieved 98.54% inhibition efficiency at 250 ppm (by PC) and 98.91% by EIS. At 50-250 ppm, polarization resistance increased from 88 Ω cm² (blank) to 1773-8106 Ω cm² (95.04%-98.91% efficiency). DIMTU exhibited long-term stability, reaching 99.64% efficiency after 72h exposure. The inhibitor showed mixed-type behavior with predominant anodic effect (Ecorr positive shift <85 mV). DIMTU performed significantly better than DIM (92.88%), TU (79.29%), and a DIM+TU physical mixture (93.10%), confirming TU was chemically incorporated into DIM rather than just mixed. Adsorption followed Langmuir isotherm with ΔGads = -45.53 kJ/mol, indicating spontaneous adsorption. Quantum chemical calculations showed HOMO distributed on imidazoline ring and S atom of TU fragment, with energy gap ΔE = 5.613 eV. GFN-xTB calculations showed DIMTU adsorbs on Fe(110) surface through S, N, C atoms of TU fragment and N of imidazoline ring (Fe-S bonds 2.203-2.312 Å, Fe-N bonds 1.935-1.963 Å, Fe-C bond 1.949 Å), with adsorption energy of -762.51 kJ/mol. The long carbon chain forms a hydrophobic barrier. XPS confirmed chemical adsorption with Fe-S bonds. DIMTU's efficiency was notably higher than other imidazoline derivatives in literature (ranging from 47.8% to 95.6%).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The experimental test results show that DIMTU has outstanding corrosion inhibition effects, with an inhibition efficiency of 98.54% at the concentration of 250 ppm."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Corrosion behaviors of Q235 carbon steel under imidazoline derivatives as corrosion inhibitors: Experimental and computational investigations - Arabian Journal of Chemistry ---
URL: https://arabjchem.org/corrosion-behaviors-of-q235-carbon-steel-under-imidazoline-derivatives-as-corrosion-inhibitors-experimental-and-computational-investigations

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Scientific Research Article: Corrosion Inhibition of Q235 Carbon Steel Using Imidazoline Derivatives

**Authors & Affiliations:** Liping Xiong, Pengjie Wang, Zhongyi He (corresponding), Qi Chen, and Renhui Zhang (corresponding) from the School of Materials Science and Engineering, East China JiaoTong University, Nanchang, China; Jibin Pu from the Key Laboratory of Marine Materials and Related Technologies, Ningbo Institute of Materials Technology and Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences.

**Published in:** Arabian Journal of Chemistry (2020), DOI: 10.1016/j.arabjc.2020.102952 (originally published by Elsevier, migrated to Scientific Scholar).

### Purpose
This study synthesized two new imidazoline derivatives (SMIF and SMID) and evaluated their corrosion inhibition performance for Q235 carbon steel in a 3.5 wt% NaCl simulated-concrete-pore (SCP) solution, using both experimental and computational approaches.

### Key Findings
- **Maximum corrosion inhibition efficiency:** 96.02% (weight-loss test) for SMIF at 4.0 g/L; electrochemical tests showed 95.95% (EIS) and 90.69% (potentiodynamic polarization) for SMIF.
- **SMIF outperformed SMID** in all tests; the phenyl group in SMIF provides stronger adsorption on the carbon steel surface compared to the methyl group in SMID.
- **Corrosion rates dropped** from 0.143 mg·cm⁻²·h⁻¹ (blank) to 0.006 mg·cm⁻²·h⁻¹ with 4.0 g/L SMIF.
- Both inhibitors act as **anodic-type corrosion inhibitors** (potential shifts of 242 mV for SMIF and 135 mV for SMID, both >85 mV threshold).
- EDS and SEM analysis confirmed the formation of a protective adsorption film on the steel surface.
- DFT and molecular dynamics simulations confirmed adsorption of inhibitor molecules on the Fe surface.
- Both inhibitors follow the **Langmuir adsorption isotherm** (linear correlation coefficient >0.99).

### Methodology
- **Synthesis:** SMIF and SMID were synthesized from oleic acid, diethylenetriamine, 1-iodobutane, and n-phenylthiourea/n-methylthiourea at ~140°C.
- **Characterization:** IR, Raman, ¹H/¹³C NMR, and elemental analysis confirmed successful synthesis.
- **Tests performed:** Weight loss (5 days immersion at 298 K), potentiodynamic polarization (Tafel), electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), SEM, EDS, and ATR-FTIR.
- **Computational:** DFT (DMol3 module) and molecular dynamics (Forcite module, COMPASS force field, NVT ensemble, 500 ps) in Materials Studio.
- **Solution used:** 0.6 mol/L KOH + 0.2 mol/L NaOH + saturated Ca(OH)₂ with 3.5 wt% NaCl.
- **Inhibitor concentrations tested:** 0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, and 4.0 g/L.

### Significance
The study demonstrates that these imidazoline derivatives exhibit potential for practical application in protecting reinforced concrete structures from chloride-induced corrosion, offering a cost-effective and convenient corrosion prevention method. The synthesized inhibitors are cationic surfactants that adsorb on the steel surface, blocking active sites and preventing corrosive ion penetration.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The maximum corrosion inhibition efficiency of weight-loss test is 96.02%. The inhibition efficiency of Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and Potentiodynamic polarization were 95.95% and 90.69%."
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://arabjchem.org/graphene-oxide-modified-with-imidazoline-quaternary-ammonium-salt-water-soluble-inhibitor-for-anticorrosion-of-the-corrosion-of-carbon-steel-in-oilfield-wastewater

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in the Arabian Journal of Chemistry (2025, Vol. 18, Article 169, DOI: 10.25259/AJC_169_2025) by Chen Xiaodong and colleagues from the School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Yulin University, Shaanxi, P.R. China. The study investigates the use of graphene oxide (GO) modified with imidazoline quaternary ammonium salt (IQAS) as a water-soluble corrosion inhibitor for carbon steel (N80) in oilfield wastewater.

METHODOLOGY: The authors prepared GO via the modified Hummers method and then acylated it with IQAS (synthesized from oleic acid, diethylenetriamine, and benzyl alkylating agent) to form a modified corrosion inhibitor. N80 carbon steel was used as the corrosion object, with oilfield wastewater from the Xingzichuan oil production plant (Yanchang Oilfield Company) as the corrosion medium. Testing was performed using electrochemical polarization curves, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), weight loss method, and surface characterization techniques including SEM, AFM, FTIR, Raman spectroscopy, XPS, and XRD.

KEY RESULTS:
- The corrosion rate of N80 steel with 0.06% GO at 40°C was 2.023 mm/a, which was 36.15% lower than the blank control group's 3.1685 mm/a.
- When 0.06% GO and 2.0% IQAS were added together, the corrosion rate dropped to 1.6494 mm/a, a 47.94% reduction compared to the blank.
- By the weight loss method (72 h at 40°C), the corrosion rate in wastewater containing 0.06% GO + 2.0% IQAS was 0.0768 mm/a, a 47.5% reduction versus the blank group, meeting industrial application standards.
- Optimal concentrations were determined to be 0.06% GO and 2.0% IQAS; excessive amounts of either reduced corrosion inhibition efficiency.

ANTI-CORROSION MECHANISM: The primary amine group of the IQAS molecule acylates with the carboxyl group of GO to form a network structure that fills the gaps of the GO lamellar layer, creating a dense protective adsorption film on the carbon steel surface. This film increases electrochemical corrosion impedance (Rs and R1) and blocks the active sites on the metal surface, reducing both anodic dissolution and cathodic hydrogen evolution reactions, thereby decreasing the corrosion current. Characterization (FTIR, Raman, XPS, SEM) confirmed the acylation reaction occurred, with amide N-C=O bonds forming at 286.21 eV and disappearance of the C=O bond peak after IQAS addition. XRD analysis showed the protective film could enrich inorganic salts (including CaCO3 and rock salt crystals) outside the anticorrosion film. The corrosion process remained under cathodic control in all conditions, and the equivalent circuit model did not change with the addition of GO and IQAS, indicating the corrosion mechanism itself was unaltered.

The research provides a novel approach for developing GO-based corrosion inhibitors for industrial oilfield wastewater applications, where GO aqueous solutions alone had been previously unreported as corrosion inhibitors.
</summary>

When 0.06% GO and 2.0% IQAS were added simultaneously, the corrosion rate was 1.6494 mm/a, which decreased by 47.94% compared with the blank control group."

SUMMARY:
<summary>

The study was authored by Ian Didiere Vázquez-Aguirre, Alvaro Torres-Islas, Edna Vázquez-Vélez, Horacio Martínez, Adrián del Pozo-Mares, and Ave María Cotero-Villegas, affiliated with the Universidad Nacional Autónoma del Estado de México, Universidad Autónoma del Estado de Morelos, and Universidad Michoacana de San Nicolás de Hidalgo in Mexico. - EIS measurements showed the fatty imidazolines formed a protective film that stabilized the patina on the bronze surface by hindering the charge transfer process.

- Raman spectroscopy and XRD analysis identified cuprite (Cu2O), tenorite (CuO), cassiterite (SnOx(OH)y), and covellite (CuS) in the patina layer.

- Inhibitor concentrations tested: 0, 10, 25, 50, and 100 ppm.

CONTEXT:
- Acid rain (pH ≤ 5.6) is a significant corrosion threat to bronze, dissolving the natural protective patina layer.
- SAE-62 bronze (Cu-Sn alloy) is widely used in architectural structures, and Mexico City has over 1400 monuments and sculptures (UNESCO World Cultural Heritage Site).
- Traditional protection methods (waxes, varnishes, benzotriazole/BTA inhibitors) have drawbacks including toxicity and environmental harm.
- This study is notable as fatty imidazolines had not previously been studied for bronze protection against acid rain.
- Rice bran oil composition: 47% oleic (monounsaturated), 33% linoleic/linolenic (polyunsaturated), and 20% stearic/palmitic (saturated) fatty acids.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: [PDF] Impact of corrosion products on performance of imidazoline ... ---
URL: https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/176177/3/Revised%20Manuscript_A.S_TLH.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article (published in Corrosion Science, 2021, Vol. 185, Article 109423) by Shamsa et al. from the University of Leeds and Schlumberger Cambridge Research, investigating the impact of corrosion products on the performance of an imidazoline-based corrosion inhibitor on X65 carbon steel in CO2 environments.

**Study Purpose and Background:**
The study addresses the critical issue that in oil and gas pipelines, corrosion inhibitors are often deployed only after internal corrosion has already begun, meaning corrosion products have already precipitated onto steel surfaces. The researchers evaluated whether pre-existing corrosion products (Fe3C and FeCO3) have antagonistic or synergistic effects on inhibitor performance, particularly regarding both uniform and localized (pitting) corrosion.

**Experimental Methodology:**
- X65 carbon steel coupons (25mm diameter, 6mm thick, 4.9 cm² exposed area) were used in a two-stage process
- Stage 1: Pre-corrosion in autoclaves at 80°C for 6, 24, and 96 hours to generate three distinct surface conditions: (i) Fe3C-rich layer, (ii) partial FeCO3 coverage, (iii) full FeCO3 coverage
- Stage 2: Pre-corroded specimens transferred to glass cells with CO2-saturated 3 wt.% NaCl brine at 80°C, tested with and without 30 ppm imidazoline corrosion inhibitor for 48 hours
- The inhibitor was a commercial imidazoline product (from M-I SWACO) synthesized from diethylenetriamine (DETA) and tall oil fatty acid (TOFA), containing 55% imidazoline (1) and amido-amine (2) components
- Techniques used: linear polarization resistance (LPR) electrochemistry, SEM, XRD, 3D surface profilometry, and in situ pH measurements

**Key Results:**

1. **Wet-ground X65 (baseline):** Inhibitor achieved 92% uniform efficiency and 95.4% localized efficiency. Pit depth reduced from 26.1 µm to 1.2 µm.

2. **Fe3C-rich layer (6h pre-corrosion):** Uniform efficiency of 95% (slightly higher than baseline due to higher bulk pH), but localized efficiency dropped dramatically to 60.7%. Slower inhibitor adsorption due to Fe3C presence. Pit depth increased from 9.0 µm to 28.0 µm (uninhibited) vs 11.0 µm (inhibited).

- The presence of corrosion products hinders inhibitor adsorption kinetics, particularly with crystalline FeCO3 layers
- FeCO3 present within pits limits inhibitor accessibility to local corrosion sites, causing continued pit growth

Key methodology: Smooth copper plates (99.98% purity) were mechanically polished, etched with concentrated nitric acid, then immersed in ammonia solution to remove copper oxides. --- SOURCE 1: Review of Corrosion Inhibiting Mechanisms in Coatings ---
URL: https://www.usbr.gov/research/publications/download_product.cfm?id=2609

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a final report (ST-2017-1703) published in September 2017 by the U.S. Department of the Interior's Bureau of Reclamation Research and Development Office, titled "Review of Corrosion Inhibiting Mechanisms in Coatings." Authors are Stephanie Prochaska and Dave Tordonato of the Materials and Corrosion Laboratory, Technical Service Center.

**Purpose/Background:** The Bureau of Reclamation historically used coatings containing toxic pigments (red lead and chromate) that provided 50+ years of service life. Modern coatings (e.g., epoxies) provide only 20-25 years, requiring more frequent and costly recoating. This literature review sought to identify nontoxic inhibitive pigments that prevent corrosion using mechanisms similar to lead and chromate pigments.

**Key Findings on Legacy Pigments:**
- Red lead (Pb3O4) pigments react with binder components to form metal soaps, which degrade into water-soluble lead salts that migrate to defects and form stable, insoluble compounds. As a secondary mechanism, lead tetroxide passivates the substrate by forming a thin, inert oxide layer.
- Chromate pigments are among the most efficient passivators; hexavalent chromium (Cr6+) reduces to trivalent chromium (Cr3+) under corrosive attack, ending the attack. Chromates are carcinogenic and were phased out by Reclamation in the 1980s-90s.

**Historical Performance Data:**
- A Reclamation analysis found the average service life of red lead primer was 64 years across their structures.
- Red lead primer on bulkhead gates at Parker Dam, California had the longest service life of 77 years.
- All repainted structures had red lead primer service lives of at least 50 years.
- Zinc chromate primers (per Federal specification TT-P-636) were used from the mid-1980s to as late as 1995; none of those structures have been repaired or recoated as of 2017.

**Three Modern Pigment Categories Researched:**

1. **Inorganic Pigments** (most promising): Four groups were reviewed—phosphates, molybdates, silicates, and ferrites. All can form metallic soaps in oleoresinous binder systems, similar to red lead. Zinc presence was important for soap formation; strontium and calcium were common additions. Zinc phosphates are versatile due to low solubility but perform poorly in accelerated testing due to a lag time for protective complex formation. Molybdates passivate steel by forming insoluble ferric molybdates but have disadvantages including premature binder aging, high cost, and toxicity concerns. Silicates can react with oleoresinous binders to form metal soaps of barium, calcium, strontium, and zinc. Ferrites also form metal soaps and promote an alkaline environment at the coating-substrate interface; all ferrite-pigmented epoxy coatings outperformed red lead pigments in the same binder in testing.

2. **Organic Pigments:** Focus on conducting polymers, especially polyaniline (PANI), which acts as a strong oxidant to steel, shifting potential toward noble direction and inducing passivation. Key results:
   - Polyaniline-coated graphite (C/PANI) achieved 97% anticorrosion efficiency (Ae), outperforming all other tested pigments including a commercially available "anticorrosion" pigment (51% Ae).
   - In a study of poly(aromatic amines), poly(m-anisidine) (PmAS) provided the best corrosion protection due to its highest chelating efficiency from its methoxy (OCH3) group.
   - Polyaniline functions similarly to chromate with self-healing properties—the steel substrate is automatically passivated if scratched or breached.
   - Bio-based aromatic acid salts (vanillic, cinnamic, ferulic acids) show potential as "green" inhibitors but are considered a novelty requiring more research.

3. **Metallic Pigments:** Zinc acts as a sacrificial pigment rather than an inhibitive one. Aluminum flake pigments (upwards of 25% by weight) form interlocking scale-like structures that are impermeable to corrosive agents and resist abrasion. Silica-coated aluminum pigments showed dramatic improvement: uncoated aluminum failed alkaline stability and boiling water tests in under 1 hour, while coated aluminum lasted ~7 hours in boiling water and over 100 hours in the alkaline stability test.

**Cost of Corrosion Context:** NACE International estimated global cost of corrosion at $2.5 trillion (3.4% of global GDP). In the U.S., corrosion costs over $276 billion, with $22.6 billion directly related to infrastructure corrosion. NACE estimates 25-30% of this cost could be saved with optimum corrosion management.

**Recommendations for Future Work:**
- Analyze current, commercially available coating systems containing the identified inhibitive pigments.
- Determine expected failure mechanisms of these coatings to predict failure timing.
- Perform accelerated laboratory testing emulating atmospheric service; pre-condition coatings in humid environments to account for pigment lag times.
- Further research conducting polymers, especially polyaniline.
- Consider engaging coatings manufacturers via cooperative agreements to develop new formulations.
- The greatest challenge is quickly and objectively testing commercial coatings to determine if they perform as well as lead- or chromate-containing coatings.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Modern coatings used by the Bureau of Reclamation have service lives of 20–25 years, whereas legacy coatings that contained red lead and chromate pigments had service lives of over 50 years."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Current and emerging trends of inorganic, organic and eco-friendly corrosion inhibitors ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/org/science/article/pii/S2046206924027815

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents a systematic review article published in RSC Advances (Volume 14, Issue 43, 1 October 2024, Pages 31877-31920) titled "Current and emerging trends of inorganic, organic and eco-friendly corrosion inhibitors." The open-access article, authored by Mahmoud A. Ahmed, Sherif Amin, and Ashraf A. Mohamed, provides a comprehensive analysis of corrosion inhibitors including both inorganic and organic compounds.

Key sections of the review cover: (1) corrosion inhibition mechanisms, (2) types of corrosion inhibitors, (3) synergistic inhibition effects, (4) inhibition performance validation, (5) comprehensive economic analysis of the corrosion inhibitor market, (6) SWOT analysis, and (7) conclusions and prospects. The review explores inhibition mechanisms, highlighting the remarkable efficiency of organic compounds attributed to heteroatoms and conjugated π-electron systems. It compares the efficacy, compatibility, and sustainability of emerging environmentally friendly corrosion inhibitors, including biopolymers from natural resources. The review emphasizes synergistic impacts between mixed corrosion inhibitors, particularly organic/organic systems, for challenging processing environments. Evaluation methods discussed include weight loss (WL) analysis, electrochemical analysis, surface analysis, and quantum mechanical calculations, as well as thermodynamics and isotherms related to corrosion inhibition.

The article includes 19 figures and 5 tables covering characteristics of inorganic corrosion inhibitors, organic corrosion inhibitors, polysaccharides, amino acids/proteins evaluated as inhibitors, and synergistic combinations. The paper has been cited 215 times and has 399 Mendeley readers.

Author biographies: Mahmoud Adel Ahmed (PhD 2024, senior service engineer at Veolia Environmental Services, focus on nanomaterials and water treatment), Sherif Amin (Chemical Service Manager at Veolia Environment, 20+ years in water treatment, B.Sc. Chemistry from Al-Azhar University 2001), and Ashraf A. Mohamed (Professor of environmental analytical chemistry at Ain Shams University, Cairo, Egypt, 35 years of research experience).

The citing articles section highlights related research on heteroatomic multiple bonded corrosion inhibitors, imidazo[1,2-a]pyrimidine-Schiff base derivatives for mild steel in HCl (96.10% and 94.22% inhibition efficiency), quinoline-based pyrazole and isoxazole derivatives (99.7% and 96.7% efficiency in 15% HCl), and corrosion inhibitors for API pipeline steels.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"This systematic review provides a thorough analysis of corrosion inhibitors, including both inorganic and organic compounds. It explores the inhibition mechanisms, highlighting the remarkable inhibitive efficiency of organic compounds attributed to the presence of heteroatoms and conjugated π-electron systems."

URL: https://www.academia.edu/11341748/Sodium_Silicate_and_Phosphate_as_Corrosion_Inhibitors_for_Mild_Steel_in_Simulated_Cooling_Water_System

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an Academia.edu page for the scientific paper "Sodium Silicate and Phosphate as Corrosion Inhibitors for Mild Steel in Simulated Cooling Water System" by Rana A Anaee (University of Technology/Iraq), published in 2014 in the Arabian Journal for Science and Engineering (DOI: 10.1007/S13369-013-0865-X). The paper is 12 pages with 857 views.

Key findings from the research:
- Sodium phosphate (1 × 10⁻² M) achieves a protection efficiency of 95.494% for mild steel
- Sodium silicate (1 × 10⁻² M) achieves a maximum protection efficiency of 74.088% in cooling water systems
- Both sodium silicate and phosphate serve as effective anodic inhibitors for mild steel corrosion
- Inhibition efficiency is significantly influenced by chloride ions, which damage protective films formed by phosphate
- The adsorption of silicate and phosphate on mild steel follows the Langmuir adsorption isotherm model
- The study used Tafel extrapolation method to analyze polarization curves and calculate corrosion parameters
- Increases in inhibitor concentration resulted in shifts of corrosion potential toward nobler values and decreased current densities
- Adsorption (ΔG°ads) values up to −20 kJ/mol indicate electrostatic (physical) adsorption between charged molecules and charged metal surfaces
- The paper includes 27 references and 14 figures, including polarization curves, cyclic polarization curves, and adsorption plots

The study compared sodium silicate and sodium phosphate individually and in binary mixtures at concentrations including 1×10⁻³, 5×10⁻³, 1×10⁻², and 0.2 mol.dm⁻³. Related research on the page covers topics such as corrosion inhibition in cooling water systems, sodium gluconate, calcium gluconate, sodium nitrite, and mixed inhibitor systems for carbon steel corrosion protection.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: Corrosion Inhibitors in Industrial Coatings ---
URL: https://www.safic-alcan.com/en-us/industry-articles/corrosion-inhibitors-industrial-coatings

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an industry article from Safic-Alcan (a specialty chemical distributor) published on May 13, 2026, covering corrosion inhibitors in industrial coatings. The article explains that corrosion costs the global economy an estimated 3-4% of GDP annually, and organic coatings are the dominant protective strategy for structural steel, marine environments, chemical processing plants, and industrial equipment.

The content covers three primary mechanisms of corrosion inhibition:

1. **Barrier Mechanism**: Physical exclusion using lamellar pigments (micaceous iron oxide, aluminium flake, talc) that create a tortuous path for water and ion diffusion. Research on pigment volume concentration (PVC) shows wollastonite and zinc phosphate outperform talc in combined anticorrosion efficiency and adhesion.

2. **Active (Passivation) Mechanism**: Sparingly soluble pigments release inhibitive ions that form passivating layers or block cathodic sites. Zinc phosphate is the most widely adopted chromate-free active inhibitor with three proposed pathways: direct phosphate ion passivation, zinc-iron complex formation, and metal soap formation with binder components. Molybdate pigments work similarly but can accelerate binder ageing and cause film embrittlement.

3. **Cathodic (Sacrificial) Mechanism**: Zinc particles act as anodes in galvanic contact with steel, requiring pigment volume concentrations above 60% for effective percolating networks. The three-coat system (zinc-rich primer/epoxy midcoat/polyurethane topcoat) is the dominant specification for structural steel bridges. Graphene-modified zinc primers can reduce zinc content while maintaining galvanic action.

The regulatory transition away from hexavalent chromium (Cr(VI)) under REACH Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 has driven development of chromate-free alternatives including: zinc phosphate and modifications, calcium-modified silica, zeolite-based pigments (with controlled release of inhibitor ions), and organic inhibitors (benzotriazole, 2-mercaptobenzothiazole).

Formulation considerations highlighted include: epoxy resins as the dominant binder for industrial anti-corrosion primers, the importance of pigment-binder compatibility testing, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) as the primary quantitative evaluation tool, and standardized testing methods (salt spray ISO 9227/ASTM B117, cyclic corrosion ISO 11997, scribe assessment ISO 4628).

Emerging technologies include smart/self-healing systems with stimuli-responsive inhibitor release — mesoporous alumina loaded with benzotriazole demonstrated 50% improvement in corrosion resistance at scratch sites. Cerium nitrate, dodecylamine, and 8-hydroxyquinoline are demonstrated encapsulatable inhibitors with pH-responsive or mechanical disruption-triggered release.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Corrosion costs the global economy an estimated 3 to 4% of GDP annually."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Phosphopolyoxometalates (Mo, W, V)  corrosion Inhibitors for Steels | Encyclopedia MDPI ---
URL: https://encyclopedia.pub/entry/58284

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article on the corrosion inhibition properties of two Keggin-type polyoxometalates (POMs): phosphovanadomolibdate acid (@PMoV, H6[PMo9V3O40]∙34H2O) and phosphovanadotungstate acid (@PWV, H6[PW9V3O40]∙14H2O), tested on S235 mild steel and SS304 austenitic stainless steel in 0.5 M sulphuric acid solution.

Key findings:
- The inhibition efficiency for S235 steel is ~90.6% for @PMoV and 69.5% for @PWV after 24 hours of immersion, showing that Mo-based POMs are more effective than W-based ones.
- For SS304 steel, the inhibition degree (as a function of Flade potential) is 4.66 for @PMoV versus 3.26 for @PWV, both proving a passivant effect.
- @PMoV and @PWV function as cathodic inhibitors for S235 steel by increasing the reduction overvoltage of hydrogen ions, and as both passivators and promoters of passivity films for SS304 steel.
- POMs act by forming protective adsorption films on the metal surface, reducing corrosion current density and slowing the corrosion process.

Methods used: potentiostatic polarization (Tafel extrapolation), chronopotentiometry (500 min open circuit potential monitoring), and weight loss/gravimetric analysis (24 h immersion). Experiments were conducted at molar concentrations of 10−2M, 10−3M, 10−4M, and 10−5M.

Synthesis: @PMoV was synthesized from NaVO3∙4H2O, NaH2PO4∙H2O, and Na2MoO4∙2H2O, yielding 14.65 g (63.5% yield, molecular mass 2305.8 g·mol−1). Characterization used FT-IR, thermal analysis (TG), and elemental analysis.

Conclusions:
- POMs with mixed addenda (V, Mo, W) show effective corrosion inhibition for both mild and stainless steels.
- POMs provide inhibition at 10−2 M or higher for S235 (efficiency ~90%), and act as passivant inhibitors for SS304 even at 10−5 M concentration.
- Compared to traditional inhibitors like chromates, polyoxometalates have very low toxicity and accept electrons without significant structural alteration, making them desirable corrosion protectors across a large scale of steels.
- Further research is needed to identify the optimal polyoxometalate ion for specific metals in given environments, and to better understand the composition/structure of metals, passive films, and POM stability.
</summary>

"The inhibition efficiency for S235 steel is about 90.6% for @PMoV, and 69.5% for @PWV after 24 h of immersion."

--- SOURCE 7: Chromate replacement: what does the future hold? | npj Materials Degradation ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41529-018-0034-5

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article published in npj Materials Degradation (volume 2, article 12, 2018) by Gharbi, Thomas, Smith, Birbilis et al., titled "Chromate replacement: what does the future hold?" The article reviews the origins of chromium replacement motivations, legislative actions aimed at reducing chromium compound use, and critically evaluates alternative corrosion prevention technologies developed since the 1980s.

Key content:
- Hexavalent chromium (Cr6+) compounds have been widely used for corrosion prevention since the second industrial revolution, but are documented carcinogens (linked to lung, nasal cancer since the 1920s; officially documented by the US HHS in 1980). Cr6+ also induces genotoxicity in aquatic and botanic life via soil/water contamination.
- REACH (Registration, Evaluation, Authorization and Restriction of Chemicals) legislation was developed in 2006, restricting chromium compound use in the EU unless authorized by the European Chemical Agency (ECHA). Authorization costs are estimated at €1.5M, with a sunset date of January 2019.
- Chromates remain the benchmark corrosion inhibitor due to their versatility, acting as both anodic and cathodic inhibitors over wide pH ranges, forming protective Cr2O3 films via self-healing mechanisms. No equally effective universal alternative has been identified.
- Aeronautical case study: F-22 aircraft switched to non-chromated primer (for environmental/health reasons), resulting in inadequate corrosion protection, and reverted to chromated primer. The F-35 program also uses non-chromated primer that has never been tested on an aircraft in a corrosive environment (program cost est. US$1.508 trillion).
- Trivalent chromium (Cr3+) conversion coatings (TCC), introduced early 1990s for Al alloys, are the most common Cr6+ replacement to date (commercialized by Henkel's Alodine T 5900 RTU, Socomore's Socosurf TCS). However, they show significantly reduced self-healing properties, and recent studies show Cr3+ may be oxidized to Cr6+ during coating growth via hydrogen peroxide (promoted by fluoride species). There are also emerging concerns about Cr3+ genotoxicity among tannery workers.
- Alternative technologies reviewed:
  1. Rare-earth-based coatings (cerium, lanthanum) - inhibit cathodic reactions but dissolve in acidic environments; supply threatened by China's near-monopolization of rare-earth market (Ce price fluctuated from US$4.35/kg to US$100/kg between 2001-2012).
  2. Vanadate-based coatings - inhibit oxygen reduction but carcinogenicity of vanadium compounds makes this alternative no longer viable.
  3. Lithium-containing coatings - Li salts intercalate into Al hydroxide matrix, forming Al-Li layered double hydroxide (LDH), providing promising corrosion resistance and self-healing properties; passed 168-hour salt spray test; not yet industrialized but shows promise comparable to hexavalent chromium.
  4. Organic coatings and nanocomposites (graphene-based) - improve barrier properties but graphene costs exceed AUD$130/kg, limiting viability.
- Smart coatings with controlled inhibitor release (responsive to pH, moisture, light) are emerging as a design direction.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"It has been documented since the 1920's that hexavalent chromium is carcinogenic in nature, after multiple studies noted an increase in the incidence of nasal and lung cancer amongst industrial workers in direct contact with Cr6+ compounds."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 8: Review of Vibrational Spectroscopy Studies of Coatings Based on Hexavalent or Trivalent Chromium Baths ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4532/6/4/47

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in Analytica (MDPI journal, 2025, Volume 6, Issue 4, article 47) titled "Review of Vibrational Spectroscopy Studies of Coatings Based on Hexavalent or Trivalent Chromium Baths" by Julio C. Avalos, Eugenia Aldeco-Pérez, Julieta Torres-González, Raul Garcia-Garcia, and German Orozco (corresponding author). The paper was submitted September 29, 2025, revised November 8, 2025, accepted November 10, 2025, and published November 14, 2025, with DOI: 10.3390/analytica6040047.

The review examines the application of vibrational spectroscopy (Raman and infrared/FTIR) to study chromium coatings, comparing hexavalent (Cr(VI)) and trivalent (Cr(III)) chromium baths used for both conversion coatings (chemical processes) and electrodeposition (electrochemical processes). Key historical context: three trivalent chromium bath patents were filed in the 19th century, but industrial production during the 20th century was based on Cr(VI) baths due to superior quality; at the beginning of the 21st century, interest in Cr(III) resumed due to lower toxicity, with systematic abandonment of Cr(VI) baths underway.

Main findings across four sections:

1. Hexavalent chromium conversion coatings: Studied extensively (especially on aluminum alloys like AA2024-T3) using FTIR techniques (ATR, DRIFTS, RAIRS, GAIRS, IRSE) and Raman spectroscopy. Synchrotron infrared microspectroscopy (SIRMS) enabled mapping of chromate oxides (820 cm⁻¹) and cyano species (2100 cm⁻¹) with <5 μm spatial resolution. The two-layer coating structure was understood, and ferricyanide was confirmed as a redox mediator in coating formation. Cr(VI) provides a self-repair mechanism by migrating to damaged/active sites (bipolar repassivation model). Chromium phosphate conversion coatings on aluminum were characterized, with film thicknesses from ~20 nm to a few micrometers.

2. Trivalent chromium conversion coatings: Studied from 2004-2023. Coatings form in two steps: (1) fluoride anions dissolve the native Al₂O₃ oxide layer; (2) interfacial pH increases causing hydroxide/oxide precipitation. The coating has two layers: an outer layer of aluminum hydroxide/oxide, zirconium oxide, and chromium hydroxide; and an inner layer rich in aluminum with oxide and fluoride species. Cr(VI) species are formed on the surface even from Cr(III)-only baths due to oxidation by hydrogen peroxide (produced by oxygen reduction). The presence of Cu(II) or Fe(II) ions suppresses Cr(VI) formation. The Raman band of Cr(VI) is approximately 3 orders of magnitude larger than Cr(III), making detection of small Cr(VI) amounts challenging.

3. Electrodeposited hexavalent chromium coatings: The mechanisms of Cr(VI) electrodeposition remain unidentified, with unclear intermediates. Vibrational spectroscopy revealed that amorphous Cr₂O₃ forms first, followed by phase transformation to crystalline Cr₂O₃. Raman laser heating causes in-situ formation of Cr₂O₃. The characteristic band at ~550-552 cm⁻¹ corresponds to the A1g vibrational mode involving Cr-O stretching in octahedrally O-coordinated Cr(III).

4. Electrodeposited trivalent chromium coatings: Approximately 880 articles evaluate Cr(III) coating quality, but very few use vibrational spectroscopy. Studies examined heat treatment effects on cobalt-chromium coatings, pulse current electrodeposition, Cr/SiC composite coatings on ferronickel alloy, and carbon analysis in coatings (sp3 carbon band ~1330 cm⁻¹). Several band assignments in the literature are questioned by the authors, who suggest revisions.

The review notes that very few studies have focused on vibrational spectroscopy of dissolved species in chromium baths—only 2 studies report Raman bands of commercial Cr(VI) conversion coating baths and only 1 electrodeposition bath study exists. Reference spectra of potassium dichromate and chromium(III) sulfate are presented as standards, and a compilation of vibrational modes is provided to facilitate band assignment. The authors conclude that spectroscopic techniques have been insufficiently applied in this field, but vibrational spectroscopy results accelerate the transition to safer Cr(III) technology.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Major vibrational spectroscopy studies have focused on the preparation of chromium coatings via chemical processes (conversion coatings), and few studies have focused on electrochemical processes (electrodeposition)."
</key_excerpts>
