- DFT/first-principle calculations showed adsorption energies on Fe(110) surface: ZnCl₂ = −1.94 eV, H₃PO₄ = −9.73 eV, Na₂MoO₄ = −2.14 eV, IL = −2.46 eV (order: H₃PO₄ > IL > Na₂MoO₄ > ZnCl₂), indicating thermodynamically favorable interactions agreeing with experimental data.
- Long-term testing in a pilot-scale cooling tower showed ~92% corrosion inhibition efficiency for combined CI + BC versus 81% for corrosion inhibitors alone.
- Surface analysis (XPS, Laser Raman spectroscopy, GDOES) confirmed adsorption of inhibitors to the metal surface.

METHODOLOGY: ASTM A53 grade B carbon steel specimens (15×30×5 mm) were used. Electrochemical methods, weight loss assays, surface analytical techniques (XPS, LRS, GDOES), DFT calculations, and quantum chemical studies were employed. The study also covered planktonic cell inhibition testing and biofilm formation inhibition.

BACKGROUND CONTEXT: The introduction explains that firewater (FW) pipeline failures occur due to under-deposit corrosion from slime formers, manganese-oxidizing bacteria (MOB), and iron-oxidizing bacteria (IOB), causing tuberculation and top-of-water-line corrosion (TWLC). Traditional treatments (chlorination and corrosion inhibitors) are often ineffective due to microbial resistance and low inhibitor efficiency in high-microbial-activity waters.

CONCLUSIONS: The combination of three non-oxidizing biocides and corrosion inhibitors (Mo, Zn, and IL) successfully enhanced CS corrosion protection, with findings validated by both experimental and computational methods. --- SOURCE 13: [PDF] In Situ Surface Studies Of Conversion Coatings For Steel And ... - DTIC ---
URL: https://apps.dtic.mil/sti/tr/pdf/ADA261016.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is a final technical report (dated 10 November 1992) submitted to the U.S. Army Research Office under Contract DAAL-03-89-K-0084, detailing "In Situ Surface Studies of Conversion Coatings for Steel and Aluminum." The work was conducted by Principal Investigators Henry W. White (University of Missouri-Columbia), Florian Mansfeld (University of Southern California), and Paul Bryant (University of Missouri-Kansas City). The report is approved for public release with unlimited distribution.

**Primary Goals:** The research aimed to develop mechanisms of corrosion protection for (1) cerium-based surface layers on aluminum alloys and aluminum/silicon carbide metal matrix composites, and (2) polyacrylic acid (PAA) complexed zinc phosphate conversion coatings on steel. Atomic force microscopy (AFM) using tunnel current control was developed and applied to these problems.

**Key Results - Cerium-Based Coatings on Al 6061-T6:**
- The protective layers consist of two principal components: a poorly ordered monohydrated aluminum oxide (boehmite, AlOOH/AI2O3·H2O) and an insoluble cerium oxide that forms at areas concentrated with impurities and alloying elements.
- Electrochemical action during surface modification fosters precipitation of cerium compounds that inhibit further attack, particularly at active sites where pits could initiate.
- The original treatment (Arnott et al.) used immersion in 1000 ppm CeCl3 for up to several weeks; Mansfeld et al. improved this with hot dilute CeCl3 and Ce(NO3)3 solutions plus anodic polarization in sodium molybdate (Na2MoO4), reducing total treatment time to six hours.
- A pretreatment process (cleaning, deoxidation, re-oxidation) was developed to standardize the surface oxide layer, since a well-formed natural oxide layer is critical for effective protection.
- Treatment DB6 (CeNO3/CeCl3/Na2MoO4) was the most effective, showing very low uniform corrosion and no localized corrosion during 60 days exposure to 0.5N NaCl.
- EIS showed a synergistic effect of Ce and Mo; treatment in either solution alone did not produce the excellent corrosion resistance of the combined treatment.
- X-ray analysis showed cerium-rich deposits were approximately circular, up to 10 μm in diameter (averaging ~3 μm), covering less than 10% of the surface.
- FT-IR spectra confirmed poorly ordered boehmite as the dominant surface phase across all treatments; no anions (cerium, nitrate, chloride, or molybdate) were detected in IR spectra.
- AFM showed "pillow-like" surface formations of 50-200 nm, independent of treatment type.
- Preliminary results for Al 7075-T6 suggest the CeCl3 step may need elimination for high-Cu alloys due to pitting concerns.

**Key Results - Zinc Phosphate Conversion Coatings on Steel:**
- Raman and micro-Raman spectra confirmed both unmodified and PAA-modified films consist predominantly of zinc phosphate dihydrate, Zn3(PO4)2·2H2O.
- PAA (molecular weight ~50,000) added to the phosphating bath significantly improves corrosion resistance and top-coat adherence by reducing crystallite size, leading to greater film ductility and fewer corrosive attack sites.
- AFM imaging of single crystallite surfaces revealed long striations with cross-striation patterns; morphologies of unmodified and modified films were generally similar with subtle differences.
- Pyramidal-shaped pits were much more prevalent on PAA-modified samples than unmodified samples (detected with Nanoscope III).
- Non-contact AFM achieved higher resolution (10-20 nm features) than contact AFM on modified films, possibly due to soft or sticky surface features.
- IR spectra showed no evidence of organic groups from PAA on film surfaces; evidence for PAA molecular segments on/in crystallites was weak, though PAA may preferentially adsorb on crystal side facets.

**Other Projects Described:**
- Cerium-treated Al/SiC metal matrix composites showed significant crystalline silicon contributions in Raman spectra of treated samples.
- Al/C interfaces treated with dilute CeCl3 became highly resistant to dissolution in water.
- A new molten salt treatment approach (SnCl2-NaCl with/without CeCl3 at 200-300°C) for Al alloys was initiated at USC.
- A new AFM design using tunnel current control was developed by Bryant and co-workers at UMKC (published in J. Vac. Sci. Tech.).
- STM imaging of solid C60/C70 (fullerite) was reported in Nature 348 (1990), revealing spherical molecules ~1 nm apart in close-packed arrays.
- Raman studies of conducting polymer polyaniline examined moisture effects on electrical conductivity.
- Equipment upgrades included a micro-Raman attachment (Oct 1990) and a Nanoscope II STM/AFM upgrade (March 1992).

**Publications and Personnel:** The report lists 15+ publications and technical reports, 20+ presentations, and participating scientific personnel with degrees earned during the project period.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: [PDF] A Review of Up-To-Date Research Knowledge on the Corrosion ... ---
URL: https://ijaem.net/issue_dcp/A%20Review%20of%20Up%20To%20Date%20Research%20Knowledge%20on%20the%20Corrosion%20Inhibiting%20Capability%20of%20Garlic%20Allicin%20Sativum%20for%20Steel%20Materials.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper is a review article published in the International Journal of Advances in Engineering and Management (IJAEM), Volume 7, Issue 01 (January 2025), pp. 104-117, authored by T.N. Guma and Jacob O. Aremo of the Department of Mechanical Engineering, Nigerian Defence Academy, Kaduna, Nigeria. The paper reviews up-to-date research knowledge on the corrosion-inhibiting capability of garlic (Allium sativum) for steel materials.

KEY FINDINGS:
- Corrosion is a monumental global economic and technological problem; steel accounts for about 90% of all global corrosion problems, and mild steel (up to 0.3% carbon) makes up about 90% of all applied steels and is responsible for 90% of steel corrosion issues.
- Synthetic corrosion inhibitors (chromate, dichromate, nitrite, nitrate) pose serious environmental and health risks, driving research into natural plant extracts as eco-friendly alternatives.
- Garlic is proven to be a very effective, safe-for-handling, biodegradable, and eco-friendly corrosion inhibitor, sustainably available worldwide.

GARLIC PRODUCTION & SAFETY:
- World garlic production is approximately 29,149,438 metric tons. China is the largest producer (20,058,388 metric tons, 76.28% share), followed by India (9.28%), Bangladesh (1.66%), South Korea (1.14%), Egypt (1.05%), and Myanmar (0.7%).
- Garlic has been used medicinally for thousands of years across numerous civilizations (China, Egypt, Greece, India, Rome), indicating its safety for human handling.

CHEMICAL COMPOSITION:
- An undamaged fresh garlic contains approximately 200 chemical compounds including sulfur-containing compounds, volatile oils, enzymes, carbohydrates, minerals, amino acids, and vitamins.
- Garlic has an unusually high proportion of sulfur-containing chemicals (13%), with key active compounds including alliin, allicin, ajoene, diallyl sulfide (DAS), diallyl disulfide (DADS), diallyl trisulfide (DATS), and allyl methyl sulfide (AMS).
- Garlic oil contains 60% diallyl disulfide; 2.62% alliin; 0.15-0.66% allicin; 0.09-0.68% γ-glutamyl-S-(E,S-propenyl)cysteine.
- Garlic oil physical properties: density/specific gravity 1.050-1.095, melting point -59.48°C, boiling point 136.32°C, pH 5.5-6.0, viscosity 9.2 mPa/s, highly flammable.

EXTRACTION METHODS:
- Major extraction methods include Soxhlet extraction, ultrasonic-assisted extraction, steam distillation, pressurized liquid extraction, supercritical-fluid extraction, and microwave extraction.
- Commercially available garlic extract types include garlic oil, prebiotic polysaccharide, aged garlic, black garlic, and garlic powder.

REVIEW OF RESEARCH STUDIES (key results):
1. Ikumapayi et al.: Garlic extract in 0.5M HCl achieved max 68% inhibitory efficiency at 8 v/v%; corrosion rate dropped from 1.66 mm/yr to 0.53 mm/yr.
2. Yang et al.: 93.26% corrosion-inhibitive efficiency for A3 steel in 5% HCl at 4.0% extract; 79.2% in 5% mud acid at 6.0% extract.
3. Afia et al.: Acid garlic essential oil reached ~95.8% inhibition efficiency at 2.5 g/L in 1M HCl at 298K; followed Langmuir adsorption isotherm; mixed-type inhibitor.
4. Barreto et al.: Garlic peel extract in 0.5M HCl was only slightly inferior to benzotriazole (BTAH) for ASTM 1020 carbon steel, offering an eco-friendly alternative.
5. Karthiga et al.: 10 mL garlic extract + 90 mL well water achieved 90% corrosion inhibition efficiency for mild steel; protective film was Fe2+-allicin complex.
6. Barreto et al.: Garlic extract achieved 90.7% efficiency and cacao extract 89% in 0.5M HCl; the mixture achieved >98% inhibition showing strong synergism.
7. Rajam et al.: 2 mL garlic extract + 25 ppm Zn2+ offered 70% inhibition efficiency for carbon steel in well water (anodic reaction control).
8. Belkaid et al.: Garlic extract in 1M H2SO4 achieved up to 90% IE for 316L stainless steel and 67% for API X60 carbon steel.
9. Joycee et al.: 100,000 ppm garlic extract + 50 ppm Zn2+ provided 87% inhibition efficiency for mild steel in simulated oil well water.
10. Yaro et al.: Garlic powder in H3PO4 achieved max 75% inhibition efficiency at 50°C and 250 ppm; followed Langmuir adsorption isotherm; mixed-type inhibitor.
11. Wei-Min and Dao-Yong: Garlic juice reached 95.4% inhibitor efficiency in 15% HCl at 80°C; 42%-64% in oil field water.
12. Fouda et al.: Allium sativum in 1M HCl is a good mixed-type inhibitor; followed Temkin's adsorption isotherm.
13. Parthipan et al.: Garlic extract (100 ppm) inhibited biocorrosion of carbon steel and stainless steel in presence of Bacillus subtilis A1 and Streptomyces parvus B7; first time garlic extract proposed as green corrosion inhibitor with biocidal activity.
14. Rodriguez-Clemente et al.: Allium sativum in 0.5M H2SO4 achieved 96% effectiveness at 400 ppm concentration.
15. Patil and Zaware: Garlic achieved 90%-95% inhibitory efficacy for steel reinforcement in concrete.
16. Maestro et al.: Garlic peel inhibited mild steel corrosion in acid (HCl), neutral (NaCl), and basic (NaOH) media; efficacy rose up to 24 hours in neutral/basic media; quantum modelling showed alliin and allicin produce more active specimens in basic conditions.
17. Ojha: 4 g/L garlic extract in 1M HCl achieved 76.47% maximum inhibition at 298K; followed Langmuir adsorption isotherm (R2=0.999).
18. Da Silvaa et al.: Garlic oil reduced microbiologically-influenced corrosion (MIC) of AISI 1020 carbon steel by sulphate-reducing bacteria more than glutaraldehyde in artificial seawater.
19. Asfia et al.: Garlic extract slowed corrosion of AISI 304 stainless steel in 0.5M HCl by up to 88%; mixed-type inhibitor following Langmuir adsorption isotherm.
20. Lu et al.: Garlic extract as post-treatment for phytic acid-based conversion coating on Q235 steel significantly improved anti-corrosion performance in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution.

CONCLUSION: Garlic is a highly effective, safe, biodegradable, and eco-friendly corrosion inhibitor for steel. However, little has been done with existing research findings for practical protection of steel materials. The review posits that garlic extracts should be considered for standardization and commercialization as practical corrosion inhibitors, or for further research.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: Allium sativum (Garlic) as green corrosion inhibitor for low carbon steel in HCl solutions | JEPT - Journal for Electrochemistry and Plating Technology ---
URL: https://www.jept.de/2015/04/14/allium-sativum-garlic-as-green-corrosion-inhibitor-for-low-carbon-steel-in-hcl-solutions

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the Journal for Electrochemistry and Plating Technology (JEPT), authored by Prof. Dr. A. S. Fouda, investigates Allium sativum (garlic) as a green corrosion inhibitor for low carbon steel in 1 M HCl solutions. The study was received on 2015-01-25, revised 2015-03-26, and accepted 2015-03-30.

**Methodology:** The inhibition properties were evaluated using four complementary techniques: potentiodynamic polarization, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), electrochemical frequency modulation (EFM), and weight loss measurements. The garlic extract was prepared by drying and grinding Allium sativum powder (20g) in 200 ml of 70% ethanol, stirring for 24 hours, evaporating the ethanol, then dissolving 1g of solid in 1000 ml of bidistilled water. Tests were conducted on low carbon steel specimens (2×2×0.2 cm) in 1 M HCl at concentrations ranging from 50–300 ppm and temperatures from 25–45°C.

**Key Findings:**
- Allium sativum proved to be a good corrosion inhibitor, acting as a mixed-type inhibitor (affecting both anodic and cathodic reactions).
- Inhibition efficiency increased with increasing inhibitor concentration but decreased with rising temperature (298–318K).
- The inhibition mechanism was physical adsorption of the extract's organo-sulphur compounds (S-alkyl-L-cysteine sulphoxides, such as allicin, and γ-glutamyl cysteines) on the metal surface.
- Adsorption followed Temkin's adsorption isotherm; calculated ΔG°ads values (around -20 kJ mol⁻¹ or lower) confirmed physical adsorption.
- EIS data showed Rct (charge transfer resistance) increased and Cdl (double layer capacitance) decreased with increasing inhibitor concentration, indicating replacement of water molecules by adsorbed inhibitor molecules.
- Nyquist plots showed a single capacitive loop in both uninhibited and inhibited solutions, indicating a single charge transfer process.
- EFM causality factors (CF-2 and CF-3) were very close to theoretical values (2.0 and 3.0), confirming good data quality.
- Results from EFM, Tafel extrapolation, and EIS methods showed good agreement.
- SEM and EDX analyses confirmed the adsorption of the inhibitor and formation of a protective thin film on the metal surface, with the surface almost unaffected by corrosion in the presence of 300 ppm extract.
- Arrhenius activation energy (Ea*) increased with inhibitor concentration, typical of physical adsorption; positive ΔH* indicated endothermic dissolution; decreasing ΔS* indicated association in the activated complex.

**Conclusions:** Allium sativum extract is a viable, environmentally friendly (biodegradable, non-toxic) green corrosion inhibitor for low carbon steel in hydrochloric acid, working through physical adsorption that forms a protective external film on the metal surface.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Allium sativum has been proved to be good inhibitor. This reduction in the corrosion rate was due to the formation of an external layer formed by S-containing film present in the extract which was adsorbed physically on the metal surface. Allium sativum acted as a mixed type of inhibitor. The inhibition efficiency increases with increasing the inhibitor concentration, but decreases with raising the temperature."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: CHARACTERIZATION AND EXTRACTION OF TANNIN FROM ARECA NUT WASTE ---
URL: https://www.ijset.in/wp-content/uploads/2015/03/032015.1831_366-372.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a research paper published on March 30, 2015 in the International Journal of Science, Engineering and Technology (ISSN: 2348-4098, Volume 3, Issue 2) by Kirankumar Rathod, M Shivaprasad, and Rajshekhar from SDM College of Engineering and Technology, Karnataka, India. The study focuses on characterizing and extracting tannin from areca nut waste and using it as a rust deactivator.

**Key Topic:** The extraction of tannins from areca nut waste using solvent extraction (leaching), characterization via UV-VIS and FTIR spectroscopy, and formulation of a rust deactivator applied to mild steel panels.

**Background on Areca Nut:**
- Areca nut is a traditional herbal medicine used in Thailand with anthelmintic, antifungal, antibacterial, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, insecticide, and larvicidal activities
- The seed contains 50-60% sugars, 15% lipids, 15% condensed tannins (phlobatannin, catechin), polyphenolics, and 0.2-0.5% alkaloids (arecoline, arecaidine, guvacine, guvacoline)
- Products derived from areca nut include: tannins/dyestuffs, fiber, timber, lipids (8-12% fat), alcohol (fermentation stimulant), poison (effective against helminthes infections), medicine, furfural, and activated carbon (25-28% yields)
- Chemical constituents: moisture 10-12%, ash 4-6%, tannin content 50-60%, specific gravity 1.54 g/cc, bulk density 0.71 g/ml

**Tannin Properties:**
- Tannins are polyphenols classified into hydrolysable and condensed (non-hydrolysable) types
- Formula: C76H52O46, molecular weight 1701.28 g/mol, melting range 198-218°C, pH ~5 (1% solution), moderate toxicity
- Soluble in water, alcohol, dilute alkalis, glycerols, and acetone; insoluble in chloroform, ether, gasoline
- Tannins act as corrosion inhibitors/rust converters by forming ferric tannate (major product), ferric vivianate, and ferric phosphate complexes. One tannin molecule replaces four water molecules during adsorption.

**Methodology:**
1. Raw material: areca nut waste slurry from areca nut industry in Kundapur, Karnataka
2. Drying in rotary dryer at 90°C
3. Identification tests: ferric chloride test (bluish-black color for hydrolysable tannins), bromine test
4. Extraction: varied feed-to-solvent ratio (1:20 to 1:30) and contact time (45-75 min)
5. Rust deactivator formulation: 5% phosphoric acid, 10% tannin aqueous, 0.25% isopropanol applied on mild steel panels (7.0 cm x 15.0 cm x 2.5 mm) rusted with 3% sodium chloride

**Key Results:**
- Maximum tannin recovery at 1:25 feed-to-solvent ratio and 60 minutes contact time
- Optimum solvent concentration: 30 ml
- Approximately 30% tannin recovery from raw sample
- FTIR analysis confirmed tannin presence in dried raw sample (ellagic acid as main constituent)
- Rust deactivator showed reduced blackspots after one week and rust was cleared without indelible marks when cleaned with sandpaper

**Conclusions:**
- Approximately 30% of tannins extracted from raw sample
- Tannins showed considerable anticorrosive property as a rust converter
- Tannin-based rust converter not effective for long-term protection in aggressive environments—only suitable for temporary corrosion protection
- Shows potential for future development in corrosion protection applications
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The areca nut, also called betel nut, is the seed of the Areca catechu palm, originally native to the Philippines but spread widely through the tropics by Austronesian migrations and trade since at least 1500 BCE. It is cultivated and naturalized across Melanesia, Micronesia, South Asia, Southeast Asia, and parts of east Africa. The nut is not a true nut but the seed of a berry-like fruit, and is commercially available in dried, cured, and fresh forms.

The nut is chewed as a mild stimulant, typically wrapped in betel (Piper betle) leaves along with slaked lime and various spices. Its consumption by approximately 600 million people worldwide, mainly of South and Southeast Asian origin, has been described as one of the greatest public health emergencies.

KEY FACTS ON TOXICITY:
- Chewing areca nut is addictive due to areca alkaloids, primarily arecoline, a partial agonist of muscarinic and nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
- It increases risk of oral, esophageal, and oropharyngeal cancers, cardiovascular disease, head and neck cancers, and oral submucous fibrosis.
- When combined with tobacco (as in gutka), risks are even higher, including fatal coronary artery disease, fatal stroke, and adverse reproductive effects.
- It can cause myocardial infarction, cardiac arrhythmias, liver damage, asthma, type II diabetes, metabolic syndrome, hypothyroidism, prostate hyperplasia, infertility, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma.
- During pregnancy, chewing areca nut formulations can cause stillbirth, premature birth, and low birth weight.
- The harm was classified in 2017 as a "neglected global public health emergency." Indian government and CAMPCO (an Indian farmer cooperative) have contested the IARC Group I classification, arguing arecoline is only classified as possibly carcinogenic (Group IIB).

CHEMISTRY: Major alkaloid is arecoline, with other compounds including arecaidine, guvacine, isoguvacine, and guvacoline. Tannins present are mainly proanthocyanidins along with catechins and arecatannin. Two new alkaloids, acatechu A and B, were recently discovered.

PRODUCTION: In 2023, world production was 2.3 million tonnes, with India providing 60% (1,369,000 tonnes). Bangladesh (341,586 tonnes) and Myanmar (262,797 tonnes) are major secondary producers. The state of Karnataka alone produced 79.97% of India's total in 2019-20.

CONSUMPTION BY REGION:
- South Asia: In India (largest consumer), preparation is called paan, sold as pan masala or supari. Poor people use it to stave off hunger. In the Maldives, chewing is popular but spitting is frowned upon. In Assam, the nut is consumed in fermented form (tamul-pan) with deep cultural and ritual significance.
- Southeast Asia: Consumption has declined in Thailand among younger generations. In the northern Philippines (Cordillera region), chewing remains prominent with restrictions and fines in urban areas like Baguio. In Indonesia it is called makan pinang or pinang.
- Oceania: In Papua New Guinea (buai), a controversial ban in Port Moresby (2014) was lifted in 2017; another limited ban was introduced in 2023. Australia bans importation, use, and sale of areca nut.
- East Asia: In Hainan and Hunan provinces of China (with Xiangtan as a processing center), consumption is widespread. In Taiwan, "betel nut beauties" sell fresh nuts from roadside shops, commonly used by blue-collar workers including taxi and truck drivers.
- Other: Legal in the US (not controlled), legal in the UK, but banned in the UAE.

CULTURE: Betel nut chewing is a significant cultural activity across South Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia, and Oceania. The oldest evidence of betel chewing comes from Duyong Cave in Palawan, Philippines (~2680±250 BCE). The practice is believed to have originated in the Philippines during the Austronesian expansion (~3000 BCE). In Vietnam, "matters of betel and areca" is synonymous with marriage. In Hinduism and Buddhism, areca nut is considered auspicious and used in religious ceremonies. In Bhutan (called doma), chewing is an essential part of life and culture, with a myth attributing its introduction to Guru Rinpoche in the 8th century. The areca nut husk (50-75% of fruit weight) serves as a construction fiber.

URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/pharmacology/articles/10.3389/fphar.2024.1407212/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive review article published in Frontiers in Pharmacology (30 May 2024, Volume 15) titled "Comprehensive insights into areca nut: active components and omics technologies for bioactivity evaluation and quality control" by Yuanyuan Sun, Jian Feng, Wencheng Hou, Huasha Qi, and Yangyang Liu from the Institute of Medicinal Plant Development, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences and Peking Union Medical College.

KEY CONTENT:

**Background:** Areca nut (AN), the fruit/seed of *Areca catechu* Linn, has both chewing and medicinal uses. More than 600 million people chew AN globally. It is classified as a Group 1 carcinogen by the IARC/WHO and is considered the world's fourth most addictive substance. Different parts have different medicinal uses: arecae pericarpium ("Da Fu Pi"), arecae semen, and arecae semen tostum (charred seeds used to promote digestion).

**Clinical Studies:** Medicinal use of AN (e.g., "Muxiang Binglang Pill" for pancreatitis recovery, "Binglang Powder" for spleen/stomach diseases, "Food Retention Relieve Oral Liquid" for child anorexia nervosa) shows no significant toxic side effects. **Alkaloids (major bioactive compounds):** At least 18 alkaloids identified in AN (total alkaloid content 0.3%-0.6%). Four major ones: arecoline (most abundant), guvacine, arecaidine, guvacoline. Arecoline has both beneficial effects (anthelmintic, antimicrobial, hypotensive, anti-inflammatory, anxiolytic, cognition-enhancing, digestive stimulation, blood glucose lowering) and adverse effects (fibrosis, cancer metastasis, cytotoxicity, reproductive toxicity, genotoxicity, cardiac toxicity, insulin resistance).

**Polyphenols and other compounds:** 88 total compounds isolated including polyphenols (catechins, procyanidins, tannins, flavonoids), triterpenes, steroids, fatty acids, and other compounds (Table 1).

**Detection Methods:** HPLC is the primary quantification method. Multiple techniques include: HPLC-UV, UHPLC-MS/MS, LC-MS-IT-TOF, MALDI-MSI (spatial distribution of 10 alkaloids), near-infrared spectroscopy, HPLC coupled with ion mobility spectrometry, and icELISA (immunoassay for arecoline using mAb-A5H12 antibody). These methods detect arecoline, arecaidine, guvacine, guvacoline, and N-nitrosoguvacoline in various matrices including hair, urine, saliva, and AN products.

**Factors Influencing Alkaloid Content:** Geographic location significantly affects content (arecoline: 0.02%-0.12% in NE Thailand vs 0.22%-0.56% in China; worldwide variation 2-10 mg/g dry weight). Growth period, processing methods (e.g., blanching, charcoal roasting), and extraction techniques also influence content.

--- SOURCE 16: Unveiling green corrosion inhibitor of Aloe vera extracts for API 5L steel in seawater environment | Scientific Reports ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-024-64715-z

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper (published in Scientific Reports, Volume 14, Article 14085, 2026) investigates the use of Aloe vera extract as an environmentally friendly ("green") corrosion inhibitor for API 5L steel in seawater environments. The study was conducted by researchers including Ahmad Royani, Muhammad Hanafi, Nabisab Mujawar Mubarak, Gadang Priyotomo, Victor Sunday Aigbodion, Siti Musabikha, and Azwar Manaf.

Key findings and data:
- The A. vera extract was produced via maceration with methanol-water (1:1 v/v) at room temperature, with extraction repeated 3×24 hours.
- Electrochemical measurements (PDP and EIS) showed the extract effectively reduces corrosion of API 5L steel in seawater.
- Optimal inhibition efficiency was approximately 83.75% (PDP) and 88.60% (EIS) with 300 mg/L of extract at 310 K.
- The highest activation energy (Ea) was 48.24 kJ/mol at 300 mg/L concentration.
- Increasing temperature and exposure duration reduced inhibition efficiency; the best exposure period was 30 minutes with 88.34% IE at 300 K with 300 mg/L.
- Inhibition occurs through adsorption of A. vera bioactive compounds on metal surfaces via a mixed inhibitor mechanism (physisorption-chemisorption).
- Dominant active compounds identified were methyl phaeophorbide (10.93) and kaempferol-3-O-rutinoside (2.91), along with 2"-O-Feruloylaloesin (3.62) and Natsudaidain (3.88).
- FT-IR analysis revealed functional groups including OH/NH bonds (3252.58 cm⁻¹), C-H stretching (2925.40 cm⁻¹), amine compounds (1024.97 cm⁻¹), C=O aromatic compounds (1583.06 cm⁻¹), and C-N/C-O groups (1397.68, 1320.92, 1256.11 cm⁻¹).
- API 5L steel (from geothermal industrial pipes) had composition of 96.17% Fe, with minor C, Si, Mn, P, S, Cr, Mo, Ni, Cu, Al, Pb, Ti, Zn.
- Synthetic seawater was prepared from salt powder (38 g per 1000 mL) containing NaCl, MgCl·6H2O, CaCl2·2H2O, Na2SO4, KCl, and NaHCO3.
- The inhibitor was classified as a mixed-type inhibitor (with cathodic tendencies at low frequencies and anodic at high frequencies) since Ecorr shifts were less than 85 mV.
- Corrosion current density decreased from 36.48 μA/cm² (no inhibitor) to between 8.25 and 7.14 μA/cm² with inhibitor concentrations of 100-300 mg/L at 300 K.
- EIS analysis showed Nyquist plots with slightly depressed semicircles, indicating charge transfer mechanism; semicircle diameter expanded with increasing inhibitor concentration, indicating protective layer formation.
- Surface analysis (FE-SEM, EDS, AFM) confirmed smoother surface morphology on steel treated with A. vera extract compared to untreated steel.

The study concludes that A. vera extract has significant potential as an environmentally friendly, cost-effective, and biodegradable alternative to traditional synthetic corrosion inhibitors (which are hazardous, toxic, and costly). This work is novel because most green inhibitor studies focus on acidic or basic conditions, whereas this study applies A. vera extract in a seawater environment.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"This corrosion inhibition is achieved by the adsorption process of A. vera bioactive on metal surfaces with a mixed inhibitor through a physisorption-chemisorption mechanism."

Alphonsa from the Department of Chemistry, St. Joseph's College (Autonomous), Trichy, India.

METHODOLOGY: An aqueous Aloe vera extract was prepared by grinding 10 g of fresh gel and making up to 100 ml with double distilled water. Carbon steel specimens (0.0267% S, 0.06% P, 0.4% Mn, 0.1% C) of dimensions 1.0 × 4.0 × 0.2 cm were immersed in well water with various inhibitor concentrations for 3 days. Corrosion rate and inhibition efficiency (IE) were measured using the weight-loss method, with corrosion products cleaned using Clarke's solution. Synergism parameters, ANOVA (F-test), biocidal efficiency (using Zobell medium), and FTIR spectroscopic analysis of protective films were also performed.

KEY RESULTS:
- Aloe vera alone showed modest IE (up to 32% at 10 ml), and Zn2+ alone showed only 5% IE at 25 ppm, but their combination reached 51% IE, demonstrating a synergistic effect.
- The ternary system of SM (100 ppm) + Zn2+ (25 ppm) + Aloe vera (10 ml) achieved 87% inhibition efficiency, the highest observed.
- Zn2+ acts as the primary synergist and Aloe vera as the secondary synergist.
- Synergism parameter (SI) values ranged from 1.67 to 7.38 (all >1), confirming significant synergistic effects.
- F-test results (F = 12.94 and F = 10.65, both exceeding the critical value of 5.32 for 1, 8 degrees of freedom at 0.05 significance level) confirmed the statistical significance of the synergistic effects.
- As immersion period increased from 1 to 7 days, IE decreased from 95% to 67%, due to chloride ion attack rupturing the protective film.
- FTIR analysis confirmed formation of Fe2+-Aloe vera complex on anodic sites and Zn(OH)2 on cathodic sites; MoO4- stretching shifted from 824 to 853 cm-1, phenolic -OH shifted from 3312 to 3385 cm-1, and C=O shifted from 1626 to 1613 cm-1.
- Adding 150 ppm of sodium dodecyl sulphate (SDS) to the formulation achieved 97% corrosion inhibition efficiency and 100% biocidal efficiency (nil colony-forming units/ml).

MECHANISM: The inhibition occurs via complexation and adsorption. Zn2+ complexes (Zn2+-SM, Zn2+-Aloe vera, Zn2+-SM-Aloe vera) form in solution. During iron dissolution, Zn(OH)2 precipitates at cathodic sites, while Fe2+-Aloe vera complexes form at anodic sites. The protective film consists of Fe2+/Fe3+ and Zn2+ complexes with SM and Aloe vera, along with Zn(OH)2 and oxides/hydroxides of iron and zinc.

CONCLUSION: The SM-Zn2+-Aloe vera ternary formulation is a potent, environmentally friendly corrosion inhibitor for carbon steel in well water. Well water parameters included pH 7.73, chloride 1450 ppm, TDS 4034 ppm, total hardness 880 ppm, and conductivity 5820 µmhos/cm.

<summary>
This is an Academia.edu page presenting a 2022 research paper titled "Investigating the Effect of Aloe-Vera Extract on the Corrosion Inhibition of Medium Carbon Steel in Seawater" by Amos Omoefe Ebebeinwe (Federal University of Technology Owerri), published in DergiPark (Istanbul University).

STUDY OVERVIEW: The research investigates aloe vera extract as a corrosion inhibitor for 0.39% carbon steel in seawater. - Corrosion rates decreased initially but showed fluctuations after 336 hours of exposure, particularly for 4% aloe vera.

CONCLUSION: Aloe vera can effectively act as a corrosion inhibitor for 0.39%C steel in seawater, though its effectiveness diminishes over prolonged exposure.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific article, published in the Journal of King Saud University - Science (2023, DOI: 10.1016/j.jksus.2023.102986), investigates the use of Aloe vera mucilage (AVM) as an eco-friendly corrosion inhibitor for bronze B66 in 3% NaCl (saline) environments. 

**Objective:** To develop a non-toxic, cost-effective, and stable green corrosion inhibitor for bronze B66 (a copper alloy with 4.87% tin, similar to archaeological bronze) in aggressive chloride media, addressing the need to replace toxic inorganic/synthetic inhibitors.

**Methodology:** 
- AVM was extracted in powder form via a newly patented process
- Testing methods included gravimetric (weight loss) measurements, potentiodynamic polarization (PDP), electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), SEM/EDX surface analysis, Density Functional Theory (DFT) quantum chemical calculations, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations

**Key Results:**
- Gravimetric study: Inhibition efficiency reached 80.97% at 750 ppm AVM (corrosion rate decreased from 3.70×10⁻⁵ to 7.04×10⁻⁶ g/h.cm²)
- Electrochemical tests: Inhibition efficiency reached 94% at 750 ppm (corrosion current density dropped from 9.48 to 0.59 μA/cm²); AVM acts as a mixed-type inhibitor affecting both anodic and cathodic reactions
- EIS: Efficiency reached 85.94% at 750 ppm, with polarization resistance increasing from 1143 to 8130 Ω.cm²
- SEM/EDX: Confirmed formation of a protective film on the bronze surface, reducing chloride attack and pitting corrosion

**Theoretical Findings:**
- The major bioactive polysaccharide in AVM is Acemannan (C66H100NO49), composed of partially acetylated mannose units linked by β-(1→4) glycosidic bonds
- DFT calculations showed the protonated form of Acemannan has better corrosion inhibition performance than the neutral form (lower energy gap: 2.768 eV vs 3.813 eV)
- MD simulations on Cu(111) surface showed protonated Acemannan lies flat on the surface with higher binding energy (3129.42 kJ/mol vs 2981.43 kJ/mol for neutral form)

**Authors:** Bouchra Benzidia, Mohammed Barbouchi, Malak Rehioui, Hind Hammouch, Hamid Erramli, and Najat Hajjaji (from Ibn Tofail University, Kenitra, Morocco and Moulay Ismail University, Meknes, Morocco).

**Conclusion:** The study supports using natural products as environmentally friendly corrosion inhibitors and shows promise for preserving bronze archaeological artifacts in museums.
</summary>

"The corrosion rate of bronze decreases with the inhibitor's presence, and its inhibitory effectiveness amplifies with higher concentrations, reaching an efficiency of 86% at 750 ppm."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific research article published in the Arabian Journal of Chemistry (2023, vol 17, article 105410) by Bi-lan Lin, Xin-xin Zhou, Tian-hu Duan, Chen Zhao, Jia-hao Zhu (Xiamen University of Technology) and Yu-ye Xu (Huaqiao University, China). The study investigates the corrosion inhibition and adsorption performance of *Ipomoea batatas L.* (sweet potato) leaf extract (IBLE) as a green, eco-friendly corrosion inhibitor for mild steel (MS) in a 1 M HCl pickling solution.

**Methods:** IBLE was extracted using ultrasonics with an ethanol-water (4:1 v/v) solution. Characterization was performed via FTIR, UV-visible spectroscopy, XPS, SEM surface observation, and electrochemical tests (OCP, EIS, PDP). DFT (Gaussian 09W, B3LYP/6-311G**(d,p)) and molecular dynamics (Materials Studio, COMPASS force field, Fe(110) surface) simulations were conducted on four representative phytochemicals: D-mannose (sugar), vitamin B2 (vitamin), quercetin (flavonoid), and protocatechualdehyde (phenolic acid).

**Key Results:**
- IBLE acts as a mixed-type corrosion inhibitor via a geometric coverage effect
- Inhibition efficiency increases with extract concentration and temperature, reaching up to 96.4% at 318 K with 5.0 g/L IBLE
- PDP results showed η_PDP up to 94.9%, 95.6%, and 96.4% at 298, 308, and 318 K respectively with 5.0 g/L extract
- Corrosion current density (i_cor) decreased from 30.0×10⁻⁵ A/cm² (blank at 298 K) to 1.54×10⁻⁵ A/cm² with 5.0 g/L IBLE
- FTIR identified functional groups including –OH, –NH, C=C, C=O, C–O, C–C, and –CH groups, plus aromatic/heteroaromatic rings
- XPS confirmed adsorption of C=C, C–N, C–N+, C=N, C=N+, C=O, C=O+, C–O, C–O+, and Fe–N bonds on the steel surface
- Adsorption follows the Langmuir isotherm (monolayer protective film)
- DFT/MD simulations confirmed active compounds adsorb on Fe(110) via physical patterns and coordinate bond formation through charge sharing with iron
- The corrosion mechanism of MS in 1 M HCl is not altered by IBLE addition
- IBLE contains sugars, vitamins, flavonoids, and phenolic acids with numerous polar functional groups that share electrons with iron atoms

**Conclusions:** IBLE is an efficient, renewable, and sustainable corrosion inhibitor for mild steel in HCl pickling media, with synergistic adsorption effects among its various active phytochemicals.
</summary>

## Abstract

In production and transportation systems of the oil industry, brine solutions contain high concentrations of chloride and dissolved CO2, which is a very corrosive medium to which carbon steel is exposed. Therefore, finding new effective and environmentally friendly corrosion inhibitors is of great importance. The effect of CeCl3 (in concentrations from 5 mg dm−3 to 20 mg dm−3) and oleic acid imidazoline (IOA) (in concentrations from 5 mg dm−3 to 20 mg dm−3) separately and their mixtures (in concentrations from 5 mg dm−3 to 15 mg dm−3 of CeCl3 and from 5 mg dm−3 to 20 mg dm−3 of IOA) as corrosion inhibitors of AISI 1018 carbon steel corrosion in simulated brine solution saturated with CO2 at 60 °C were examined by means of weight-loss testing, electrochemical measurements (polarization resistance, linear polarization with Tafel extrapolation, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy) and surface analyses (scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy analyses, Raman spectroscopy and X-ray diffraction). All test methods showed a higher efficiency of compounds′ mixtures (from 62.77% to 97.94%) and a higher degree of corrosion protection compared to the action of individual compounds (efficiency from 3.43% to 94.61% for IOA and from 57.58% to 96.27% for CeCl3). Imidazoline, a common corrosion inhibitor in CO2-saturated systems, most likely forms a surface film with voids via its adsorption on steel surface, while cerium carbonate tends to fill these voids by creating a more compact film. In this way, a denser and thicker surface film is formed.

## 1. Introduction

Carbon capture, utilization and storage (CCUS) is considered an effective way of reducing CO2 emissions, and it is often used for enhanced oil recovery purposes (CO2-EOR) [[1](#B1-coatings-15-00093),[2](#B2-coatings-15-00093),[3](#B3-coatings-15-00093),[4](#B4-coatings-15-00093),[5](#B5-coatings-15-00093),[6](#B6-coatings-15-00093)]. It is known that the produced fluids are quite corrosive media (they contain oil, water, chlorides, acids and dissolved gases) that impair the integrity and useful properties of transportation pipelines and tubing [[7](#B7-coatings-15-00093),[8](#B8-coatings-15-00093),[9](#B9-coatings-15-00093)].

In oil and gas production and transport pipelines, as well as in carbon capture storage systems, corrosion of the inner walls of the pipes, due to the presence of CO2, results in pipeline rupture, the loss of production and transport fluid, economic losses and ecological disaster [[10](#B10-coatings-15-00093),[11](#B11-coatings-15-00093),[12](#B12-coatings-15-00093),[13](#B13-coatings-15-00093),[14](#B14-coatings-15-00093)]. Situations are much worse when high chloride concentrations are present as well as turbulent hydrodynamic conditions [[15](#B15-coatings-15-00093)].

Most pipelines for systems containing CO2 (oil and gas production, geothermal systems, carbon capture, utilization and storage systems) are made of carbon steel. Although carbon steel is subject to corrosion in exposed conditions, the reason for its wide application is due to its favorable metallurgical properties as well as economic profitability [[16](#B16-coatings-15-00093),[17](#B17-coatings-15-00093),[18](#B18-coatings-15-00093)].

One of the oldest and most common methods of protecting metals from corrosion is the application of corrosion inhibitors [[19](#B19-coatings-15-00093)]. Corrosion inhibitors are defined as substances that, added in small amounts, slow down or prevent metal corrosion [[20](#B20-coatings-15-00093)]. In the past, the only factor in selecting an inhibitor was its effectiveness, while its environmental impact was neglected. In addition, it was believed that effective corrosion inhibitors could not be environmentally friendly, and environmentally friendly compounds could not be effective corrosion inhibitors [[21](#B21-coatings-15-00093)].

Fortunately, nowadays, the selection and application of corrosion inhibitors has moved from an exclusively economic aspect to taking into account environmental factors, i.e., it is necessary to satisfy the so-called E3 concept (efficiency, economy and ecology). Before 1960, the only criterion that had to be met when choosing an inhibitor was effectiveness, and the following were widely used: chromates, phosphates, nitrates, borates, silicates and zinc compounds. Although extremely effective as corrosion inhibitors and economically viable, today’s chromates (like most inorganic inhibitors) are banned for health and safety reasons. From 1960 to 1980, the focus when choosing inhibitors was on the economic aspect; so polyphosphates, gluconates, vanadates, molybdates, carboxylates and surface-active chelates were used. Tannins, vitamins, natural compounds and polymers were widely used from 1980 to 1995 when ecology was the main required property of the inhibitor. From 1995 until today, inhibitors must be environmentally friendly, which is why compounds like rare earth metal compounds, multifunctional organic compounds, mixtures of rare earth metals and organic/inorganic compounds and the encapsulation of inhibitors are preferred [[21](#B21-coatings-15-00093),[22](#B22-coatings-15-00093)].

Chemicals in the general sense, and thus non-ecological corrosion inhibitors, cause numerous environmental problems, which is why the development of “green chemistry” that also applies to corrosion inhibitors has occurred. “Green chemistry” refers to chemicals and chemical processes that reduce or eliminate the negative impact on the environment since they reduce waste products, do not contain toxic compounds and improve efficiency [[23](#B23-coatings-15-00093)].

Scientists invest a lot of effort in finding and producing inhibitors that are both highly effective and low in toxicity. Such inhibitors are called “environmentally friendly”, “green inhibitors” or “environmentally acceptable inhibitors” [[24](#B24-coatings-15-00093),[25](#B25-coatings-15-00093)].

In the eighties of the last century, the development of a new group of corrosion inhibitors, salts of rare earth metals (REM), began. Their development was slow, and they did not reach the importance of organic inhibitors despite their significant effectiveness. Among the rare earth salts, lanthanoids stand out as effective corrosion inhibitors. Cerium, praseodymium, neodymium, lanthanum and ytterbium ions showed very high inhibitory effectiveness on aluminum alloys [[26](#B26-coatings-15-00093),[27](#B27-coatings-15-00093)].

Small animal studies of cerium compounds have shown low toxicity, which can be related to other lanthanides. Lanthanides are economically competitive products, and the relative prevalence of some of them (e.g., cerium) makes them additionally acceptable. The chemical properties of the lanthanides, for example the low solubility of their oxides and hydroxides, make them particularly suitable for corrosion inhibition [[28](#B28-coatings-15-00093),[29](#B29-coatings-15-00093),[30](#B30-coatings-15-00093),[31](#B31-coatings-15-00093)]. Excellent corrosion inhibition is attributed to the high reactivity of rare earths. In the articles, the formation of a protective film and the inhibition of the cathodic corrosion reaction have been proven [[32](#B32-coatings-15-00093),[33](#B33-coatings-15-00093),[34](#B34-coatings-15-00093),[35](#B35-coatings-15-00093),[36](#B36-coatings-15-00093),[37](#B37-coatings-15-00093)].

Imidazolines are a special class of corrosion inhibitors that have proven to be highly effective, and therefore, they have a wide range of applications in protection against CO2 corrosion. In addition to being highly effective in protecting against CO2 corrosion, they are also available and environmentally friendly. To further improve their effectiveness, commercial forms of imidazolines are most often mixtures of imidazolines and other compounds, i.e., these are imidazoline derivatives [[38](#B38-coatings-15-00093)]. Imidazoline derivatives are organic compounds based on nitrogen that act as cationic surfactants, depending on the nature of the hydrocarbon substituting group attached to the carbon or nitrogen atom of the imidazole ring [[39](#B39-coatings-15-00093)]. The imidazoline head (with free electron pairs on nitrogen atoms and delocalized π-electrons) binds to the metal surface, while the hydrophobic tail represents a kind of barrier against the diffusion of water ions [[40](#B40-coatings-15-00093)]. The inhibitory effect is attributed to physical (electrostatic interaction of the inhibitor molecule and the metal) or chemical adsorption (sharing or transfer of electrons between the inhibitor and the metal) on the metal surface, resulting in the formation of a protective film [[39](#B39-coatings-15-00093)].

The examination of the synergistic effect of the compounds is carried out with the assumption of an increase in the inhibitory effectiveness in corrosion protection, as well as due to a reduction in the doses of chemicals [[38](#B38-coatings-15-00093),[41](#B41-coatings-15-00093),[42](#B42-coatings-15-00093),[43](#B43-coatings-15-00093),[44](#B44-coatings-15-00093),[45](#B45-coatings-15-00093),[46](#B46-coatings-15-00093)]. The synergistic action involving rare earth metal salts as corrosion inhibitors is rarely investigated; therefore, the aim of this work is to examine the potentially synergistic action of rare earth salt, CeCl3 and imidazoline based compounds.

In this work, the joint/synergistic effect of cerium chloride and imidazoline on the corrosion of carbon steel in a simulated brine solution saturated with CO2 at 60 °C (which corresponds to the average temperature of the transported fluid in the oil industry) was tested. The inhibitory action of individual components as well as their synergistic action was tested using the mass loss method as well as the electrochemical methods of potentiodynamic polarization, measurement of polarization resistance and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy. The surface analysis of carbon steel samples was examined using scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction and Raman spectroscopy.

## 2. Materials and Methods

The tested alloy is the AISI 1018 carbon steel with the chemical composition determined via optical emission spectrometry on a GDS 850 Leco spectrophotometer, MI, USA, and it is composed of the following (wt.%): 0.35 C, 0.35 Si, 1.09 Mn, 0.007 P, 0.024 S, 0.09 Cr, 0.07 Ni, 0.01 Mo, 0.10 Cu, <0.01 V and Fe balance. The steel has a ferrite–pearlite microstructure, as shown in [Figure 1](#fig_body_display_coatings-15-00093-f001).

![Coatings 15 00093 g001](/coatings/coatings-15-00093/article_deploy/html/images/coatings-15-00093-g001-550.jpg)

**Figure 1.**
The ferrite–pearlite microstructure of the tested AISI 1018 carbon steel scanned with an Olympus GX51 light microscope, Tokyo, Japan, magnification 1000×.

The carbon steel surface area for tests using the mass loss method was 23.72 cm2, while for electrochemical tests, the surface area exposed to the action of the tested electrolyte was 1 cm2. Before testing, the carbon steel samples were wet sanded with a silicon carbide abrasive paper up to 1200 grit, washed with double distilled water, degreased in 96% ethanol and dried in a stream of air.

The tested electrolyte is composed of 800 mL of chloride–carbonate solution (synthetic brine solution, SBS) saturated with CO2, both without and with inhibitors (individually and in a mixture). The chloride–carbonate solution was prepared by dissolving 30.0 g dm−3 NaCl, 0.1 g dm−3 NaHCO3 and 0.1 g dm−3 CaCO3 in distilled water. The chloride–carbonate solution was saturated with CO2 by bubbling CO2 for 1 h before the start of the measurement and continued during the experiment. The composition of the tested electrolyte corresponds to the composition of natural, stratified waters of oil deposits in Croatia, except that the chloride content has been increased to carry out corrosion tests under severe conditions. The pH value of the prepared solution was 5.3. The pH value was measured with a Portable Waterproof pH meter HI991300, Hanna Instruments, Bedfordshire, UK, (pH accuracy ±0.1 pH, pH range 0.0–14.0). The chemicals used for the preparation of simulated brine solution were analytical grade and produced by Sigma Aldrich, Darmstadt, Germany. In the experiment, imidazoline oleic acid (IOA), produced by Sigma Aldrich, Darmstadt, Germany, and cerium chloride, also produced by Sigma Aldrich, Darmstadt, Germany, as corrosion inhibitors were used. The chemical structures of imidazoline based on oleic acid and cerium chloride are shown in [Figure 2](#fig_body_display_coatings-15-00093-f002).

![Coatings 15 00093 g002](/coatings/coatings-15-00093/article_deploy/html/images/coatings-15-00093-g002-550.jpg)

**Figure 2.**
Chemical structures of (**a**) oleic acid imidazoline-based compound and (**b**) cerium chloride anhydrate.

Both tested compounds were added individually in concentrations of 5 mg dm−3, 10 mg dm−3, 15 mg dm−3 and 20 mg dm−3, while the inhibitor mixture consisted of 5 mg dm−3, 10 mg dm−3, 15 mg dm−3 or 20 mg dm−3 IOA with the addition of 5 mg dm−3, 10 mg dm−3 or 15 mg dm−3 CeCl3 to each of these concentrations. The concentrations of individual components used in this work are arbitrary and lower than those reported in the literature for similar test systems. The aim in selecting concentrations was to achieve satisfactory efficacy at as low a concentration of individual components and as low a concentration of their mixtures as possible, i.e., use the lowest possible doses of chemicals.

All measurements were carried out at a temperature of 60 ± 1 °C with stirring at a speed of 300 rpm; they were repeated at least three times, and very good reproducibility of the results was achieved (relative standard deviation was less than 5%).

### 2.1. Mass Loss Measurements

Tests using the mass loss method were performed in accordance with the ASTM G-1 standard. Before immersion in the tested electrolyte, the steel coupons were prepared in the previously described manner (treated with sandpaper, washed, degreased and dried) and weighed on an analytical balance with an accuracy of ±0.1 mg. After 72 h of exposure to the tested electrolytes, the coupons were taken out, and their surfaces were cleaned with a Clarke′s solution (ASTM G 1-03 pickling solution consists of 5% stannous chloride and 2% antimony trioxide in concentrated hydrochloric acid), washed with distilled water, degreased with 96% ethanol, dried in a stream of air and weighed again on an analytical balance. The chemicals used for the preparation of Clarke′s solution and the ethanol used for degreasing were analytical grade and produced by Sigma Aldrich, Darmstadt, Germany. All tests were performed at least four times, and very good reproducibility of the obtained measurement results was achieved.

### 2.2. Electrochemical Measurements

Electrochemical corrosion tests were performed on an EG&G PAR 378 potentiostat/galvanostat, IL, USA, in conjunction with the Power Suite software 2.41. An electrochemical cell with a three-electrode system was connected to the potentiostat. The working electrode was a sample of tested carbon steel AISI 1018, with a circular cross-section, inserted into the holder of the working electrode, so that the surface of the steel exposed to the action of the electrolyte was 1 cm2. A saturated calomel electrode was used for the reference electrode, and two graphite rods were used for the counter electrodes.

The electrochemical measurements were performed after 24 h of stabilization of the working electrode at the open circuit potential.

Linear polarization curves in a narrow range of potential were recorded, ±10 mV in relation to the open circuit potential with a scanning rate of 0.1660 mV s**−**1, from which the polarization resistances were determined.

Potentiodynamic polarization recordings were performed in a potential range of ±250 mV in relation to the open circuit potential with a scanning rate of 0.1660 mV s**−**1. Corrosion rates were calculated using the Tafel extrapolation method. The method includes extrapolation of the linear cathodic and linear anodic parts of the polarization curve to their intersection, which corresponds to the corrosion current and corrosion potential from which the software calculates the corrosion rates.

Electrochemical impedance spectra were recorded at an open circuit potential, in the frequency range from 100 kHz to ~10 mHz and an excitation signal of 5 mV. The ZSimpWin software 3.21 was used to analyze the recorded impedance spectra.

### 2.3. Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) and Energy-Dispersive X-Ray Spectroscopy (EDS) Analyses

The morphology of the carbon steel surface products after 72 h of exposure to systems with single components and their mixtures was examined by a scanning electron microscope (SEM) JEOL JSM6510LV, Tokyo, Japan, while the chemical properties of the surface products were determined via energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). Analyses of the carbon steel were performed after exposure to the system in the presence of individual components separately at concentrations of 15 mg dm−3 CeCl3 and 15 mg dm−3 IOA and in the presence of a mixture of 15 mg dm−3 CeCl3 and 15 mg dm−3 IOA. This combination of the compounds was chosen because most of the test methods showed the highest inhibitory effectiveness at precisely this concentration of the mixture. The samples analyzed were previously sputtered with gold.

### 2.4. Raman Spectroscopy

The Raman spectra of the carbon steel surface corrosion products were obtained using a Bruker Senterra II confocal Raman microscope, Karlsruhe, Germany, with a 50× long working distance objective. Raman excitation was performed with a Torus single frequency of 532 nm, continuous-wave laser at a laser power of 25 mW and a laser spot diameter of 2–3 μm. Spectra were collected in the 50–4250 cm**−**1 wavenumber range using a grating with 1200 lines/mm, with an acquisition time of 30 s. The calibration was automatic using SureCAL technology, Brucker, Karlsruhe, Germany. The peak positions were obtained using curve fitting in the Opus software (Base Package).

The samples were analyzed in their original form, without prior preparation, after 72 h of exposure to systems with single components (15 mg dm−3 CeCl3; 15 mg dm−3 IOA) and their mixtures (of 15 mg dm−3 CeCl3 and 15 mg dm−3 IOA).

### 2.5. Powder X-Ray Diffraction Analysis (PXRD)

The samples of pure carbon steel AISI 1018 and those of carbon steel after 72 h of exposure to the synthetic brine solution saturated with CO2 and with the addition of 15 mg dm−3 CeCl3 were analyzed using the powder method on a Panalytical Empyrean diffractometer, Malvern, UK. Copper radiation (Kα 1.541874 Å) was used for the analysis with the following recording conditions: U = 45 kV, I = 40 mA, scan area 3–70° 2Θ, step height 0.0131°, scan rate 0.041683°/s, primary beam divergence 1/2° and PIXcel3D-Medipix3 1 × 1 line detector. Recorded diffractograms were interpreted using the High Score Plus 4.9 (2020) computer program, which uses the PDF-2 database.

The effectiveness of the inhibitor was calculated from the corrosion rates according to Equation (2):where is the corrosion rate of carbon steel in the system without inhibitor, and is the corrosion rate of carbon steel in the system with individual inhibitor or in the presence of individual inhibitors’ mixtures.

The measured mass loss, i.e., the calculated corrosion rate of carbon steel in a chloride–carbonate solution saturated with CO2 at 60 °C is is in accordance with literature data [[47](#B47-coatings-15-00093)].

The corrosion rate of carbon steel in the presence of cerium(III) chloride is lower (from 0.52 mm year−1 to 0.56 mm year−1) compared to the uninhibited system (1.57 mm year−1); however, the corrosion rates and inhibitor effectiveness do not change significantly with increasing CeCl3 concentration ( from 0.52 mm year−1 to 0.56 mm year−1, i.e., IE from 64.24% to 66.88%). The lowest corrosion rate of carbon steel, i.e., the highest effectiveness with the addition of CeCl3, was achieved at a concentration of 10 mg/L (vcorr = 0.52 mm year−1, IE = 66.88 ± 0.15%).

The system in the presence of an imidazoline-based oleic acid inhibitor showed a decrease in the corrosion rate (from 1.02 mm year−1 to 0.17 mm year−1) and an increase in effectiveness (from 35.03% to 89.17%) with an increase in the concentration of the inhibitor (from 5 mg dm−3 to 20 mg dm−3). The highest inhibitory efficiency, IE = 89.17%, was achieved via IOA at a concentration of 20 mg/L.

The synergistic effect of the mixture of two compounds, IOA and CeCl3, as corrosion inhibitors is expressed through a synergistic parameter, S, which is determined according to Equation (3) [[48](#B48-coatings-15-00093),[49](#B49-coatings-15-00093)]:where IEIOA and are the inhibition efficiencies of individual compounds, respectively, while is the inhibition efficiency of a mixture of IOA and CeCl3. Values of the synergistic parameter greater than one indicate a synergistic effect of the compounds, while values less than one indicate their antagonistic action [[49](#B49-coatings-15-00093),[50](#B50-coatings-15-00093)].

Mixtures of compounds IOA and CeCl3, in most of combinations, show synergistic action (S > 1) and higher inhibitory effectiveness (from 81.53% to 96.82%) compared to individual components (IE is from 64.24% to 66.88% for CeCl3 and from 35.03% to 89.17% for IOA). The highest inhibitory efficiency, IE = 96.82%, was achieved at a mixture concentration of 15 mg/dm3 CeCl3 and 15 mg/dm3 IOA.

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

In all tested systems, in the presence of individual components, CeCl3 and IOA as well as their mixtures, a shift in corrosion potentials in the positive direction, an increase in polarization resistance values and a decrease in corrosion rates compared to the blank system were observed. The efficacies of the tested compounds as corrosion inhibitors, individually and in their mixture, were calculated from the corrosion rate values according to Equation (2). The synergistic effect of each compound’s mixture was calculated according to Equation (3).

In the case of IOA, an increase in polarization resistance, from 275.1 Ω cm−2 to 3555.1 Ω cm−2, with an increase in concentrations from 5 mg dm−3 to 20 mg dm−3 of IOA is observed. The corrosion rate decreases from 1.115 mm year**−**1 to 0.077 mm year**−**1, and the effectiveness of IOA as a corrosion inhibitor increases from 11.8% to 92.89%. IOA achieved its highest effectiveness, 92.89%, at a concentration of 20 mg dm−3.

The values of polarization resistances, Rp, for CeCl3 show an increase (from 508.4 Ω cm−2 to 3082.9 Ω cm−2) with an increasing concentration (from 5 mg dm−3 to 20 mg dm−3). The corrosion rates range from 0.232 mm year**−**1 to 0.055 mm year**−**1, and the effectiveness of CeCl3 as a corrosion inhibitor increases from 81.66% to 95.65%. In the system with CeCl3 as a corrosion inhibitor, the highest efficiency, 95.65%, was achieved at the highest concentration of the compound, 20 mg dm−3. Compared to the action of IOA alone, CeCl3 alone shows greater effectiveness in protecting AISI 1018 carbon steel from corrosion under the tested conditions.

Mixtures of 5 mg dm−3 CeCl3 and IOA (from 5 mg dm−3 to 20 mg dm−3) do not show an increase in polarization resistance compared to the individual components. However, at higher concentrations of CeCl3 (10 mg dm−3 and 15 mg dm−3) in mixtures with IOA (5 mg dm−3, 10 mg dm−3, 15 mg dm−3 and 20 mg dm−3), an increase in polarization resistances is observed compared to the individual components. In mixtures of 15 mg dm−3 CeCl3 added to IOA, the highest values of polarization resistance were achieved. Tests at the highest concentrations of the tested mixtures (20 mg dm−3 IOA in a mixture with 5 mg dm−3, 10 mg dm−3 and 15 mg dm−3 CeCl3) show a decrease in resistance compared to the values of polarization resistances achieved at previous lower concentrations. A possible explanation is that for organic compounds, which IOA is, a critical micellar concentration has been reached [[51](#B51-coatings-15-00093)]. The lowest corrosion rate, 0.026 mm year−1, and the highest inhibitory efficacy, 97.94%, were achieved in the presence of a mixture of 15 mg dm−3 CeCl3 and 15 mg dm−3 IOA. Although most combinations of CeCl3 and IOA mixtures show better performance in corrosion protection of AISI 1018 carbon steel under the tested conditions, compared to the individual components, a synergistic effect (S > 1) was demonstrated only for the 5 mg dm−3 CeCl3 and 5 mg dm−3 IOA combination.

The mechanism of CO2 carbon steel corrosion has been a controversial subject for decades. The system is very complex, involving many chemically and electrochemically active species in an acidic CO2/H2O system. CO2 dissolves in water, which then reacts chemically with water to form a weak carbonic acid, H2CO3, which dissociates in two steps. In the first step, it dissociates into a hydrogen ion, H+, and a bicarbonate ion, , which in the second step, dissociates into a hydrogen ion, H+, and a carbonate ion, , according to the following reactions:

Water as a solvent can dissociate according to the following reaction:

Under the tested conditions, the anodic corrosion reaction is the oxidation of iron from steel according to the following reaction:

Cathodic reactions of CO2 corrosion involve the reduction of the hydrogen ions, H+, either directly or via other weak acids present in the system (), according to the following reactions [[52](#B52-coatings-15-00093)]:

It was found that under the test conditions analogous to those in this work, carbonic acid affects the limiting cathodic current but has no effect on the charge transfer current. The charge transfer current depends only on pH, indicating that hydrogen ion reduction is the main cathodic reaction (this mechanism is called the “buffering effect”) according to Reaction 10. The direct reduction of carbonic acid is insignificant compared to the reduction of hydrogen ions [[52](#B52-coatings-15-00093),[53](#B53-coatings-15-00093)].

The polarization curve recorded on carbon steel after 24 h of exposure to the inhibitor-free system (black curve in [Figure 4](#fig_body_display_coatings-15-00093-f004) and [Figure 5](#fig_body_display_coatings-15-00093-f005)) shows cathodic corrosion currents partly influenced by mass transfer, while the anodic polarization curves show a linear dependence of current and potential, indicating a region of active dissolution, i.e., iron oxidation [[54](#B54-coatings-15-00093)].

In the presence of IOA, an inhibitory effect on the cathodic and anodic process was observed, i.e., a shift in the cathodic and anodic polarization curves towards lower values of the corrosion current density and thus lower corrosion rates. Such an inhibitory action is more pronounced with an increase in the concentration of IOA, which is evident from the polarization curves ([Figure 4](#fig_body_display_coatings-15-00093-f004)) as well as the kinetic parameters contained in [Table 3](#table_body_display_coatings-15-00093-t003). The slopes of the anodic Tafel lines in the presence of IOA change slightly (68.30 mV dec−1–94.09 mV dec−1) compared to the value of the slope in the uninhibited solution (75.01 mV dec−1), which points to the effect of IOA in the way that it adsorbs on the metal surface, blocks the active sites and prevents the anodic reaction from taking place rather than changing the mechanism of the anodic reaction [[13](#B13-coatings-15-00093),[14](#B14-coatings-15-00093),[51](#B51-coatings-15-00093)]. The dominant cathodic reduction reaction in the test conditions (CO2-saturated brine solution, pH ≈ 5) is the reduction of hydrogen ions produced via the dissociation of carbonic acid. The slope of the cathodic Tafel line of the uninhibited system is high (410.69 mV dec−1) in electrolytes due to the influence of diffusion of H+ ions on the cathodic reaction. In the presence of IOA, a decrease in the slope of the cathodic Tafel line (406.04 mV dec−1–152.81 mV dec−1) is observed, but it is still high, indicating the influence of diffusion on the cathodic process [[15](#B15-coatings-15-00093)]. In the presence of IOA, the corrosion potential is shifted towards more positive values (from −689 mV to −582 mV), which indicates a preference for inhibiting the anodic reaction and is associated with the formation of a protective film [[17](#B17-coatings-15-00093),[51](#B51-coatings-15-00093)]. At higher concentrations of IOA (from 10 mg dm−3 to 20 mg dm−3), the corrosion potential shift in the anodic direction is greater than 85 mV compared to the system without inhibitors, classifying it as an anodic type of corrosion inhibitor under the tested conditions [[18](#B18-coatings-15-00093),[19](#B19-coatings-15-00093),[20](#B20-coatings-15-00093),[21](#B21-coatings-15-00093),[22](#B22-coatings-15-00093),[23](#B23-coatings-15-00093),[51](#B51-coatings-15-00093)]. It slows down corrosion by reducing the rate of the anodic metal dissolution process. The values of inhibitory effectiveness, shown in [Table 2](#table_body_display_coatings-15-00093-t002), increase with the increase in IOA concentration and reach a maximum value of 94.61% at a concentration of 15 mg dm−3, which is attributed to the binding of imidazoline molecules to the metal surface. The structure of IOA ([Figure 2](#fig_body_display_coatings-15-00093-f002)a) shows the existence of delocalized electrons in the imidazole ring as well as a free electron pair on the nitrogen atoms. The adsorption of IOA on the surface of carbon steel AISI 1018 can be explained in the way that IOA can donate these π-electrons and free electron pairs to the empty d-orbitals of iron [[55](#B55-coatings-15-00093),[56](#B56-coatings-15-00093)].

The presence of CeCl3 causes a shift in the corrosion potential slightly in the positive direction (from −677 mV to −699 mV) compared to the blank system (−713 mV). At all tested CeCl3 concentrations, a displacement of the cathodic and anodic branches of the polarization curves towards lower corrosion currents is observed. The corrosion current densities (from 17.87 μA cm−2 to 4.67 μA cm−2) and corrosion rates (from 0.207 mm year−1 to 0.054 mm year−1) are significantly lower compared to the values recorded for the same concentrations in the presence of IOA (from 117.0 μA cm−2 to 6.72 μA cm−2 and from 1.358 mm year−1 to 0.078 mm year−1) and the blank system (124.6 μA cm−2, 1.446 mm year−1). CeCl3 significantly reduced the slope of the cathodic Tafel line (from 211.92 mV dec−1 to 117.50 mV dec−1) compared to the blank system (410.69 mV year−1), as shown in [Figure 4](#fig_body_display_coatings-15-00093-f004) and [Table 3](#table_body_display_coatings-15-00093-t003), indicating the effect of CeCl3 on the cathodic reaction. The sustained high slopes of the cathodic Tafel lines indicate the influence of diffusion on the cathodic reaction [[15](#B15-coatings-15-00093)]. The slopes of the anodic Tafel line are significantly lower (from 47.30 mV dec−1 to 23.37 mV dec−1) compared to the uninhibited system (75.01 mV dec−1), indicating an influence of CeCl3 on the anodic corrosion reaction of ferrous oxidation. The effectiveness of CeCl3 in protecting AISI 1018 carbon steel from corrosion increases with increasing concentration (from 5 mg dm−3 to 15 mg dm−3). However, a deviation from this trend was observed at the highest tested concentration (20 mg dm−3), where a slight increase in the corrosion rate and a decrease in inhibitory efficiency, compared to values at 15 mg dm−3 CeCl3, were observed, which can be explained by the increase in chloride concentration when adding a higher concentration of CeCl3 [[33](#B33-coatings-15-00093),[57](#B57-coatings-15-00093),[58](#B58-coatings-15-00093),[59](#B59-coatings-15-00093)]. CeCl3 showed the behavior of a mixed corrosion inhibitor with a predominant influence on the anodic process. The highest inhibitory efficiency, 96.27%, was shown by CeCl3 at a concentration of 15 mg dm−3, which potentially can be attributed to the formation of cerium carbonate under the tested conditions [[57](#B57-coatings-15-00093)].

The corrosion potential values for all tested compound mixtures show a shift in the anodic direction compared to the blank system (−713 mV). The range of corrosion potential for the compound mixtures ranges from −660 mV to −625 mV; in some mixtures, only a negligible increase in potential (slightly above 85 mV) compared to the uninhibited system was observed. The values of corrosion currents and corrosion rates are very low in the presence of the compounds′ mixtures, which are already at low concentrations of compounds. The slopes of the cathodic and anodic Tafel lines in the presence of the mixtures of compounds are comparable or lower to those determined in the systems with the individual components, indicating the effect of the mixtures of compounds on the cathodic and anodic corrosion reactions. The mixture of tested compounds blocks the metal surface and reduces the areas available for cathodic and anodic reactions to occur [[57](#B57-coatings-15-00093)]. From the above results, the mixture of CeCl3 and IOA compounds showed the activity of a mixed corrosion inhibitor with a significant effect on the anodic reaction of iron oxidation. The highest inhibitory efficiency, 97.78%, was shown by the mixture composed of 15 mg dm−3 CeCl3 and 15 mg dm−3 IOA. Most of the mixtures of compounds did not show synergistic action, since as individual components, they achieved high inhibitory efficiency. Nonetheless, an enhanced corrosion protection effect was certainly noted compared to individual compounds. This webpage is a scientific research article published in the MDPI journal "Coatings" (Volume 15, Issue 1, Article 93) in January 2025, titled "Individual and Joint Effect of Oleic Acid Imidazoline and CeCl3 on Carbon Steel Corrosion in CO2-Saturated Brine Solution." The paper is classified as an Open Access, Feature Paper, and Editor's Choice article.

**Authors & Affiliations:**
- Tihomir Borko (INA, d.d., Zagreb, Croatia)
- Gordana Bilić (Faculty of Mining, Geology and Petroleum Engineering, University of Zagreb) - corresponding author
- Katarina Žbulj (Faculty of Mining, Geology and Petroleum Engineering, University of Zagreb)
- Helena Otmačić Ćurković (Faculty of Chemical Engineering and Technology, University of Zagreb)

**DOI:** 10.3390/coatings15010093
**Submission/Publication dates:** Submitted 12 December 2024, Revised 8 January 2025, Accepted 12 January 2025, Published 15 January 2025.

**Objective:**
The study investigates the individual and synergistic corrosion inhibition effects of cerium chloride (CeCl3, 5-20 mg dm⁻³) and oleic acid imidazoline (IOA, 5-20 mg dm⁻³) on AISI 1018 carbon steel in a CO2-saturated simulated brine solution at 60 °C (representing average oil industry transport fluid temperature).

**Methodology:**
- Weight-loss testing per ASTM G-1 standard (72 h exposure)
- Electrochemical measurements: linear polarization (±10 mV), potentiodynamic polarization with Tafel extrapolation (±250 mV), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (100 kHz to ~10 mHz)
- Surface analyses: SEM with EDS, Raman spectroscopy, and powder X-ray diffraction
- The simulated brine solution (synthetic brine solution, SBS) contained 30.0 g dm⁻³ NaCl, 0.1 g dm⁻³ NaHCO3, and 0.1 g dm⁻³ CaCO3, pH 5.3, saturated with CO2
- The steel (AISI 1018) had a ferrite-pearlite microstructure with composition: 0.35 C, 0.35 Si, 1.09 Mn, 0.007 P, 0.024 S, 0.09 Cr, 0.07 Ni, 0.01 Mo, 0.10 Cu, <0.01 V, Fe balance

**Key Results:**
- CeCl3 alone showed IE from 57.58% to 96.27%; highest efficiency (96.27%) at 15 mg dm⁻³
- IOA alone showed IE from 3.43% to 94.61%; highest efficiency (94.61%) at 15 mg dm⁻³ (from potentiodynamic polarization)
- Mixtures showed higher efficiency (62.77% to 97.94%) compared to individual compounds
- Highest inhibitory efficiency (IE = 96.82% by mass loss; 97.94% by linear polarization; 97.78% by Tafel) was achieved at 15 mg dm⁻³ CeCl3 + 15 mg dm⁻³ IOA mixture
- A synergistic effect (S > 1) was demonstrated only for the lowest concentration combination (5 mg dm⁻³ CeCl3 + 5 mg dm⁻³ IOA), with S ≈ 1.07 and IE = 87.48%
- Corrosion rates: blank system ~1.446-1.57 mm year⁻¹; best mixture achieved 0.026 mm year⁻¹

**Mechanism:**
- IOA acts as an anodic-type inhibitor at higher concentrations, adsorbing on the metal surface via π-electrons and free electron pairs donated to empty d-orbitals of iron
- CeCl3 behaves as a mixed inhibitor with predominant influence on the anodic process; cerium carbonate likely forms protective film
- The proposed mechanism: imidazoline forms a surface film with voids via adsorption, while cerium carbonate fills these voids, creating a denser and thicker protective film
- The mixture acts as a mixed corrosion inhibitor with significant effect on the anodic iron oxidation reaction

**Context/Background:**
The research addresses CO2 corrosion in oil industry production and transportation systems, which is a major cause of pipeline rupture, economic losses, and ecological disasters. The study aligns with the "green chemistry" approach and the E3 concept (efficiency, economy, and ecology), as both rare earth salts (like CeCl3) and imidazolines are considered environmentally friendly corrosion inhibitors.

# Mercaptopropionic acid-modified oleic imidazoline as a highly efficient corrosion inhibitor for carbon steel in CO 2-saturated formation water

Author links open overlay panel Ziqi Zheng a, [Junying Hu a](https://www.sciencedirect.com/author/55499392900/junying-hu), [Noam Eliaz b](https://www.sciencedirect.com/author/7003877801/noam-eliaz), Li Zhou c, Xi Yuan c, [Xiankang Zhong a](https://www.sciencedirect.com/author/24339786700/xiankang-zhong)
