Fig. 1 shows the steel specimens after extraction from the FA mortars in the 130
presence and absence of chlorides for 720 days of experimentation. The steel specimens 131
embedded in the mortars without chlorides present tiny amounts of corrosion products 132
on a practically smooth surface, indicating that the steel was in the passive state in this 133
new cementitious system. The steel specimens extracted from the chloride-polluted 134
mortars present small fragments of the mortars on their surface and in some regions 135
corrosion product layers are also observed. The amount of corrosion products formed 136
was higher in the presence of 2% chlorides and the steel surface was fully coated in both 137
FAA and FAB mortars. 138
The Raman spectra of iron oxides/hydroxides can be divided into two regions 139
[26]: (i) 1200 to 600 cm−1 for both FeOH bending and FeO stretching vibration 140
regions; and (ii) 600 to 200 cm−1, this region includes absorptions overlapping of lattice 141
vibrations as well as molecular frequencies. FeO stretching vibrations can also be 142
absorbed below 400 cm−1. 143

In order to identify and locate the phases of the corrosion layers on the rebar, 256
including those poorly crystallised, investigations with Raman micro-spectroscopy have 257
been carried out in recent years. In such work the authors have always controlled the 258
laser power, because some iron oxides are very sensitive to laser exposure. Bouchar et 259
al. [28] used density filters to control the laser power on a sample under 100 μW. 260
Moreover, Singh et al. [29] observed that the Raman spectrum presented significant 261
noise when a laser power of less than 1.5 mW was used. El Mendili et al. [30] 262
investigated the stability of the γ-Fe2O3 nanoparticles under laser irradiation with laser 263
powers from 0.08 to 48 mW on the sample and thermal treatment (300-1400ºC). At 15 264
mW and 350ºC the vibration modes of maghemite had vanished and low intensity bands 265
attributed to the hematite phase appear in the Raman spectra. These vibration modes 266
became stronger with increase of the laser power and the thermal treatment. Thus the 267
laser power is a very important parameter when making measurements and it must also 268
be taken into account that the laser output needs to be modified depending on the 269
wavelength of the incident laser and the matrix studied. 270
Tables 2 and 3 show Raman peaks and the different iron corrosion products 271
formed in each cementitious matrix with different laser powers using wavelengths of 272
532 and 633 nm. According to Chitty et al. [31] the corrosion system was made up of a 273
multilayer structure constituted of a metallic substrate (M), a dense corrosion product 274
-- 11 of 31 --
12
layer (DPL), a transformed medium (TM) and a binder (B). In the light of Raman 275
results presented in this paper, different iron compounds and heterogeneous dense 276
corrosion product layers (DPL) were observed on the steel extracted from alkali 277
activated fly ash mortars. The type of iron phases formed was dependent on the type of 278
alkaline solution used in the activation of fly ash and the amount of chloride added to 279
the cementitious system, while the heterogeneous DPL was associate with the detection 280
of two regions: dark and light. The difference in the colour of the rusts was associated 281
with different thickness in the dense product layer. Previous authors also considered that 282
the DPL thicknesses increased with the age of the sample, however in our case 283
thickness depend on the aggressive solution. A higher thickness of DPL and detection 284
of more crystalline compounds were observed in the dark areas. The corrosion products 285
in the light regions were poor crystallized phases of iron oxyhydroxide while the 286
products in the dark regions were goethite, except for FAB mortar in the presence of 287
0.4% Cl¯ where lepidocrocite was formed. These results are in good agreement with 288
precedent data published on dense corrosion product layer of steel embedded in 289
concrete [5, 32]. However, neither Fe3O4, FeO nor akaganeite were detected in these 290
corrosion layers, no formation of the latter compound indicated that the amount of 291
chlorine was not enough in the DPL to stabilise this phase. Additionally Hostis et al. 292
[33] only found FeO, Fe3O4 as a tinny layer before embedded in concrete and the 293
corrosion phases formed were mainly iron oxyhydroxides (goethite). 294
Regarding the influence of the studied matrix (the type of alkaline solution used 295
in the activation of fly ash), it should be remembered that the FA was activated with two 296
alkaline solutions, one constituted only by NaOH (to manufacture FAA mortars) and 297
other consisting of a mixture of NaOH and waterglass (to manufacture the FAB 298
mortars). The matrix obtained with the solution containing a small amount of waterglass 299
-- 12 of 31 --
13
(15%) was denser and more compact, and therefore chloride ion mobility to the steel 300
surface was more hindered and the corrosion process was more restricted [34]. The iron 301
corrosion products formed on the steel surface embedded in the FAB mortars were iron 302
oxyhydroxides with low crystallinity, lepidocrocite and goethite, while poor crystallized 303
phases of iron oxyhydroxides and goethite were detected in those formed on the FAA 304
mortars. In addition, the aggressivity of the medium (the amount of chloride added to 305
the cementitious system: 0.4 and 2% chlorides) also affected the nature of the corrosion 306
products. In the FAB mortar with 0.4% chlorides (FAB0.4) with a dense matrix and 307
lower amount of chlorides, slightly aggressive medium, lepidocrocite was formed. 308
The goethite present in the DPL is considered electrochemically stable. In 309
contrast, lepidocrocite plays an active role in the corrosion mechanisms [35]. The 310
dissolution of this phase in the wet stages is facilitated by slightly acidic media, leading 311
to the dissolution of lepidocrocite and the precipitation of amorphous ferric 312
oxyhydroxide upon drying. Finally, the amorphous ferric oxyhydroxide is transformed 313
to goethite [36]. As such, the FAB mortar with 0.4% chlorides may be an insufficiently 314
aggressive medium to promote the evolution of the rust in just 720 days, compared to 315
the rest of the mortars, where the evolution of lepidocrocite to goethite has indeed taken 316
place. Therefore, the characteristics of the cementitious matrices and the percentage of 317
chloride ions influenced the nature of the iron phases. 318

could be obtained with laser powers between 0.025 and 0.25 mW for a wavelength of 321
532 nm (more energy) and with laser powers of 0.25 to 2.5 mW for a wavelength of 633 322
nm. 323

Conclusions 336
The main corrosion products generated on the surface of steel embedded in 337
activated fly ash mortars in the presence of chlorides were poorly crystallised phases of 338
iron oxyhydroxides, goethite (α-FeOOH) and lepidocrocite (-FeOOH). 339
The iron products formed should be studied with a laser line of 532 nm and a 340
power from 0.025 to 0.25 mW or with a laser line of 633 nm and a power greater than 341
2.5 mW. The spectra obtained with the 532 nm line and 0.0005 mW or with the 633 nm 342
line and 0.25 mW presented low resolution, no peak or only small peaks were detected. 343
For the wavelength of 532 nm the phases formed: oxyhydroxides with low 344
crystallinity, goethite and lepidocrocite, were transformed into hematite or modified 345
hematite at a power equal to or above 0.5 mW. The spectra recorded with this line with 346
5 mW showed fluorescence. 347

This is a scientific research paper (published in a materials science journal) by M. Criado, S. Martínez-Ramirez, and J.M. Bastidas from three CSIC institutes in Madrid, Spain. The study uses Raman spectroscopy to characterize corrosion products on reinforcing steel embedded in alkali-activated fly ash (AAFA) mortars containing 0.4% and 2% chlorides (NaCl added relative to binder weight).

**Methodology:**
- Carbon steel electrodes (0.45% C, 0.22% Si, 0.72% Mn, with traces of Cr, Ni, Cu) were embedded in type F fly ash mortars from Aboño, Asturias, Spain.
- The fly ash (51.78% SiO2, 27.80% Al2O3, 6.18% Fe2O3; 41.23% reactive silica; 65.60% vitreous phase) was activated using two alkaline solutions: (1) 8M NaOH (FAA mortars) and (2) 85% 10M NaOH + 15% waterglass (FAB mortars), with liquid/solid ratio of 0.45 and sand/AAFA ratio of 2:1.
- Mortars were cured at 85°C in saturated water vapor for 20 hours; specimens stored at ~95% RH for up to 720 days.
- Raman spectra were recorded directly on extracted steel surfaces using two excitation wavelengths (532 nm and 633 nm) with laser power scans (532 nm: 0.0005–5 mW; 633 nm: 0.25–25 mW).

**Key Findings:**
1. Steel in mortars without chlorides remained passive (tiny amounts of corrosion products); higher corrosion occurred with 2% chlorides.
2. Main corrosion products identified: iron oxyhydroxides with low crystallinity, goethite (α-FeOOH), and lepidocrocite (γ-FeOOH). Neither magnetite (Fe3O4), FeO, nor akaganeite were detected.
3. The 532 nm laser line caused transformation of corrosion products (oxyhydroxides, goethite, lepidocrocite) into hematite or "modified hematite" at powers ≥0.5 mW, and produced fluorescence at 5 mW (loss of peak definition).
4. The 633 nm laser line did NOT cause phase transformation or fluorescence — all phases remained stable under laser heat.
5. Optimal measurement conditions: 532 nm line at 0.025–0.25 mW, or 633 nm line at powers between 2.5–25 mW.
6. FAB mortars (with waterglass) produced a denser, more compact matrix that hindered chloride mobility and restricted corrosion. Corrosion products in FAB included lepidocrocite (especially at 0.4% chlorides), while FAA mortars yielded mainly low-crystallinity oxyhydroxides and goethite.
7. Dark regions on steel surfaces had thicker dense product layers and more crystalline compounds (goethite), while light regions had poorly crystallized oxyhydroxides. In FAB with 0.4% chlorides, lepidocrocite formed (an electrochemically active phase that typically evolves to goethite).
8. The nature of iron phases depended on the alkaline activator type and chloride content, with the FAB 0.4% chloride system being insufficiently aggressive to evolve lepidocrocite to goethite within 720 days.

## Abstract

The application of Raman spectroscopy in the study of the corrosion of steel reinforcement in concrete is critically reviewed. The Raman effects of all the possible products formed during passivation and corrosion are individually reviewed first with an attempt to identify the characteristic peaks and corresponding assignments, which could potentially be a useful reference for future application. The capability of Raman spectroscopy in characterising the passivation and corrosion process under real conditions are then demonstrated and critically reviewed. Finally, the challenges and potential solutions of using Raman spectroscopy are discussed together with some perspectives for future work.

This webpage is a critical review article titled "Application of Raman Spectroscopy in the study of the corrosion of steel reinforcement in concrete: A critical review," published in Cement and Concrete Composites (Volume 143, Article 105231, October 2023) by Elsevier. The article is open access under a Creative Commons license and was authored by Tangwei Mi, Jing Jing Wang, Colum McCague, and Yun Bai. The DOI is 10.1016/j.cemconcomp.2023.105231.

The review critically examines the use of Raman spectroscopy for studying corrosion of steel reinforcement in concrete. The article is structured around several key sections: (1) an introduction, (2) background, (3) Raman spectra of possible products formed during passivation and corrosion of mild steel, (4) characterisation of passivation and corrosion processes of reinforcing steel using Raman spectroscopy, (5) challenges and potential solutions, (6) perspectives for future research, and (7) concluding remarks.

Key content areas include: the Raman effects of all possible products formed during passivation and corrosion (reviewed individually to identify characteristic peaks and assignments), the capability of Raman spectroscopy to characterise passivation and corrosion under real conditions, and discussion of challenges with potential solutions for future work. The article contains 33 figures and 14 tables covering Raman shifts for ferrous hydroxide, wüstite, magnetite, green rust (GR), and other corrosion products. The article has been cited 77 times and has 74 Mendeley readers and 1 news mention. Data availability is noted as available on request.
args.key_excerpts: "The application of Raman spectroscopy in the study of the corrosion of steel reinforcement in concrete is critically reviewed. The Raman effects of all the possible products formed during passivation and corrosion are individually reviewed first with an attempt to identify the characteristic peaks and corresponding assignments, which could potentially be a useful reference for future application."

### Key Takeaways

*    Silicate network depolymerization by modifiers creates non-bridging oxygens, and Raman band evolution (Q3–Q0) provides a practical readout of connectivity and composition-dependent structure. 
*    Additives such as CaO, MgO, and Al2O3 improve chemical durability, while B2O3 lowers thermal expansion and enhances thermal-shock resistance in borosilicate formulations. 
*    Chemical strengthening via Na+/K+ ion exchange in molten salts generates surface compression in thin plates but is process-intensive; Gorilla Glass has progressed through multiple generations toward glass-ceramic variants. 
*    Confocal/depth-profile Raman can interrogate device stacks in situ, showing near-surface spectral shifts consistent with ion diffusion and identifying underlying PET-like layers, inorganic crystallinity, and unexpected carbon films. 
*    Nuclear-waste immobilization by vitrification demands engineered durability and impermeability over geologic timescales, positioning spectroscopic structure–property correlations as a useful optimization tool for waste-form design.

**Because its properties can be controlled by composition and manufacturing history, glass has been used since the Stone Age when obsidian was chipped to make sharp objects for hunting and cutting. The Romans actually manufactured glass for holding and storing liquids. But we are interested in modern uses, where the physical and chemical properties can be controlled with composition and history. Because of its transparency in the visible region of the spectrum, glass is used for containers, windows, electronic devices, and optics. However, common glasses are quite brittle: They can easily shatter, producing large, sharp shards that can destroy the products’ uses and are quite dangerous. Raman spectroscopy has been used for more than 50 years to follow the changes in the structure of glasses with composition. In this column, we survey what is known and how Raman spectroscopy has been applied to the development of materials important to technology.**

## **Introduction and Background**

Glasses are solid amorphous materials without the long-range order of crystals. They are often formed by melt-quenching a supercooled liquid, and the ability to form a glass during rapid cooling is known as its glass-forming ability. Although glasses can be formed from a variety of metal oxides (or even sulfides), we will consider silicate-based glasses here. Valence considerations determine that each silicon atom is bound to four oxygen atoms, but the angles included at the silicon atoms are distorted from those in crystalline phases. Although pure amorphous silica (SiO 2) is a useful material, especially for fiber optics, it is difficult to use for many applications because of its high melting temperature and high fabrication costs. Consequently, many glasses contain alkali and alkaline elements, aluminum, and boron.

As one can imagine, the physical and chemical properties will reflect the elemental composition. Many common glasses based on alkali or alkaline earth elements are susceptible to corrosion. Consequently, CaO, MgO, and Al 2 O 3 are added to improve chemical stability. Boron trioxide (B 2 O 3) is also used to improve glass physical characteristics: it lowers thermal expansion, making it useful for applications where the glass will experience large thermal excursions.

Raman spectra have been measured by many authors to understand the structures that determine the properties. McMillan published extensive spectra of these glasses in the early 1980s, showing composition and polarization dependence.1,2 A more recent publication of the MgO/CaO sodium aluminosilicate glasses follows the Raman spectra as a function of composition 3; one of the authors is John Mauro, who was at Corning when the article was published but is now head of the Materials Science and Engineering group at Pennsylvania State University. He continues to collaborate with Corning on the improvements to Gorilla Glass, originally used for cell phone covers in 2007, which will be discussed later in this article.

The spectra of glasses have been interpreted in terms of the connectivity of the glass network. Any SiO 2 structure will have four Si–O bonds at each silicon atom when, for example, alkali ions are added to silica, the Si–O–Si bonds are broken, leaving SiO NB bonds, where NB denotes non-bridging oxygen. There can be three, two, one, or zero bonding oxygens (BOs). McMillan and Piriou 4 in their Figure 4 summarize the Raman behavior for =Si=, ≡SiO, = SiO 2, -SiO 3, and SiO 4; bands appear respectively at 450, 800, and 1050–1250 cm-1; 500–600, 775, and 1050 cm-1; 500–650 and 1000 cm-1; 700 and 900 cm-1; and 850 cm-1. Almeida and Santos denote non-bonding oxygen bands Q 3, Q 2, Q 1, Q 0, and these can be followed in the spectra of sodium silicate glasses.5 In Figure 3.4 of Reference 5, Q 3 appears near 1100 cm-1 for 60–90% silicate. Q 2 appears near 950 cm-1 for 50–70% silicate. Another band between 520 and 650 cm-1 appears for glasses with 50–80% silicate. Figure 3.4 in Reference 5 conveniently illustrates the appearance and shift of these bands in a sodium silicate glass as a function of sodium concentration.

The Raman spectra of alkali borosilicate glasses have been studied by Osipov et al.6 In this system, there are Q 4, Q 3, (BO 4/2]- tetrahedrons, BO 3/2 triangles, and BØ 2/2 O- triangles (at low SiO 2 content).

For technology applications such as electronic devices, including cell phone covers, the biggest problem is the susceptibility to fractures. Although the theoretical tensile strength of glass is higher than that of many metals, the presence of microscopic flaws, such as scratches on the surface, leads to susceptibility to fracture. Techniques for toughening have been developed to make glasses robust against fracture.

An early method for toughening glass, especially for car windshields, was to sandwich two glass layers around a layer of polymer with the same index of refraction as the glass. Because of the index match, there are no ghost images. This is called laminated glass. When it breaks, it breaks into granular chunks, which are less likely to cause penetration than jagged shards.

Glass can also be tempered with a thermal tempering process. It is heated above its glass transition temperature and cooled rapidly with forced air drafts so quickly that the inner portion remains molten.

However, the big breakthrough for toughening the glass was to ion-exchange the sodium-containing finished glass piece in a molten alkali salt, such as KNO 3, where K+ ions replace Na+ ions at the surface.7 The larger K+ ions produce compression at the surface of plates as thin as 100 µm. Typical conditions are ~475°C for 16 h, making this an expensive process.8 The process was developed at Corning in the early 1960s and used on the original Apple iPhone in June 2007 under the brand name Gorilla Glass. Since its first use, Gorilla Glass has undergone at least 10 generations of improvements, which included the use of glass ceramics in January 2025.9 Glass ceramics are mixtures of crystalline and amorphous phases, which are heat-treated for controlled nucleation and are also resistant to thermal shock because of the thermal expansion coefficient of the crystalline phase being negative and that of the amorphous phase being positive. At approximately 70% crystallinity, the thermal expansion coefficient is close to 0, and the material can tolerate temperature changes up to 1000 °C.

The next section presents representative spectra of several glasses, illustrating how Raman spectroscopy can be useful for characterizing these materials. And then, we show some spectra of Gorilla glasses, indicating the engineering developed to harden them.

## **Raman Spectra of Some Glasses**

Figures 1a and 1b show the Raman spectra of seven glasses and crystalline quartz as examples of the Raman spectra of some of these materials. From top to bottom are spectra of a glass frying pan, a microscope slide, a drinking glass, a small laboratory glass container, then labware, colloidal silica, tetrasil (amorphous quartz) and crystalline quartz at the bottom. The spectra were all acquired with the 532 nm green laser and full-scale spectra are shown in Figure 1a out to 4000 cm-1. Clearly, some of the spectra have significant backgrounds, which will appear different when excited at different wavelengths. Glasses with alkali composition especially will often show these fluorescent backgrounds because of small amounts of iron contamination. To compare spectra, use of a green laser for excitation is recommended if possible. In addition, expansion of the spectrum of colloidal silica in the 3600 cm-1 region shows clear evidence for OH functionality. The region below 1400 cm-1 for all the glasses is expanded in Figure 1b to more clearly show the differences that reflect their varying compositions.

In summary, the spectra in Figure 1 indicate that the Raman spectra even of amorphous materials with broad bands can be useful in estimating the composition of glasses. Unfortunately, I do not have a set of glasses of known composition that I could have measured for identification purposes, so if you are going to use Raman spectra to study glasses, I recommend that you acquire the publications that I have cited, as well as others of relevance.

## **Gorilla Glass**

Having established that Raman spectra can be used to identify commercial materials, I wanted to measure Gorilla Glass and confirm what the literature says is the origin of the mechanical strength. However, since I do not have access to materials except in my Horiba (iPhone 14) and personal (iPhone 15) phones, and I did not want to peel off the protection cover, I looked for a way to measure the phone’s glass _in situ_.

Figure 2 shows the results of measuring a depth profile of the glass next to the protector on the front face of my iPhone 14. On the bottom right are the spectra that I extracted using classical least squares (CLS). Although multiple curve resolution (MCR) is often useful in this case, I could see the glass spectrum changing as I surfed the file, but the changes were too subtle to be captured by MCR. It appeared that the thickness of the spectrum of the glass on the top surface was approximately 20 µm. Interestingly, the difference between that spectrum and the spectrum of the bulk glass is subtly different, which may not be too surprising for a soda alkali glass into which potassium had diffused. Note that my goal was only to see evidence for potassium diffusion. If you want to use the spectra to characterize physical characteristics, a more extensive study would be needed. For a start spectra of glasses with known potassium and sodium, the compositions need to be recorded as references, and if you are trying to engineer a glass, you will need to understand what the Raman spectra are saying about the atomic connectivity.

## **Summary and Discussion**

The Raman spectra of glasses exhibit bands that are quite broad, but a review of the literature, coupled with some representative spectra, shows that the spectra can be used to differentiate glasses of different compositions. By comparing the spectra of glasses with systematically varying compositions, researchers have been able to characterize the types of bonding in the glass-forming network as composition is varied. Our goal at the beginning of this project was to document the diffusion of potassium into soda alkali glasses for the Gorilla Glass covers of cell phones. However, the technology has been changing rapidly, so we were also able to document the presence of polymers, inorganic crystals, and even carbon films in these protective layers.

I would also like to make some further comments about a unique contemporary use of glass. As of October 2025, site managers at the Hanford Tank Waste Treatment and Immobilization Plant have begun sealing medium- and low-level nuclear waste in glass for storage in stainless steel containers for geological disposal.11 Because radioactive isotopes last for tens of thousands of years, there are significant challenges involved in storing this material. These include chemical durability and impermeability to avoid leaching radioactive elements into groundwater. The composition and method for vitrification have to be engineered to fulfill these requirements. Scientists have been working on this since the 1970s, considering both glasses and ceramics for this purpose.12,13 The cited articles provide a wealth of information on what has been done so far and where in the world ongoing activity is taking place. There is no Raman information in these publications, but the materials engineer who wants to optimize a glass (or ceramic) formula could determine which material parameters are important for this application and then use Raman spectroscopy to characterize what is being made.

This article, published May 18, 2026 in the Molecular Spectroscopy Workbench column of Spectroscopy Online, is authored by Fran Adar and examines how Raman spectroscopy has been applied to understanding glass structure and its contemporary technological uses.

**Key Points:**

**Introduction/Background:**
- Glasses are amorphous solids without long-range crystalline order, typically formed by melt-quenching supercooled liquids. Silicate-based glasses are the focus, though glasses can form from various metal oxides.
- Pure amorphous silica (SiO2) has high melting temperature and fabrication costs, so alkali, alkaline earth, aluminum, and boron are added to modify properties.
- CaO, MgO, and Al2O3 improve chemical stability/corrosion resistance; B2O3 lowers thermal expansion and improves thermal-shock resistance.
- Raman interpretation is based on glass network connectivity: adding alkali ions breaks Si–O–Si bonds, creating non-bridging oxygens (NB). Bands are designated Q3, Q2, Q1, Q0. Q3 appears near 1100 cm-1 (60-90% silicate), Q2 near 950 cm-1 (50-70% silicate), with additional bands between 520-650 cm-1.
- Key literature includes McMillan's early 1980s spectra, Almeida and Santos' work, Osipov et al. on alkali borosilicate glasses, and Bechgaard et al. (2017) on MgO/CaO sodium aluminosilicate glasses (with co-author John Mauro, now at Penn State, who collaborates with Corning).

**Glass Toughening Technologies:**
- Laminated glass: two glass layers sandwiching a polymer layer with matching refractive index to avoid ghost images; breaks into granular chunks.
- Thermal tempering: heating above glass transition temperature and rapid cooling.
- Chemical strengthening via ion exchange: Na+ ions in glass replaced by larger K+ ions from molten KNO3 at ~475°C for ~16 hours, producing surface compression in plates as thin as 100 µm. This is an expensive process developed at Corning in the early 1960s.
- Gorilla Glass was first used on the original Apple iPhone in June 2007. It has undergone at least 10 generations of improvements, including glass ceramics (January 2025, Corning Gorilla Armor 2). Glass ceramics combine crystalline and amorphous phases, are resistant to thermal shock, and at ~70% crystallinity have near-zero thermal expansion, tolerating temperature changes up to 1000°C.

**Raman Spectra of Representative Glasses:**
- Figure 1 shows spectra of seven glasses and crystalline quartz (acquired with 532 nm green laser): a Corning glass frying pan, microscope slide, drinking glass, lab container, labware (PYREX), colloidal silica, tetrasil (amorphous quartz), and crystalline quartz.
- Glass frying pan spectrum matches borosilicate cooking glass composition (~80% SiO2, 13% B2O3, 4% Na2O/K2O, 2-3% Al2O3).
- Microscope slide and drinking glass spectra are essentially identical, matching soda lime glass.
- Lab container spectrum matches CaO/MgO-Na2O-Al2O3-SiO2 glasses with Al2O3 at 10.7%, SiO2 at 65.2-65.3%, Na2O at 15.7-15.8%, CaO or MgO at 8%.
- Labware (PYREX) matches borosilicate glass with 80.54% SiO2, 12.70% B2O3, 3.54% Na2O, 0.64% K2O, 2.53% Al2O3.
- Colloidal silica spectrum is similar to amorphous silica but lacks defect bands near 490 and 610 cm-1, and shows OH bands between 3550-3800 cm-1.
- Alkali-containing glasses often show fluorescent backgrounds due to iron contamination; green laser excitation is recommended.

**Gorilla Glass In Situ Analysis:**
- Depth-profile Raman spectroscopy was performed on iPhone 14 and iPhone 15 screens in situ without removing protective covers.
- iPhone 14: The glass spectrum on the top surface was ~20 µm thick. Subtle differences between surface and bulk glass spectra are consistent with potassium diffusion into a soda alkali glass. Below the glass layer were two polyester layers: a classic PET (polyethylene terephthalate) layer and a layer with PET bands at different intensities.
- iPhone 15: MCR analysis identified layers including PET, an inorganic crystalline phase, and—surprisingly—a film of amorphous carbon at approximately 400 µm depth.
- iPhone 14 camera cover plate was identified as sapphire (hard phase of Al2O3) with a thin glass layer underneath; sapphire is used for small plates because it is hard and feasible to manufacture at that size, but prohibitively expensive for full front surfaces.

**Nuclear Waste Vitrification:**
- As of October 2025, the Hanford Tank Waste Treatment and Immobilization Plant began sealing medium- and low-level nuclear waste in glass for storage in stainless steel containers for geological disposal.
- Radioactive isotopes last tens of thousands of years, requiring engineered chemical durability and impermeability to prevent leaching into groundwater.
- Scientists have worked on this since the 1970s, considering both glasses and ceramics. Raman spectroscopy is positioned as a useful tool for optimizing waste-form design, though cited articles on this topic contain no Raman data directly.

**References cited include:** McMillan & Piriou (1982, 1983), Bechgaard et al. (2017), Almeida & Santos (2015), Osipov et al. (2013), Kistler (1962), Varshneya (2010), Corning Gorilla Armor 2 announcement (January 2025), Manghnani et al. (2011), Samuels/C&EN (2026), Thorpe et al. (2021), and Gregg et al. (2025).
args.key_excerpts: "Silicate network depolymerization by modifiers creates non-bridging oxygens, and Raman band evolution (Q3–Q0) provides a practical readout of connectivity and composition-dependent structure." — Key Takeaways

## Abstract

In this study, carbon quantum dots (CQDs) were successfully synthesized from garlic peel, with size dimensions confirmed by TEM and DLS analyses and photochemical properties validated by UV–vis and fluorescence spectroscopy. FTIR revealed chemical similarities with the precursor, while XPS revealed the presence of nitrogen and sulfur, indicating endogenous doping. The anticorrosive performance of the CQDs was demonstrated through gravimetric, electrochemical impedance, potentiodynamic polarization, and surface analyses including scanning electron microscopy, atomic force microscopy, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy. The CQDs exhibited high inhibition efficiencies with sustained performance over time, achieving maximum inhibition efficiencies of 79% for 2 h and 96% for 24 h, as determined by gravimetric studies. This inhibition was primarily mediated through physical interactions, as indicated by temperature-dependent studies. Electrochemical measurements further confirm that the CQDs act as mixed-type inhibitors, exhibiting a predominant anodic effect. Surface analyses confirmed the formation of a protective and hydrophobic film on the steel surface. XPS, DLS, and zeta potential studies, along with Arrhenius equation analysis, demonstrated that the film forms through physical and chemical interactions between mild steel and quantum dot aggregates. These findings highlight the potential of using agro-industrial waste, such as garlic peel, as a sustainable precursor for the synthesis of effective corrosion inhibitors.

---

---

## 1. Highlights

* 1.

  Synthesized carbon quantum dots (CQDs) from garlic peel using acid hydrolysis.
* 2.

  Achieved up to 79 and 96% inhibition efficiency for mild steel in 1 mol L–1 HCl after 2 and 24 h, respectively.
* 3.

  The inhibition mechanism involves both physical and chemical interactions between CQD aggregates and the steel surface.
* 4.

  Surface analysis revealed hydrophobic protective film formation by CQDs on steel, reducing metal dissolution.
* 5.

  Presents a sustainable and potential use of agro-waste to produce carbon quantum dots and effective inhibitors of corrosion.

## 2. Introduction

Mild steel (MS) is one of the most widely used materials in the industry due to its low cost, mechanical properties, the possibility of recycling, and machinability without losing its properties. *,*  Therefore, it is widely used in the industry, especially in the oil industry. MS is the standard pipeline material that transports oil, gas, water, and other fluids. The transportation of such products favors corrosion and incrustation (formation of oxides), which slows or prevents the passage of fluids.

One way to avoid this problem is to acid pickle MS to remove oxides. *,,*  Hydrochloric acid is usually used in this method due to its low cost and ability to form water-soluble metal chlorides. *,,*  Despite the procedure’s effectiveness, the acid corrodes the steel, causing damage to industrial pipelines. *,,*  Therefore, the industry makes extensive expenditures for repairing and replacing pipes. *−*

Organic corrosion inhibitors are widely used to minimize metal degradation. These compounds act by adsorbing onto the metal surface, forming a protective layer that prevents direct contact with the corrosive medium, protecting the active corrosion sites. *,*  These molecules are present in their structure compounds such as N, S, P, and/or O that allow adsorption onto the carbon steel surface by physical and/or chemical interactions. Other characteristics, such as multiple bonds and aromatic rings, also increase interactions. *,*

Thus, carbon quantum dots (CQDs), which are nanoparticles smaller than 10 nm, are excellent candidates as corrosion inhibitors due to their potential richness in functional groupsdepending on the synthesis method and starting materialswhich allows for easy modification of their chemical structure.

In recent years, certain research groups have taken a green approach by developing methodologies for synthesizing CQDs derived from biomass residues. *−*  The use of raw materials is favorable to the environment and the inhibitory efficiency of the synthesized CQDs, as the organic residue is rich in O, N, P, and S. *−*  With the increase in population, food production grows exponentially, resulting in the production of large amounts of agro-industrial waste that often goes untreated, thereby increasing environmental pollution.

Recent literature has highlighted various biomass sources for CQD synthesis with effective corrosion inhibition properties. For example, pitaya and grapefruit peels have yielded CQDs with inhibition efficiencies above 94% in hydrochloric acid environments, demonstrating their assertive protective behavior against corrosive attacks on mild steel surfaces. *,*  Zheng et al. reported that CQDs synthesized from biomass waste can self-assemble on metal surfaces, forming uniform and adherent protective films that hinder electrolyte access and reduce corrosion rates. Long et al. and Kamaruzzaman et al. further advanced the field by developing CQDs doped with nitrogen and sulfur, demonstrating improved corrosion resistance due to enhanced surface interactions with the metal substrate, which confirmed the role of heteroatom doping in the inhibitor performance. *,*  Furthermore, recent studies by Zamindar et al. and Verma et al. have emphasized green synthesis approaches for CQDs, highlighting the importance of using environmentally benign precursors while achieving high corrosion inhibition efficiencies, thereby aligning with global sustainability goals. *,*  These advancements demonstrate the versatility of CQDs from various biomass sources and reinforce the ongoing trend toward ecofriendly and high-performance corrosion inhibitors.

Despite the advances, few studies have thoroughly investigated garlic peel, a high-sulfur agricultural waste, as a precursor for CQDs for corrosion protection. Garlic (*Allium sativum*) is used in many cultures worldwide as a food seasoning and has been cultivated on a large scale for centuries. *,*  Garlic peel is generated as waste during garlic processing and contributes to environmental pollution, like most agro-industrial waste. *,−*  Approximately 3.3 billion tons of CO2 are generated from untreated agro-industrial waste each year, which increases the greenhouse effect and, consequently, global warming. Part of the CO2 released comes from burning waste from garlic production, which amounts to 3.5 million tons annually.

A range of bioactive compounds is found in garlic bulbs and skin, primarily aromatic compounds and organosulfur compounds, including flavonoids, polyphenols, allicin, and alliin, as well as polysaccharides, which can facilitate the incorporation of several functional groups into the structure of CQDs. Such compositional characteristics and the high carbon content of garlic skin are desirable in CQDs, making the residue an excellent candidate as a precursor for synthesizing carbon quantum dots with compositional sulfur.

Therefore, this work aimed to produce CQDs from garlic (*A. sativum*) peel and their application as a green corrosion inhibitor for mild steel in a 1 mol L–1 HCl solution, a low-carbon technology that can reduce part of the burning and pollution associated with waste from garlic production.

## 3. Materials and Methods

### 3.1. Carbon Quantum Dot Synthesis

For the synthesis of carbon quantum dots, 1 g of previously crushed garlic peel (*A. sativum*) was added to a round-bottom flask with 20 mL of 1 mol L–1 sulfuric acid solution prepared from 98% sulfuric acid (purchased from ISOFAR). The mixture was heated under reflux in a heating mantle at 200 °C for 2 h and then filtered through a 0.45 μm pore-size membrane to remove residues of garlic peel and large particles. The filtered solution was dialyzed for 48 h using a 1 kDa membrane with a capacity of 20 mL (PUR-A-LYZER) to remove smaller residues, with water exchange twice daily. Subsequently, vacuum filtration filtered the solution through a 0.22 μm pore membrane (KASVI) to remove the remaining solid residues. Afterward, the remaining solution was dried with a rotary evaporator. The dried material was resuspended as a stock solution of 1 mg mL–1. This method yielded approximately 10% of the produced CQD. ### 3.2. Characterization

The morphological characteristics, chemical composition, and optical properties of quantum dots were analyzed by using several techniques, such as transmission electron microscopy (TEM), dynamic light scattering (DLS), Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, Raman spectroscopy, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), Zeta potential measurement, UV–vis spectroscopy, and fluorimetry.

TEM investigation was performed by dropping the carbon quantum dot (CQD) solution onto a lacey carbon-coated copper grid (Cu grid). The characterization was carried out by using a JEOL JEM-2100 Plus transmission electron microscope, operating at an accelerating voltage of 200 kV.

DLS measurements were conducted with an Anton Paar Litesizer 500, utilizing a 0.2 mg mL–1 dispersion of CQDs in DMF. FTIR analysis was performed on a Nicolet 6700 FTIR spectrometer, with samples prepared in KBr and spectra recorded in the 400 to 4000 cm–1 range. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was performed using an ultrahigh vacuum system (ScientaOmicron) with a nonmonochromatic Al Kα X-ray source (hν = 1486.6 eV), operating at 15 kV and 20 mA. The survey scan covered an energy range from 0 to 1100 eV, while high-resolution spectra were obtained based on the sample composition at an energy setting of 30 eV.

Raman spectra were collected using a Confocal Raman Microscope (SENTERRA II) with a 532 nm laser excitation. The UV–vis spectrum was measured from 200 to 700 nm with a Shimadzu UV-1800 spectrophotometer, and fluorescence measurements were taken by using a Shimadzu RF 5301 cuvette fluorimeter. Fluorometric analysis employed excitation wavelengths in increments of 300 to 500 nm. For these experiments, a 0.2 mg mL–1 suspension was used for the UV–vis analysis, and a 1 mg mL–1 suspension was used for the fluorescence spectroscopy.

Lastly, the stability of the particles was assessed through Zeta potential measurements using an Anton Paar Litesizer 500. Samples at a concentration of 1 mg mL–1 in Milli-Q water underwent 60 runs at a potential of 200 V and a temperature of 25 °C.

### 3.3. Mild Steel Surface Preparation

The corrosion tests utilized mil steel with the following composition: carbon (C), 0.18%; manganese (Mn), 0.30%; phosphorus (P), 0.04%; sulfur (S), 0.05%, with trace amounts of silicon (Si) and iron (Fe) making up the balance. Before the corrosion analyses were conducted by gravimetry, the mild steel plates, each with a surface area of approximately 13 cm2, were polished using sandpaper with grits of 100, 320, and 600 mesh. After abrading, the plates were thoroughly cleaned with deionized water. A smaller mild steel plate with a surface area of about 0.8 cm2 was employed for the electrochemical tests.

### 3.6. Surface Analysis

The effect of corrosive media on the surface of mild steel was assessed by using contact angle measurements, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), atomic force microscopy (AFM), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS).

Scanning electron microscopy images were acquired using a FEG-SEM JEOL JSM-IT700HR microscope, operated at 5 kV with secondary electron detection. To determine the hydrophobicity of the surfaces, contact angles were measured with an automatic tensiometer (Teclis Instrument, France) fitted with a 2.11 mm diameter aluminum needle. Measurements were performed at room temperature (20.3 °C) and 56% relative humidity. 2 μL of ultrapure water (resistivity 18.2 MΩ cm) was placed on each surface to evaluate the surface homogeneity. The needle and syringe were thoroughly cleaned before each measurement. For each sample, three independent measurements were taken at different spots. The contact angle was recorded once the droplet reached a stable shape, typically around 25 s after deposition. The final contact angle values were averaged to provide a representative result.

AFM imaging was conducted using a NanoWizard instrument from JPK, operating in intermittent contact mode with a silicon probe with a spring constant of 3 N m–1 and a resonance frequency of approximately 70 kHz. The root-mean-square (RMS) surface roughness was calculated for 30 mm × 30 mm images using the JPK software to estimate surface texture. The RMS values were derived from the average of 10 measurements.

X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy was conducted using an ultrahigh vacuum system (Specs System equipped with a Phoibos 150 Hemispherical analyzer) with a nonmonochromatic Al Kα X-ray source (hν = 1486.6 eV), operating at 15 kV and 20 mA. The survey scan covered an energy range from 0 to 1100 eV, while high-resolution spectra were obtained based on the sample composition at an energy setting of 30 eV.

## 4. Results and Discussion

### 4.1. Carbon Quantum Dot Characterization

One important physical property for characterizing carbon quantum dots (CQDs) is their size, typically less than 10 nm in diameter. Therefore, the nanomaterials produced were characterized by TEM and DLS. As shown in [Figure](#fig2) A, the sample exhibits a narrow size distribution. Additionally, [Figure](#fig2) B confirms that the synthesized particles are smaller than 10 nm. In both images, the absence of lattice fringes suggests that the material has an amorphous nature. From the TEM image, a histogram ([Figure](#fig2) C) of the obtained nanomaterials was created, revealing that the carbon quantum dots were successfully produced and had an average size of 3.17 ± 0.07 nm.

In addition to having a size smaller than 10 nm, photoluminescence is another essential characteristic of carbon quantum dots (CQDs). [Figure](#fig4)  illustrates the emission spectrum of CQDs synthesized at different excitation wavelengths. This figure highlights the photoluminescent behavior of the CQDs. Three distinct emission peaks are observed when the sample is excited with UV light at wavelengths of 300, 310, and 320 nm. These peaks indicate the presence of CQD particles with varying sizes, as shown in [Figure](#fig2) , which produces different excitation peaks. *,*  Other excitation wavelengths also fail to show emission focused on a single peak, further suggesting diversity in nanoparticle sizes in aqueous media, thereby supporting the results obtained from dynamic light scattering (DLS). The highest emission intensity occurs at 440 nm when excited with UV light at a wavelength of 340 nm. As the UV excitation wavelength increases, the corresponding peak shifts to longer emission wavelengths, resulting in a consequent decrease in the intensity. The other emission peaks exhibit similar behavior, indicating that the synthesized CQDs have an irregular distribution of functional groups on their surfaces. *−*  Thus, it is possible to say that the emission wavelength of the produced CQD is directly dependent on the excitation wavelength of the UV light. Considering that the highest emission spectrum occurs at a high energy wavelength (340 nm), it is possible to say that its bandgap is also high, a characteristic only possible for smaller than 10 nm, which proves once again the synthesis of CQD.

The elemental composition is a crucial aspect for the application of CQDs as corrosion inhibitors, as the presence of functional groups can facilitate the adsorption of CQDs on the metal surface, thereby directly influencing the inhibitory activity. *,,*  The chemical and structural information on CQDs synthesized from garlic peel can be observed in the FTIR spectrum ([Figure](#fig5) ). From the spectrum, it is possible to perceive several bands in the garlic peel and the CQD synthesized from it. A broad and intense band is observed in both spectra at 3440 cm–1, indicating the presence of axial deformation vibrations of O–H and N–H, which suggests the existence of amino and/or hydroxyl groups on the CQD surface. *−*  The band at 2930 cm–1 can be associated with the axial deformation vibration of the C–H bond. *−*  The band wavelengths of 1620 and 1425 cm–1 correspond to the vibrations of CC bonds, indicating the presence of aromatic ring systems within the CQD structure. The bands at 1425 and 1620 cm–1 can also be associated with the vibrations of the axial deformation of the CN bond and the carbonyl group (CO), respectively. *,,*  Additionally, a small band at 1325 cm–1 is likely related to the axial vibration of the N–H bond. The intense band seen in the CQD spectrum at 1130 cm–1 is associated with the vibration of the C–O bond. The vibration associated with the axial distortion of the SO–O bond corresponds to a wavenumber of 1115 cm–1. Additionally, the band observed around 620 cm–1 can be linked to the angular distortion vibration of the C–H bond. The FTIR analysis provide evidence for the presence of hydrophilic groups, which contribute to the solubility of the synthesized carbon quantum dots (CQDs) in water, which is a desirable characteristic of the material. Furthermore, this analysis indicates that the chemical composition of the raw materials was effectively transferred to the synthesized CQDs. This key aspect will be examined in more detail through XPS measurements.

To perform electrochemical tests and study the influence of the inhibitor, the system must be in a steady state. The open-circuit potential (OCP) graph versus immersion time ([Figure](#fig8) ) shows that up to 7200 s, all systems are in a steady-state OCP. Furthermore, it is observed that in the presence of the inhibitor, as the concentration increases, there is a shift of the OCP to more anodic potentials, indicating that the inhibitor influences the electrochemical processes at the MS surface.

The Nyquist and Bode plots obtained by electrochemical tests are shown in [Figure](#fig9) . It is possible to observe a capacitive loop in the medium without an inhibitor ([Figure](#fig9) A), which is directly linked to the capacitance of the electric double layer and the charge transfer resistance. With the addition and increase in inhibitor concentration, the loop tends to grow, indicating the formation of a protective film of the inhibitor on the mild steel surface capable of protecting it against the action of H+ and Cl– ions. An inductive loop can also appear with the addition of the inhibitor, primarily at high inhibitor concentrations (300 ppm), which is associated with the relaxation of species, such as (FeH)ads and FeOHads. Both species are intermediates of cathodic and anodic reactions and can interact with the inhibitor, influencing the corrosion inhibition efficiency. *,*  Another possibility for an inductive loop in systems with inhibitors is relaxation of the inhibitory molecule onto the metallic surface.

Characterization techniques are essential tools for corroborating the results obtained in corrosion tests and observing the influence of the inhibitor’s presence on the metal surface. This is a peer-reviewed scientific research article published in ACS Omega (July 22, 2025; DOI: 10.1021/acsomega.5c03224) by researchers from Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ), INMETRO, and Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Rio de Janeiro (Brazil). The study demonstrates the synthesis of carbon quantum dots (CQDs) derived from garlic peel (Allium sativum) and their application as a green corrosion inhibitor for mild steel in 1 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid (HCl) solution.

METHODOLOGY: CQDs were synthesized via acid hydrolysis — 1 g of crushed garlic peel was refluxed in 20 mL of 1 mol L⁻¹ sulfuric acid at 200 °C for 2 h, followed by filtration, dialysis (48 h, 1 kDa membrane), vacuum filtration, and rotary evaporation. The synthesis yielded approximately 10% CQDs. Characterization was performed using TEM, DLS, FTIR, Raman spectroscopy, XPS, zeta potential, UV–vis spectroscopy, and fluorimetry. Corrosion tests included gravimetric analysis, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), potentiodynamic polarization, SEM, AFM, and contact angle measurements.

KEY RESULTS:
- CQDs had an average size of 3.17 ± 0.07 nm (TEM) and 2.29 nm hydrodynamic diameter (DLS), confirming sub-10 nm nanoparticles. The material was amorphous with no lattice fringes.
- FTIR and XPS confirmed the presence of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and sulfur (endogenous doping), including functional groups such as O–H, N–H, C–N, C–S, C=O, and COOH.
- Gravimetric tests showed maximum inhibition efficiencies of 79% after 2 h and 96% after 24 h immersion in 1 mol L⁻¹ HCl.
- CQDs act as mixed-type inhibitors with a predominant anodic effect, confirmed by electrochemical polarization and Tafel analysis.
- At 300 ppm, EIS showed 71.4% inhibition efficiency (via charge transfer resistance), while Tafel analysis showed 68.0% (via corrosion current density) and 71.8% (via polarization resistance).
- Temperature-dependent studies (25–55 °C) revealed decreasing inhibition efficiency at higher temperatures (from 77.5% at 35 °C down to 46.7% at 55 °C), indicating primarily physical (electrostatic) adsorption. Activation energy was 65.1 kJ/mol with inhibitor vs. 46.1 kJ/mol without.
- Langmuir adsorption isotherm best fit the data (R² = 0.9964), suggesting monolayer adsorption.
- Surface analysis confirmed formation of a hydrophobic protective film (contact angle increased from 69° to 80° with inhibitor vs. decreasing to 38° without inhibitor), and SEM/AFM showed reduced surface roughness in the presence of CQDs.
- The garlic peel-derived CQDs achieved 95.8% maximum efficiency at 200 ppm, comparable to other biomass-derived CQDs (pitaya peel 95.6%, grapefruit peel 94.1%, sugar cane bagasse 94.0%, pumpkin seeds 94.6%).

CONCLUSION: The study highlights the sustainable use of garlic peel agro-industrial waste as a precursor for effective carbon quantum dot corrosion inhibitors, addressing both corrosion protection for mild steel in acidic environments and environmental concerns regarding agro-waste (approximately 3.5 million tons of garlic production waste burned annually, contributing to 3.3 billion tons of CO2 from untreated agro-industrial waste globally).

## Abstract

Natural materials (NMs) have emerged as better alternatives for the mitigation of corrosion of metals. NMs can be used as both inhibitors and coatings; however, they have been used mostly as inhibitors. In this work, ethanol extract of garlic peel (EEGP) has been synthesized and investigated by Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) and UV-visible spectroscopy (UVS). The results have confirmed that biomolecules are present in the prepared extract. EEGP has been coated on mild steel (MS) by drop casting (DC) in layers (one and two). The coated MS have been examined in 0.5 M NaCl by open circuit potential (OCP) and potentiodynamic polarization (PDP) measurements. The results have shown that EEGP protect MS in 0.5 M NaCl with the maximum efficiency of 71%. The conditions of bare, coated, and corroded MS have been visually monitored through camera images and atomic force microscopy (AFM), which advocates that EEGP protect MS. Based on the results, a schematic for corrosion prevention of MS by EEGP coatings has also been proposed.

The material selection and design are onboard methods, whereas coatings, inhibitors, and cathodic protection are infield methods. Since this work is focused on corrosion control using infield methods, coating has been selected because it is an effective, durable, and efficient method of corrosion control. There are many methods of applying coatings on metallic substrate [[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#ref-CR12 "Syed JA, Lu H, Tang S, Meng X. This work aims to synthesis ethanolic extract of garlic peels (EEGP), to coat EEGP on MS in layers by drop casting (DC), and to test coated MS in 0.5 M NaCl. For coating by DC, a volatile solvent is necessary. Among various solvents, ethanol is selected because it is biologically safe and stable at room temperature for long days [[28](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#ref-CR28 "Neto OZS, Batista EAC, Meirelles AJdA. The employment of ethanol as solvent to extract Brazil nut oil. J Clean Prod. 2018;180:866–75.")]. Garlic is scientifically known as Allium sativum and belongs to _Lillaceae_ family. The cloves of garlic bulb are utilized for various purposes for its tremendous benefits, including medicines and dishes [[29](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#ref-CR29 "Richard S, Rivlin. Historical perspective on the use of Garlic. J Nutr. 2001;131:S951–4.")]. Garlic is rich in organo-sulphur compounds and hence used to control corrosion in steel [[30](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#ref-CR30 "Parthipan P, Elumalai P, Narenkumar J, Machuca LL, Murugan K, Karthikeyan OP, et al. The electrochemical study of the Garlic extract as a corrosion inhibitor for brass in the nitric acid solution. Mater Chem Phys. 2024;312:128516.")]. Garlic is reported to contain flavonoids, Allicin, disulphide, and trisulphides [[32](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#ref-CR32 "Pereira SSAA, Pêgas MM, Fernández TL, Magalhães M, Schöntag TG, Lago DC. Allium sativum as corrosion inhibitor for carbon steel in sulfuric acid. Int J Electrochem Sci. 2014;9:5924–36.")]. Garlic peels are also used as inhibitors for its potential properties [[34](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#ref-CR34 "Barreto LS, Almeida TF, Santos AM, Tokumoto MS, Cotting F, Capelossi VR. Evaluation of vegetable residues as corrosion inhibitors. Res Soc Dev. 2021;10:e28710817409."), [35](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#ref-CR35 "Barreto LS, Tokumoto MS, Melo ICGHG, Amado FDR, Capelossi VR. Evaluation of the anticorrosion performance of Peel Garlic extract as corrosion inhibitor for ASTM 1020 carbon steel in acidic solution. Matéria (Rio J) 22, e11852, 2017.")]. However, garlic peel extract has never been used to date as alone coating material as per our knowledge. The EEGP has been investigated by UVS, FTIRS, PDP measurements, and camera images. The EEGP is found effective to prevent MS as per investigation.

## 2 Experimental works

### 2.1 Materials

Sodium chloride (NaCl; 99.5%) and Ethanol (C2H5OH; ≥ 99.9%) were obtained from Sigma Aldrich. Doble distilled (DD) water for cleaning purpose and making NaCl solutions was obtained from the installed plant in the university. MS specimen of 1cm 2 having a thickness of 1 mm was used in the experiments. The chemical composition (wt%) of the specimen was: 0.17% Carbon (C), 0.35% Silicon (Si), 0.42% Manganese (Mn), 0.05% Sulphur (S), 0.01% Copper (Cu), 0.20% Phosphorus (P), 0.01% Nitrogen (N), and the remaining iron.

### 2.2 Preparation of extract

**Fig. 2**

![Image 8: Fig. 2](https://media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1007%2Fs43938-026-00110-6/MediaObjects/43938_2026_110_Fig2_HTML.png)

[Full size image](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6/figures/2)

Process for the synthesis of the extract

For the preparation, the method explained in Jha et al. [[22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#ref-CR22 "Jha VK, Jana S, Pal. S, Ji G, Prakash R. Thin-Film coating of the hydrophobic Lotus leaf on copper by the floating film transfer method and investigation on the corrosion behavior of coated copper in saline water. Ind Eng Chem Res. 2023;62:85–95.")] has been used. Garlic bulbs were purchased in the local market of Haryana, India. The cloves were separated from the bulb and peeled carefully. The garlic peels are washed thoroughly by DD water. The peels were dried in sunlight for about 10–12 days. Afterwards, the dried peels were grinded in a kitchen grinder to obtain reduced size of peels. The 3.5 g of dried peels were dissolved in 50 mL ethanol and put on stirring at 550 RPM for 24 h. After the process, the solution was put on bath-ultrasonicator for 15 min and filtered afterwards using Whatman Grade-1 paper. At the end, filtered solution (EEGP) was stored in sealed container and used in the experiments. The process is explained schematically also in Fig. [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#Fig2).

### 2.3 Layer-wise coating of EEGP on MS

MS specimen of 1 × 1 cm 2 was cut from a big sheet. The specimens were cleaned by ethanol and compressed air to remove any possible dirt and contamination from the surface. Afterwards, they were abraded by emery papers (200 to 2000 grit) followed by cleaning with ethanol and tissue papers. A 25 µl of EEGP was taken and a drop was released on the center of the specimen (stage-1). The solution spread over the surface due to high energy of ethanol and grew (stage-2&3). The drop covers the maximum surface and remains in open air condition for 15 min (stage-4). After evaporation of ethanol, a thin layer of EEGP on MS had been created (stage-5). Similarly, two more layers were cast on MS. These coated MS specimens were used in experiments. The process has already been explained in Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#Fig1).

### 2.4 Corrosion testing

The corrosion experiments had been carried out on prepared MS specimens using the Gamry Potentiostat workstation (IFC-1010-28152). Three electrode assembly was used, where Ag/AgCl, platinum wire, and MS specimens were used as reference, auxiliary, and working electrodes, respectively [[36](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#ref-CR36 "Ji G, Mangla B, Umoren SA, Sharma A. Generation of layers of pointed gourd seed extract on mild steel using drop casting and testing of their corrosion behavior in salty water. Moroccan J Chem. 2024;12:1839–51."),[37](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#ref-CR37 "Bairagi H, Vashishth P, Narang R, Shukla SK, Mangla B. Protection of mild steel from corrosion in an aggressive chloride media through chitosan-CeO2 nanocomposite: experimental and computational studies. Corros Commun. 2024;14:58–71."),[38](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#ref-CR38 "Kumar H, Dhanda T. Cyclohexylamine an effective corrosion inhibitor for mild steel in 0.1 N H2SO4: experimental and theoretical (molecular dynamics simulation and FMO) study. J Mol Liq. 2021;327:114847.")]. A consistent open-circuit potential (OCP) was reached by letting the MS specimens in NaCl for 40 min (approximately) without applying any external potential or current. Afterwards, Tafel polarization tests had been performed in the potential range of OCP ± 250 mV at scan rate of 3 mv per second. The obtained polarization curves were fitted, and protection efficiency (µ p) had been calculated by the formula given below [[39](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#ref-CR39 "Ji G, Singh MK, Kumar V. Deposition of layers of ethanolic extract of waste pineapple crown on mild steel through drop casting and examination of their corrosion behavior. J Solid Waste Technol Manage. 2024;50:766–74.")]:

$$\:{\mu\:}_{P}\left(\%\right)=\frac{{i}_{corr}^{0}-{i}_{corr}^{p}\:}{{i}_{corr}^{0}}$$

 (1) 

where _i_ _0_ _corr_ and _i_ _p_ _corr_ were the current densities for bare and coated MS specimens.

### 2.5 Characterization and surface morphology

A Shimadzu UV-Vis spectrophotometer (UV-3600 PLUS) and Perkin FTIR spectrophotometer having 4500 –550 cm− 1 were used to test the EEGP. The surface morphology was clicked by a 10 megapixels mobile camera. The NT-MDT, made in Russia AFM microscope was also used to capture surface morphology in 3D.

### 3.2 Electrochemical testing

#### 3.2.1 OCP

The OCP and PDP curves are shown in Figs. [4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#Fig4) and [5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#Fig5). It was noticed that OCP of coated MS specimens were lower than bare MS in NaCl. Also, the OCP value for G2 (2-layer EEGP coated MS) was lower than G1(1-layer EEGP coated MS). This could suggest that EEGP was cathodic with respect to bare MS [[41](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#ref-CR41 "Salehinasab H, Majidi R, Danaee I, Vrsalović L, Saliminasab S, Zarei D. Engineering a zinc-rich Ethyl silicate coating based on nickel oxide nanoparticles for improving anticorrosion performance. Hybrid Adv 5, 2024,100132.")]. The OCP values for G1 and G2 were going down with during the first 600 s of immersion. Hence, additional 30 minutes was given to stabilize the OCPs prior to perform PDP measurements.

#### 3.2.2 Potentiodynamic polarization (PDP)

The PDP graphs shown in Fig. [5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#Fig5) indicated that equilibrium corrosion potential (E corr) of coated MS shifted toward cathodic potentials with respect to E corr of bare MS, which supported the findings based on OCP values. The curves for bare and coated MS were following same pattern, which meant that nature of corrosion reactions was not changed by EEGP coatings [[42](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#ref-CR42 "Li W, He Q, Zhang S, Pei C, Hou B. Some new Triazole derivatives as inhibitors for mild steel corrosion in acidic medium. J Appl Electrochem. 2008;38:289–95.")]. To obtain E corr and i corr, the curves have been fitted and values are listed in Table [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#Tab1). The E corr of G1 was anodic with respect to E corr of bare MS, whereas E corr of G2 was cathodic. The Ecorr shifts (< 85 mV) further suggest that EEGP behaves as a mixed-type inhibitor, with a slight cathodic tendency for G2 [[43](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#ref-CR43 "Ferreira ES, Giancomelli C, Giacomelli FC, Spinelli A. Evaluation of inhibitor effect of L ascorbic acid on the corrosion of mild steel. Mater Chem Phys. 2004;83:129–34.")]. However, the values of anodic and cathodic Tafel slopes (β a and β c) could predict that both cathodic and anodic corrosion reactions were suppressed by the EEGP coatings. The variations in both anodic and cathodic Tafel slopes in the presence of EEGP films indicate that the inhibitor suppresses both anodic and cathodic reactions, confirming its mixed-type inhibition behavior.

The camera images of bare and EEGP coated (G1 and G2) MS are shown in Fig.[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#Fig6)a–c. A clean surface of MS in with bright silver colour was noticed in Fig.[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#Fig6)a. The yellowish EEGP layer could be easily seen in Fig.[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#Fig6)b. However, it was noticed that 1 layer of EEGP could not cover whole surface of MS. In contrast, darker yellowish layer of EEGP was seen in Fig.[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#Fig6)c. Also, the surface coverage of MS by G2 was greater than G1 as per the camera images. Based on camera images, it could be stated that EEGP layers covered the MS surface effectively.

The corroded bare and coated MS surfaces were analysed by AFM because camera images could not give exact comparison of corroded surfaces. The 3D AFM images were shown in Fig. [7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#Fig7)a–c. The corroded MS surface was looking rough in the image (Fig. [7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#Fig7)a). The high roughness of the surface could be guessed from the height of the Z-axis (depth) scale. The surface of G1 was smoother than corroded MS; however, it was lesser smooth in comparison of G2’s surface. The surface condition was slightly better than MS in G1, which could be guessed from the height scale. In contrast, much smoother surface was seen in G2. For quantitative comparison, average surface roughness (R a) is a good parameter [[45](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#ref-CR45 "Evgeny B, Hughes T, Eskin D. Effect of surface roughness on corrosion behaviour of low carbon steel in inhibited 4 M hydrochloric acid under laminar and turbulent flow conditions. Corros Sci. 2016;103:196–205.")]– [[46](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#ref-CR46 "Bairagi H, Vashishth P, Ji G, Shukla SK, Ebenso EE, Mangla B. Polymers and their composites for corrosion Inhibition application: Development, advancement, and future scope–A critical review. Corros Commun. 2024;15:79–94.")]. The R a values of 151 nm, 95 nm, and 43 nm were measured for corroded MS, G1, and G2 respectively indicating that EEGP effectively protected MS in NaCl solution. However, the most effective protection was acknowledged in case of G2. The reason was evident in the camera images, i.e., more surface coverage of MS by G2 than G1.

Optical microscopy (OM) was employed to examine the cross-sectional surfaces of bare and coated MS samples for additional evidence. The cross-sectional thickness of bare MS was measured as 922.843 μm, which served as the baseline. For G1-coated MS, the thickness increased to 960.64 μm, representing a coating layer addition of 37.797 μm. The G2-coated MS exhibited a greater thickness of 982.44 μm, indicating a 59.597 μm coating layer, which was noticeably thicker than G1. After intense corrosion exposure in NaCl solution, the bare MS thickness increased to 943.004 μm due to the deposition of yellow corrosion products on the surface. In contrast, the G1-coated MS showed a thickness of 953.1 μm after corrosion, with a coating loss of 7.54 μm (19.9% damage), indicating moderate protective capability with some localized coating deterioration. The G2-coated MS demonstrated superior performance, with its thickness slightly reduced to 977.76 μm, corresponding to only 4.68 μm coating loss (7.9% damage). This minimal reduction confirmed that the inhibitor layer remained largely intact and provided enhanced barrier protection.

[Full size image](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6/figures/7)

3D AFM images of**a** mild steel,**b** single layer EEGP coated MS (G1), and**c** double layer EEGP coated MS (G2) corroded in 0.5 M NaCl

### 3.4 Mechanism for prevention by EEGP

The experimental results revealed that EEGP contained organo-sulfur compounds (confirmed by FTIR peaks at 720.67 cm⁻¹ for C-S and 1044.28 cm⁻¹ for S = O) and potentially other phytochemicals including flavonoids (indicated by carbonyl peaks at 1618 cm⁻¹ and UV-Vis absorption in the 250–350 nm range). These bioactive compounds adsorbed onto the MS surface, forming a protective barrier layer. The corrosion reactions at the MS surface were significantly slowed down due to the strong barrier effect of EEGP layers, which was well reflected in OCP, PDP, and AFM measurements. Based on results, a schematic had been prepared and shown in Fig.[8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#Fig8). Mild steel was covered by EEGP layers. However, 1 layer of EEGP could not cover the whole surface of MS. The 2 layers of EEGP covered the greater surface than G1; however, it also could not cover the whole surface. The incomplete coverage created microchannels on the surface, which were obviously present in greater amounts in G1 than G2. The bare MS had the largest area exposed to NaCl. Hence, Cl−, OH−, and O 2 could react freely with the surface of bare MS. The Cl− and OH− could react with Fe+ (or Fe++ and Fe+++) and made iron chlorides and hydroxides (major corrosion products), whereas O 2 could be reduced on the bare surface. Due to these aggressive corrosion reactions, a high corrosion of MS in NaCl was observed. On the other hand, occurrence of these reactions on the surface was made limited by EEGP layers due to restricted surface exposure. Since, surface in G2 was more covered than G1, greater protection was observed in G2. The EEGP was also coated in 3 layers (G3) on MS; however, any significant improvement in protection was not achieved. Hence, the results for G3 had not been discussed.

**Fig. 8**

![Image 14: Fig. 8](https://media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1007%2Fs43938-026-00110-6/MediaObjects/43938_2026_110_Fig8_HTML.png)

[Full size image](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6/figures/8)

schematic for mechanism of corrosion prevention by EEGP

## 4 Conclusion

The extract of garlic peels was successfully synthesised using ethanol. The EGP was characterised by UV-vis and FTIR spectroscopy, which confirmed that EEGP was rich in organo-sulphur compounds. The EEGP coating on MS was done by drop casting and tested for their corrosion behaviour by OCP and PDP measurements. The significant decrease in i corr for G1 and G2 portrayed that EEGP effectively protected MS in 0.5 M NaCl. The more prominent decrease was observed for G2. Hence, greater corrosion protection was achieved in G2 (77%) than G1(55%). The camera images suggested that EEGP covered greater surface of MS in G2 than in G1. Due to greater coverage, the surface was lesser damaged in G2 than in G1; however, a heavy damage was observed in bare MS in AFM images. This was also shown in schematic introduced based on overall results (Fig.[8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43938-026-00110-6#Fig8)). The damage could also be analysed by R a values obtained for bare MS, G1, and G2 in AFM images. Based on overall investigation it could be said that EEGP protected MS in layer wise manner up to 2 layers.

args.summary:
This is an open-access research article published in the journal "Discover Chemical Engineering" (Volume 6, article 13, 2026) on March 21, 2026. The study investigates the use of ethanol extract of garlic peel (EEGP) as a corrosion protection coating for mild steel (MS) in saline medium (0.5 M NaCl).

**Methodology:**
- Garlic peels (purchased from local market in Haryana, India) were washed, dried in sunlight for 10-12 days, ground, and 3.5 g dissolved in 50 mL ethanol and stirred at 550 RPM for 24 hours, then ultrasonicated for 15 min and filtered
- EEGP was characterized via FT-IR and UV-visible spectroscopy, confirming presence of organo-sulphur compounds (FTIR peaks at 720.67 cm⁻¹ for C-S and 1044.28 cm⁻¹ for S=O) and potential flavonoids (carbonyl peaks at 1618 cm⁻¹, UV-Vis absorption 250-350 nm)
- EEGP was coated on MS (1 cm², 1 mm thick) via drop casting in one (G1) and two (G2) layers
- Corrosion testing used open circuit potential (OCP) and potentiodynamic polarization (PDP) measurements via a Gamry Potentiostat workstation with Ag/AgCl reference, platinum wire auxiliary, and MS working electrodes
- Surface analysis used camera images, atomic force microscopy (AFM), and optical microscopy

**Key Results:**
- EEGP achieved up to 71% (stated in AI summary) corrosion protection; PDP data showed protection efficiency of 55% for G1 (single layer) and 77% for G2 (double layer)
- EEGP acts as a mixed-type inhibitor, with slight cathodic tendency for G2 (Ecorr shifts < 85 mV)
- AFM surface roughness (Ra): 151 nm for bare corroded MS, 95 nm for G1, 43 nm for G2
- Cross-sectional thickness measurements: bare MS 922.843 μm; G1 coated 960.64 μm (37.797 μm coating); G2 coated 982.44 μm (59.597 μm coating). After corrosion, G1 showed 19.9% coating damage, G2 only 7.9% damage
- Coating in 3 layers (G3) showed no significant additional improvement

**Conclusion:** EEGP protects mild steel in a layer-wise manner up to 2 layers via drop casting, acting as a sustainable, green corrosion inhibitor/coating. The study is notable as garlic peel extract had never previously been used as a standalone coating material (only as an inhibitor). Authors: Bindu Mangla, Gopal Ji, Kajal Kajal, Kanak Rawat, Harshita Kaushik, Khushi Mittal, Rashmi Sehrawat, Priya Vashishth, Himanshi Bairagi, D. K. Sharma, and Harish Kumar.
args.key_excerpts: "The results have shown that EEGP protect MS in 0.5 M NaCl with the maximum efficiency of 71%."
