**Arecoline** is a [cholinergic agent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cholinergic_agent "Cholinergic agent"), [stimulant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stimulant "Stimulant"), and [naturally occurring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_product "Natural product") [alkaloid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkaloid "Alkaloid") found in [areca (betel) nuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Areca_nut "Areca nut") of the [areca palm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Areca_palm "Areca palm") (*Areca catechu*) found in [South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Asia "South Asia") and [Southeast Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Asia "Southeast Asia").[[1]](#cite_note-VolginBashirzadeAmstislavskaya2019-1)[[3]](#cite_note-StokesPinoHagan2022-3) Its effects, depending on the dose, include [stimulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stimulation "Stimulation"), [alertness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alertness "Alertness"), increased [concentration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concentration "Concentration"), [cognitive enhancement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nootropic "Nootropic"), [elation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mood_lift "Mood lift"), [euphoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euphoriant "Euphoriant"), [pro-sexual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aphrodisiac "Aphrodisiac") effects, [relaxation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mental_relaxation "Mental relaxation"), [reduced anxiety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anxiolytic "Anxiolytic"), and [sedation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sedation "Sedation"), as well as [addiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drug_addiction "Drug addiction") and [withdrawal symptoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drug_withdrawal "Drug withdrawal") upon [discontinuation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drug_discontinuation "Drug discontinuation").[[1]](#cite_note-VolginBashirzadeAmstislavskaya2019-1) Its effects are described as subtle and it has been likened to a strong cup of [coffee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffee "Coffee").[[3]](#cite_note-StokesPinoHagan2022-3) There are also other active constituents of areca nuts, but arecoline is the key active component, with a percentage of ~0.3 to 0.6%.[[1]](#cite_note-VolginBashirzadeAmstislavskaya2019-1) Areca nuts are [administered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drug_administration "Drug administration") by [chewing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chewing "Chewing") for 5 to 20 minutes without [swallowing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swallowing "Swallowing").[[1]](#cite_note-VolginBashirzadeAmstislavskaya2019-1)

[Side effects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Side_effect "Side effect") of arecoline include [hypersalivation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypersalivation "Hypersalivation"), [hypotension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypotension "Hypotension"), [vertigo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertigo "Vertigo"), [miosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miosis "Miosis"), [tremor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tremor "Tremor"), and [bradycardia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bradycardia "Bradycardia"), among others.[[1]](#cite_note-VolginBashirzadeAmstislavskaya2019-1) Other adverse effects can include [extrapyramidal syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extrapyramidal_syndrome "Extrapyramidal syndrome") and [seizures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seizure "Seizure").[[1]](#cite_note-VolginBashirzadeAmstislavskaya2019-1) Addiction and [dependence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drug_dependence "Drug dependence") can occur, with withdrawal symptoms including [mood swings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mood_swing "Mood swing"), [anxiety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anxiety "Anxiety"), [irritability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irritability "Irritability"), and [insomnia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insomnia "Insomnia").[[1]](#cite_note-VolginBashirzadeAmstislavskaya2019-1) Rarely, [psychosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychosis "Psychosis") can occur during withdrawal in heavy users.[[1]](#cite_note-VolginBashirzadeAmstislavskaya2019-1) Areca nut use, the primary method of consuming arecoline, is highly associated with [oral disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oral_disease "Oral disease") and [oral cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oral_cancer "Oral cancer").[[3]](#cite_note-StokesPinoHagan2022-3) [Overdose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overdose "Overdose") of arecoline can be treated with [antimuscarinic drugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antimuscarinic_drug "Antimuscarinic drug") like [atropine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atropine "Atropine") or [scopolamine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scopolamine "Scopolamine").[[1]](#cite_note-VolginBashirzadeAmstislavskaya2019-1)

The drug acts as a [non-selective](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binding_selectivity "Binding selectivity") [partial agonist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_agonist "Partial agonist") of [muscarinic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscarinic_acetylcholine_receptor "Muscarinic acetylcholine receptor") and [nicotinic acetylcholine receptors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicotinic_acetylcholine_receptor "Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor").[[1]](#cite_note-VolginBashirzadeAmstislavskaya2019-1) The major [metabolite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metabolite "Metabolite") of arecoline, [arecaidine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arecaidine "Arecaidine"), is a [GABA reuptake inhibitor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GABA_reuptake_inhibitor "GABA reuptake inhibitor").[[1]](#cite_note-VolginBashirzadeAmstislavskaya2019-1) The subjective effects of arecoline appear to be mediated by muscarinic acetylcholine receptors and not by nicotinic acetylcholine receptors based on [animal studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_study "Animal study").[[1]](#cite_note-VolginBashirzadeAmstislavskaya2019-1)[[4]](#cite_note-MeltzerRosecrans1981-4) However, its [mechanism of action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanism_of_action "Mechanism of action") is still yet to be fully understood and other activities have also been described.[[3]](#cite_note-StokesPinoHagan2022-3)[[5]](#cite_note-HorensteinQuadriStokes2019-5) The stimulant and addictive effects of arecoline are thought to be due to increased [dopaminergic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dopaminergic "Dopaminergic") [neurotransmission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neurotransmission "Neurotransmission") in the [mesolimbic pathway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesolimbic_pathway "Mesolimbic pathway") of the [brain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brain "Brain").[[6]](#cite_note-OsborneKoWu2017-6)[[3]](#cite_note-StokesPinoHagan2022-3)[[1]](#cite_note-VolginBashirzadeAmstislavskaya2019-1) In terms of [chemical structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_structure "Chemical structure"), arecoline is closely related to [nicotinic acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicotinic_acid "Nicotinic acid").[[1]](#cite_note-VolginBashirzadeAmstislavskaya2019-1)

The use of arecoline, in the form of areca nuts, dates back several thousand years, including in [Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand "Thailand"), [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"), and [Polynesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesia "Polynesia").[[1]](#cite_note-VolginBashirzadeAmstislavskaya2019-1) Arecoline was first [isolated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_isolation "Chemical isolation") in 1888 by Ernst Jahns and its [synthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_synthesis "Chemical synthesis") was first proposed in 1891, with its [chemical structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_structure "Chemical structure") confirmed in 1907.[[1]](#cite_note-VolginBashirzadeAmstislavskaya2019-1) The first complete synthesis was reported by Fritz Chemnitius at Jena University (Germany) in 1926. Arecoline, in the form of areca nuts, is used by more than 600 million people worldwide (~10–20% of the global population), and is the fourth most commonly used [psychoactive drug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychoactive_drug "Psychoactive drug") in the world after [alcohol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcohol_(drug) "Alcohol (drug)"), [nicotine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicotine "Nicotine"), and [caffeine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caffeine "Caffeine").[[1]](#cite_note-VolginBashirzadeAmstislavskaya2019-1)[[3]](#cite_note-StokesPinoHagan2022-3) Despite [globalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Globalization "Globalization"), arecoline is unusual among [recreational drugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recreational_drug "Recreational drug") in that its use is still predominantly confined to [Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia "Asia"), though its use has been increasing and spreading in part due to the [Internet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet "Internet").[[1]](#cite_note-VolginBashirzadeAmstislavskaya2019-1)[[3]](#cite_note-StokesPinoHagan2022-3) Chewing areca nuts is said to be as familiar to various Asian peoples as chewing gum is to Americans.[[1]](#cite_note-VolginBashirzadeAmstislavskaya2019-1) The countries in which areca nut production are highest include [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"), [Myanmar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myanmar "Myanmar"), [Malaysia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia "Malaysia"), [Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia "Indonesia"), and [Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh").[[1]](#cite_note-VolginBashirzadeAmstislavskaya2019-1) Arecoline and areca nut sale and consumption are not generally [controlled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Controlled_substance "Controlled substance") throughout the world, with a few exceptions.[[1]](#cite_note-VolginBashirzadeAmstislavskaya2019-1)

## Uses

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Arecoline&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Uses")]

### Recreational

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Arecoline&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Recreational")]

In many Asian cultures, the [areca nut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Areca_nut "Areca nut") is chewed along with [betel leaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betel_leaf "Betel leaf") to obtain a [stimulating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stimulant "Stimulant") effect.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

### Medical

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Arecoline&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Medical")]

Arecoline has been used medicinally as an [antihelmintic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antihelmintic "Antihelmintic") (a drug against parasitic worms).[[8]](#cite_note-pmid12121538-8) It paralyzes tapeworms.[[9]](#cite_note-ReferenceA-9)

### Traditional medicine

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Arecoline&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Traditional medicine")]

Arecoline has been used in [traditional medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_medicine "Traditional medicine") in [Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia "Asia") for thousands of years.[[1]](#cite_note-VolginBashirzadeAmstislavskaya2019-1)

## Adverse effects

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Arecoline&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Adverse effects")]

### Overdose

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Arecoline&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Overdose")]

The [LD50](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Median_lethal_dose "Median lethal dose") of arecoline is 100 mg/kg, when administered subcutaneously in mice.[[10]](#cite_note-Merck-10) The minimum lethal dose (MLD) values of arecoline in mice, dogs, and horses is 100 mg/kg, 5 mg/kg and 1.4 mg/kg respectively.[[9]](#cite_note-ReferenceA-9)

### Toxicity

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Arecoline&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Toxicity")]

Current science is confident that areca nut chewing is [carcinogenic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carcinogenic "Carcinogenic"). Research suggests this is probably at least partly because of arecoline itself, although it could also be from the other constituents of the nut as well, some of which are precursors to [nitrosamines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrosamine "Nitrosamine") that form in the mouth during chewing. Section 5.5 Evaluation on page 238 of IARC Monograph 85-6 states the following:[[11]](#cite_note-isbn_9789283212850-11)

> * [...]
> * There is sufficient evidence in humans for the carcinogenicity of betel quid without tobacco. Betel quid without tobacco causes oral cancer.
> * There is sufficient evidence in experimental animals for the carcinogenicity of betel quid without tobacco.
> * There is sufficient evidence in experimental animals for the carcinogenicity of betel quid with tobacco.
> * There is sufficient evidence in experimental animals for the carcinogenicity of areca nut.
> * There is sufficient evidence in experimental animals for the carcinogenicity of areca nut with tobacco.
> * There is limited evidence in experimental animals for the carcinogenicity of arecoline.
> * There is inadequate evidence in experimental animals for the carcinogenicity of arecaidine.
> * [...]

The toxicity of arecoline can be partially mitigated by [vitamins C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_C "Vitamin C") and [E](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_E "Vitamin E") in mice.[[12]](#cite_note-12)

#### Mechanisms of toxicity

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Arecoline&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Mechanisms of toxicity")]

Arecoline is "obviously cytotoxic" to cultures of hepatocytes, bone marrow cells, lymphocytes, neuronal cell, myoblasts and endothelial cells.[[9]](#cite_note-ReferenceA-9)

Arecoline generates excessive [reactive oxygen species](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reactive_oxygen_species "Reactive oxygen species") (ROS) in a number of cell types, including oral epithelial cells and neuronal cells. In adult mice, arecoline is toxic to the testes and liver via ROS generation.[[9]](#cite_note-ReferenceA-9)

Arecoline is also genotoxic, being able to induce DNA damage and mutation in several cell cultures.[[9]](#cite_note-ReferenceA-9) Mice chronically exposed to arecoline show relaxation of their [chromatin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromatin "Chromatin") structure.[[13]](#cite_note-carcinogen-Saikia-13)

## Pharmacology

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Arecoline&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Pharmacology")]

### Pharmacodynamics

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Arecoline&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Pharmacodynamics")]

Arecoline is the primary active ingredient responsible for the central nervous system effects of the areca nut. Arecoline has been compared to [nicotine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicotine "Nicotine"); however, nicotine agonizes [nicotinic acetylcholine receptors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicotinic_acetylcholine_receptor "Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor"), whereas arecoline is primarily a partial agonist of [muscarinic acetylcholine receptors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscarinic_acetylcholine_receptor "Muscarinic acetylcholine receptor"),[[14]](#cite_note-pmid3600615-14)[[15]](#cite_note-pmid1704434-15) leading to its [parasympathetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parasympathetic "Parasympathetic") effects. In [frogs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xenopus "Xenopus"), arecoline also acts as an [antagonist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Receptor_antagonist "Receptor antagonist") (or very weak partial agonist) at [α4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CHRNA4 "CHRNA4") and [α6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CHRNA6 "CHRNA6")-containing [nicotinic acetylcholine receptors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicotinic_acetylcholine_receptor "Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor") and as a silent antagonist at [α7 nicotinic receptors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CHRNA7 "CHRNA7"), which may account for its anti-inflammatory activity.[[16]](#cite_note-16) Arecoline also inhibits [AMPK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AMP-activated_protein_kinase "AMP-activated protein kinase") through generation of [ROS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reactive_oxygen_species "Reactive oxygen species") in several types of cells.[[17]](#cite_note-pmid21440488-17)

AN (Areca Nut) is a vasodilator mainly due to the presence of arecoline. It also has anti-thrombosis and anti-atherogenic effects by increasing plasma nitric oxide, eNos, and mRNA expression and decreasing IL-8 along with other downregulations.[[9]](#cite_note-ReferenceA-9) It increases the level of testosterone by stimulating Leydig's cells as well as levels of FSH and LH.[[18]](#cite_note-pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov-18)[[19]](#cite_note-19) It also activates HPA axis and stimulates CRH release. It prevents the dysfunction of B cells of the pancreas from high fructose intake.[[9]](#cite_note-ReferenceA-9) Arecoline has the ability to stimulate the digestive system through the activation of [muscarinic receptors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscarinic_receptor "Muscarinic receptor"). Areca nut water extract could increase the contractions of gastric smooth muscle and muscle strips of the duodenum, ileum, and colon significantly. This activity could be caused by arecoline.[[9]](#cite_note-ReferenceA-9)

### Pharmacokinetics

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Arecoline&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Pharmacokinetics")]

Arecoline is metabolized by both kidneys and liver.[[20]](#cite_note-20) Currently, 11 metabolites of arecoline are documented among which *N*-methylnipecotic acid was found to be a major metabolite of both arecoline and [arecaidine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arecaidine "Arecaidine").[[21]](#cite_note-pmid16780361-21) Lime, which is traditionally mixed to crushed areca nuts prior to consumption, is said to hydrolyse almost all arecoline to [arecaidine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arecaidine "Arecaidine"), a GABA reuptake inhibitor.[[22]](#cite_note-JohnstonKrogsgaard-Larsen1975-22) Arecaidine is also formed during liver metabolism of arecoline in rats.[[21]](#cite_note-pmid16780361-21)

Arecoline is very efficiently absorbed through oral musoca, with 85% bioavailbility. Maximum plasma concentration is reached within 3 minutes.[[23]](#cite_note-23)

Orally ingested arecoline is extensively metabolized in rats, with the vast majority of the dose being converted to arecaidine and arecoline *N*-oxide.[[24]](#cite_note-24)

## Chemistry

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Arecoline&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Chemistry")]

Arecoline is a colorless odorless oily liquid.[[1]](#cite_note-VolginBashirzadeAmstislavskaya2019-1) It is a [base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Base_(chemistry) "Base (chemistry)"), and its conjugate acid has a pKa ~ 6.8.[[10]](#cite_note-Merck-10) Arecoline is volatile in steam, miscible with most organic solvents and water, but extractable from water by [ether](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diethylether "Diethylether") in presence of dissolved salts. Being basic, arecoline forms salts with acids. The salts are crystalline, but usually [deliquescent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hygroscopy#Deliquescence "Hygroscopy"): the hydrochloride, arecoline•HCl, forms needles, m.p. 158 °C;[[10]](#cite_note-Merck-10) the hydrobromide, arecoline•HBr, forms slender prisms, mp. 177–179 °C from hot [methanol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methanol "Methanol"); the [aurichloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chloroauric_acid "Chloroauric acid"), arecoline•HAuCl4, is an oil, but the [platinichloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chloroplatinic_acid "Chloroplatinic acid"), arecoline2•H2PtCl6, mp. 176 °C, crystallizes from water in orange-red rhombohedrons. The [methiodide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methiodide "Methiodide") forms glancing prisms, mp. 173–174 °C.

### Synthesis

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Arecoline&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Synthesis")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/Arecoline_synthesis_CN118812418.svg/500px-Arecoline_synthesis_CN118812418.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Arecoline_synthesis_CN118812418.svg)

2024 method:[[25]](#cite_note-25) Also see:[[26]](#cite_note-26)[[27]](#cite_note-27)

The double [Michael reaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_reaction "Michael reaction") between methyl acrylate [96-33-3] (**1**) and aqueous methylamine (**2**) gave N,N-Bis(-methoxycarbonylethyl)methylamine [105-71-5] (**3**). [Dieckmann cyclization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dieckmann_cyclization "Dieckmann cyclization") led to 1-Methyl-3-carbomethoxy-4-piperidone [13221-89-1] (**4**). The reduction of the ketone group with sodium borohydride gave N-Methyl-3-carbomethoxy-4-hydroxypiperidine, PC3029557 (**5**). Reaction with methanesulfonyl chloride followed by addition of hydrobromic acid completed the synthesis of arecoline hydrobromide (**6**). N.B. compound #4 is similar to a compound used in the synthesis of [GSK1360707F](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GSK1360707F "GSK1360707F").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/Arecoline_synthesis.svg/500px-Arecoline_synthesis.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Arecoline_synthesis.svg)

Synthesis:[[28]](#cite_note-28)[[1]](#cite_note-VolginBashirzadeAmstislavskaya2019-1) Chinese:[[29]](#cite_note-29)

Fischer esterification of [nicotinic acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicotinic_acid "Nicotinic acid") (niacin) (**1**) gives [methyl nicotinate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methyl_nicotinate "Methyl nicotinate") (**2**). Alkylation with [methyl iodide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methyl_iodide "Methyl iodide") then gives 3-methoxycarbonyl-1-methylpyridinium iodide (**3**). Hydride reduction with an agent such as potassium borohydride thus gives the tetrahydropyridine (**4**). Salt formation with [HBr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_bromide "Hydrogen bromide") completes the synthesis (**5**).

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/Arecoline_synthesis2.svg/500px-Arecoline_synthesis2.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Arecoline_synthesis2.svg)

Secondary method:[[30]](#cite_note-30)

A double Mannich reaction between methylamine (**1**), acetaldehyde (**2**) and [formaldehyde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formaldehyde "Formaldehyde") (**3**) in the presence of [hydroxylamine hydrochloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydroxylamine_hydrochloride "Hydroxylamine hydrochloride") is supposed to have delivered 1-methyl-1,2,5,6-tetrahydropyridine-3-carbaldehyde oxime hydrochloride (**4**) as the product. Dehydration of the aldoxime to the nitrile occurs upon treatment with acetic anhydride giving 3-cyano-1-methyl-1,2,5,6-tetrahydropyridine (**5**). Functional group interconversion of the nitrile to the methyl carboxylate ester then occurs upon acid-catalyzed treatment in methanol, and then conversion to the HBr salt completes the synthesis. N.B. Although the first step is not very high yielding, if one substitutes methoxyamine for hydroxylamine procedure could be used for a [one-pot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One-pot "One-pot") synthesis of [milameline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milameline "Milameline").

### Chemical precursor

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Arecoline&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Chemical precursor")]

Arecoline is used in the [synthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_synthesis "Chemical synthesis") of a variety of other [drugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drug "Drug"), including [paroxetine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paroxetine "Paroxetine"),[[31]](#cite_note-31)[[32]](#cite_note-32) [femoxetine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Femoxetine "Femoxetine"), [nocaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nocaine "Nocaine"), [DMNPC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DMNPC "DMNPC"), [piquindone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piquindone "Piquindone"),[[33]](#cite_note-33) [PC10058081](https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/10058081) ([epiboxidine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epiboxidine "Epiboxidine") type), [FT-0731096](https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/14235519) [114724-56-0], piper-[brasofensine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brasofensine "Brasofensine")[[34]](#cite_note-34) piper-[Tesofensine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tesofensine "Tesofensine")[[35]](#cite_note-35) and [BRN 0023391](https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/11971445) [102206-67-7].

### Analogues

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Arecoline&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Analogues")]

[Analogues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structural_analog "Structural analog") of and related compounds to arecoline include [arecaidine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arecaidine "Arecaidine"), [guavacoline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guavacoline "Guavacoline"), [guvacine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guvacine "Guvacine"), [nipecotic acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nipecotic_acid "Nipecotic acid"), [nicotinic acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicotinic_acid "Nicotinic acid"), [muscarine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscarine "Muscarine"), [SKF-89976A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SKF-89976A "SKF-89976A"), [tiagabine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiagabine "Tiagabine"), and [CI-966](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CI-966 "CI-966"). [Xanomeline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xanomeline "Xanomeline"), the anti-schizophrenia component in the approved drug [xanomeline/trospium chloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xanomeline/trospium_chloride "Xanomeline/trospium chloride"), also has structural similarities to arecoline.[[36]](#cite_note-pmid35758639-36)

## Research

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Arecoline&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Research")]

Owing to its [muscarinic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscarine "Muscarine") and nicotinic agonist properties, arecoline has shown improvement in the learning ability of healthy volunteers. Since one of the hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease is a cognitive decline, arecoline was suggested as a treatment to slow down this process. Arecoline administered intravenously did indeed show modest verbal and spatial [memory improvement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_improvement "Memory improvement") in Alzheimer's patients,[[37]](#cite_note-Alzheimer's-37) though due to arecoline's possible carcinogenic properties (see [§ Toxicity](#Toxicity)), it is not the first drug of choice for this degenerative disease.[[37]](#cite_note-Alzheimer's-37)

Anecdotal reports indicate that it has a short-lived effect against schizophrenia. Among male schizophrenia patients, higher areca nut consumption is associated with weaker symptoms. It inspired the development of [xanomeline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xanomeline "Xanomeline").[[36]](#cite_note-pmid35758639-36) It enhances learning and memory in rodents.[[9]](#cite_note-ReferenceA-9)

## Veterinary use

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Arecoline&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Veterinary use")]

In 2012, [Chinese Ministry of Agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Ministry_of_Agriculture "Chinese Ministry of Agriculture") listed arecoline [hydrobromide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrobromide "Hydrobromide") as an abolished [veterinary drug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veterinary_drug "Veterinary drug") and stopped its production and use.[[38]](#cite_note-38)

## Arecoline — Wikipedia Article Summary

**Overview:** Arecoline is a cholinergic agent, stimulant, and naturally occurring alkaloid found in areca (betel) nuts of the areca palm (*Areca catechu*), native to South and Southeast Asia. It is the key active component of areca nuts, comprising approximately 0.3–0.6% of the nut. Its effects (dose-dependent) include stimulation, alertness, increased concentration, cognitive enhancement, elation, euphoria, pro-sexual effects, relaxation, reduced anxiety, and sedation, as well as addiction and withdrawal symptoms upon discontinuation. Effects are described as subtle, likened to a strong cup of coffee.

**Uses:**
- **Recreational:** Chewed with betel leaf in many Asian cultures for its stimulating effect.
- **Medical:** Used medicinally as an antihelmintic (paralyzes tapeworms).
- **Traditional medicine:** Used in Asian traditional medicine for thousands of years.

**Adverse Effects & Toxicity:**
- Side effects include hypersalivation, hypotension, vertigo, miosis, tremor, bradycardia, extrapyramidal syndrome, and seizures.
- Withdrawal symptoms include mood swings, anxiety, irritability, and insomnia; rarely psychosis in heavy users.
- LD50 is 100 mg/kg (subcutaneous, mice). MLD: 100 mg/kg (mice), 5 mg/kg (dogs), 1.4 mg/kg (horses).
- Areca nut chewing is carcinogenic (confirmed by IARC). IARC Monograph 85-6 found sufficient evidence for carcinogenicity of betel quid and areca nut in humans/animals, but only limited evidence for arecoline itself.
- Arecoline is cytotoxic to multiple cell types, generates reactive oxygen species, and is genotoxic (induces DNA damage/mutation).
- Toxicity partially mitigated by vitamins C and E in mice.
- Overdose treated with antimuscarinic drugs like atropine or scopolamine.

**Pharmacology:**
- Acts as a non-selective partial agonist of muscarinic and nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
- Its major metabolite, arecaidine, is a GABA reuptake inhibitor.
- Subjective effects appear mediated by muscarinic receptors (not nicotinic) per animal studies.
- Stimulant/addictive effects thought to be due to increased dopaminergic neurotransmission in the mesolimbic pathway.
- Chemically closely related to nicotinic acid.
- Metabolized by kidneys and liver; 11 documented metabolites.
- Very efficiently absorbed through oral mucosa with 85% bioavailability; peak plasma concentration within 3 minutes.
- Lime mixed with areca nuts hydrolyzes almost all arecoline to arecaidine.

**Chemical/Physical Data:**
- Formula: C8H13NO2; Molar mass: 155.197 g/mol
- Colorless, odorless oily liquid; melting point 27°C; boiling point 209°C; density 1.0495 g/cm³
- pKa ~6.8; forms crystalline (usually deliquescent) salts.
- IUPAC name: Methyl 1-methyl-1,2,5,6-tetrahydropyridine-3-carboxylate
- CAS: 63-75-2; PubChem CID: 2230

**Synthesis:** Multiple methods exist, including a 2024 method using double Michael reaction/Dieckmann cyclization, a Fischer esterification of nicotinic acid route, and a double Mannich reaction route.

**History & Prevalence:**
- Use dates back several thousand years (Thailand, China, Polynesia).
- First isolated in 1888 by Ernst Jahns; structure confirmed 1907; first complete synthesis 1926 by Fritz Chemnitius.
- Used by 600+ million people worldwide (~10–20% of global population); fourth most used psychoactive drug after alcohol, nicotine, and caffeine.
- Use predominantly confined to Asia; major producing countries include India, China, Myanmar, Malaysia, Indonesia, and Bangladesh.
- Not generally controlled worldwide.

**Chemical Precursor:** Arecoline is used to synthesize paroxetine, femoxetine, nocaine, DMNPC, piquindone, epiboxidine-type compounds, brasofensine, tesofensine, and others.

**Analogues/Related:** Arecaidine, guavacoline, guvacine, nipecotic acid, nicotinic acid, muscarine, tiagabine, xanomeline (anti-schizophrenia drug), and others.

**Research:** Showed modest verbal/spatial memory improvement in Alzheimer's patients (IV administration), but carcinogenic properties make it not a first-choice drug. Anecdotal short-lived effect against schizophrenia; higher areca consumption associated with weaker symptoms in male schizophrenia patients. Inspired development of xanomeline. Enhances learning/memory in rodents.

**Veterinary Use:** Arecoline hydrobromide was listed as an abolished veterinary drug by the Chinese Ministry of Agriculture in 2012.

Betel quid without tobacco causes oral cancer." — IARC Monograph 85-6, "There is limited evidence in experimental animals for the carcinogenicity of arecoline." — IARC Monograph 85-6, Arecoline is used by more than 600 million people worldwide (~10–20% of the global population), and is the fourth most commonly used psychoactive drug in the world after alcohol, nicotine, and caffeine., "Arecoline is 'obviously cytotoxic' to cultures of hepatocytes, bone marrow cells, lymphocytes, neuronal cell, myoblasts and endothelial cells." — Liu et al. 2016 review, Arecoline is very efficiently absorbed through oral mucosa, with 85% bioavailability. Maximum plasma concentration is reached within 3 minutes.

## Abstract

Areca nut (Areca catechu L. AN), which is the dried, mature seed of the palm species Areca catechu L., is consumed by over 600 million individuals, predominantly in South Asia, East Africa, and certain regions of the tropical Pacific. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) has classified it as a species carcinogenic to humans and designated it as a Group 1 human carcinogen. Arecoline, which has attracted attention for its therapeutic potential in the treatment of mental illness and the relief of gastrointestinal disorders, is the main active alkaloid in the areca nut. However, in 2020, the IARC said that arecoline might be a “probable human carcinogen”. Arecoline can cause various types of cellular damage, primarily leading to the destruction of cell morphology, reduced survival rates, abnormal physiological functions, and even cell apoptosis. The research on its toxic mechanisms includes several aspects, such as increased levels of reactive oxygen species, autophagy, epigenetic dysregulation, and immune dysfunction, but these research findings are scattered and lack systematic integration. This article summarizes the effect mechanisms of arecoline on the oral cavity, neurological and cardiovascular systems, and other organs, as well as embryogenesis, and provides detailed and valuable insights for the clinical practice and targeted therapy of arecoline.

[arecoline](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=arecoline); [toxic effects](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=toxic+effects); [biological activity](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=biological+activity); [organ systems](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=organ+systems)

## 1. Introduction

The areca (betel) nut, derived from the seed of the areca nut palm, ranks as the world’s most prevalent harmful and addictive substance, following tobacco, ethanol, and caffeine [[1](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B1-foods-13-03825)]. In 1992, the World Health Organization (WHO) recognized the areca nut and tobacco as direct causative agents of oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC). Subsequently, in 2003, the WHO classified the areca nut as a primary carcinogen [[2](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B2-foods-13-03825)]. To date, more than an estimated 600 million individuals are habitual users of chewing the areca nut, with most in Central and South Asia, Southeast Asia, and Melanesia, including India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Malaysia, Taiwan, and other countries [[1](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B1-foods-13-03825),[3](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B3-foods-13-03825)]. The pharmacological and toxicological effects of the areca nut are dose-dependent. At low doses, it exhibits repellent and anti-inflammatory properties, enhances gastrointestinal function, modulates blood lipid levels, and offers protection against atherosclerosis. Additionally, it has been noted to have antidepressant effects. However, prolonged consumption of the areca nut can lead to adverse reactions in the human body and may be associated with malignant diseases, such as cirrhosis and oral submucosal fibrosis, among other toxicological effects [[3](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B3-foods-13-03825),[4](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B4-foods-13-03825)].

Arecoline (N-methyl-1,2,5, 6-tetrahydropyridine-3-carboxylate methyl ester), the primary alkaloid found in areca, has garnered significant interest within the realms of medicine and biology due to its pharmacological properties and toxic effects. Recent advancements in research pertaining to the physiological functions of areca alkaloids have led scholars to increasingly recognize their detrimental effects on human health. These encompass cellular damage to vital organs, such as the brain, heart, lungs, digestive tract, and genital system, as well as alterations in cell morphology. Such damage can precipitate conditions like oral submucosal fibrosis and various forms of cancer [[5](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B5-foods-13-03825)]. Furthermore, prolonged consumption of the areca nut may result in damage to both the reproductive and urinary systems. This could potentially impair sperm count and activity, as well as affect the acrosomal reaction of sperm and its ability to fertilize [[5](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B5-foods-13-03825)]. It significantly impacts the functionality of the nervous system, suppresses its cellular antioxidant capacity, results in oxidative stress damage, and elevates the prevalence of nervous system disorders [[6](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B6-foods-13-03825),[7](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B7-foods-13-03825)]. However, some studies have shown that low doses of arecoline in the areca nut have therapeutic effects for some diseases [[4](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B4-foods-13-03825)], such as its role in bone disease [[8](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B8-foods-13-03825)], Parkinson’s disease models [[9](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B9-foods-13-03825)], and Alzheimer’s disease [[10](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B10-foods-13-03825),[11](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B11-foods-13-03825),[12](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B12-foods-13-03825)]. To comprehensively understand the multifaceted nature of areca alkaloids, numerous studies have been conducted. These investigations encompass quality improvement techniques and extraction and analysis methodologies, as well as the metabolism of areca alkaloids in various environments. These studies offer valuable insights into the areca nut and its alkaloid constituents, suggesting potential avenues for the formulation of novel therapeutic approaches.

In this work, we searched the following databases using arecoline, toxicity, and biological activity as the keywords: The Web of Science, Science Direct, and PubMed. Three authors independently screened the titles and abstracts of all relevant papers in recent years, followed by full-text screening. Any conflicts were resolved by the three authors through discussion and consultation with a fourth author. Finally, 95 articles were reviewed, and the research content was summarized, focusing on the types, detection methods, pharmacological effects of arecoline, and its effects on different human organs, aiming to review and prospect for the related fields of arecoline and provide references for subsequent studies.

## 2. Species and Identification Method of Areca Alkaloids

The alkaloids in the areca nut are mainly pyridine alkaloids, and the total alkaloids are about 0.3~0.7%. It has been reported that about 20 alkaloids ([Figure 1](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#fig_body_display_foods-13-03825-f001)) are found in the areca nut, among which arecoline, arecaidine, guvacoline, and guvacine are the most common [[12](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B12-foods-13-03825),[13](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B13-foods-13-03825),[14](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B14-foods-13-03825),[15](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B15-foods-13-03825),[16](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B16-foods-13-03825)]. The chemical structure of areca alkaloids has double bonds at the exact location of the ring and contains ester bonds and nitromethyl functional groups, and its chemical structure is shown in [Figure 1](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#fig_body_display_foods-13-03825-f001) [[16](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B16-foods-13-03825)]. Arecoline and norarecoline are hydrolyzed products of arecaidine and norecaidine. The separation, purification, and determination methods of these four alkaloids have been studied and explored. The extraction methods of areca alkaloids mainly include solvent extraction, ultrasonic-assisted extraction, subcritical water extraction, and supercritical CO 2 extraction [[17](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B17-foods-13-03825),[18](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B18-foods-13-03825)]. Currently, the primary detection methods for arecoline that have reached a significant level of maturity encompass high-performance liquid chromatography, ultra-high performance liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry, microchip capillary electrophoresis with contactless conductance detection, and gas chromatography–mass spectrometry [[17](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B17-foods-13-03825)]. Dai et al. [[19](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B19-foods-13-03825)] employed near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) to quantify the primary active components of the areca nut, namely, gallic acid, tannins, catechin, and arecoline. The quantification of these four active components was further enhanced using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). By integrating these findings, a rapid near-infrared detection model for the main active substances in the areca nut was established. Pan et al. [[20](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B20-foods-13-03825)] devised a method utilizing ultra-high performance liquid chromatography–MS/MS (UPLC-M S/MS) to simultaneously quantify areca alkaloids in rat plasma, following oral administration of the areca extract. This method also facilitated pharmacokinetic studies that indirectly elucidated the metabolic relationship of the four areca alkaloids in vivo. Furthermore, Pan [[21](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B21-foods-13-03825)] introduced a rapid, selective, and accurate high-performance liquid chromatography–electrospray ionization tandem mass spectrometry (LC-ESI-MS/MS) technique for the concurrent quantification of arecoline, arecaidine, and arecoline n-oxide in rat plasma. This comprehensive approach effectively validated their pharmacokinetic post-oral arecoline administration.

## 3. Toxicological Effects of Areca Nut

Arecoline is a key medicinal component of the areca nut and is soluble in water, ethanol, ether, and chloroform [[21](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B21-foods-13-03825)]. Extensive studies have linked it to the onset of various diseases. The ingestion of the areca nut has been associated with an elevated risk of developing oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), oral submucosal fibrosis (OSF), and head and neck cancer. Furthermore, it is implicated in DNA damage and a range of systemic diseases, including atherosclerosis and cardiovascular disease [[22](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B22-foods-13-03825)]. Modern toxicological studies have reported that arecoline has oral submucosal fibrogenic toxicity, reproductive toxicity, hepatorenal toxicity, immunosuppressive toxicity, and neurotoxicity, and it has been observed to induce cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, and cytotoxicity in human oral endothelial cells [[23](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B23-foods-13-03825)], as well as having cytotoxic and genotoxic effects in hepatocytes [[24](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B24-foods-13-03825)], bone marrow cells (BMCs) [[25](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B25-foods-13-03825)], lymphocytes (PBLs) [[26](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B26-foods-13-03825)], and neuronal cells [[27](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B27-foods-13-03825)]. Moreover, arecoline has been implicated in neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson’s disease [[9](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B9-foods-13-03825)].

In recent years, many researchers have conducted in-depth studies on the pharmacological effects of areca alkaloids. The effects of areca alkaloids on various organs are shown in [Table 1](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#table_body_display_foods-13-03825-t001). It can be seen from the table that arecoline affects the oral system, the brain nervous system, the cardiovascular system, the gastrointestinal system, the liver system, and even embryos to varying degrees, and different doses of arecoline have different effects on each organ.

## 4. Effects on Inducing Oral Fibrosis and Oral Diseases

The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) has designated the areca nut and its principal constituents as Group 1 carcinogens [[41](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B41-foods-13-03825)]. Oral cancer ranks as the seventh most prevalent cause of cancer-related mortality globally, with an estimated 710,000 cases annually. Dishearteningly, only 40–50% of those diagnosed survive beyond five years [[42](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B42-foods-13-03825)]. The elevated incidence of oral cancer is intimately associated with habits such as areca nut chewing, smoking, and alcohol consumption. Arecoline, a compound found in the areca nut, triggers the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and contributes to DNA damage during oral cancer progression [[43](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B43-foods-13-03825)]. Oxidative stress plays a pivotal role in this malignancy, primarily affecting DNA and proteins in normal cells, leading to carcinogenic mutations and the malignant transformation of the oropharyngeal mucosa and enhancing the progression and invasiveness of OSCC cells [[44](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B44-foods-13-03825)]. Both areca extract (ANE) and areca alkaloid exhibit genotoxic properties, promoting increased levels of ROS and resulting in chromosomal aberrations in mammalian cells [[1](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B1-foods-13-03825)]. [Figure 2](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#fig_body_display_foods-13-03825-f002) presents potential mechanisms through which arecoline contributes to oral submucosal fibrosis (OSF) and oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) [[45](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B45-foods-13-03825)].

### 4.1. Oral Submucosal Fibrosis (OSF)

Oral submucosal fibrosis (OSF) is a chronic oral mucosal disease characterized by chronic inflammation processes and persistent fibrosis proliferation. It represents a precancerous lesion that is causally associated with the consumption of the areca nut. As indicated by epidemiological studies, the primary etiological factor associated with OSF is chewing the areca nut [[46](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B46-foods-13-03825)]. Consumption of the areca nut has been demonstrated to exert a detrimental impact on the oral mucosa, precipitating inflammatory responses and fibrosis. This is attributed to the impairment of T-cell activation and the subsequent stimulation of the production of transforming growth factor β (TGF-β1), prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), transforming growth factor-α (TNF-α), and interleukin-6 (IL-6), which are pivotal in the pathogenesis of both cancer and OSF [[47](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B47-foods-13-03825),[48](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B48-foods-13-03825)].

It has been demonstrated that the primary pathway associated with OSF is linked to a number of inflammatory mediators. These include but are not limited to transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) [[49](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B49-foods-13-03825)], PGE2, IL-6, TNF-α, and cyclooxygenase 2 (Cox-2). TGF-β is a pivotal mediator in the pathogenesis of OSF [[48](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B48-foods-13-03825)]. Areca-derived substances, such as arecaolin, induce keratinocytes to secrete a considerable amount of TGF-β by upregulating the TGF-β signaling pathway, which further affects the transformation of oral mucosal fibroblasts into myofibroblasts and deepens the role of fibrosis. Currently, the TGF-β pathway is understood to play a role in inhibiting collagen degradation and activating the inhibitor of the plasma plasminogen activator in the process of fibrotic diseases, affecting the balance between matrix metalloproteinases and inhibitors at DNA and protein levels, promoting the mesenchymal transformation of epithelial cells and resulting in the imbalance of collagen metabolism. Nevertheless, the induction of arecoline has been observed to elicit an overt oxidative stress response in fibroblasts, culminating in DNA damage, lipid peroxidation, and cellular death [[50](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B50-foods-13-03825),[51](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B51-foods-13-03825),[52](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B52-foods-13-03825)], thus promoting the induction of oral cancer. Concurrently, research has demonstrated that aprocoline can modulate phosphoinositide 3-kinase/protein kinase B (PI3K-Akt) and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathways. This modulation promotes the expression of inflammatory mediators, such as IL-6 and interleukin 8 (IL-8), induces collagen hyperplasia, and contributes to the development of oral submucosal fibrosis [[52](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B52-foods-13-03825),[53](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B53-foods-13-03825)]. In the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase-Akt pathway, the expression of protein kinase B (AKT1) is increased by activating the AKT1 protein downstream, which intensifies the expression and accumulation of the phosphorylated AKT (p-AKT) protein [[54](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B54-foods-13-03825)]. In the MAPK pathway, by upregulating the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) protein, the activity of the downstream AP-1 complex protein c-jun and c-fos transcription factors is induced to increase and promote their aggregation to the nucleus.

Another pathway of OSF is arecaine’s induction of epithelial–mesenchymal transformation (EMT) in human buccal mucosal fibroblasts (BMFs), which is a key factor in promoting tumor progression and fibrosis [[55](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B55-foods-13-03825)]. In the context of carcinogenesis and metastasis, the expression of specific proteins and enzymes is enhanced, leading to epithelial–mesenchymal transformation (EMT) and the subsequent activation of EMT-associated proteins. This process can be influenced by a variety of chemical compounds, such as ROS, TGF-β, Notch receptor-1, and inflammatory cytokines [[56](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B56-foods-13-03825)]. Zinc Finger E-box Binding Homeobox 1 (ZEB1) functions as a transcription factor, regulating its target genes via its protein-binding domain, with a particular emphasis on e-cadherin. The alkaloid arecoline has been demonstrated to induce the formation of α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA)-positive stress fibers in cells that express the transcription factor ZEB1 in a manner that is dependent on the presence of the BMF protein. Furthermore, arecoline has been demonstrated to induce collagen contraction in the BMF. Chromatin immunoprecipitation demonstrated that arecoline enhanced the binding of ZEB1 to the α-SMA promoter in the BMF, thereby inducing the BMF to undergo transdifferentiation into myofibrocytes. Subsequently, it promotes extracellular matrix (ECM) accumulation and participates in the pathogenesis of OSF [[57](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B57-foods-13-03825),[58](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B58-foods-13-03825)].

### 4.2. Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma (OSCC)

Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is a malignant tumor that can occur in various parts of the mouth, including the lips, tongue, salivary glands, gums, floor of the mouth, oropharynx, and buccal mucosa. Oral cancer ranks as the seventh most prevalent cause of cancer-related deaths globally, with an annual estimation of 378,500 new cases. Notably, half of the oral cancer-related fatalities occur in Southeast Asia [[59](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B59-foods-13-03825)]. OSF is a precancerous lesion of OSCC and can precede the diagnosis of OSCC [[60](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B60-foods-13-03825)]. Statistics show that the incidence of OSCC accounts for about 90% of oral malignancies. According to the Global Cancer Observatory (GCO), the incidence of OSCC will increase by about 40% by 2040, and the mortality rate will gradually increase [[61](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B61-foods-13-03825)]. Epidemiological research has demonstrated a strong correlation between the act of chewing the areca nut and the incidence of OSCC. The areca line found in the areca nut exhibits mutagenic and carcinogenic properties, thereby increasing the likelihood of malignant tumor development in patients with oral submucous fibrosis (OSMF) [[62](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B62-foods-13-03825)]. Concurrently, research has indicated that arecoline may contribute to the development of OSCC by inducing heightened oxidative stress, epigenetic irregularities, and immune system dysfunction [[28](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B28-foods-13-03825),[63](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B63-foods-13-03825),[64](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B64-foods-13-03825)].

Oral cancer is caused by the accumulation of oxidative stress in normal cells, resulting in damage to DNA and proteins. This leads to the development of carcinogenic mutations and malignant transformation of the oropharyngeal mucosa. Consequently, the progression and invasiveness of OSCC cells are enhanced. It has been demonstrated that oxidative stress can promote the occurrence, progression, and resistance to therapy of tumors by damaging the DNA of cells. This leads to the accumulation of mutations and genomic instability and results in the reprogramming of cell metabolism and signaling pathways [[65](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B65-foods-13-03825)]. The administration of arecoline has been demonstrated to induce an increase in ROS production and a reduction in the expression of antioxidant enzymes, which, in turn, results in DNA damage and the inhibition of DNA repair activity. This ultimately leads to the accumulation of error-prone DNA replication and mutation [[66](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B66-foods-13-03825),[67](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B67-foods-13-03825)]. The administration of 100–200 μg/mL of arecoline resulted in DNA damage, the induction of phosphorylated ATM (p-ATM) and phosphorylated ATR (p-ATR) expression, and an increase in genotoxicity. Arecoline oxidative metabolites (ANOs) have been demonstrated to exhibit high levels of cytotoxicity, DNA damage, and proliferation activity in the initial stages of chewing arecoline. Furthermore, they have been shown to stimulate extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK), JNK, p38, and pro-inflammatory cytokines through peroxide stress and induce an increase in ROS, thus increasing the risk of OSCC [[68](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B68-foods-13-03825)].

## 5. Effects on the Nervous System

The nervous system is a functional collection of cells, tissues, and organs that enables the body to react to both internal and external stimuli in a controlled manner. The human nervous system can be broadly categorized into two principal sections: the central nervous system (CNS), which encompasses both the brain and the spinal cord, and the peripheral nervous system, which is constituted by the cranial and spinal nerves. The primary role of the human nervous system is to act as a central control, coordinating and regulating the functions of various organs and systems within the body. This ensures that the human body operates as a cohesive unit. The system controls movement, regulates the endocrine system, maintains cardiovascular stability, manages respiration, oversees the digestive system, and regulates the immune system, among other functions [[69](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B69-foods-13-03825),[70](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B70-foods-13-03825),[71](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B71-foods-13-03825)].

Consumption of the areca nut has been observed to produce a range of effects on the central nervous system. These include the induction of euphoria, palpitations, and salivation, as well as an increase in perspiration. Additionally, it has been noted to improve cognitive impairment and reduce anxiety. The nut also carries addictive properties and can suppress hunger while simultaneously enhancing physical activity [[72](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B72-foods-13-03825)]. Arecoline, the main alkaloid in arecoline, easily crosses the blood–brain barrier (BBB) [[9](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B9-foods-13-03825)] and stimulates nicotinic and muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, thus stimulating the central nervous system. The specific mechanisms of influence on the nervous system include neuron damage and nerve signal transmission. Arecoline induces neurotoxicity via oxidative stress-mediated apoptotic signaling. This process elevates reactive ROS levels, diminishes antioxidant concentrations, and impedes the protective mechanisms against ROS, thereby leading to neuronal damage [[27](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B27-foods-13-03825)]. Arecoline concentrations, ranging from 50 to 200 μM, have been observed to disrupt neuronal redox homeostasis, subsequently inducing neuronal cell death [[27](https://www.mdpi.com/2304-8158/13/23/3825#B27-foods-13-03825)]. It was observed that the administration of arecoline resulted in the disruption of the autophagy flux in PC12 cells, which manifested as an increase in the number of autophagy vacuoles. Additionally, the levels of LC3II/LC3I and p62 expression were elevated in PC12 cells following the administration of arecoline. These changes led to a notable decrease in the viability of PC12 cells, thereby indicating a neurotoxic effect of arecoline on these cells [[73](https://www.mdpi.com/

This is a scientific review article titled "Recent Advance on Biological Activity and Toxicity of Arecoline in Edible Areca (Betel) Nut: A Review," published in the journal Foods (2024, Volume 13, Issue 23, Article 3825; DOI: 10.3390/foods13233825). The article belongs to the Food Toxicology section.

**Authors and Affiliations:** Gang Huang, Deyong Zeng, Tisong Liang, Yaping Liu, Fang Cui, Haitian Zhao, and Weihong Lu, affiliated with the Harbin Institute of Technology (School of Chemical Engineering and Chemistry; Chongqing Research Institute; School of Medicine and Health Sciences), China.

**Publication Timeline:** Submitted 16 October 2024; Revised 14 November 2024; Accepted 24 November 2024; Published 27 November 2024.

**Key Content Summary:**

1. **Areca Nut Background:** The areca (betel) nut (Areca catechu L.) is consumed by over 600 million individuals, predominantly in South Asia, East Africa, and tropical Pacific regions. The IARC has classified it as a Group 1 human carcinogen. Arecoline is the main active alkaloid.

2. **Carcinogenicity Classification:** In 2020, IARC indicated arecoline might be a "probable human carcinogen." WHO recognized areca nut as a primary carcinogen in 2003 and, in 1992, linked it to oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC).

3. **Alkaloid Species and Detection:** Areca nut contains about 20 pyridine alkaloids (0.3–0.7% total), with arecoline, arecaidine, guvacoline, and guvacine being most common. Extraction methods include solvent extraction, ultrasonic-assisted extraction, subcritical water extraction, and supercritical CO₂ extraction. Detection methods include HPLC, UPLC-MS/MS, microchip capillary electrophoresis, GC-MS, and near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS).

4. **Toxicological Effects:** Arecoline has oral submucosal fibrogenic toxicity, reproductive toxicity, hepatorenal toxicity, immunosuppressive toxicity, and neurotoxicity. It induces cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, and cytotoxicity.

5. **Oral Diseases:** 
   - OSF (Oral Submucosal Fibrosis) is a precancerous lesion caused by areca nut chewing, involving TGF-β, PGE2, IL-6, TNF-α, and COX-2 pathways. Arecoline modulates PI3K-Akt and MAPK pathways, induces epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), and promotes collagen accumulation.
   - OSCC (Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma) is the 7th most prevalent cause of cancer-related mortality globally (~710,000 cases annually; 378,500 new cases). Arecoline causes DNA damage via ROS production, epigenetic irregularities, and immune dysfunction.

6. **Nervous System Effects:** Arecoline crosses the blood–brain barrier, stimulates nicotinic and muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, induces neurotoxicity via oxidative stress-mediated apoptotic signaling, and disrupts autophagy flux in PC12 cells. It causes euphoria, palpitations, salivation, increased perspiration, and has addictive properties. Concentrations of 50–200 μM disrupt neuronal redox homeostasis.

7. **Methodology:** The review searched Web of Science, Science Direct, and PubMed databases using keywords (arecoline, toxicity, biological activity), and 95 articles were reviewed by three independent authors with conflicts resolved by a fourth author.

8. **Review Structure:** Sections cover species and identification methods of areca alkaloids, toxicological effects, oral fibrosis and oral diseases (OSF and OSCC), effects on the nervous system, cardiovascular system, reproductive organs, and other organs, plus conclusions and prospects.

# Comprehensive insights into areca nut: active components and omics technologies for bioactivity evaluation and quality control

### Yuanyuan Sun

### Jian Feng

### Wencheng Hou

### Huasha Qi

### Yangyang Liu

**Edited by:**
[Wei Peng](https://loop.frontiersin.org/people/715217/overview), Chengdu University of Traditional Chinese Medicine, China

**Reviewed by:**
[Qin Wan Huang](https://loop.frontiersin.org/people/637619/overview), Chengdu University of Traditional Chinese Medicine, China

[Mengmeng Zhang](https://loop.frontiersin.org/people/2718041/overview), Shaanxi University of Chinese Medicine, China

\*Correspondence: Yangyang Liu, yyliu@implad.ac.cn

Received 2024 Mar 26; Accepted 2024 May 6; Collection date 2024.

This is an open-access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY). No use, distribution or reproduction is permitted which does not comply with these terms.

## Abstract

Areca nut (AN), the fruit or seed of *Areca catechu* Linn, has many uses, including chewing and medicinal purposes. It has sparked worries about health due to the presence of alkaloids. Chewing AN may have a variety of negative consequences; however, the medicinal use of AN has no notable adverse effects. To completely understand and effectively use AN, researchers have investigated its chemical makeup or biological activity, analyzed the variations between different AN species and different periods, and improved extraction and processing procedures. Today, an increasing number of researchers are exploring the underlying reasons for AN variations, as well as the molecular mechanisms of biosynthesis of chemical components, to comprehend and change AN at the genetic level. This review presents an overview of the clinical study, pharmacology, and detection of the main bioactive components in AN, and the main factors influencing their content, delving into the omics applications in AN research. On the basis of the discussions and summaries, this review identifies current research gaps and proposes future directions for investigation.

**Keywords:** areca nut, active components, pharmacology, quality detection, influencing factors, omics, clinical study

## Graphical Abstract

[![graphic file with name FPHAR_fphar-2024-1407212_wc_abs.jpg](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/f539/11169615/351e82ad0ca5/FPHAR_fphar-2024-1407212_wc_abs.jpg)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/core/lw/2.0/html/tileshop_pmc/tileshop_pmc_inline.html?title=Click%20on%20image%20to%20zoom&p=PMC3&id=11169615_FPHAR_fphar-2024-1407212_wc_abs.jpg)

![graphic file with name FPHAR_fphar-2024-1407212_wc_abs.jpg](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/f539/11169615/351e82ad0ca5/FPHAR_fphar-2024-1407212_wc_abs.jpg)

## 1 Introduction

*Areca catechu* is a monoecious, perennial and evergreen tree belonging to the palm family ([Figure 1A](#F1)). It grows in the tropical climates of Asia, East Africa, and the Pacific, particularly in South and Southeast Asian countries. It is now believed that *A. catechu* originated in Indonesia, Malaysia, or the Philippines ([Rooney, 1995](#B103); [Lim, 2012](#B73); [World Health Organization. Regional Office for the Western Pacific, 2012](#B144); [Manimekalai et al., 2018](#B85); [Joo et al., 2020](#B61)). After thousands of years of evolution, it has become a significant economic tree species in certain regions, such as Indonesia and Vietnam. Hainan Province is the largest producer of *A. catechu* in China ([Yang et al., 2018](#B156)). In addition to its contribution to the agricultural economies of the countries where it is grown, *A. catechu* has an important place in the religious, cultural, and social milieus of the rural people. Areca nut (AN) is the fruit of *A. catechu* ([Figures 1B, C](#F1)), and it is not only used to chew; however, different parts of it have different medicinal values. The immature fruit is boiled and dried, and the husk obtained after removing the seeds is called arecae pericarpium (“Da Fu Pi” in Chinese) ([Figure 1D](#F1)), whereas the husk obtained after processing the mature fruit is called “Da Fu Mao” ([Figure 1G](#F1)). Their primary functions include moving qi, soothing the middle, disinhibiting water, and relieving swelling. The mature fruit is boiled and dried, and the husk is removed, resulting in therapeutic seeds known as arecae semen ([Figure 1E](#F1)). The charred seeds are known as arecae semen tostum ([Figure 1F](#F1)). For seeds, the arecae semen is mainly used to kill parasites, and the arecae semen tostum is mainly used to promote digestion. In this review, the term AN is used to refer to both the fruit and the seed of *A. catechu* without distinction. The fresh young fruit (usually harvested at around 4 months) are chewed with various ingredients in different regions. It is estimated that more than 600 million people chew AN ([Warnakulasuriya and Chen, 2022](#B143)). Unfortunately, AN is considered the world’s fourth most addictive substance and is classified as a Group 1 carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) of the World Health Organization ([IARC Working Group on the Evaluation of Carcinogenic Risks to Humans, 2007](#B57)). In traditional medicinal applications, the processing of traditional Chinese medicine has been proven by numerous studies to enhance efficacy and reduce toxicity. To cater to individuals with diverse constitutions and address various primary symptoms, China has long employed the technique of charcoal roasting to transform arecae semen into arecae semen tostum. Arecae semen has the strongest medicinal properties and is not recommended for frail individuals. By contrast, Arecae semen tostum offers milder effects with less adverse effects while alleviating food stagnation. Researchers have already compared the chemical compositions of AN, in addition to the influence of different processing methods on these chemical components. Distinct parts of AN and various processing techniques can lead to significant changes in the active ingredients.

### FIGURE 1.

[![FIGURE 1](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/f539/11169615/14c9d8619a7a/fphar-15-1407212-g001.jpg)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/core/lw/2.0/html/tileshop_pmc/tileshop_pmc_inline.html?title=Click%20on%20image%20to%20zoom&p=PMC3&id=11169615_fphar-15-1407212-g001.jpg)

![FIGURE 1](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/f539/11169615/14c9d8619a7a/fphar-15-1407212-g001.jpg)

The plant, fruit, husk, and seed of *Areca catechu*. **(A)** Plant *A. catechu*. **(B)** Fresh and tender fruit. **(C)** Ripe fruit. **(D)** Arecae pericarpium. **(E)** Arecae semen. **(F)** Arecae semen tostum. **(G)** Da Fu Mao.

Although it is true that the medicinal and edible uses of seeds and fruit should not be confused, alkaloids, the main active ingredients that cause the positive effects, also play a major role in the negative effects. As a result, the public is afraid of pharmaceuticals and preparations that contain arecae semen or arecae semen tostum. Nevertheless, the adverse clinical events associated with medicinal seeds are relatively rare and controllable. Ancient books contain no records of arecae semen’s toxicity and usually consider it nontoxic. Only a few records mention likely side effects, such as “fever and injury to vital energy”, emphasizing that it should not be used by those with weak constitutions or those who do not have specific indications for its use ([Sun et al., 2017](#B119)).

This review provides an overview of the clinical study and observation of AN, and two main categories of bioactive compounds in the fruit and seeds of *A. catechu*: alkaloids and polyphenolic substances. It describes their pharmacological effects and potential adverse effects, and summarizes recent literature on the main detected substances, quantification methods, and influencing factors. Subsequently, the application of omics technologies in AN research is discussed, encompassing aspects such as *A. catechu* germplasm, metabolites, and bioactive properties, with the aim of offering a reference for better utilization and quality determination of AN.

## 2 Clinical study of AN

### 2.1 Clinical study of medicinal AN

AN is commonly used in therapeutic settings as a proprietary Chinese medicine. These formulas were proposed by traditional Chinese physicians a hundred or a thousand years ago and were enhanced during use. There have been no reports of clinically significant toxic side effects of the use of AN for medicinal purposes. “Muxiang Binglang Pill” has the effect of eliminating food-induced stagnation, and its combination with Western medicine in the comprehensive treatment of mild acute pancreatitis can effectively promote the recovery of intestinal function and improve its overall clinical efficacy ([Wang, 2024](#B135)). The clinical efficacy of employing “Binglang Powder” in conjunction with acupoint massage in the treatment of patients with spleen and stomach diseases is remarkable, effectively relieving symptoms, reducing inflammatory reactions in the spleen and stomach, and improving spleen and stomach function ([Liu, 2021](#B77)). Moreover, AN can promote the recovery of gastrointestinal function after gynecological abdominal surgery, and its mechanism of action may be related to the modulation of the level of motilin, a brain-gut peptide hormone ([Liang et al., 2020](#B72)). “Food Retention Relieve Oral Liquid” is composed of 10 medicines, including Galli Gigerii Endothelium Corneum, Sparganii Rhizoma, Curcumae Rhizoma, and Arecae semen. It has good clinical efficacy in the treatment of anorexia nervosa in children ([Wan, 2010](#B130); [Sun et al., 2014](#B118)). “Jinyingzi Binglang Decoction” is effective in treating patients with chronic, intractable diarrhea ([Zhang, 2014](#B168)). “Food Retention and Cough Relieve Oral Liquid for Children” is composed of Crataegi Fructus, Arecae semen, and eight other medicines that are effective in the treatment of pediatric cough and have the advantages of few toxic side effects and ease of use ([Di, 2015](#B24)). “Binglang Shisanwei Pill,” in combination with psychological care, can effectively improve the symptoms of depression and increase satisfaction in clinical care ([Gu, 2021](#B38)). Furthermore, in animal parasite therapy, arecoline hydrobromide is useful in the eradication of cattle tick *Rhipicephalus microplus* infections in calves, and clinical safety has been determined by examining hematological characteristics and performing skin irritation assays in calves infested with ticks ([Jain et al., 2021](#B58)).

### 2.2 Clinical observation of chewing AN

AN chewing often leads to oral problems. Clinical analysis of 189 cases of oral submucosal fibrous degeneration in a hospital in Zhengzhou (a city in China) showed that the onset of oral submucous fibrosis (OSF) predominantly occurs in males, with a tendency for rejuvenation. Age, chewing time, and chewing amount are related to OSF disease severity ([Yu et al., 2022](#B161)). [Tang et al. (2018)](#B123) conducted a clinical analysis of 86 cases of OSF caused by AN chewing; the higher the frequency and duration of AN chewing, the greater the probability of the disease. The majority of patients with OSF have initial symptoms of mucosal irritation pain and limited mouth opening. Most patients also have a smoking habit, which has a synergistic effect on the occurrence of OSF. In oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) patients with an chewing habit, tumors are relatively well differentiated, and the buccal and tongue areas are the most common sites of OSCC ([Shao et al., 2021](#B108)). Long-term AN chewing may lead to different degrees of tooth abrasion. By reviewing the medical records of patients with oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) between 1999 and 2013, [Chen et al. (2020)](#B15) found that HPV-OPSCC accounted for the majority of OPSCC in areas where AN chewing is endemic. The combination of alcohol/betel nut chewing/smoking exposure has a significant negative impact on disease-free survival and overall survival.

## 3 Alkaloid

Alkaloids display a wide range of biological functions and may pose potential health threats. They are typical constituents and bioactive compounds found in AN, with presence primarily limited to *A. catechu* in the palm family. Presently, at least 18 alkaloids have been identified in AN ([Table 1](#T1)) ([Peng et al., 2015](#B95); [Tang et al., 2017](#B122); [Cao et al., 2019](#B9)); however, there is a notable dearth of dedicated research on the isolation and identification of alkaloids in the seed. The total alkaloid content in AN varies between 0.3% and 0.6% ([Han, 2010](#B43)). Arecoline is commonly considered the most abundant alkaloid, followed by guvacine, arecaidine, and guvacoline. These four alkaloids not only constitute a significant portion of the alkaloids in AN but are also major active substances ([Oliveira et al., 2021](#B90)). Hence, researchers often rely on measuring the content of arecoline or these four alkaloids as evidence of AN efficacy or toxicity. Furthermore, experiments have shown that different regions, growth stages, and processing methods can significantly influence the alkaloid content of AN.
