Cite this article:  Zeleke ZZ. Extraction of essential oil from lemon and orange peel by Clevenger apparatus:Comparative GC\_MS analysis of chemical composition, from Debre Berehan Market town Amahara Region Ethiopia. Ann Biotechnol. 2022; 5(1): 1026.

**Keywords**: Waste; Essential oil; Limonene; Peel; GC-MS.

### Abstract

The peel of orange and lemon fruits is considered as a waste. It is used as a source of essential oils that can be applicable for food flavoring agent, pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, and soap and detergent factories. In this work, essential oils were extracted from lemon (1.56%) and orange (3.55%) peels by hydro distillation. The physiochemical properties of oils were recorded. The chemical composition of the oils was also analyzed by GC-MS. Orange peel oil contained four compounds with limonene (95.19%) as major component and lemon peel oil composed of 12 compounds of which limonene (49.74%) was the main compound.

### Introduction

Citrus (family Rutaceae) is one of the most widespread genera all over the world due to its prominent production. It comprises 140 genus and 1,300 species, Citrus sinensis (sweet orange), Citrus limon (lemon), Citrus paradis (grape fruits), Citrus medica (Citron), Citrus aurantifolia (lime), Citrus grandis (shaddock), Citrus reticulate (tangerine) and citrus aurantium (sour orange) are some of important fruits of genus citrus [1-8]. Citrus fruits are very popular in many parts of the world because of their distinctive taste and aroma as well as multiple health benefits to mankind [9]. These plants grow in tropical and subtropical regions of the world. Orange and lemon trees lemon are the three most important and abundant citrus species in the world [10,11].

      Most of citrus plants are planted for consuming freshly at home. Orange and lemon fruits are consumed fresh or industrially processed as juice [12-15]. The juice industries produce mainly juices from the endocarp or pulp parts of citrus fruits. However, the industries discard byproducts including peels or flavedo, albedo, seeds and pulp residues as waste. The waste having more than half of the original weight of the fruit is disposed outside their compound which has high potential to affect the environment. All byproducts of citrus plants may have importance if they are recommended to use them based on research findings [16,17].

      The chemical compositions of the plants are mainly affected by the part of plant analyzed, growing condition, variation of species, plant pretreatment, extraction methods, place of origin, maturity. The chemical constituents may present in all parts of the plant but the amount varies from one organ of plant to another [18-20].

      Citrus fruits and their peels are the rich sources of vitamins, minerals, sugars, carbohydrates, fats, proteins, organic acids, dietary fibers and secondary metabolites like flavonoids, terpenoids, coumarins, alkaloids and essential oils [11]. Citrus plants are rich sources of citric acid (vitamin C) which causes their fruits sour due to low pH (2-3) [21-23]. The juices also contain fragrance compounds like hydrocarbons, alcohols, aldehydes, esters, ketones and some oxygenated terpenes [24]. Reportedly, the peels of citrus plants contain many biologically active compounds that are extensively applied for flavoring beverages, foods, perfumes, cosmetics, etc. [5,25]. Flavonoids are the major constituents of dry citrus fruits as well as citrus peels [17].

      Essential oils are volatile odoriferous or aromatic oily liquids extracted from different plants parts. Numerous plants contain essential oils, however, parts of plants, which serve as the major source of essential oil can be different. Plant essential oils are usually the complex mixture of both polar and nonpolar compounds including terpenoids and oxygenated aromatic compounds [26]. The essential oils extracted from the peels of citrus peels are complex mixtures; of which 85%-99% are volatile and 1%-15% are non-volatile. The volatile components contain a mixture of monoterpene, sesquiterpene and their oxygenated derivatives but non-volatile compounds contains hydrocarbons, flavonoids, sterols, fatty acids, coumarins, waxes and carotenoids [1,27].

      The main chemical components of lemon and orange essential oils are Limonene (1), Alpha- Terpene (2), Γ-Terpinene (3), Α-Terpineol (4), Β-Pinene (5), Α-Pinene (6), Myrcene (7), Linalool (8), Geraneryl acetate (9), Neral (10), Nerol (11), Valencene (12), Octanal (13), Decanal (14), Geraniol (15), Sabinene (16), Linalyl Acetate (17), Terpinen-4-ol (18), Citronella (19), Heptanal (20), O-cymene (21), P-cymene (22), 2-Undecanone (23), 3-Carene (24), Beta-bisaboline (25), caryopellene (26), citral (27). Limonene (1) is the major constituent of lemon essential oil as well as other citrus essential oils. Also lemon oil has some aldehyde molecules (0.13% -1.50%) [18,19,23,24,28].

[![...](figures/biotechnology-1026-001.gif "Scheme 1: Structures of some compounds found in essential oils from the lemon and orange peels. ")](#)

Scheme 1:  Structures of some compounds found in essential oils from the lemon and orange peels.

      Different studies reveled that Limonene (1) is found in citrus essential oils accounting for 32%- 98% [1,27]. It is a colorless to colored liquid monoterpene at room temperature depending on the source; in some fruits it has strong odour. It takes its name from lemon. It exists as (R)- limonene in orange and (S)- limonene in lemon. It is insoluble in water but soluble in alcohol and ether which has boiling point of 74OC [19,29].

      The peels can be used as possible sources of compounds that can be applicable for the manufacture of chemicals, flavorings and fragrances, paints, cosmetics, and animal feed supplement instead of their disposal. The aim of this study was to investigate the comparative essential oil chemical constituents of the waste peels of orange and lemon by GC-MS.

#### Experimental procedure

**Hydro distillation of fresh orange and lemon peels**

      The washed lemon and orange peels were crushed in order to reduce their size. The edible portion and white spongy portion (albedo) was separated from the peel by crusher. The crushed samples were used to isolate an essential oil by hydro distillation as follows. Crushed pieces of lemon peels (225 g) were placed in to 1000 ml round bottom flask and 720 ml of distilled water was added to it. After addition of boiling chips the flask was heated slowly for two hours. The distillate forms two layers in the Clevenger apparatus with organic compounds at upper and hydrosol at bottom. The organic phase was collected by small bottles and dried with anhydrous sodium sulfate. The weight of essential oil was measured and the percentage yield of oil was calculated. Similarly crushed pieces (225g) of Lemon peel were subjected to hydro distillation by same procedure above. The same procedure was carried out twice for orange peel extraction essential oils.

**GC-MS analysis of essential oils**

      GC-MS analyses were performed at Addis Ababa University. The instrument was fitted with a fused silica capillary column (30 m x 250 μm, i.d. 0.25 μm film thickness). The oven temperature was programmed from 60°C (2 min) to 240°C (20 min.) at 3°C/min. The injector and detector temperatures were 250°C and 280oC respectively. Oil samples of 0.2 μl were injected into the GC with a split ratio of 1:50. Helium was the carrier gas at a flow rate of 2 ml/min. The MS was obtained with an ionization voltage of 70 eV, ion source at 230°C. MS data were acquired in the scan mode in the m/z range 40-650. Identification was made based on a comparison of their retention indices and MS data compared to those from the NIST 107 and Wiley 229 spectral libraries (National Institute of Standards and Technology) [29,30].

### Results and discussion

Essential oils were isolated from fresh orange and lemon peels by hydro distillation (Clevenger apparatus) and subjected to GC-MS analysis.

      The weight of the essential oils were measured and their percentage were calculated relative to mass of fresh peels of both lemon and orange (Table 1). The average yield of essential oils obtained from lemon and orange peels were determined as 1.56% and 3.55%, respectively. Orange peel has essential oil twice of lemon. Literature shows the closer percentage yield of orange essential oil (3%) [31] With this work.

**GC-MS analysis of essential oils of orange and lemon peels**

      The GC--MS data of lemon essential oil (Table 5) showed the identification of 12 components with monoterpene hydrocarbons (76.56%), aliphatic aldehyde (0.77%), monoterpene aldehydes (14.39%), monoterpene alcohols (2.3%), sesquiterpenes (4.97%) and ketone (1.02%) as main constituents. The major monoterpenes limonene (49.74%), β-pinene (17.13%), γ-terpinene (7.52), o-cymene (2.17%), sesquiterpenes of β-bisabolene (2.4%), β-caryophyllene (1.45%),

      trans α-bergamotene (1.12%), carbonyls citral (14.39%), heptanal (0.77%), 2-undecanone (1.02%), and alcohols α-terpineol (1.44%) and terpinen-4-ol (0.86%) were detected. Terpenes particularly monoterpenes were dominant components in the lemon essential oils.

![table 1](../img/table_icon.png)  Table 1

Table 1: Percentage composition of essential oils.

![table 2](../img/table_icon.png)  Table 2

Table 2: Chemical composition of lemon and orange essential oils.

      Four compounds were detected in orange peel essential oil (99.99%), namely, monoterpenes (97.11%) and N-methyl-1, 3-propanediamine (2.88%). The monoterpenes were limonene (95.19), beta-myrcene (1.09) and 3-carene (0.83). The major and common component of both essential oils was limonene (32%-98%) as reported in [1].

      The differences in chemical constituents of essential oil were assumed due to their genetic characteristics [1,30,32,33,34].

[![...](figures/biotechnology-1026-002.gif " ")](#)

### Conclusion and recommendations

This work was intended to comparative study and chemical compositions of lemon and orange peels in the area as an alternative method to reduce municipal wastes by converting these waste materials into useful products. The percentage yield of peel essential oil from orange (3.55%) was higher than that of lemon essential oil (1.56%). The chemical compositions of the essential oils isolated from orange and lemon peels, as identified by GC-MS analysis, were dominated by limonene. The chemical composition of orange peel essential oil includes limonene (95.19%), 3,3-dimethyl-4-methylamino-2-one (2.88%), beta-myrcene (1.09%) and 3-carene (0.83%) whereas the lemon peel essential oil was compose of limonene (49.74%), beta-pinene (17.13), citral (12.39%), gamma-tepinene (7.52%), beta-bisaboline (2.4%) and o-cymene (2.17%).

#### Recommendation

      For further study it is important to isolate the major component by different isolation technique and elucidate its structure and cover comparative bioassay studies.

This is a peer-reviewed research article published in the Annals of Biotechnology (ISSN: 2637-4927) by Zelalem Zayse Zeleke from Wachemo University, Ethiopia. The study investigates the extraction of essential oils from lemon and orange peels obtained from Debre Berehan Market town in the Amhara Region of Ethiopia, using a Clevenger apparatus and hydro-distillation, followed by comparative GC-MS analysis of their chemical compositions. The research was received on May 19, 2022, accepted on June 14, 2022, and published online on June 16, 2022. The article is published under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.

Key findings: Essential oil yields were 1.56% from lemon peel and 3.55% from orange peel (orange peel yield being about twice that of lemon, consistent with literature reporting ~3% for orange). GC-MS analysis identified 12 compounds in lemon peel essential oil and 4 compounds in orange peel essential oil. The major component in both oils was limonene—comprising 95.19% of orange peel oil (along with beta-myrcene 1.09% and 3-carene 0.83%) and 49.74% of lemon peel oil (along with beta-pinene 17.13%, citral 14.39%, gamma-terpinene 7.52%, beta-bisabolene 2.4%, and o-cymene 2.17%). Lemon oil chemical classes included monoterpene hydrocarbons (76.56%), monoterpene aldehydes (14.39%), sesquiterpenes (4.97%), monoterpene alcohols (2.3%), ketones (1.02%), and aliphatic aldehydes (0.77%).

Methodology: Fresh peels (225g) were crushed and hydro-distilled in a 1000ml round-bottom flask with 720ml distilled water for two hours in a Clevenger apparatus. GC-MS analysis was performed at Addis Ababa University using a fused silica capillary column (30m x 250μm, 0.25μm film), with oven temperature programmed from 60°C (2 min) to 240°C (20 min) at 3°C/min, helium carrier gas at 2 ml/min, and identification based on NIST 107 and Wiley 229 spectral libraries.

Background context: Citrus peels are typically discarded as waste by juice industries (constituting over half the fruit's original weight), posing environmental concerns. This research demonstrates the value of converting this waste into essential oils useful for food flavoring, pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, and soap/detergent industries. The differences in chemical constituents between the two oils were attributed to genetic characteristics of the plant species. The author recommends further studies to isolate major components, elucidate their structures, and conduct comparative bioassay studies. The author declares no conflict of interest.

--- SOURCE 1: Utilization of Green Tea as Environmentally Friendly ... ---
URL: https://www.electrochemsci.org/papers/vol10/100201855.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in the International Journal of Electrochemical Science (Vol. 10, 2015, pages 1855-1872) by researchers from the Egyptian Petroleum Research Institute (EPRI) in Cairo, Egypt (A.M. Alsabagh, M.A. Migahed, M. Abdelraouf, and E.A. Khamis). The study investigates the use of green tea extract (GTEs) from Camellia Sinensis as an environmentally friendly corrosion inhibitor for carbon steel in both 1M HCl and 0.5M H2SO4 acidic solutions.

METHODOLOGY: The researchers used weight loss measurements (7-day immersion at 303 K), potentiodynamic polarization, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) techniques. The green tea extract was prepared by boiling 1.5g of dried Lipton green tea bags in 250ml of distilled water. Steel specimens had a composition of 0.09% C, 0.29% Si, 1.66% Mn, 0.017% P, 0.005% S, 0.33% Cr, 0.19% Ni, 0.71% Mo, and remainder Fe. FTIR confirmed the presence of catechin functional groups (O-H, C=C aromatic rings, and C-O bonds). Quantum calculations for catechin monomers (EC, EGC, ECG, EGCG) were performed using the PM3 method in Hyperchem 8.0.

KEY RESULTS: 
- Maximum inhibition efficiency of 81.47% in 1M HCl and 71.65% in 0.5M H2SO4 was achieved at 500 ppm concentration of green tea extract.
- Corrosion rate decreased and inhibition efficiency increased with increasing extract concentration in both acid solutions.
- Corrosion rates (k) decreased from 18.52 to 3.43 mg cm-2 hr-1 in 1M HCl, and from 22.43 to 5.25 mg cm-2 hr-1 in 0.5M H2SO4 at 500 ppm.
- Adsorption followed the Langmuir adsorption isotherm with a correlation coefficient of 0.971, adsorption equilibrium constant Kads of 757.1 M-1, and standard free energy of adsorption (ΔG°ads) of -16.70 kJ mol-1, indicating physical adsorption via electrostatic interaction.
- Potentiodynamic polarization showed the extract acts as a mixed-type inhibitor, with inhibition efficiencies of 80.5% (1M HCl) and 70.11% (0.5M H2SO4) at 500 ppm.
- EIS results showed increasing charge transfer resistance (Rct) and decreasing double layer capacitance (Cdl) with inhibitor concentration, with inhibition efficiencies of 81.98% (HCl) and 73.68% (H2SO4) at 500 ppm.
- All three techniques showed good agreement in inhibition efficiency values.
- SEM analysis confirmed adsorption of extract molecules on the carbon steel surface, showing a protective film formation.
- Quantum calculations showed EGCG monomer had the highest number of aromatic rings (3) and OH groups (8), suggesting it contributes most to corrosion inhibition.

CONCLUSIONS: Green tea extract acts as an effective, biodegradable, non-toxic, and environmentally friendly corrosion inhibitor for carbon steel in acidic media. The inhibition mechanism involves physical adsorption of extract components (catechins, caffeine, alkaloids, polyphenols) onto the metal surface, following the Langmuir adsorption isotherm. The extract performed better in 1M HCl than in 0.5M H2SO4 due to the higher H+ ion concentration in H2SO4 affecting inhibitor adsorption.
</summary>

"Maximum inhibition efficiency was found (81.47%) in 1M HCl, whereas, it was (71.65%) in 0.5M H2SO4 at concentration 500 ppm."

--- SOURCE 2: Green and Black Tea (Camellia sinensis) Extracts as ... ---
URL: http://www.idosi.org/wasj/wasj35%286%2917/21.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in World Applied Sciences Journal (Vol 35, Issue 6, pages 985-992, 2017) by L.E. Yahaya, S.O. Aroyeun, S.O. Ogunwolu, C.O. Jayeola, and R.O. Igbinadolor from the End-Use Research Division, Cocoa Research Institute of Nigeria, Ibadan, Nigeria. The study investigates the corrosion inhibition properties of Green Tea Extract (GTE) and Black Tea Extract (BTE) from Camellia sinensis on mild steel in 1.0 M HCl acid medium.

Key findings include:
- Both extracts effectively inhibited mild steel corrosion, with maximum inhibition efficiencies of 83.1% (GTE) and 81.7% (BTE) at 0.25 g/L inhibitor concentration in 1.0 M HCl.
- Minimum corrosion rates of 1.2 mm/yr (GTE) and 1.28 mm/yr (BTE) were achieved at 0.25 g/L.
- Inhibition efficiency increased with increasing extract concentration up to 0.25 g/L, then plateaued; it decreased with increasing temperature (303K to 323K), indicating physisorption.
- Adsorption of both inhibitors on mild steel followed the Langmuir adsorption isotherm (r² = 0.9995 for GTE and 0.9997 for BTE), confirming monolayer formation.
- Thermodynamic parameters showed negative free energy of adsorption values (GTE: -10.48 kJ/mol; BTE: -9.98 kJ/mol), indicating spontaneous adsorption. Negative enthalpy values (GTE: -6.60 kJ/mol; BTE: -2.3 kJ/mol) showed exothermic reactions, and positive entropy values (GTE: 13.02 J/K; BTE: 25.8 J/K) confirmed spontaneity.
- Values below -20 kJ/mol for free energy confirmed physisorption (electrostatic interaction) rather than chemisorption.
- FTIR analysis confirmed the formation of active compound-Fe²⁺ complexes on the mild steel surface, with shifts in functional group peaks (e.g., CO groups, C=O, OH) and new peaks corresponding to Fe-H and Fe=O bonds.
- Tea contains polyphenols (catechins such as EGCG, ECG, EGC, EC) with high complexation affinity to metals, which explains the inhibition mechanism.

Methods: Mild steel coupons (1x1 cm) were tested via gravimetric (weight loss) measurements at 303, 313, and 323 K in 1.0 M HCl. Extracts were prepared by defatting with n-hexane and extracting with methanol. FTIR spectroscopy was used for surface analysis. The study concludes that GTE and BTE from Camellia sinensis represent promising, inexpensive, and environmentally friendly corrosion inhibitors for mild steel in acid environments, addressing the need for eco-friendly alternatives to toxic synthetic corrosion inhibitors.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 13: A review of plant extracts as green corrosion inhibitors for CO2 corrosion of carbon steel | npj Materials Degradation ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41529-021-00201-5

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article published in npj Materials Degradation (Volume 6, Article 5, 2022) titled "A review of plant extracts as green corrosion inhibitors for CO2 corrosion of carbon steel." The article has 24k accesses and 176 citations, authored by Basit Raza Fazal, Thomas Becker, Brian Kinsella, and Katerina Lepkova (Curtin University affiliations).

KEY CONTENT:

1. PURPOSE: The review analyzes plant-extract-based green corrosion inhibitors for mitigating CO2 corrosion of carbon steel in oil and gas pipelines, and also extends to strong acid (HCl, H2SO4) corrosion since such products are expected to prevent weak acid corrosion from CO2.

2. CO2 CORROSION MECHANISM: CO2 dissolves in water forming carbonic acid (H2CO3) which is corrosive to carbon steel. Iron carbonate (FeCO3) is the main corrosion product. The "buffer effect mechanism" proposed by Remita et al. holds that proton reduction is the only cathodic reaction, with H2CO3 equilibrium supplying hydrogen ions. For temperatures below 50-60°C, hydration of CO2 to carbonic acid controls cathodic reaction kinetics. Iron carbonate scale is loose and porous at 40-60°C (leading to higher corrosion rates), but solubility decreases at high pH (>6.5) and high temperatures (≥80°C). Corrosion rate increases with CO2 partial pressure and flow rate (in non-scaling conditions).

3. CORROSION INHIBITORS: Synthetic commercial formulations typically contain quaternary ammonium salts, fatty acids, fatty amines/diamines, imidazolines, and O/S/P-containing compounds. Adsorption occurs via four mechanisms: hydrolysis of organic compounds, donor-acceptor exchanges with π-electrons of aromatic rings, interactions between unshared electron pairs of O/N/S atoms and vacant d-orbitals of iron, and d-orbital electron interactions. Many synthetic inhibitors are toxic (e.g., zinc synergists pose environmental hazards).

4. PLANT EXTRACTS: Plants contain phytochemicals (terpenoids, polyphenols, organic acids) with electronic structures resembling conventional synthetic inhibitors. They are non-toxic, biodegradable, economical to extract, and can be sourced from fruit, leaves, bark, roots, seeds, or peels. However, the complex composition makes full understanding of inhibition mechanisms difficult. The majority of research does not elucidate synergistic combinations with commercial inhibitor formulations, requiring significant optimization.

5. ENVIRONMENTAL REGULATIONS: Acceptance schemes include Oslo and Paris Commission (PARCOM), North Sea scheme (UK, Norway, Denmark, Netherlands), US Scheme, and Harmonized Mandatory Control System. North Sea criteria: biodegradability >60% in 28 days, marine toxicity EC50/LC50 >10 mg/L, bioaccumulation log(Po/w) <3.

6. EVALUATION TECHNIQUES: 
   - Electrochemical methods: Linear Polarisation Resistance (LPR), Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS), Tafel extrapolation, and Electrochemical Noise (ECN, used in only a few studies despite potential for detecting localized corrosion).
   - Inhibitor classification: anodic if Ecorr displacement ≥+85mV, cathodic if ≥-85mV, mixed type if less.
   - Adsorption isotherms: physisorption (8-25 kJ/mol), chemisorption (>40 kJ/mol), mixed (25-40 kJ/mol). Langmuir isotherm gives best fit for most studies.
   - Surface characterization: SEM (most common), AFM, SECM, FTIR, and quantum chemical calculations (HOMO/LUMO, electronegativity, fraction of electrons transferred).

CONCLUSION: Plant extracts appear as promising alternatives to commercial synthesized inhibitors, but significant optimization is required. Further development of plant extracts as corrosion inhibitors is of significant interest.
</summary>

- The corrosion rate of carbon steel in HCl is more than twice that in H2SO4.
- Organic compounds were developed as corrosion inhibitors in the petroleum industry in the 1950s.

**Corrosion Mechanism:** The overall reaction for iron in HCl is Fe + 2H+ → Fe²⁺ + H₂. The anodic dissolution involves adsorbed intermediates [FeOH]ads and [FeClOH]ads, both involved in rate-determining steps. Cathodic reactions involve hydrogen evolution through (FeH)ads intermediates.

**Inhibition Mechanism:** Organic compounds form a thin layer on the metal surface through a substitution reaction with water molecules at the metal/solution interface. The size ratio (x) depends on inhibitor geometry—planar inhibitors provide higher surface coverage. Adsorption typically initiates via physisorption (van der Waals or Coulombic forces) and propagates via chemisorption (electron donation from heteroatoms like S, N, P, O and conjugated groups to iron's d-orbitals). A retro-donation mechanism also occurs where electrons transfer back from iron to inhibitor anti-bonding orbitals. Electron-releasing substituents (-NH₂, -OH, -OCH₃, -CH₃) make better inhibitors than electron-withdrawing ones (-NO₂, -CN, -COOH).

**Evaluation Methods (Section 3.1):**
1. **Weight Loss (WL):** Computes corrosion rate (C_WL = K×W/(A×t×ρ), where ρ=7.86 g·cm⁻³ for carbon steel, K=8.76×10⁴), then calculates inhibition efficiency. Accurate but time-consuming, cannot evaluate localized corrosion.
2. **Potentiodynamic Polarization (PDP):** Obtains E_corr and i_corr from Tafel extrapolation. If E_corr shift > 85 mV, inhibitor is anodic/cathodic type; if < 85 mV, it's a mixed type.
3. **Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS):** Nondestructive, analyzes corrosion inhibitor films using parameters like R_s, R_ct, C_dl, C_c, and Warburg resistance.
4. **Electrochemical Frequency Modulation (EFM):** Nondestructive, directly gives i_corr, Tafel slopes, and causality factors without prior knowledge of Tafel constants.
5. **Other methods:** FTIR peak intensities, electrochemical noise (EN), hydrogen evolution (HE) measurements, temperature-based reaction number methods, cyclic voltammetry (CV), potential of zero charge (PZC) measurements, and scanning vibrating electrode technique (SVET).

**Adsorption Isotherms (Section 3.2):** Six adsorption isotherm models are evaluated to identify the most fitted model: Langmuir, Temkin, Freundlich, Frumkin, El-Awady, and Flory-Huggins. Thermodynamic parameters (K_ads, ΔG_ads, ΔH_ads, ΔS_ads) are used to distinguish physisorption vs. chemisorption. The Freundlich isotherm's 1/n value between 0 and 1 indicates favorable adsorption; greater than 1 indicates unfavorable.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific article from Spectroscopy Online (June 1, 2022, Spectroscopy Supplements, Volume 37, Issue s6, Pages 8–18) titled "In situ Raman Spectroscopy Monitors the Corrosion of Mild Steel in a Salt Fog Chamber." The article reports the first use of in situ Raman spectroscopy to detect the formation, growth, and evolution of corrosion products on metal surfaces inside a working salt fog chamber.

**Background:** Corrosion costs approximately 3.4% of global GDP. Standardized tests like the neutral salt spray (NSS) test (e.g., EN ISO 9227, ASTM B117) accelerate corrosion for research, but these aggressive environments are not suitable for many analytical methods.

**Methodology:** A custom tabletop corrosion chamber (glass basin 45×25×30 cm) was used with a 10×10 cm mild steel (DC04, voestalpine Stahl GmbH) sample. The sample was corroded over 8 days in alternating cycles: 48h salt fog, 48h drying, 72h salt fog, and 24h drying. Salt fog was generated from a neutral 5.0 wt% NaCl solution at 35±2°C using a floating ultrasonic fog generator. Drying occurred at 23±2°C with 40-60% relative humidity. A hermetically enclosed Raman probe (Wasatch Photonics WP-785-R-SR-LMMFC-25 spectrometer with 450 mW, 785 nm diode laser) pointed perpendicular to the sample surface, with spectra recorded at 6-minute intervals (1s integration, 25 averages). Sample weight was monitored online via a balance. Salt fog reduced Raman signal intensity by approximately 50%.

**Key Results:**
- During the first salt fog phase, bands at 297 and 378 cm⁻¹ signaled onset of corrosion with formation of α-FeO(OH) (goethite).
- During the first drying phase, bands at 289, 402, 489, and 604 cm⁻¹ indicated formation of hematite (α-Fe₂O₃) through dehydration of iron oxyhydroxides.
- Bands at 647 cm⁻¹ and 1078 cm⁻¹ were assigned to magnetite (Fe₃O₄) and siderite (FeCO₃), respectively. Siderite formation indicated reaction with CO₂ from laboratory atmosphere during drying.
- During the second salt fog phase, bands at 306, 346, 376, and 525 cm⁻¹ indicated lepidocrocite (γ-FeO[OH]) formation; magnetite persisted due to its stability.
- A shift in the dominant Raman band from 374-376 cm⁻¹ to ~400 cm⁻¹ was observed during drying phases, interpreted as FeO(OH) → Fe₂O₃ transformation.
- Physical drying occurred within 1-2 hours (evidenced by weight changes), while chemical conversion from oxyhydroxides to oxides took about 30 hours — a key finding showing chemical transformation is much slower than physical drying.
- MCR-ALS (multivariate curve resolution alternating least squares) analysis identified four components assigned to "FeO(OH)," "Fe₂O₃," "FeCO₃," and an unidentified "other components" species.

**Conclusion:** A compact Raman spectroscopy setup can successfully monitor complex corrosion processes in a salt fog chamber, providing detailed chemical insights (formation of goethite after ~2h of salt fog, conversion to hematite, magnetite stability, lepidocrocite formation) that would otherwise be inaccessible. This approach represents a valuable tool for corrosion mechanism research and for evaluating the corrosion resistance of newly developed coatings and alloys.

**Funding/Acknowledgments:** The work was funded by COMET (Competence Centers for Excellent Technologies) program via FFG, from the iMESA project (FFG 865864, CEST-K1, 2019–2022), with support from voestalpine Stahl GmbH, Recendt GmbH, and Wasatch Photonics. Authors are affiliated with CEST Competence Center for Electrochemical Surface Technology GmbH (Linz, Austria), Vienna University of Technology, Research Center for Non Destructive Testing GmbH (Linz, Austria), Wasatch Photonics, and voestalpine Stahl GmbH.

--- SOURCE 1: SERS detection of 1,4-bis(2-aminoethyl)piperazine functionalized GO (AEP-GO) on X60 carbon steel surface in 15% HCl solution ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10685366

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed research article published in Heliyon (2023 Nov 10;9(11):e22158, DOI: 10.1016/j.heliyon.2023.e22158, PMID: 38034666, PMCID: PMC10685366) by Kabiru Haruna, Tawfik A. Saleh, and Ahmad A. Sorour from the Interdisciplinary Research Center for Advanced Materials and Department of Chemistry at King Fahd University of Petroleum & Minerals, Dhahran, Saudi Arabia. The corresponding author is Kabiru Haruna (kabiru.haruna@kfupm.edu.sa). The article is open access under CC BY-NC-ND license.

STUDY OBJECTIVE: The study used a silver nanoparticle (AgNPs) anchored transparent tape sensor to detect 1,4-bis(2-aminoethyl)piperazine functionalized graphene oxide (AEP-GO) adsorbed on X60 carbon steel surfaces in 15% HCl solution using surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS). This represents the first time SERS was used to detect inhibitor molecules on carbon steel (a non-plasmonic material).

KEY METHODOLOGY:
- AgNPs were synthesized at room temperature by reduction of silver nitrate with hydroxylamine hydrochloride (Leopold and Lendl method).
- AgNPs sensor was fabricated using a translucent adhesive tape pressed onto an array of AgNPs in a watch glass.
- Carbon steel coupons were immersed in different AEP-GO concentrations (1, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 ppm) for 24 hours.
- SERS signals were collected using a LabRAM Horiba Raman spectrophotometer at 633 nm laser excitation, 50x objective lens, 600 gr/mm gratings, 60s acquisition, 2s accumulation.
- DFT calculations were performed using Gaussian 09 at B3LYP level with 6-31G basis sets for C, N, O, H atoms and SDD basis set for the Ag cluster (Four-Ag cluster).

KEY RESULTS:
- AgNPs absorption maximum at 456 nm with fwhm beyond 100 nm, indicating polydispersed nanoparticles with average particle size ~70 nm (predominantly spherical).
- AEP-GO showed characteristic Raman peaks at 1320 cm⁻¹ (D-band) and 1583 cm⁻¹ (G-band) typical of graphitic structures.
- Without the AgNPs sensor, no visible Raman peaks were detected on steel surfaces; with the sensor, AEP-GO peaks were visible even at the lowest concentration of 1 ppm.
- Strong linear correlation between SERS intensity and AEP-GO concentration (5-25 ppm) with R² = 0.9976.
- Limit of detection (LOD) is far below 1 ppm (signal-to-noise ratio >3 at 1 ppm), compared to 1.2 ppm reported for benzotriazole on aluminum alloy in similar SERS tape studies.
- Excellent reproducibility with less than 3% intensity fluctuation across three randomly selected spots at 25 ppm.
- DFT calculations revealed silver atoms preferentially approach the oxygen atom at the GO epoxy group (not carbonyl or hydroxyl groups) due to its lesser stability. The epoxy C-O bond distance increased from 1.443 Å (AEP-GO) to 1.488 Å (AEP-GO_Ag adduct) due to epoxy ring opening. Calculated Ag-O bond distance was 2.081 Å, and Ag-Ag bonds ranged 2.734-2.879 Å (mean 2.791 Å, close to experimental value of 2.850 Å).

CONCLUSIONS: SERS signal intensity increased with AEP-GO concentration, corroborating prior weight loss and electrochemical studies. The appearance of characteristic Raman bands confirmed inhibitor adsorption on the steel surface, blocking it from aggressive acid attack. The fabricated SERS tape sensor is versatile with no substrate material restrictions and can be used to track corrosion inhibitor dynamic adsorption regardless of metal type.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"SERS detection enabled the extreme amplification of Raman signals emitted by inhibitor molecules in order to describe their adsorption behavior on metallic/alloy surfaces."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in the journal Surface Technology (2025, Vol. 54, Issue 12, pp. 49-60, DOI: 10.16490/j.cnki.issn.1001-3660.2025.12.004) titled "Analysis of Inhibition Properties of Amino Acid Corrosion Inhibitor on CO2 Corrosion of Carbon Steel." The authors are YAN Kunfeng, YANG Jiang (corresponding author), ZHAO Xiaolong, MA Shufan from the College of Petrochemical Engineering, Liaoning Petrochemical University (Fushun, China), and WANG Yefei and YANG Zhen from China Petroleum University (East China, Qingdao).

STUDY OVERVIEW: The research investigated the corrosion inhibition properties of two bio-based amino acid-derived inhibitors — N-octylglycine sodium (OCT, C8 alkyl chain) and N-dodecylglycine sodium (DOD, C12 alkyl chain) — on N80 carbon steel in CO2-saturated brine environments.

METHODOLOGY: The inhibitors were synthesized and characterized using Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. - Inhibition efficiency increased with inhibitor concentration, exceeding 94% at 100 mg/L of DOD.
- EIS showed that the capacitive arc radius increased with both concentration and carbon chain length.
- The inhibitors behaved as mixed-type inhibitors; corrosion current density decreased as concentration and carbon chain length increased.
- Weight loss and electrochemical test results were consistent.
- SEM showed significantly reduced corrosion on N80 steel with DOD; the surface was smooth with clear grinding marks.
- XPS confirmed both inhibitors formed a protective film via chemisorption.
- Quantum chemical calculations showed DOD had a smaller HOMO-LUMO energy gap than OCT, indicating higher electron transfer capability and more effective adsorption.

CONCLUSION: DOD (C12 chain) demonstrated superior corrosion inhibition compared to OCT (C8 chain), forming a more effective adsorbed film that provides higher corrosion resistance in CO2-saturated brine environments. The study concludes that amino acid-based corrosion inhibitors with longer alkyl chains give better performance.

--- SOURCE 3: Amino acids and their derivatives as corrosion inhibitors for ... ---
URL: https://arabjchem.org/amino-acids-and-their-derivatives-as-corrosion-inhibitors-for-metals-and-alloys

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a peer-reviewed review article titled "Amino acids and their derivatives as corrosion inhibitors for metals and alloys" published in the Arabian Journal of Chemistry (Volume 13, pages 740-771), authored by B. El Ibrahimi, A. Jmiai, L. Bazzi, and S. El Issami from the Chemistry-Physics Team, Department of Chemistry, Faculty of Sciences, University Ibn Zohr, Agadir, Morocco. The corresponding author is B. El Ibrahimi (brahimmhm@gmail.com). The article was originally published by Elsevier and migrated to Scientific Scholar.

KEY CONTENT SUMMARY:

1. INTRODUCTION & CONTEXT: Corrosion costs about 2-4% of gross national product globally, and approximately 25% of corrosion costs are avoidable. Corrosion affects economics, safety, and environmental damage. Published corrosion research papers increased from 35 in 1907 to 10,655 by 2003. Fontana defined eight forms of corrosion. Vernon (1957) outlined four corrosion prevention methods: modification of procedure, environment, metal, and protective coatings.

2. ECO-FRIENDLY CORROSION INHIBITORS: Due to strict environmental regulations (toxicity, biodegradability, bioaccumulation criteria), researchers have shifted toward green corrosion inhibitors. These are classified as organic or inorganic. Plant extracts, drugs, biopolymers (chitosan, cellulose), surfactants, and ionic liquids have been investigated. Rare earth compounds (CeCl3, LaCl3) show excellent inhibition but face limitations including difficult separation, environmental waste from extraction, and market instability. Amino acids are highlighted as particularly promising because they are non-toxic, biodegradable, soluble in aqueous media, relatively cheap, and easy to produce at high purity. Amino acids contain at least one carboxyl (—COOH) group and one amino (—NH2) group bonded to the same α-carbon. Twenty physiological amino acids exist, and the biotechnological production occurs at million-ton scale with 5-7% annual growth. About 6 million tons of l-glutamate and l-lysine are produced annually by fermentation worldwide.

3. RESEARCH DISTRIBUTION: Over half of published research (1970-2017) on amino acid corrosion inhibitors focuses on iron and its alloys, followed by copper and its alloys, aluminium and its alloys, and other metals.

4. COPPER AND ITS ALLOYS: Benzotriazole (BTA) was the most used copper corrosion inhibitor for decades but has been restricted due to high toxicity. Key findings include:
   - Gomma and Wahdanb (1994): Alanine, aspartic acid, glutamine, and lysine tested on copper in 1M HCl; inhibition efficiency follows Ala > Glu > Asp-A > Lys at 10⁻³M, but sequence changes at 10⁻⁵M, showing concentration importance.
   - Moretti and Guidi (2002): Tryptophan shows good inhibition of copper in aerated sulfuric acid, and photodegradation over 6 months did not affect its efficiency.
   - Petrovic et al. (2012) and Simonović et al. (2014): Cysteine was physically adsorbed with slight chemisorption in neutral/alkaline solutions, mainly chemisorbed in acidic solution (pH 2); better activity in alkaline and acidic than neutral solutions.
   - Zhang et al. (2005): In aerated 0.5M HCl, inhibition efficiency order was cysteine > alanine > BTA, all acting as anodic inhibitors.
   - Matos et al. (2004): Cysteine forms a Cu(I)–cysteine complex film on copper surface.
   - Barouni et al.: Cysteine and methionine showed best inhibition for linear chain amino acids, tryptophan for nonlinear chain, in nitric acid; good linear correlation between inhibition efficiency and calculated quantum parameters using AM1 and MNDO methods.
   - Khaled (2010): Methionine derivatives in nitric acid showed efficiency MITO2 (90.7%) > MITO > MIT (81.6%) at 5×10⁻³M.
   - Dai and Zhang (2012): Glutamic acid and aspartic acid adsorb on Cu(001) via polar sites; glutamic acid has higher efficiency.
   - Wang et al. (2013): Polyaspartic acid (PASP) acts as mixed-type inhibitor; synergy with imidazole reached 89.8% at 1 g/L PASP alone and 95.4% for PASP + 0.5 g/L IM formulation.
   - Milošev et al. (2013): In 0.5M HCl at 10mM, inhibition efficiency was cysteine (50%) > histidine ≈ arginine (25%) > threonine ≈ tyrosine ≈ tryptophan (12%) > methionine (10%) > glycine (3%); alanine and leucine modestly accelerated corrosion.
   - For copper-nickel alloys: Glycine is an efficient inhibitor for Cu-Ni alloys in neutral NaCl; cysteine inhibits Cu10Ni alloy in sulfide-polluted salt water with synergistic effect when mixed with KI; cysteine protects Cu30Ni alloy and bronze.

5. IRON AND ITS ALLOYS: Half of all published amino acid corrosion inhibitor research focuses on iron and alloys. Key findings:
   - Abd-El-Nabey et al. (1985): Methionine was best among cysteine, cystine, methionine, and alanine for mild steel in 1N H2SO4; adsorption occurs in two steps (monolayer followed by second layer).
   - Özcan (2008): Cystine provides 86% inhibition at 5mM against mild steel corrosion in sulfuric acid.
   - Su et al. (2014): Hydrolysate of excess sewage sludge (EES) containing 15 kinds of amino acids can serve as ecofriendly corrosion inhibitor for steel in HCl.
   - Hluchan et al. (1988): Among 22 amino acids and 4 related compounds for iron in de-aerated 1M HCl, best common amino acid was tryptophan; best related compound was 3,5-diiodotyrosine (87% at 10mM). Hydroxyproline, creatine, cystine, and cysteine acted as corrosion accelerators.
   - Zerfaoui et al. (2004b): Methionine was best among five amino acids in citric acid media, reaching 90% inhibition at pH 5; compounds were cathodic-type inhibitors.
   - Ashassi-Sorkhabi et al. (2004): Alanine, glycine, and leucine inhibited steel in HCl with efficiency ranging 28-91% via physical adsorption.
   - Amin et al. (2009a,b): Glycine acts as mixed-type inhibitor for low alloy steel in 0.5M HCl.
   - Khaled and Abdel-Shafi (2013): Arginine showed 60% efficiency in 1M HCl and 79% in 3.5% NaCl at 0.9 g/L; mixed-type inhibitor.
   - Bobina et al. (2013): Histidine and tryptophan showed up to 80% inhibition at 10⁻²M for carbon steel in acetic acid/acetate medium via physical adsorption.
   - Oguzie et al. (2007b): Cysteine promoted corrosion at low concentrations but inhibited at higher concentrations for low carbon steel; methionine inhibited mild steel in sulfuric acid with enhanced efficiency when KI was added.
   - El-Deab (2011): 5mM cysteine + 25µM Cu²⁺ reached 95% inhibition in de-aerated sulfuric acid, attributed to Cu(I)-cysteine complex and/or cysteine self-assembly monolayer.
   - Gowri et al. (2013): Glutamic acid with Zn²⁺ showed synergistic effect, increasing efficiency from 35% at 200 ppm to 87% with 25 ppm zinc ions for carbon steel in sea water.
   - Mobin et al. (2016): Cysteine at 500 ppm with surfactants gave: Cys + TX (97.76%) > Cys + SDS (95.09%) > Cys + CPC (91.99%) > Cys alone (85.62%) for mild steel in 1M HCl.
   - Morad (2008): In 5% sulfamic acid at 40°C and 1000 µM, inhibition order was acetylcysteine (97.3%) > cysteine (94.3%) > cystine (92.7%) > S-benzylcysteine (91.7%) > methionine (86.5%); compounds chemically adsorbed.
   - Amin et al. (2010a): Glycine derivative GlyD1 showed 96% efficiency vs. glycine alone (74% at 5mM) for cold-rolled steel in 1M HCl.
   - Amin and Ibrahim (2011): In 4M H2SO4, GlyD1 (98%) > GlyD2 (76%) > Gly (64%) at 5mM.
   - Gupta et al. (2016): Three lysine derivatives (SB-1, SB-2, SB-3) showed 94%, 92%, and 91% inhibition respectively for mild steel in 1M HCl; SB-3's highest efficiency was due to strong electron-releasing —N(CH3)2 group.
   - Vikneshvaran and Velmathi (2017): Two l-tryptophan derivatives showed good inhibition for mild steel in 1M HCl; S2 performed better due to strong electron-donating ability and additional phenyl rings.

6. COMPUTATIONAL METHODS: Quantum chemical calculations (DFT, HF, AM1, MNDO) and molecular dynamics simulations are increasingly used to explain inhibition mechanisms. For example, Zor et al. (2009) used HF/6-311G(d,p) to show methionine inhibits iron more than tyrosine via electrostatic interaction. Amin et al. (2010b) found inhibition efficiency increases with increasing EHOMO energy and decreasing ELUMO energy, energy gap, and dipole moment for alanine, cysteine, and S-methyl cysteine on iron in 1M HCl.

7. ARTICLE STRUCTURE: The review is organized in two parts — the first presents published work by metal type (copper, iron, aluminium, and other metals), and the second discusses factors affecting inhibition ability, computational modeling, action mechanisms, and new trends including self-assembly monolayers and smart coating treatments. Tables A1 and A2 in Appendix A summarize additional studies.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 10: Organic Compounds as Corrosion Inhibitors for Carbon Steel ... ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8954067

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive review article published in Materials (Basel) on March 9, 2022, titled "Organic Compounds as Corrosion Inhibitors for Carbon Steel in HCl Solution: A Comprehensive Review." The article is authored by Liangyuan Chen and Dongzhu Lu (from the Open Studio for Marine Corrosion and Protection, Pilot National Laboratory for Marine Science and Technology, Qingdao, China, and the Institute of Oceanology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) and Yanhu Zhang (Institute of Advanced Manufacturing and Modern Equipment Technology, Jiangsu University, Zhenjiang, China). The paper has DOI 10.3390/ma15062023, PMC ID PMC8954067, and PMID 35329474. It is an open-access article under the Creative Commons CC BY 4.0 license.

**Purpose and Scope:** The review focuses on the corrosion inhibition performance of organic compounds and (nano)materials for carbon steel in 1.0 M HCl solution systems. It aims to conduct comparative studies to select the best-suited inhibitor type (low concentration/high inhibition efficiency, nontoxic, and cost-effective synthesis). Organic compounds are classified into six types: drug molecules, ionic liquids, surfactants, plant extracts, polymers, and polymeric nanoparticles. Statistical analysis is performed specifically on data from the carbon steel/1.0 M HCl solution system.

**Key Background Information:**
- Corrosion inhibitors are the most economical and commonly used method to retard metal corrosion compared to metal constituent optimization and coating technology.
- Carbon steel corrosion is most studied due to its high strength, low cost, and widespread availability, particularly in chemical and petrochemical industries where it contacts strong acidic solutions.
- 1.0 M HCl is the standard test medium because most metal chlorides are water-soluble, and HCl is effective as an acid detergent for chemical cleaning.
- The reaction rate of iron oxide with HCl is over three times faster than with H2SO4.
- The corrosion rate of carbon steel in HCl is more than twice that in H2SO4.
- Organic compounds were developed as corrosion inhibitors in the petroleum industry in the 1950s.

**Corrosion Mechanism:** The overall reaction for iron in HCl is Fe + 2H+ → Fe²⁺ + H₂. The anodic dissolution involves adsorbed intermediates [FeOH]ads and [FeClOH]ads, both involved in rate-determining steps. Cathodic reactions involve hydrogen evolution through (FeH)ads intermediates.

**Inhibition Mechanism:** Organic compounds form a thin layer on the metal surface through a substitution reaction with water molecules at the metal/solution interface. The size ratio (x) depends on inhibitor geometry—planar inhibitors provide higher surface coverage. Adsorption typically initiates via physisorption (van der Waals or Coulombic forces) and propagates via chemisorption (electron donation from heteroatoms like S, N, P, O and conjugated groups to iron's d-orbitals). A retro-donation mechanism also occurs where electrons transfer back from iron to inhibitor anti-bonding orbitals. Electron-releasing substituents (-NH₂, -OH, -OCH₃, -CH₃) make better inhibitors than electron-withdrawing ones (-NO₂, -CN, -COOH).

**Evaluation Methods (Section 3.1):**
1. **Weight Loss (WL):** Computes corrosion rate (C_WL = K×W/(A×t×ρ), where ρ=7.86 g·cm⁻³ for carbon steel, K=8.76×10⁴), then calculates inhibition efficiency. Accurate but time-consuming, cannot evaluate localized corrosion.
2. **Potentiodynamic Polarization (PDP):** Obtains E_corr and i_corr from Tafel extrapolation. If E_corr shift > 85 mV, inhibitor is anodic/cathodic type; if < 85 mV, it's a mixed type.
3. **Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS):** Nondestructive, analyzes corrosion inhibitor films using parameters like R_s, R_ct, C_dl, C_c, and Warburg resistance.
4. **Electrochemical Frequency Modulation (EFM):** Nondestructive, directly gives i_corr, Tafel slopes, and causality factors without prior knowledge of Tafel constants.
5. **Other methods:** FTIR peak intensities, electrochemical noise (EN), hydrogen evolution (HE) measurements, temperature-based reaction number methods, cyclic voltammetry (CV), potential of zero charge (PZC) measurements, and scanning vibrating electrode technique (SVET).

**Adsorption Isotherms (Section 3.2):** Six adsorption isotherm models are evaluated to identify the most fitted model: Langmuir, Temkin, Freundlich, Frumkin, El-Awady, and Flory-Huggins. Thermodynamic parameters (K_ads, ΔG_ads, ΔH_ads, ΔS_ads) are used to distinguish physisorption vs. chemisorption. The Freundlich isotherm's 1/n value between 0 and 1 indicates favorable adsorption; greater than 1 indicates unfavorable.
</summary>

8. The uniform inhibitor layer mitigates the formation of iron chloride/hydroxide intermediates by blocking chloride diffusion through the oxide/hydroxide layer.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an open-access review article published in the Journal of Saudi Chemical Society (Volume 29, article number 20, 2025) on August 19, 2025, titled "Review of organic corrosion inhibitors: application with respect to the main functional group." The article has 9,566 accesses and 38 citations.

Authors: Darya Puzikova, Gulinur Khussurova, Xeniya Leontyeva, Oleg Kholkin, Nail Kenzin, Murat Zhurinov, and Svetlana Peshaya.

MAIN TOPIC: The review provides a comprehensive analysis of corrosion mechanisms, classification systems, and practical applications of corrosion inhibitors, with emphasis on organic corrosion inhibitors based on imidazolines, phosphonates, and urotropine for protecting oilfield and refinery equipment. Imidazoline-based inhibitors form hydrophobic barriers on metal surfaces; phosphonates are effective at high temperatures; urotropine is efficient in acidizing operations for well stimulation. The review also examines synergistic effects of combined inhibitors and addresses environmental/toxicological concerns of conventional inhibitors.

KEY DATA POINTS:
- According to NACE, the annual cost of corrosion control in the oil and gas sector is ~$1.372 billion, broken down as: onshore pipelines/facilities (~$589 million), well pipes ($463 million), and capital expenses ($320 million).
- The global oilfield corrosion and scale inhibitors market was valued at USD 1820.9 million in 2023, expected to reach USD 2144.7 million by 2030 (2.4% CAGR, 2024–2030).
- Corrosion inhibitor concentrations in corrosive fluid range from 1 to 15,000 mg/L (0.0001 to 1.5 wt.%).

CORROSION TYPES DISCUSSED: Hydrogen sulfide ("acid") corrosion from sour oils (H2S content can reach 500 mg/L+), CO2 ("sweet") corrosion causing pitting, oxygen corrosion, and naphthenic acid corrosion (active at 200–400°C in refinery equipment). H2S can be generated by sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB). Sulfur compounds can cause hydrogen embrittlement and cracking.

CORROSION INHIBITOR CLASSIFICATIONS:
1. By protection mechanism: 
   - Protective coating inhibitors (passivation films 30–200 Å thick, precipitated films, adsorption films)
   - Neutralizing inhibitors (nitrogen-containing amines like monoethanolamine, diethanolamine, methylamine that neutralize H+, H2S, CO2)
   - Absorbent/sorption inhibitors (e.g., sodium sulfite, ammonium bisulfate, hydrazine binding oxygen)
2. By chemical composition: Inorganic vs. organic inhibitors. Inorganic inhibitors include nitrites, chromates, borates, molybdates, phosphates, polyphosphates, silicates, and zinc salts. They can act anodically (via anions like CrO4²⁻, NO2⁻) or cathodically (via cations like Ca²⁺, Zn²⁺, Ni²⁺). Cathodic inhibitors work by shifting corrosion potential to more negative values, reducing oxygen, or increasing hydrogen release potential. Examples include arsenic trioxide, zinc sulfate, nickel sulfate, magnesium hydroxide, zinc hydroxide. Disadvantages of inorganic inhibitors include toxicity, inability to decompose, effectiveness only in presence of oxygen, and susceptibility to bacterial influence.

The article emphasizes that corrosion remains a significant challenge in the oil and gas industry affecting all production stages, and highlights the urgent need for sustainable, environmentally friendly corrosion inhibitor alternatives.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 8: Current and emerging trends of inorganic, organic and eco ... ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11460216

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a scientific review article published in RSC Advances (2024 Oct 8, Vol 14, Issue 43, article 31877, DOI: 10.1039/d4ra05662k) titled "Current and emerging trends of inorganic, organic and eco-friendly corrosion inhibitors." The article was written by Mahmoud A. Ahmed (Ain Shams University, Cairo, Egypt and Veolia Water Technologies), Sherif Amin (Veolia Water Technologies), and Ashraf A. Mohamed (Ain Shams University). It was received Aug 5, 2024 and accepted Sep 23, 2024. PMCID: PMC11460216, PMID: 39380647.

The systematic review provides a comprehensive analysis of corrosion inhibitors, covering both inorganic and organic compounds. Key topics include:

1. **Corrosion mechanisms**: Adsorption mechanisms (chemisorption involving coordinate bonding via π-electrons and non-bonding electrons, and physisorption via electrostatic attractions) and electrochemical mechanisms (anodic, cathodic, and mixed inhibitors). Adsorption type can be determined thermodynamically: |ΔG°ads| > 40 kJ/mol indicates chemisorption, while |ΔG°ads| < 20 kJ/mol indicates physisorption.

2. **Inorganic inhibitors**: Detailed coverage of nitrite, molybdate, and silicate inhibitors. 
   - Nitrite inhibitors convert ferrous to ferric ions, forming a passive oxide film (primarily magnetite). Performance depends on pH (effective at pH ≥6, promotes corrosion below pH 4), temperature, and chloride levels.
   - Molybdate inhibitors form a dual-layer protective film (outer layer of Fe2(MoO4)3, inner layer of ferric hydroxide/oxide). Effective molybdate concentration varies with aggressive ion levels (70 ppm in deionized water, up to 1000 ppm with high chloride).
   - Silicate inhibitors form protective silicate coatings on metal surfaces, with self-healing properties.

3. **Table 1** presents inhibition efficiency data for various inorganic inhibitors: Zn²⁺ (83.3% IE), sodium silicate (74.0%), sodium phosphate (95%), silicate-phosphate (62.3%), sodium vanadate (99.85%), sodium nitrite (up to 99.06%), sodium molybdate (88.99-98.5% across various environments), sodium tungstate (30.71-97%), and combinations such as sodium tungstate + ZnSO₄ (84.81%).

4. **Organic inhibitors**: Work primarily by adsorption, using polar groups (–OH, –OCH₃, –COOH, –NH₂, –CONH₂, etc.) containing heteroatoms and π-electrons. Can bind via chemisorption and/or physisorption.

5. **Eco-friendly/green inhibitors**: Biopolymers (polypeptides, polysaccharides like cellulose, starch, chitosan, nucleic acids, lignin) are highlighted as promising alternatives. They are biodegradable, non-toxic, renewable, and cost-effective. Plant extracts (e.g., Euphorbia heterophylla L.) and drugs are also explored.

6. **Synergistic effects**: Mixed inhibitor systems show enhanced performance, e.g., polyaspartic acid (PASP) alone gave 61% inhibition efficiency at 2.0 g/L, but with zinc ions increased to 97% at 0.5 g/L. PASP-threonine showed superior inhibition compared to PASP alone.

7. **Evaluation methods**: Weight loss (WL) analysis, electrochemical analysis (PDP, EIS), surface analysis (SEM, XPS, AES), and quantum mechanical calculations are discussed as tools for evaluating inhibitor performance.

The review serves as a resource for researchers, engineers, and practitioners in corrosion control, offering insights and future directions for environmentally friendly corrosion inhibition strategies.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in the Journal of Materials Research and Technology (JMRT), 2020, vol. 9(4), pages 8723-8734, by Fernando Cotting (Chemical Engineering Department, Federal University of Minas Gerais, Brazil) and Idalina Vieira Aoki (Chemical Engineering Department of Polytechnic School of the University of São Paulo, Brazil). The study evaluates a corrosion inhibitor system consisting of a mixture of a long-chain silanol (octyltriethoxysilanol, derived from octyltriethoxysilane/Silquest A137) doped with cerium(III) chloride for protecting 1020 carbon steel in 0.1 mol L–1 NaCl (neutral chloride) solution.

METHODOLOGY: Carbon steel samples (3 cm × 4 cm × 0.1 cm) were ground, degreased in acetone, and treated in 2.5% NaOH solution to activate surface hydroxyl groups. The silane was hydrolyzed in an ethanol/water (50/50 v/v) solution acidified to pH 5.0 with acetic acid, sonicated for 5 min, and stirred for 24 h at room temperature. Silane concentration was kept constant at 400 ppm, while Ce(III) ion concentrations varied at 25, 50, and 100 ppm. Tests included electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), linear polarization resistance (Rp), potentiodynamic polarization curves, scanning vibrating electrode technique (SVET), contact angle measurements, and Raman spectroscopy.

KEY RESULTS: The best performance was achieved with 400 ppm octylsilanol + 50 ppm Ce(III) ions, yielding approximately 96-97.8% inhibition efficiency (I.E.) in 0.1 mol L–1 NaCl. At 100 ppm Ce(III), efficiency decreased to 88.1%. The Rp values increased from 1.7 kΩ cm² (blank) to 77.3 kΩ cm² (best condition), with 46.9% I.E. for octylsilanol alone (proving silanol alone is insufficient) versus 97.8% with 50 ppm Ce(III). The inhibitor system was classified as mixed-type with more pronounced anodic behavior, based on polarization curves. Contact angle measurements showed the treated surface became hydrophobic (111.9°±1.1°) versus 58.1°±2.3° for untreated steel. Raman spectroscopy confirmed the presence of persistent adsorbed silanol films (Si–OH and Si–O–C stretching peaks) and cerium hydroxide precipitates (Ce(III) peak at ~450 cm–1) on the steel surface even after removal from the inhibitor solution.

MECHANISM: The inhibition occurs via a synergistic dual mechanism — octylsilanol adsorbs on anodic sites forming a hydrophobic protective barrier, while Ce(III) ions react with hydroxyls generated during oxygen reduction at cathodic sites to precipitate Ce(OH)3, blocking cathodic reactions. The silanol adsorption reduces exposed surface area, while cerium hydroxide precipitation provides additional protection at cathodic regions.

ECONOMIC/TOXICITY COMPARISON: The authors compared the studied inhibitors to traditional ones. Octyltriethoxysilane costs ~100 USD/kg with low toxicity and fair degradability, while cerium(III) chloride costs 818 USD/kg (low toxicity, fair degradability). Traditional inhibitors like zinc chromate (6,600 USD/kg, very high toxicity), 2-mercaptobenzimidazole (228 USD/kg, very high toxicity), sodium benzoate (41 USD/kg, low toxicity, excellent degradability but requires 57,600 ppm for only 53.2% efficiency), and sodium molybdate (513 USD/kg, moderate toxicity) were compared. The studied mixture was more efficient and cheaper than reputable traditional inhibitors, with 50 ppm Ce(III) achieving ~96% efficiency versus >250 ppm needed for Ce(III) alone.

LONGEVITY: EIS with immersion time (up to 48 h) showed four stages of film formation: rapid adsorption (0-4 h), film breakdown (4-8 h), re-adsorption and self-assembly (8-24 h), and stabilization (24-48 h). SVET measurements confirmed fast and persistent protection, with no significant anodic or cathodic ionic currents observed even after 24-48 h of immersion in inhibited solutions. The protective film remained effective after 48 h of immersion.
</summary>

<summary>
This document is a final technical report (dated 10 November 1992) submitted to the U.S. Army Research Office under Contract DAAL-03-89-K-0084, detailing "In Situ Surface Studies of Conversion Coatings for Steel and Aluminum." The work was conducted by Principal Investigators Henry W. White (University of Missouri-Columbia), Florian Mansfeld (University of Southern California), and Paul Bryant (University of Missouri-Kansas City). The report is approved for public release with unlimited distribution.

**Primary Goals:** The research aimed to develop mechanisms of corrosion protection for (1) cerium-based surface layers on aluminum alloys and aluminum/silicon carbide metal matrix composites, and (2) polyacrylic acid (PAA) complexed zinc phosphate conversion coatings on steel. Atomic force microscopy (AFM) using tunnel current control was developed and applied to these problems.

**Key Results - Cerium-Based Coatings on Al 6061-T6:**
- The protective layers consist of two principal components: a poorly ordered monohydrated aluminum oxide (boehmite, AlOOH/AI2O3·H2O) and an insoluble cerium oxide that forms at areas concentrated with impurities and alloying elements.
- Electrochemical action during surface modification fosters precipitation of cerium compounds that inhibit further attack, particularly at active sites where pits could initiate.
- The original treatment (Arnott et al.) used immersion in 1000 ppm CeCl3 for up to several weeks; Mansfeld et al. improved this with hot dilute CeCl3 and Ce(NO3)3 solutions plus anodic polarization in sodium molybdate (Na2MoO4), reducing total treatment time to six hours.
- A pretreatment process (cleaning, deoxidation, re-oxidation) was developed to standardize the surface oxide layer, since a well-formed natural oxide layer is critical for effective protection.
- Treatment DB6 (CeNO3/CeCl3/Na2MoO4) was the most effective, showing very low uniform corrosion and no localized corrosion during 60 days exposure to 0.5N NaCl.
- EIS showed a synergistic effect of Ce and Mo; treatment in either solution alone did not produce the excellent corrosion resistance of the combined treatment.
- X-ray analysis showed cerium-rich deposits were approximately circular, up to 10 μm in diameter (averaging ~3 μm), covering less than 10% of the surface.
- FT-IR spectra confirmed poorly ordered boehmite as the dominant surface phase across all treatments; no anions (cerium, nitrate, chloride, or molybdate) were detected in IR spectra.
- AFM showed "pillow-like" surface formations of 50-200 nm, independent of treatment type.
- Preliminary results for Al 7075-T6 suggest the CeCl3 step may need elimination for high-Cu alloys due to pitting concerns.

**Key Results - Zinc Phosphate Conversion Coatings on Steel:**
- Raman and micro-Raman spectra confirmed both unmodified and PAA-modified films consist predominantly of zinc phosphate dihydrate, Zn3(PO4)2·2H2O.
- PAA (molecular weight ~50,000) added to the phosphating bath significantly improves corrosion resistance and top-coat adherence by reducing crystallite size, leading to greater film ductility and fewer corrosive attack sites.
- AFM imaging of single crystallite surfaces revealed long striations with cross-striation patterns; morphologies of unmodified and modified films were generally similar with subtle differences.
- Pyramidal-shaped pits were much more prevalent on PAA-modified samples than unmodified samples (detected with Nanoscope III).
- Non-contact AFM achieved higher resolution (10-20 nm features) than contact AFM on modified films, possibly due to soft or sticky surface features.
- IR spectra showed no evidence of organic groups from PAA on film surfaces; evidence for PAA molecular segments on/in crystallites was weak, though PAA may preferentially adsorb on crystal side facets.

**Other Projects Described:**
- Cerium-treated Al/SiC metal matrix composites showed significant crystalline silicon contributions in Raman spectra of treated samples.
- Al/C interfaces treated with dilute CeCl3 became highly resistant to dissolution in water.
- A new molten salt treatment approach (SnCl2-NaCl with/without CeCl3 at 200-300°C) for Al alloys was initiated at USC.
- A new AFM design using tunnel current control was developed by Bryant and co-workers at UMKC (published in J. Vac. Sci. Tech.).
- STM imaging of solid C60/C70 (fullerite) was reported in Nature 348 (1990), revealing spherical molecules ~1 nm apart in close-packed arrays.
- Raman studies of conducting polymer polyaniline examined moisture effects on electrical conductivity.
- Equipment upgrades included a micro-Raman attachment (Oct 1990) and a Nanoscope II STM/AFM upgrade (March 1992).

**Publications and Personnel:** The report lists 15+ publications and technical reports, 20+ presentations, and participating scientific personnel with degrees earned during the project period.

--- SOURCE 1: [PDF] A Review of Up-To-Date Research Knowledge on the Corrosion ... ---
URL: https://ijaem.net/issue_dcp/A%20Review%20of%20Up%20To%20Date%20Research%20Knowledge%20on%20the%20Corrosion%20Inhibiting%20Capability%20of%20Garlic%20Allicin%20Sativum%20for%20Steel%20Materials.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper is a review article published in the International Journal of Advances in Engineering and Management (IJAEM), Volume 7, Issue 01 (January 2025), pp. 104-117, authored by T.N. Guma and Jacob O. Aremo of the Department of Mechanical Engineering, Nigerian Defence Academy, Kaduna, Nigeria. The paper reviews up-to-date research knowledge on the corrosion-inhibiting capability of garlic (Allium sativum) for steel materials.

KEY FINDINGS:
- Corrosion is a monumental global economic and technological problem; steel accounts for about 90% of all global corrosion problems, and mild steel (up to 0.3% carbon) makes up about 90% of all applied steels and is responsible for 90% of steel corrosion issues.
- Synthetic corrosion inhibitors (chromate, dichromate, nitrite, nitrate) pose serious environmental and health risks, driving research into natural plant extracts as eco-friendly alternatives.
- Garlic is proven to be a very effective, safe-for-handling, biodegradable, and eco-friendly corrosion inhibitor, sustainably available worldwide.

GARLIC PRODUCTION & SAFETY:
- World garlic production is approximately 29,149,438 metric tons. China is the largest producer (20,058,388 metric tons, 76.28% share), followed by India (9.28%), Bangladesh (1.66%), South Korea (1.14%), Egypt (1.05%), and Myanmar (0.7%).
- Garlic has been used medicinally for thousands of years across numerous civilizations (China, Egypt, Greece, India, Rome), indicating its safety for human handling.

CHEMICAL COMPOSITION:
- An undamaged fresh garlic contains approximately 200 chemical compounds including sulfur-containing compounds, volatile oils, enzymes, carbohydrates, minerals, amino acids, and vitamins.
- Garlic has an unusually high proportion of sulfur-containing chemicals (13%), with key active compounds including alliin, allicin, ajoene, diallyl sulfide (DAS), diallyl disulfide (DADS), diallyl trisulfide (DATS), and allyl methyl sulfide (AMS).
- Garlic oil contains 60% diallyl disulfide; 2.62% alliin; 0.15-0.66% allicin; 0.09-0.68% γ-glutamyl-S-(E,S-propenyl)cysteine.
- Garlic oil physical properties: density/specific gravity 1.050-1.095, melting point -59.48°C, boiling point 136.32°C, pH 5.5-6.0, viscosity 9.2 mPa/s, highly flammable.

EXTRACTION METHODS:
- Major extraction methods include Soxhlet extraction, ultrasonic-assisted extraction, steam distillation, pressurized liquid extraction, supercritical-fluid extraction, and microwave extraction.
- Commercially available garlic extract types include garlic oil, prebiotic polysaccharide, aged garlic, black garlic, and garlic powder.

REVIEW OF RESEARCH STUDIES (key results):
1. Ikumapayi et al.: Garlic extract in 0.5M HCl achieved max 68% inhibitory efficiency at 8 v/v%; corrosion rate dropped from 1.66 mm/yr to 0.53 mm/yr.
2. Yang et al.: 93.26% corrosion-inhibitive efficiency for A3 steel in 5% HCl at 4.0% extract; 79.2% in 5% mud acid at 6.0% extract.
3. Afia et al.: Acid garlic essential oil reached ~95.8% inhibition efficiency at 2.5 g/L in 1M HCl at 298K; followed Langmuir adsorption isotherm; mixed-type inhibitor.
4. Barreto et al.: Garlic peel extract in 0.5M HCl was only slightly inferior to benzotriazole (BTAH) for ASTM 1020 carbon steel, offering an eco-friendly alternative.
5. Karthiga et al.: 10 mL garlic extract + 90 mL well water achieved 90% corrosion inhibition efficiency for mild steel; protective film was Fe2+-allicin complex.
6. Barreto et al.: Garlic extract achieved 90.7% efficiency and cacao extract 89% in 0.5M HCl; the mixture achieved >98% inhibition showing strong synergism.
7. Rajam et al.: 2 mL garlic extract + 25 ppm Zn2+ offered 70% inhibition efficiency for carbon steel in well water (anodic reaction control).
8. Belkaid et al.: Garlic extract in 1M H2SO4 achieved up to 90% IE for 316L stainless steel and 67% for API X60 carbon steel.
9. Joycee et al.: 100,000 ppm garlic extract + 50 ppm Zn2+ provided 87% inhibition efficiency for mild steel in simulated oil well water.
10. Yaro et al.: Garlic powder in H3PO4 achieved max 75% inhibition efficiency at 50°C and 250 ppm; followed Langmuir adsorption isotherm; mixed-type inhibitor.
11. Wei-Min and Dao-Yong: Garlic juice reached 95.4% inhibitor efficiency in 15% HCl at 80°C; 42%-64% in oil field water.
12. Fouda et al.: Allium sativum in 1M HCl is a good mixed-type inhibitor; followed Temkin's adsorption isotherm.
13. Parthipan et al.: Garlic extract (100 ppm) inhibited biocorrosion of carbon steel and stainless steel in presence of Bacillus subtilis A1 and Streptomyces parvus B7; first time garlic extract proposed as green corrosion inhibitor with biocidal activity.
14. Rodriguez-Clemente et al.: Allium sativum in 0.5M H2SO4 achieved 96% effectiveness at 400 ppm concentration.
15. Patil and Zaware: Garlic achieved 90%-95% inhibitory efficacy for steel reinforcement in concrete.
16. Maestro et al.: Garlic peel inhibited mild steel corrosion in acid (HCl), neutral (NaCl), and basic (NaOH) media; efficacy rose up to 24 hours in neutral/basic media; quantum modelling showed alliin and allicin produce more active specimens in basic conditions.
17. Ojha: 4 g/L garlic extract in 1M HCl achieved 76.47% maximum inhibition at 298K; followed Langmuir adsorption isotherm (R2=0.999).
18. Da Silvaa et al.: Garlic oil reduced microbiologically-influenced corrosion (MIC) of AISI 1020 carbon steel by sulphate-reducing bacteria more than glutaraldehyde in artificial seawater.
19. Asfia et al.: Garlic extract slowed corrosion of AISI 304 stainless steel in 0.5M HCl by up to 88%; mixed-type inhibitor following Langmuir adsorption isotherm.
20. Lu et al.: Garlic extract as post-treatment for phytic acid-based conversion coating on Q235 steel significantly improved anti-corrosion performance in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution.

CONCLUSION: Garlic is a highly effective, safe, biodegradable, and eco-friendly corrosion inhibitor for steel. --- SOURCE 1: Carbon Quantum Dots Derived from Garlic (Allium sativum) Peel as Corrosion Inhibitor for Mild Steel in HCl Solution - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12332664

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific research article published in ACS Omega (July 22, 2025; DOI: 10.1021/acsomega.5c03224) by researchers from Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ), INMETRO, and Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Rio de Janeiro (Brazil). The study demonstrates the synthesis of carbon quantum dots (CQDs) derived from garlic peel (Allium sativum) and their application as a green corrosion inhibitor for mild steel in 1 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid (HCl) solution.

METHODOLOGY: CQDs were synthesized via acid hydrolysis — 1 g of crushed garlic peel was refluxed in 20 mL of 1 mol L⁻¹ sulfuric acid at 200 °C for 2 h, followed by filtration, dialysis (48 h, 1 kDa membrane), vacuum filtration, and rotary evaporation. The synthesis yielded approximately 10% CQDs. Characterization was performed using TEM, DLS, FTIR, Raman spectroscopy, XPS, zeta potential, UV–vis spectroscopy, and fluorimetry. Corrosion tests included gravimetric analysis, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), potentiodynamic polarization, SEM, AFM, and contact angle measurements.

KEY RESULTS:
- CQDs had an average size of 3.17 ± 0.07 nm (TEM) and 2.29 nm hydrodynamic diameter (DLS), confirming sub-10 nm nanoparticles. The material was amorphous with no lattice fringes.
- FTIR and XPS confirmed the presence of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and sulfur (endogenous doping), including functional groups such as O–H, N–H, C–N, C–S, C=O, and COOH.
- Gravimetric tests showed maximum inhibition efficiencies of 79% after 2 h and 96% after 24 h immersion in 1 mol L⁻¹ HCl.
- CQDs act as mixed-type inhibitors with a predominant anodic effect, confirmed by electrochemical polarization and Tafel analysis.
- At 300 ppm, EIS showed 71.4% inhibition efficiency (via charge transfer resistance), while Tafel analysis showed 68.0% (via corrosion current density) and 71.8% (via polarization resistance).
- Temperature-dependent studies (25–55 °C) revealed decreasing inhibition efficiency at higher temperatures (from 77.5% at 35 °C down to 46.7% at 55 °C), indicating primarily physical (electrostatic) adsorption. Activation energy was 65.1 kJ/mol with inhibitor vs. 46.1 kJ/mol without.
- Langmuir adsorption isotherm best fit the data (R² = 0.9964), suggesting monolayer adsorption.
- Surface analysis confirmed formation of a hydrophobic protective film (contact angle increased from 69° to 80° with inhibitor vs. decreasing to 38° without inhibitor), and SEM/AFM showed reduced surface roughness in the presence of CQDs.
- The garlic peel-derived CQDs achieved 95.8% maximum efficiency at 200 ppm, comparable to other biomass-derived CQDs (pitaya peel 95.6%, grapefruit peel 94.1%, sugar cane bagasse 94.0%, pumpkin seeds 94.6%).

CONCLUSION: The study highlights the sustainable use of garlic peel agro-industrial waste as a precursor for effective carbon quantum dot corrosion inhibitors, addressing both corrosion protection for mild steel in acidic environments and environmental concerns regarding agro-waste (approximately 3.5 million tons of garlic production waste burned annually, contributing to 3.3 billion tons of CO2 from untreated agro-industrial waste globally).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The CQDs exhibited high inhibition efficiencies with sustained performance over time, achieving maximum inhibition efficiencies of 79% for 2 h and 96% for 24 h, as determined by gravimetric studies." "The inhibition mechanism involves both physical and chemical interactions between CQD aggregates and the steel surface." "Surface analysis revealed hydrophobic protective film formation by CQDs on steel, reducing metal dissolution." "Electrochemical measurements further confirm that the CQDs act as mixed-type inhibitors, exhibiting a predominant anodic effect." "These findings highlight the potential of using agro-industrial waste, such as garlic peel, as a sustainable precursor for the synthesis of effective corrosion inhibitors."
</key_excerpts>
