--- SOURCE 2: [PDF] A Review of Up-To-Date Research Knowledge on the Corrosion ... ---
URL: https://ijaem.net/issue_dcp/A%20Review%20of%20Up%20To%20Date%20Research%20Knowledge%20on%20the%20Corrosion%20Inhibiting%20Capability%20of%20Garlic%20Allicin%20Sativum%20for%20Steel%20Materials.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper is a review article published in the International Journal of Advances in Engineering and Management (IJAEM), Volume 7, Issue 01 (January 2025), pp. 104-117, authored by T.N. Guma and Jacob O. Aremo of the Department of Mechanical Engineering, Nigerian Defence Academy, Kaduna, Nigeria. The paper reviews up-to-date research knowledge on the corrosion-inhibiting capability of garlic (Allium sativum) for steel materials.

KEY FINDINGS:
- Corrosion is a monumental global economic and technological problem; steel accounts for about 90% of all global corrosion problems, and mild steel (up to 0.3% carbon) makes up about 90% of all applied steels and is responsible for 90% of steel corrosion issues.
- Synthetic corrosion inhibitors (chromate, dichromate, nitrite, nitrate) pose serious environmental and health risks, driving research into natural plant extracts as eco-friendly alternatives.
- Garlic is proven to be a very effective, safe-for-handling, biodegradable, and eco-friendly corrosion inhibitor, sustainably available worldwide.

GARLIC PRODUCTION & SAFETY:
- World garlic production is approximately 29,149,438 metric tons. China is the largest producer (20,058,388 metric tons, 76.28% share), followed by India (9.28%), Bangladesh (1.66%), South Korea (1.14%), Egypt (1.05%), and Myanmar (0.7%).
- Garlic has been used medicinally for thousands of years across numerous civilizations (China, Egypt, Greece, India, Rome), indicating its safety for human handling.

CHEMICAL COMPOSITION:
- An undamaged fresh garlic contains approximately 200 chemical compounds including sulfur-containing compounds, volatile oils, enzymes, carbohydrates, minerals, amino acids, and vitamins.
- Garlic has an unusually high proportion of sulfur-containing chemicals (13%), with key active compounds including alliin, allicin, ajoene, diallyl sulfide (DAS), diallyl disulfide (DADS), diallyl trisulfide (DATS), and allyl methyl sulfide (AMS).
- Garlic oil contains 60% diallyl disulfide; 2.62% alliin; 0.15-0.66% allicin; 0.09-0.68% γ-glutamyl-S-(E,S-propenyl)cysteine.
- Garlic oil physical properties: density/specific gravity 1.050-1.095, melting point -59.48°C, boiling point 136.32°C, pH 5.5-6.0, viscosity 9.2 mPa/s, highly flammable.

EXTRACTION METHODS:
- Major extraction methods include Soxhlet extraction, ultrasonic-assisted extraction, steam distillation, pressurized liquid extraction, supercritical-fluid extraction, and microwave extraction.
- Commercially available garlic extract types include garlic oil, prebiotic polysaccharide, aged garlic, black garlic, and garlic powder.

REVIEW OF RESEARCH STUDIES (key results):
1. Ikumapayi et al.: Garlic extract in 0.5M HCl achieved max 68% inhibitory efficiency at 8 v/v%; corrosion rate dropped from 1.66 mm/yr to 0.53 mm/yr.
2. Yang et al.: 93.26% corrosion-inhibitive efficiency for A3 steel in 5% HCl at 4.0% extract; 79.2% in 5% mud acid at 6.0% extract.
3. Afia et al.: Acid garlic essential oil reached ~95.8% inhibition efficiency at 2.5 g/L in 1M HCl at 298K; followed Langmuir adsorption isotherm; mixed-type inhibitor.
4. Barreto et al.: Garlic peel extract in 0.5M HCl was only slightly inferior to benzotriazole (BTAH) for ASTM 1020 carbon steel, offering an eco-friendly alternative.
5. Karthiga et al.: 10 mL garlic extract + 90 mL well water achieved 90% corrosion inhibition efficiency for mild steel; protective film was Fe2+-allicin complex.
6. Barreto et al.: Garlic extract achieved 90.7% efficiency and cacao extract 89% in 0.5M HCl; the mixture achieved >98% inhibition showing strong synergism.
7. Rajam et al.: 2 mL garlic extract + 25 ppm Zn2+ offered 70% inhibition efficiency for carbon steel in well water (anodic reaction control).
8. Belkaid et al.: Garlic extract in 1M H2SO4 achieved up to 90% IE for 316L stainless steel and 67% for API X60 carbon steel.
9. Joycee et al.: 100,000 ppm garlic extract + 50 ppm Zn2+ provided 87% inhibition efficiency for mild steel in simulated oil well water.
10. Yaro et al.: Garlic powder in H3PO4 achieved max 75% inhibition efficiency at 50°C and 250 ppm; followed Langmuir adsorption isotherm; mixed-type inhibitor.
11. Wei-Min and Dao-Yong: Garlic juice reached 95.4% inhibitor efficiency in 15% HCl at 80°C; 42%-64% in oil field water.
12. Fouda et al.: Allium sativum in 1M HCl is a good mixed-type inhibitor; followed Temkin's adsorption isotherm.
13. Parthipan et al.: Garlic extract (100 ppm) inhibited biocorrosion of carbon steel and stainless steel in presence of Bacillus subtilis A1 and Streptomyces parvus B7; first time garlic extract proposed as green corrosion inhibitor with biocidal activity.
14. Rodriguez-Clemente et al.: Allium sativum in 0.5M H2SO4 achieved 96% effectiveness at 400 ppm concentration.
15. Patil and Zaware: Garlic achieved 90%-95% inhibitory efficacy for steel reinforcement in concrete.
16. Maestro et al.: Garlic peel inhibited mild steel corrosion in acid (HCl), neutral (NaCl), and basic (NaOH) media; efficacy rose up to 24 hours in neutral/basic media; quantum modelling showed alliin and allicin produce more active specimens in basic conditions.
17. Ojha: 4 g/L garlic extract in 1M HCl achieved 76.47% maximum inhibition at 298K; followed Langmuir adsorption isotherm (R2=0.999).
18. Da Silvaa et al.: Garlic oil reduced microbiologically-influenced corrosion (MIC) of AISI 1020 carbon steel by sulphate-reducing bacteria more than glutaraldehyde in artificial seawater.
19. Asfia et al.: Garlic extract slowed corrosion of AISI 304 stainless steel in 0.5M HCl by up to 88%; mixed-type inhibitor following Langmuir adsorption isotherm.
20. Lu et al.: Garlic extract as post-treatment for phytic acid-based conversion coating on Q235 steel significantly improved anti-corrosion performance in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution.

CONCLUSION: Garlic is a highly effective, safe, biodegradable, and eco-friendly corrosion inhibitor for steel. However, little has been done with existing research findings for practical protection of steel materials. The review posits that garlic extracts should be considered for standardization and commercialization as practical corrosion inhibitors, or for further research.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Garlic is capable of performing its various usage functions due to the effects of a variety of its functional groups such sulfur-containing compounds with strong biological activity."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Allium sativum (Garlic) as green corrosion inhibitor for low carbon ... ---
URL: https://www.jept.de/2015/04/14/allium-sativum-garlic-as-green-corrosion-inhibitor-for-low-carbon-steel-in-hcl-solutions

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the Journal for Electrochemistry and Plating Technology (JEPT), authored by Prof. Dr. A. S. Fouda, investigates Allium sativum (garlic) as a green corrosion inhibitor for low carbon steel in 1 M HCl solutions. The study was received on 2015-01-25, revised 2015-03-26, and accepted 2015-03-30.

**Methodology:** The inhibition properties were evaluated using four complementary techniques: potentiodynamic polarization, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), electrochemical frequency modulation (EFM), and weight loss measurements. The garlic extract was prepared by drying and grinding Allium sativum powder (20g) in 200 ml of 70% ethanol, stirring for 24 hours, evaporating the ethanol, then dissolving 1g of solid in 1000 ml of bidistilled water. Tests were conducted on low carbon steel specimens (2×2×0.2 cm) in 1 M HCl at concentrations ranging from 50–300 ppm and temperatures from 25–45°C.

**Key Findings:**
- Allium sativum proved to be a good corrosion inhibitor, acting as a mixed-type inhibitor (affecting both anodic and cathodic reactions).
- Inhibition efficiency increased with increasing inhibitor concentration but decreased with rising temperature (298–318K).
- The inhibition mechanism was physical adsorption of the extract's organo-sulphur compounds (S-alkyl-L-cysteine sulphoxides, such as allicin, and γ-glutamyl cysteines) on the metal surface.
- Adsorption followed Temkin's adsorption isotherm; calculated ΔG°ads values (around -20 kJ mol⁻¹ or lower) confirmed physical adsorption.
- EIS data showed Rct (charge transfer resistance) increased and Cdl (double layer capacitance) decreased with increasing inhibitor concentration, indicating replacement of water molecules by adsorbed inhibitor molecules.
- Nyquist plots showed a single capacitive loop in both uninhibited and inhibited solutions, indicating a single charge transfer process.
- EFM causality factors (CF-2 and CF-3) were very close to theoretical values (2.0 and 3.0), confirming good data quality.
- Results from EFM, Tafel extrapolation, and EIS methods showed good agreement.
- SEM and EDX analyses confirmed the adsorption of the inhibitor and formation of a protective thin film on the metal surface, with the surface almost unaffected by corrosion in the presence of 300 ppm extract.
- Arrhenius activation energy (Ea*) increased with inhibitor concentration, typical of physical adsorption; positive ΔH* indicated endothermic dissolution; decreasing ΔS* indicated association in the activated complex.

**Conclusions:** Allium sativum extract is a viable, environmentally friendly (biodegradable, non-toxic) green corrosion inhibitor for low carbon steel in hydrochloric acid, working through physical adsorption that forms a protective external film on the metal surface.
</summary>

"Allium sativum has been proved to be good inhibitor. This reduction in the corrosion rate was due to the formation of an external layer formed by S-containing film present in the extract which was adsorbed physically on the metal surface. Allium sativum acted as a mixed type of inhibitor. The inhibition efficiency increases with increasing the inhibitor concentration, but decreases with raising the temperature."

--- SOURCE 6: Arecoline - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arecoline

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Arecoline — Wikipedia Article Summary

**Overview:** Arecoline is a cholinergic agent, stimulant, and naturally occurring alkaloid found in areca (betel) nuts of the areca palm (*Areca catechu*), native to South and Southeast Asia. It is the key active component of areca nuts, comprising approximately 0.3–0.6% of the nut. Its effects (dose-dependent) include stimulation, alertness, increased concentration, cognitive enhancement, elation, euphoria, pro-sexual effects, relaxation, reduced anxiety, and sedation, as well as addiction and withdrawal symptoms upon discontinuation. Effects are described as subtle, likened to a strong cup of coffee.

**Uses:**
- **Recreational:** Chewed with betel leaf in many Asian cultures for its stimulating effect.
- **Medical:** Used medicinally as an antihelmintic (paralyzes tapeworms).
- **Traditional medicine:** Used in Asian traditional medicine for thousands of years.

**Adverse Effects & Toxicity:**
- Side effects include hypersalivation, hypotension, vertigo, miosis, tremor, bradycardia, extrapyramidal syndrome, and seizures.
- Withdrawal symptoms include mood swings, anxiety, irritability, and insomnia; rarely psychosis in heavy users.
- LD50 is 100 mg/kg (subcutaneous, mice). MLD: 100 mg/kg (mice), 5 mg/kg (dogs), 1.4 mg/kg (horses).
- Areca nut chewing is carcinogenic (confirmed by IARC). IARC Monograph 85-6 found sufficient evidence for carcinogenicity of betel quid and areca nut in humans/animals, but only limited evidence for arecoline itself.
- Arecoline is cytotoxic to multiple cell types, generates reactive oxygen species, and is genotoxic (induces DNA damage/mutation).
- Toxicity partially mitigated by vitamins C and E in mice.
- Overdose treated with antimuscarinic drugs like atropine or scopolamine.

**Pharmacology:**
- Acts as a non-selective partial agonist of muscarinic and nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
- Its major metabolite, arecaidine, is a GABA reuptake inhibitor.
- Subjective effects appear mediated by muscarinic receptors (not nicotinic) per animal studies.
- Stimulant/addictive effects thought to be due to increased dopaminergic neurotransmission in the mesolimbic pathway.
- Chemically closely related to nicotinic acid.
- Metabolized by kidneys and liver; 11 documented metabolites.
- Very efficiently absorbed through oral mucosa with 85% bioavailability; peak plasma concentration within 3 minutes.
- Lime mixed with areca nuts hydrolyzes almost all arecoline to arecaidine.

**Chemical/Physical Data:**
- Formula: C8H13NO2; Molar mass: 155.197 g/mol
- Colorless, odorless oily liquid; melting point 27°C; boiling point 209°C; density 1.0495 g/cm³
- pKa ~6.8; forms crystalline (usually deliquescent) salts.
- IUPAC name: Methyl 1-methyl-1,2,5,6-tetrahydropyridine-3-carboxylate
- CAS: 63-75-2; PubChem CID: 2230

**Synthesis:** Multiple methods exist, including a 2024 method using double Michael reaction/Dieckmann cyclization, a Fischer esterification of nicotinic acid route, and a double Mannich reaction route.

**History & Prevalence:**
- Use dates back several thousand years (Thailand, China, Polynesia).
- First isolated in 1888 by Ernst Jahns; structure confirmed 1907; first complete synthesis 1926 by Fritz Chemnitius.
- Used by 600+ million people worldwide (~10–20% of global population); fourth most used psychoactive drug after alcohol, nicotine, and caffeine.
- Use predominantly confined to Asia; major producing countries include India, China, Myanmar, Malaysia, Indonesia, and Bangladesh.
- Not generally controlled worldwide.

**Chemical Precursor:** Arecoline is used to synthesize paroxetine, femoxetine, nocaine, DMNPC, piquindone, epiboxidine-type compounds, brasofensine, tesofensine, and others.

**Analogues/Related:** Arecaidine, guavacoline, guvacine, nipecotic acid, nicotinic acid, muscarine, tiagabine, xanomeline (anti-schizophrenia drug), and others.

**Research:** Showed modest verbal/spatial memory improvement in Alzheimer's patients (IV administration), but carcinogenic properties make it not a first-choice drug. Anecdotal short-lived effect against schizophrenia; higher areca consumption associated with weaker symptoms in male schizophrenia patients. Inspired development of xanomeline. Enhances learning/memory in rodents.

**Veterinary Use:** Arecoline hydrobromide was listed as an abolished veterinary drug by the Chinese Ministry of Agriculture in 2012.
</summary>

**Authors and Affiliations:** Gang Huang, Deyong Zeng, Tisong Liang, Yaping Liu, Fang Cui, Haitian Zhao, and Weihong Lu, affiliated with the Harbin Institute of Technology (School of Chemical Engineering and Chemistry; Chongqing Research Institute; School of Medicine and Health Sciences), China.

**Publication Timeline:** Submitted 16 October 2024; Revised 14 November 2024; Accepted 24 November 2024; Published 27 November 2024.

**Key Content Summary:**

1. **Areca Nut Background:** The areca (betel) nut (Areca catechu L.) is consumed by over 600 million individuals, predominantly in South Asia, East Africa, and tropical Pacific regions. The IARC has classified it as a Group 1 human carcinogen. Arecoline is the main active alkaloid.

2. **Carcinogenicity Classification:** In 2020, IARC indicated arecoline might be a "probable human carcinogen." WHO recognized areca nut as a primary carcinogen in 2003 and, in 1992, linked it to oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC).

3. **Alkaloid Species and Detection:** Areca nut contains about 20 pyridine alkaloids (0.3–0.7% total), with arecoline, arecaidine, guvacoline, and guvacine being most common. Extraction methods include solvent extraction, ultrasonic-assisted extraction, subcritical water extraction, and supercritical CO₂ extraction. Detection methods include HPLC, UPLC-MS/MS, microchip capillary electrophoresis, GC-MS, and near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS).

4. **Toxicological Effects:** Arecoline has oral submucosal fibrogenic toxicity, reproductive toxicity, hepatorenal toxicity, immunosuppressive toxicity, and neurotoxicity. It induces cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, and cytotoxicity.

5. **Oral Diseases:** 
   - OSF (Oral Submucosal Fibrosis) is a precancerous lesion caused by areca nut chewing, involving TGF-β, PGE2, IL-6, TNF-α, and COX-2 pathways. Arecoline modulates PI3K-Akt and MAPK pathways, induces epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), and promotes collagen accumulation.
   - OSCC (Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma) is the 7th most prevalent cause of cancer-related mortality globally (~710,000 cases annually; 378,500 new cases). Arecoline causes DNA damage via ROS production, epigenetic irregularities, and immune dysfunction.

6. **Nervous System Effects:** Arecoline crosses the blood–brain barrier, stimulates nicotinic and muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, induces neurotoxicity via oxidative stress-mediated apoptotic signaling, and disrupts autophagy flux in PC12 cells. It causes euphoria, palpitations, salivation, increased perspiration, and has addictive properties. Concentrations of 50–200 μM disrupt neuronal redox homeostasis.

7. **Methodology:** The review searched Web of Science, Science Direct, and PubMed databases using keywords (arecoline, toxicity, biological activity), and 95 articles were reviewed by three independent authors with conflicts resolved by a fourth author.

8. **Review Structure:** Sections cover species and identification methods of areca alkaloids, toxicological effects, oral fibrosis and oral diseases (OSF and OSCC), effects on the nervous system, cardiovascular system, reproductive organs, and other organs, plus conclusions and prospects.
</summary>

**Key Topics Covered:**

1. **Background**: Areca nut (AN) is the fruit/seed of *Areca catechu* Linn, a palm tree grown in tropical Asia, East Africa, and the Pacific, especially South/Southeast Asia. Hainan Province is China's largest producer. Over 600 million people chew AN. It is considered the world's fourth most addictive substance and is classified as a Group 1 carcinogen by the IARC/WHO. However, medicinal use of AN shows no notable adverse effects. Different parts have distinct medicinal uses: Arecae pericarpium ("Da Fu Pi"), Arecae semen, Arecae semen tostum (charred), and "Da Fu Mao."

2. **Clinical Studies**: 
   - Medicinal AN is used in traditional Chinese medicine formulations (e.g., Muxiang Binglang Pill for acute pancreatitis, Binglang Powder for spleen/stomach diseases, Food Retention Relieve Oral Liquid for pediatric anorexia, Jinyingzi Binglang Decoction for chronic diarrhea, Binglang Shisanwei Pill for depression).
   - Chewing AN is linked to oral submucous fibrosis (OSF), oral squamous cell carcinoma, tooth abrasion, and oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma. Frequency/duration of chewing correlates with disease severity.

3. **Alkaloids**: At least 18 alkaloids identified in AN. Total alkaloid content ranges 0.3%-0.6%. Four major alkaloids: arecoline (most abundant), guvacine, arecaidine, and guvacoline. 
   - **Beneficial effects**: Anthelmintic, antimicrobial, hypotensive, anti-inflammatory, nervous system effects (anxiolytic, cognition enhancement, lifespan extension via GAR2/PLCβ pathway), digestive system effects, endocrine effects, and anticancer activity against basal cell carcinoma.
   - **Adverse effects**: Fibrosis (especially oral submucous fibrosis), cancer cell metastasis (oral cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma via PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway), cytotoxicity (cytotoxic above 10 μg/mL, suppresses epithelial cell viability at 0.025-12.5 μg/mL), reproductive toxicity, genotoxicity (inhibits p53, induces DNA damage), cardiac toxicity, intestinal inflammation, bronchial smooth muscle contraction, insulin resistance, and diabetes.

5. **Chemical Compounds**: A comprehensive table lists 88+ compounds isolated from AN, categorized as alkaloids (18), polyphenols (29+), triterpenes (6+), steroids (5+), fatty acids (16), and other compounds (11+).

6. **Table 2** summarizes pharmacological activities and toxicity of AN alkaloids across beneficial effects (parasites, microbial infection, blood pressure, inflammation, nervous/digestive/endocrine systems, cancer) and adverse effects (cancer metastasis, fibrosis, cytotoxicity, reproductive toxicity, genotoxicity, and other effects) with relevant references and model organisms.

The review identifies research gaps and proposes future directions for investigating AN at the genetic level using omics technologies (germplasm, metabolites, bioactive properties) for better utilization and quality control of AN.

--- SOURCE 1: Individual and Joint Effect of Oleic Acid Imidazoline and CeCl3 on Carbon Steel Corrosion in CO2-Saturated Brine Solution ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2079-6412/15/1/93

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a scientific research article published in the MDPI journal "Coatings" (Volume 15, Issue 1, Article 93) in January 2025, titled "Individual and Joint Effect of Oleic Acid Imidazoline and CeCl3 on Carbon Steel Corrosion in CO2-Saturated Brine Solution." The paper is classified as an Open Access, Feature Paper, and Editor's Choice article.

**Authors & Affiliations:**
- Tihomir Borko (INA, d.d., Zagreb, Croatia)
- Gordana Bilić (Faculty of Mining, Geology and Petroleum Engineering, University of Zagreb) - corresponding author
- Katarina Žbulj (Faculty of Mining, Geology and Petroleum Engineering, University of Zagreb)
- Helena Otmačić Ćurković (Faculty of Chemical Engineering and Technology, University of Zagreb)

**DOI:** 10.3390/coatings15010093
**Submission/Publication dates:** Submitted 12 December 2024, Revised 8 January 2025, Accepted 12 January 2025, Published 15 January 2025.

**Objective:**
The study investigates the individual and synergistic corrosion inhibition effects of cerium chloride (CeCl3, 5-20 mg dm⁻³) and oleic acid imidazoline (IOA, 5-20 mg dm⁻³) on AISI 1018 carbon steel in a CO2-saturated simulated brine solution at 60 °C (representing average oil industry transport fluid temperature).

**Methodology:**
- Weight-loss testing per ASTM G-1 standard (72 h exposure)
- Electrochemical measurements: linear polarization (±10 mV), potentiodynamic polarization with Tafel extrapolation (±250 mV), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (100 kHz to ~10 mHz)
- Surface analyses: SEM with EDS, Raman spectroscopy, and powder X-ray diffraction
- The simulated brine solution (synthetic brine solution, SBS) contained 30.0 g dm⁻³ NaCl, 0.1 g dm⁻³ NaHCO3, and 0.1 g dm⁻³ CaCO3, pH 5.3, saturated with CO2
- The steel (AISI 1018) had a ferrite-pearlite microstructure with composition: 0.35 C, 0.35 Si, 1.09 Mn, 0.007 P, 0.024 S, 0.09 Cr, 0.07 Ni, 0.01 Mo, 0.10 Cu, <0.01 V, Fe balance

**Key Results:**
- CeCl3 alone showed IE from 57.58% to 96.27%; highest efficiency (96.27%) at 15 mg dm⁻³
- IOA alone showed IE from 3.43% to 94.61%; highest efficiency (94.61%) at 15 mg dm⁻³ (from potentiodynamic polarization)
- Mixtures showed higher efficiency (62.77% to 97.94%) compared to individual compounds
- Highest inhibitory efficiency (IE = 96.82% by mass loss; 97.94% by linear polarization; 97.78% by Tafel) was achieved at 15 mg dm⁻³ CeCl3 + 15 mg dm⁻³ IOA mixture
- A synergistic effect (S > 1) was demonstrated only for the lowest concentration combination (5 mg dm⁻³ CeCl3 + 5 mg dm⁻³ IOA), with S ≈ 1.07 and IE = 87.48%
- Corrosion rates: blank system ~1.446-1.57 mm year⁻¹; best mixture achieved 0.026 mm year⁻¹

**Mechanism:**
- IOA acts as an anodic-type inhibitor at higher concentrations, adsorbing on the metal surface via π-electrons and free electron pairs donated to empty d-orbitals of iron
- CeCl3 behaves as a mixed inhibitor with predominant influence on the anodic process; cerium carbonate likely forms protective film
- The proposed mechanism: imidazoline forms a surface film with voids via adsorption, while cerium carbonate fills these voids, creating a denser and thicker protective film
- The mixture acts as a mixed corrosion inhibitor with significant effect on the anodic iron oxidation reaction

**Context/Background:**
The research addresses CO2 corrosion in oil industry production and transportation systems, which is a major cause of pipeline rupture, economic losses, and ecological disasters. The study aligns with the "green chemistry" approach and the E3 concept (efficiency, economy, and ecology), as both rare earth salts (like CeCl3) and imidazolines are considered environmentally friendly corrosion inhibitors.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"All test methods showed a higher efficiency of compounds′ mixtures (from 62.77% to 97.94%) and a higher degree of corrosion protection compared to the action of individual compounds (efficiency from 3.43% to 94.61% for IOA and from 57.58% to 96.27% for CeCl3)."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Scientific Research Article: Corrosion Inhibition of Q235 Carbon Steel Using Imidazoline Derivatives

**Authors & Affiliations:** Liping Xiong, Pengjie Wang, Zhongyi He (corresponding), Qi Chen, and Renhui Zhang (corresponding) from the School of Materials Science and Engineering, East China JiaoTong University, Nanchang, China; Jibin Pu from the Key Laboratory of Marine Materials and Related Technologies, Ningbo Institute of Materials Technology and Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences.

**Published in:** Arabian Journal of Chemistry (2020), DOI: 10.1016/j.arabjc.2020.102952 (originally published by Elsevier, migrated to Scientific Scholar).

### Purpose
This study synthesized two new imidazoline derivatives (SMIF and SMID) and evaluated their corrosion inhibition performance for Q235 carbon steel in a 3.5 wt% NaCl simulated-concrete-pore (SCP) solution, using both experimental and computational approaches.

### Key Findings
- **Maximum corrosion inhibition efficiency:** 96.02% (weight-loss test) for SMIF at 4.0 g/L; electrochemical tests showed 95.95% (EIS) and 90.69% (potentiodynamic polarization) for SMIF.
- **SMIF outperformed SMID** in all tests; the phenyl group in SMIF provides stronger adsorption on the carbon steel surface compared to the methyl group in SMID.
- **Corrosion rates dropped** from 0.143 mg·cm⁻²·h⁻¹ (blank) to 0.006 mg·cm⁻²·h⁻¹ with 4.0 g/L SMIF.
- Both inhibitors act as **anodic-type corrosion inhibitors** (potential shifts of 242 mV for SMIF and 135 mV for SMID, both >85 mV threshold).
- EDS and SEM analysis confirmed the formation of a protective adsorption film on the steel surface.
- DFT and molecular dynamics simulations confirmed adsorption of inhibitor molecules on the Fe surface.
- Both inhibitors follow the **Langmuir adsorption isotherm** (linear correlation coefficient >0.99).

### Methodology
- **Synthesis:** SMIF and SMID were synthesized from oleic acid, diethylenetriamine, 1-iodobutane, and n-phenylthiourea/n-methylthiourea at ~140°C.
- **Characterization:** IR, Raman, ¹H/¹³C NMR, and elemental analysis confirmed successful synthesis.
- **Tests performed:** Weight loss (5 days immersion at 298 K), potentiodynamic polarization (Tafel), electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), SEM, EDS, and ATR-FTIR.
- **Computational:** DFT (DMol3 module) and molecular dynamics (Forcite module, COMPASS force field, NVT ensemble, 500 ps) in Materials Studio.
- **Solution used:** 0.6 mol/L KOH + 0.2 mol/L NaOH + saturated Ca(OH)₂ with 3.5 wt% NaCl.
- **Inhibitor concentrations tested:** 0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, and 4.0 g/L.

### Significance
The study demonstrates that these imidazoline derivatives exhibit potential for practical application in protecting reinforced concrete structures from chloride-induced corrosion, offering a cost-effective and convenient corrosion prevention method. The synthesized inhibitors are cationic surfactants that adsorb on the steel surface, blocking active sites and preventing corrosive ion penetration.
</summary>

The study analyzed two specific molecular models: GAOH-2Fe (two Fe atoms interacting with O atoms at positions 3, 4, and 5) and GACOO-1Fe (one Fe atom interacting with the carboxylate group). Analytical techniques used include FTIR, Raman spectroscopy, fluorescence spectroscopy, UV-vis absorption, and DFT calculations. Iron complexation causes significant fluorescence quenching, which facilitates Raman inspection of historical manuscripts by reducing background interference. The pH decrease upon metal complexation is identified as a contributing factor to the acidification of iron gall inks and subsequent degradation of paper. The material is classified as a pigment (black color), instrumentally verified with confirmed certainty level.

--- SOURCE 1: Review of Corrosion Inhibiting Mechanisms in Coatings ---
URL: https://www.usbr.gov/research/publications/download_product.cfm?id=2609

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a final report (ST-2017-1703) published in September 2017 by the U.S. Department of the Interior's Bureau of Reclamation Research and Development Office, titled "Review of Corrosion Inhibiting Mechanisms in Coatings." Authors are Stephanie Prochaska and Dave Tordonato of the Materials and Corrosion Laboratory, Technical Service Center.

**Purpose/Background:** The Bureau of Reclamation historically used coatings containing toxic pigments (red lead and chromate) that provided 50+ years of service life. Modern coatings (e.g., epoxies) provide only 20-25 years, requiring more frequent and costly recoating. This literature review sought to identify nontoxic inhibitive pigments that prevent corrosion using mechanisms similar to lead and chromate pigments.

**Key Findings on Legacy Pigments:**
- Red lead (Pb3O4) pigments react with binder components to form metal soaps, which degrade into water-soluble lead salts that migrate to defects and form stable, insoluble compounds. As a secondary mechanism, lead tetroxide passivates the substrate by forming a thin, inert oxide layer.
- Chromate pigments are among the most efficient passivators; hexavalent chromium (Cr6+) reduces to trivalent chromium (Cr3+) under corrosive attack, ending the attack. Chromates are carcinogenic and were phased out by Reclamation in the 1980s-90s.

**Historical Performance Data:**
- A Reclamation analysis found the average service life of red lead primer was 64 years across their structures.
- Red lead primer on bulkhead gates at Parker Dam, California had the longest service life of 77 years.
- All repainted structures had red lead primer service lives of at least 50 years.
- Zinc chromate primers (per Federal specification TT-P-636) were used from the mid-1980s to as late as 1995; none of those structures have been repaired or recoated as of 2017.

**Three Modern Pigment Categories Researched:**

1. **Inorganic Pigments** (most promising): Four groups were reviewed—phosphates, molybdates, silicates, and ferrites. All can form metallic soaps in oleoresinous binder systems, similar to red lead. Zinc presence was important for soap formation; strontium and calcium were common additions. Zinc phosphates are versatile due to low solubility but perform poorly in accelerated testing due to a lag time for protective complex formation. Molybdates passivate steel by forming insoluble ferric molybdates but have disadvantages including premature binder aging, high cost, and toxicity concerns. Silicates can react with oleoresinous binders to form metal soaps of barium, calcium, strontium, and zinc. Ferrites also form metal soaps and promote an alkaline environment at the coating-substrate interface; all ferrite-pigmented epoxy coatings outperformed red lead pigments in the same binder in testing.

2. **Organic Pigments:** Focus on conducting polymers, especially polyaniline (PANI), which acts as a strong oxidant to steel, shifting potential toward noble direction and inducing passivation. Key results:
   - Polyaniline-coated graphite (C/PANI) achieved 97% anticorrosion efficiency (Ae), outperforming all other tested pigments including a commercially available "anticorrosion" pigment (51% Ae).
   - In a study of poly(aromatic amines), poly(m-anisidine) (PmAS) provided the best corrosion protection due to its highest chelating efficiency from its methoxy (OCH3) group.
   - Polyaniline functions similarly to chromate with self-healing properties—the steel substrate is automatically passivated if scratched or breached.
   - Bio-based aromatic acid salts (vanillic, cinnamic, ferulic acids) show potential as "green" inhibitors but are considered a novelty requiring more research.

3. **Metallic Pigments:** Zinc acts as a sacrificial pigment rather than an inhibitive one. Aluminum flake pigments (upwards of 25% by weight) form interlocking scale-like structures that are impermeable to corrosive agents and resist abrasion. Silica-coated aluminum pigments showed dramatic improvement: uncoated aluminum failed alkaline stability and boiling water tests in under 1 hour, while coated aluminum lasted ~7 hours in boiling water and over 100 hours in the alkaline stability test.

**Cost of Corrosion Context:** NACE International estimated global cost of corrosion at $2.5 trillion (3.4% of global GDP). In the U.S., corrosion costs over $276 billion, with $22.6 billion directly related to infrastructure corrosion. NACE estimates 25-30% of this cost could be saved with optimum corrosion management.

**Recommendations for Future Work:**
- Analyze current, commercially available coating systems containing the identified inhibitive pigments.
- Determine expected failure mechanisms of these coatings to predict failure timing.
- Perform accelerated laboratory testing emulating atmospheric service; pre-condition coatings in humid environments to account for pigment lag times.
- Further research conducting polymers, especially polyaniline.
- Consider engaging coatings manufacturers via cooperative agreements to develop new formulations.
- The greatest challenge is quickly and objectively testing commercial coatings to determine if they perform as well as lead- or chromate-containing coatings.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Modern coatings used by the Bureau of Reclamation have service lives of 20–25 years, whereas legacy coatings that contained red lead and chromate pigments had service lives of over 50 years."
</key_excerpts>

This webpage presents a systematic review article published in RSC Advances (Volume 14, Issue 43, 1 October 2024, Pages 31877-31920) titled "Current and emerging trends of inorganic, organic and eco-friendly corrosion inhibitors." The open-access article, authored by Mahmoud A. Ahmed, Sherif Amin, and Ashraf A. Mohamed, provides a comprehensive analysis of corrosion inhibitors including both inorganic and organic compounds.

Key sections of the review cover: (1) corrosion inhibition mechanisms, (2) types of corrosion inhibitors, (3) synergistic inhibition effects, (4) inhibition performance validation, (5) comprehensive economic analysis of the corrosion inhibitor market, (6) SWOT analysis, and (7) conclusions and prospects. The review explores inhibition mechanisms, highlighting the remarkable efficiency of organic compounds attributed to heteroatoms and conjugated π-electron systems. It compares the efficacy, compatibility, and sustainability of emerging environmentally friendly corrosion inhibitors, including biopolymers from natural resources. The review emphasizes synergistic impacts between mixed corrosion inhibitors, particularly organic/organic systems, for challenging processing environments. Evaluation methods discussed include weight loss (WL) analysis, electrochemical analysis, surface analysis, and quantum mechanical calculations, as well as thermodynamics and isotherms related to corrosion inhibition.

--- SOURCE 4: Corrosion Inhibitors in Industrial Coatings ---
URL: https://www.safic-alcan.com/en-us/industry-articles/corrosion-inhibitors-industrial-coatings

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an industry article from Safic-Alcan (a specialty chemical distributor) published on May 13, 2026, covering corrosion inhibitors in industrial coatings. The article explains that corrosion costs the global economy an estimated 3-4% of GDP annually, and organic coatings are the dominant protective strategy for structural steel, marine environments, chemical processing plants, and industrial equipment.

The content covers three primary mechanisms of corrosion inhibition:

1. **Barrier Mechanism**: Physical exclusion using lamellar pigments (micaceous iron oxide, aluminium flake, talc) that create a tortuous path for water and ion diffusion. Research on pigment volume concentration (PVC) shows wollastonite and zinc phosphate outperform talc in combined anticorrosion efficiency and adhesion.

2. **Active (Passivation) Mechanism**: Sparingly soluble pigments release inhibitive ions that form passivating layers or block cathodic sites. Zinc phosphate is the most widely adopted chromate-free active inhibitor with three proposed pathways: direct phosphate ion passivation, zinc-iron complex formation, and metal soap formation with binder components. Molybdate pigments work similarly but can accelerate binder ageing and cause film embrittlement.

3. **Cathodic (Sacrificial) Mechanism**: Zinc particles act as anodes in galvanic contact with steel, requiring pigment volume concentrations above 60% for effective percolating networks. The three-coat system (zinc-rich primer/epoxy midcoat/polyurethane topcoat) is the dominant specification for structural steel bridges. Graphene-modified zinc primers can reduce zinc content while maintaining galvanic action.

The regulatory transition away from hexavalent chromium (Cr(VI)) under REACH Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 has driven development of chromate-free alternatives including: zinc phosphate and modifications, calcium-modified silica, zeolite-based pigments (with controlled release of inhibitor ions), and organic inhibitors (benzotriazole, 2-mercaptobenzothiazole).

Formulation considerations highlighted include: epoxy resins as the dominant binder for industrial anti-corrosion primers, the importance of pigment-binder compatibility testing, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) as the primary quantitative evaluation tool, and standardized testing methods (salt spray ISO 9227/ASTM B117, cyclic corrosion ISO 11997, scribe assessment ISO 4628).

Emerging technologies include smart/self-healing systems with stimuli-responsive inhibitor release — mesoporous alumina loaded with benzotriazole demonstrated 50% improvement in corrosion resistance at scratch sites. Cerium nitrate, dodecylamine, and 8-hydroxyquinoline are demonstrated encapsulatable inhibitors with pH-responsive or mechanical disruption-triggered release.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: Phosphopolyoxometalates (Mo, W, V)  corrosion Inhibitors for Steels | Encyclopedia MDPI ---
URL: https://encyclopedia.pub/entry/58284

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article on the corrosion inhibition properties of two Keggin-type polyoxometalates (POMs): phosphovanadomolibdate acid (@PMoV, H6[PMo9V3O40]∙34H2O) and phosphovanadotungstate acid (@PWV, H6[PW9V3O40]∙14H2O), tested on S235 mild steel and SS304 austenitic stainless steel in 0.5 M sulphuric acid solution.

Key findings:
- The inhibition efficiency for S235 steel is ~90.6% for @PMoV and 69.5% for @PWV after 24 hours of immersion, showing that Mo-based POMs are more effective than W-based ones.
- For SS304 steel, the inhibition degree (as a function of Flade potential) is 4.66 for @PMoV versus 3.26 for @PWV, both proving a passivant effect.
- @PMoV and @PWV function as cathodic inhibitors for S235 steel by increasing the reduction overvoltage of hydrogen ions, and as both passivators and promoters of passivity films for SS304 steel.
- POMs act by forming protective adsorption films on the metal surface, reducing corrosion current density and slowing the corrosion process.

Methods used: potentiostatic polarization (Tafel extrapolation), chronopotentiometry (500 min open circuit potential monitoring), and weight loss/gravimetric analysis (24 h immersion). Experiments were conducted at molar concentrations of 10−2M, 10−3M, 10−4M, and 10−5M.

Synthesis: @PMoV was synthesized from NaVO3∙4H2O, NaH2PO4∙H2O, and Na2MoO4∙2H2O, yielding 14.65 g (63.5% yield, molecular mass 2305.8 g·mol−1). Characterization used FT-IR, thermal analysis (TG), and elemental analysis.

Conclusions:
- POMs with mixed addenda (V, Mo, W) show effective corrosion inhibition for both mild and stainless steels.
- POMs provide inhibition at 10−2 M or higher for S235 (efficiency ~90%), and act as passivant inhibitors for SS304 even at 10−5 M concentration.
- Compared to traditional inhibitors like chromates, polyoxometalates have very low toxicity and accept electrons without significant structural alteration, making them desirable corrosion protectors across a large scale of steels.
- Further research is needed to identify the optimal polyoxometalate ion for specific metals in given environments, and to better understand the composition/structure of metals, passive films, and POM stability.

--- SOURCE 7: Chromate replacement: what does the future hold? | npj Materials Degradation ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41529-018-0034-5

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article published in npj Materials Degradation (volume 2, article 12, 2018) by Gharbi, Thomas, Smith, Birbilis et al., titled "Chromate replacement: what does the future hold?" The article reviews the origins of chromium replacement motivations, legislative actions aimed at reducing chromium compound use, and critically evaluates alternative corrosion prevention technologies developed since the 1980s.

Key content:
- Hexavalent chromium (Cr6+) compounds have been widely used for corrosion prevention since the second industrial revolution, but are documented carcinogens (linked to lung, nasal cancer since the 1920s; officially documented by the US HHS in 1980). Cr6+ also induces genotoxicity in aquatic and botanic life via soil/water contamination.
- REACH (Registration, Evaluation, Authorization and Restriction of Chemicals) legislation was developed in 2006, restricting chromium compound use in the EU unless authorized by the European Chemical Agency (ECHA). Authorization costs are estimated at €1.5M, with a sunset date of January 2019.
- Chromates remain the benchmark corrosion inhibitor due to their versatility, acting as both anodic and cathodic inhibitors over wide pH ranges, forming protective Cr2O3 films via self-healing mechanisms. No equally effective universal alternative has been identified.
- Aeronautical case study: F-22 aircraft switched to non-chromated primer (for environmental/health reasons), resulting in inadequate corrosion protection, and reverted to chromated primer. The F-35 program also uses non-chromated primer that has never been tested on an aircraft in a corrosive environment (program cost est. US$1.508 trillion).
- Trivalent chromium (Cr3+) conversion coatings (TCC), introduced early 1990s for Al alloys, are the most common Cr6+ replacement to date (commercialized by Henkel's Alodine T 5900 RTU, Socomore's Socosurf TCS). However, they show significantly reduced self-healing properties, and recent studies show Cr3+ may be oxidized to Cr6+ during coating growth via hydrogen peroxide (promoted by fluoride species). There are also emerging concerns about Cr3+ genotoxicity among tannery workers.
- Alternative technologies reviewed:
  1. Rare-earth-based coatings (cerium, lanthanum) - inhibit cathodic reactions but dissolve in acidic environments; supply threatened by China's near-monopolization of rare-earth market (Ce price fluctuated from US$4.35/kg to US$100/kg between 2001-2012).
  2. Vanadate-based coatings - inhibit oxygen reduction but carcinogenicity of vanadium compounds makes this alternative no longer viable.
  3. Lithium-containing coatings - Li salts intercalate into Al hydroxide matrix, forming Al-Li layered double hydroxide (LDH), providing promising corrosion resistance and self-healing properties; passed 168-hour salt spray test; not yet industrialized but shows promise comparable to hexavalent chromium.
  4. Organic coatings and nanocomposites (graphene-based) - improve barrier properties but graphene costs exceed AUD$130/kg, limiting viability.
- Smart coatings with controlled inhibitor release (responsive to pH, moisture, light) are emerging as a design direction.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in Analytica (MDPI journal, 2025, Volume 6, Issue 4, article 47) titled "Review of Vibrational Spectroscopy Studies of Coatings Based on Hexavalent or Trivalent Chromium Baths" by Julio C. Avalos, Eugenia Aldeco-Pérez, Julieta Torres-González, Raul Garcia-Garcia, and German Orozco (corresponding author). The paper was submitted September 29, 2025, revised November 8, 2025, accepted November 10, 2025, and published November 14, 2025, with DOI: 10.3390/analytica6040047.

The review examines the application of vibrational spectroscopy (Raman and infrared/FTIR) to study chromium coatings, comparing hexavalent (Cr(VI)) and trivalent (Cr(III)) chromium baths used for both conversion coatings (chemical processes) and electrodeposition (electrochemical processes). Key historical context: three trivalent chromium bath patents were filed in the 19th century, but industrial production during the 20th century was based on Cr(VI) baths due to superior quality; at the beginning of the 21st century, interest in Cr(III) resumed due to lower toxicity, with systematic abandonment of Cr(VI) baths underway.

Main findings across four sections:

1. Hexavalent chromium conversion coatings: Studied extensively (especially on aluminum alloys like AA2024-T3) using FTIR techniques (ATR, DRIFTS, RAIRS, GAIRS, IRSE) and Raman spectroscopy. Synchrotron infrared microspectroscopy (SIRMS) enabled mapping of chromate oxides (820 cm⁻¹) and cyano species (2100 cm⁻¹) with <5 μm spatial resolution. The two-layer coating structure was understood, and ferricyanide was confirmed as a redox mediator in coating formation. Cr(VI) provides a self-repair mechanism by migrating to damaged/active sites (bipolar repassivation model). Chromium phosphate conversion coatings on aluminum were characterized, with film thicknesses from ~20 nm to a few micrometers.

2. Trivalent chromium conversion coatings: Studied from 2004-2023. Coatings form in two steps: (1) fluoride anions dissolve the native Al₂O₃ oxide layer; (2) interfacial pH increases causing hydroxide/oxide precipitation. The coating has two layers: an outer layer of aluminum hydroxide/oxide, zirconium oxide, and chromium hydroxide; and an inner layer rich in aluminum with oxide and fluoride species. Cr(VI) species are formed on the surface even from Cr(III)-only baths due to oxidation by hydrogen peroxide (produced by oxygen reduction). The presence of Cu(II) or Fe(II) ions suppresses Cr(VI) formation. The Raman band of Cr(VI) is approximately 3 orders of magnitude larger than Cr(III), making detection of small Cr(VI) amounts challenging.

3. Electrodeposited hexavalent chromium coatings: The mechanisms of Cr(VI) electrodeposition remain unidentified, with unclear intermediates. Vibrational spectroscopy revealed that amorphous Cr₂O₃ forms first, followed by phase transformation to crystalline Cr₂O₃. Raman laser heating causes in-situ formation of Cr₂O₃. The characteristic band at ~550-552 cm⁻¹ corresponds to the A1g vibrational mode involving Cr-O stretching in octahedrally O-coordinated Cr(III).

4. Electrodeposited trivalent chromium coatings: Approximately 880 articles evaluate Cr(III) coating quality, but very few use vibrational spectroscopy. Studies examined heat treatment effects on cobalt-chromium coatings, pulse current electrodeposition, Cr/SiC composite coatings on ferronickel alloy, and carbon analysis in coatings (sp3 carbon band ~1330 cm⁻¹). Several band assignments in the literature are questioned by the authors, who suggest revisions.

The review notes that very few studies have focused on vibrational spectroscopy of dissolved species in chromium baths—only 2 studies report Raman bands of commercial Cr(VI) conversion coating baths and only 1 electrodeposition bath study exists. Reference spectra of potassium dichromate and chromium(III) sulfate are presented as standards, and a compilation of vibrational modes is provided to facilitate band assignment. The authors conclude that spectroscopic techniques have been insufficiently applied in this field, but vibrational spectroscopy results accelerate the transition to safer Cr(III) technology.
</summary>

"Major vibrational spectroscopy studies have focused on the preparation of chromium coatings via chemical processes (conversion coatings), and few studies have focused on electrochemical processes (electrodeposition)."

--- SOURCE 11: Phosphate conversion coating - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphate_conversion_coating

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Phosphate Conversion Coating (Wikipedia Article Summary)

**Definition and Overview:** Phosphate conversion coating is a chemical treatment applied to steel parts that creates a thin adhering layer of iron, zinc, or manganese phosphates. It improves corrosion resistance and lubrication, or serves as a foundation for subsequent coatings/painting. It is one of the most common types of conversion coating and is also known as phosphate coating, phosphatization, phosphatizing, or phosphating. The trade term "Parkerizing" is used especially when applied to firearms and military equipment. The coating is typically applied via a dilute solution of phosphoric acid with soluble iron, zinc, and/or manganese salts, using sponging, spraying, or immersion. It can also be used on aluminium, zinc, cadmium, silver, and tin.

**History:** Phosphatizing of firearms was discovered around 1910 when it was found that converting steel surfaces to phosphate significantly improved corrosion resistance. It remained very popular in the USA until the 1940s when more modern metal finishing methods were introduced.

**Types of Phosphate Coatings:**
- **Manganese phosphate**: Used for both corrosion resistance and lubricity; applied only by immersion.
- **Iron phosphate**: Typically used as a base for further coatings or painting; applied by immersion or spraying.
- **Zinc phosphate**: Used for corrosion resistance, as a lubricant-holding layer, and as a paint/coating base; applied by immersion or spraying; can also be applied to galvanized steel.

**Process:** The process exploits the low solubility of phosphates at medium or high pH. The bath contains phosphoric acid (H3PO4) with iron, zinc, or manganese cations. The acid reacts with iron metal, producing hydrogen gas and iron cations, raising local pH until phosphates become insoluble and deposit on the surface. An oxidizer (e.g., sodium nitrite) is often added to consume hydrogen gas that would otherwise slow the reaction. An "activation" bath with titanium compounds may precede the main step. Coating performance depends on crystal structure and thickness—a dense microcrystalline structure with low porosity is best for corrosion resistance/painting, while coarse grain impregnated with oil is best for wear resistance. These factors are controlled by bath concentration, composition, temperature, and time.

**Parkerizing (Early History):**
- Development began in Britain and continued by the Parker family in the US.
- "Parkerizing," "Parkerize," and "Parkerized" are registered US trademarks of Henkel Adhesives Technologies (now largely generic use).
- First used on large scale for US military firearms during World War II.
- Key patent milestones:
  - 1869: British inventor William Alexander Ross, patent 3119 (earliest phosphating work).
  - 1906: Thomas Watts Coslett, British patent 8667; US patent 870,937 (1907) for iron phosphating.
  - 1913: Frank Rupert Granville Richards, US patent 1,069,903 for manganese phosphating.
  - 1915: Clark W. Parker and son Wyman C. Parker founded Parker Rust-Proof Phosphating Company of America.
  - 1919: R. D. Colquhoun, US patent 1,311,319 for improved manganese phosphating.
  - 1930: Baker and Dingman, US patent 1,761,186—reduced processing time to one-third by heating to 500-550°F.
  - 1938: Romig, US patent 2,132,883 for zinc phosphating (using strategic materials available in America during war).
  - 1942: Darsey, US patent 2,293,716—improved zinc phosphating by adding copper (reducing acidity requirements) and chlorate, allowing lower operating temperatures (115-130°F). This energy-efficient zinc process became the most common during WWII.

**Parkerizing (Later Developments):** Glock GmbH uses a black Parkerizing process as a topcoat over a Tenifer (ferritic nitrocarburizing) process for pistol slides. Stovetop Parkerizing recipes and kits are sold by major gun-parts distributors such as Brownells.

**Uses:**
1. **Painting primer**: Effective surface preparation providing excellent adhesion and electric isolation.
2. **Corrosion resistance**: Coatings are porous, requiring impregnation with oil, paint, or sealant; results in a tightly adhering dielectric (insulating) layer protecting against electrochemical and under-paint corrosion.
3. **Wear resistance**: Zinc and manganese coatings help break in wear-prone components and prevent galling.
4. **Lubrication**: Zinc phosphate, though abrasive by itself, can become a lubricating layer for cold forming when treated with sodium stearate (soap), forming zinc stearate—a thin, insoluble, hydrophobic layer useful even in extreme deformation like wire drawing.

**Limitations:** Parkerizing cannot protect non-ferrous metals (aluminium, brass, copper) or steels with high nickel content or stainless steel; passivation is used for other metals.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Phosphate conversion coating is a chemical treatment applied to steel parts that creates a thin adhering layer of iron, zinc, or manganese phosphates to improve corrosion resistance or lubrication or as a foundation for subsequent coatings or painting."
</key_excerpts>

- Too high acid ratio caused difficulty in film formation; too low acid ratio produced coarse-grained microstructures

--- SOURCE 1: Group Theory Problems ---
URL: https://faculty.csbsju.edu/frioux/group/SymmetryProblemsX.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage contains a comprehensive collection of Group Theory problems applied to molecular vibrational spectroscopy, likely from a university-level inorganic or physical chemistry course. The problems require students to use point group symmetry analysis to determine IR and Raman activity, vibrational mode types (stretch vs. bend), and symmetry labels for various molecules.

Key molecules covered and their assigned point groups:
- CH4, CD4 (Td): fill in tables with stretch/bend designations, symmetry labels, and IR/Raman activity
- CH2D2 (C2v), CH3D (C3v): complete frequency tables
- Formaldehyde: 6 vibrational frequencies (2843, 2776, 1501, 1251, 1746, 1167 cm⁻¹), all IR and Raman active (A1, B1, B2 symmetries)
- PH3/PD3 (C3v): assign stretches and bends
- BCl3: determine if trigonal planar (D3h) or trigonal pyramidal (C3v); bands at 995 (IR+Raman), 480 (IR), 471 (Raman), 244 (IR+Raman)
- CH3CN: 12 vibrational DOF but only 8 fundamentals observed in IR (explain degeneracies/overlaps)
- Methane: two IR absorptions (bend at 1306, stretch at 3019 cm⁻¹) consistent with Td; predict Raman active modes
- XeF4: determine tetrahedral vs. square planar (absorptions at 161, 291, 586 IR; 218, 524, 554 Raman)
- Cubane (C8H8, Oh): 42 vibrational DOF, only 3 IR active modes; predict Raman active modes
- Dodecahedrane (C20H20, Ih): 3 IR bands (2945, 1298, 728) and 8 Raman frequencies consistent with icosahedral symmetry
- SF4: C2v see-saw structure per VSEPR, 8 coincidences between IR and Raman
- Al2H6 (dialane, D2h): B1u (1932, 836), B2u (1268, 632), B3u (1915, 1408, 702) cm⁻¹
- C60 Buckminsterfullerene (Ih): 4 IR active and 10 Raman active modes
- P4 (Td): Raman at 614, 372 and IR+Raman at 466 cm⁻¹; isotopic substitution to C3v
- Tetrahedrane (C4H4, Td): predict IR and Raman active modes (not yet synthesized)
- cis/trans/1,1-difluoroethene (C2v/C2h/C2v): distinguish isomers spectroscopically
- CH3Cl (C3v): frequencies at 3017, 2937, 1452, 1355, 1017, 732 cm⁻¹
- Diborane (D2h): 18 vibrational DOF, 9 Raman and 9 IR active modes, no coincidences
- Cyclopropane (D3h): complete vibrational table
- PX5 and MoF5 (D3h trigonal bipyramidal): symmetry analysis with Γuma and Γbonds
- [PtCl4]²⁻ (D4h): IR at 320, 183, 93; Raman at 332, 314, 170 cm⁻¹
- [BrF2]⁻ and [BrF2]⁺: identify which spectrum belongs to which ion
- [ClO4]⁻ (Td): consistent with Td symmetry (1102, 935, 628, 462 cm⁻¹)
- N2F2: determine cis (C2v) vs. trans (C2h)
- Benzene (D6h): 4 IR active modes at 675, 1035, 1479, 3036 cm⁻¹; π orbital symmetry analysis
- Allene (D2d), ethene/deuterated ethene (D2h), BH3 (D3h), CH4 (Td) H-orbital analyses
- cis/trans/1,1-dichloroethene: complete symmetry tables
- Pyrazine (D2h): confirm vibrational table
- InCl5²⁻: determine C4v vs. D3h (data supports C4v: 6 IR, 9 Raman, 6 coincidences)
- C10H8 isomers (azulene C2v, fulvalene D2h, naphthalene D2h): distinguish via spectroscopy
- Propellane (D3h): symmetry analysis with/without bridging C-C bond

The problems incorporate historical references including Eaton and Cole's 1964 cubane synthesis (JACS 1964, 86, 3157), Paquette's dodecahedrane work (JACS 1983, 105, 5446), dialane synthesis (Science, March 28, 2003), and XeF4 references (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1963, 85, 1927; J. Phys. Chem. 1971, 54, 5247).

Key spectroscopic principles exercised include: IR active modes require dipole change (transform as x, y, z), Raman active modes require polarizability change (transform as quadratic functions), and coincidence rules (centrosymmetric molecules show no IR-Raman coincidences).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Cubane, C8H8, has 42 vibrational degrees of freedom, but only three IR active modes. Cubane belongs to the octahedral point group. Show that group theory predicts three IR active modes."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: 7.2: Identifying all IR- and Raman-active vibrational modes ... ---
URL: https://chem.libretexts.org/Courses/Saint_Marys_College_Notre_Dame_IN/CHEM_431%3A_Inorganic_Chemistry_(Haas)/CHEM_431_Readings/07%3A_Vibrational_Spectroscopy/7.02%3A_Identifying_all_IR-_and_Raman-active_vibrational_modes_in_a_molecule

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an educational webpage from Chemistry LibreTexts (CHEM 431: Inorganic Chemistry, Fall 2020, by Dr. Kathryn Haas at Saint Mary's College) that explains how to identify all IR- and Raman-active vibrational modes in a molecule using symmetry and group theory. The page uses water (H₂O) as a case study to demonstrate a four-step process:

1. **Step 1: Find the reducible representation (Γ_modes)** for all normal modes by assigning an axis system to each atom and determining the character (trace) of the transformation matrix for each symmetry operation. For water (point group C₂ᵥ, with operations E, C₂, σᵥ, σᵥ'), the Γ_modes is found to be 9, -1, 3, 1 for E, C₂, σᵥ, σᵥ' respectively.

2. **Step 2: Break Γ_modes into irreducible representations** using the reduction formula: (# of i) = (1/h) × Σ(operations in class × χ_Γ × χ_i). For water, this yields Γ_modes = 3A₁ + 1A₂ + 3B₁ + 2B₂ (9 total irreducible representations).

3. **Step 3: Subtract rotations and translations** to isolate vibrational modes. Rotations correspond to R_x, R_y, R_z in the character table; translations have the same symmetry as x, y, z axes. For water: (3A₁ + 1A₂ + 3B₁ + 2B₂) − (A₁ + B₁ + B₂ rotations) − (A₁ + B₁ + B₂ translations) = 2A₁ + 1B₁. This matches the 3N−6 = 3 vibrational modes expected for a non-linear molecule.

4. **Step 4: Determine IR and Raman activity.** IR selection rule: a vibration is IR-active if it changes the molecular dipole moment (modes with symmetry of x, y, or z axes). Raman selection rule: a vibration is Raman-active if it changes molecular polarizability (modes with symmetry of binary products xy, xz, yz, x², y², z²). For water's vibrations (2A₁ + 1B₁), all are both IR-active and Raman-active, predicting two possible IR peaks and three possible Raman peaks.

Key formulas: Linear molecule degrees of freedom = 3N−5; Non-linear molecule degrees of freedom = 3N−6. The page notes that group theory predicts what is *possible* but actual spectra may show overlapping or off-scale peaks. An exercise asks students to apply the same analysis to tetrachloroplatinate(II) square planar complex. The page is shared under a CC BY-NC-SA license.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"If a vibration results in the change in the molecular dipole moment, it is IR-active. In the character table, we can recognize the vibrational modes that are IR-active by those with symmetry of the x,y, and z axes."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Molecular Vibrations Explained (IR & Raman Made Simple) ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WNfg2CQEV4A

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This educational YouTube video by Inorganic Chemistry Tutor (published January 5, 2026) explains molecular vibrations and their connection to character tables for IR and Raman spectroscopy. The video covers:

**Fundamental Concepts:**
- A molecule with n atoms has 3n degrees of freedom, divided into translation (3), rotation, and vibration
- Linear molecules have 3n-5 vibrational degrees of freedom; nonlinear molecules have 3n-6
- Examples: Sodium (single atom) = 0 vibrational modes; CO2 (linear) = 4 vibrational modes; H2O (nonlinear) = 3 vibrational modes
- Some vibrational modes can be degenerate (same energy, different atomic motion directions)

**Vibrational Mode Visualization:**
- CO2: symmetric stretch, asymmetric stretch, and two degenerate perpendicular bending modes
- H2O: symmetric stretch, asymmetric stretch, and scissoring/bending mode

**IR vs. Raman Activity:**
- A mode is IR active if it changes the molecular dipole moment (analogy: marble changing color position)
- A mode is Raman active if it changes polarizability, how easily the electron cloud deforms (analogy: balloon)
- The symmetric stretch of CO2 is IR inactive but Raman active (classic example)
- Mutual exclusion principle: for molecules with a center of symmetry, IR-active vibrations are Raman-inactive and vice versa

**Using Character Tables:**
- If a vibrational mode transforms like X, Y, or Z, it is IR active
- If a mode transforms like x², y², z², or xy, it is Raman active
- Method: determine point group, apply symmetry operations to find reducible representation, reduce it to irreducible representations, and consult the character table

**Worked Examples:**
1. **H2O (C2V point group):** Reducible representation 2 0 0 2 reduces to A1 and B2; all three vibrational modes are both IR and Raman active (3 IR peaks expected)
2. **XY3 molecules like SO3/BF3 (D3h point group):** 6 vibrational modes reduce to A1' (Raman only), E' (IR and Raman, doubly degenerate), and A2'' (IR only); SO3 shows 2 IR absorption bands despite 6 vibrational modes
3. **SF6 (Oh point group):** 15 vibrational modes reduce to A1g, Eg, T1u, T2g, T2u; due to center of inversion and mutual exclusion principle, only T1u (triply degenerate) is IR active, so SF6 shows just one IR absorption band

The video concludes that symmetry and character tables allow chemists to predict vibrational modes and IR/Raman activity without tracking every bond motion manually.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"For linear molecules, we have 3n - 5 vibrational degrees of freedom. And for nonlinear molecules, we have 3n - 6 vibrational degrees of freedom."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Raman active modes ---
URL: https://www.doitpoms.ac.uk/tlplib/raman/active_modes.php

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This page is from the DoITPoMS (Dissemination of IT for the Promotion of Materials Science) Teaching & Learning Package on Raman Spectroscopy, specifically covering "Raman active modes." It explains the spectroscopic selection rule for Raman scattering: for a vibrational mode to be Raman active, it must involve a change in the polarisability (α) of the molecule, expressed as (dα/dq)e ≠ 0, where q is the normal coordinate and e is the equilibrium position.

Key points covered include:
- Raman and IR spectroscopy are complementary techniques; the IR selection rule requires a change in dipole moment, while Raman requires a change in polarisability. For centrosymmetric molecules, Raman-active modes are IR-inactive and vice versa (rule of mutual exclusion).
- The mathematical derivation shows how polarisability oscillating at the molecular vibration frequency (νvib) interacts with the incident photon's oscillating electric field (frequency νp) to produce three scattering outcomes: Rayleigh scattering (νp), Stokes scattering (νp – νvib), and anti-Stokes scattering (νp + νvib). If polarisability does not change, only Rayleigh scattering occurs.
- For solids, vibrations are quantised as phonons determined by the crystal structure. The same selection rule applies, and phonons generally have lower frequencies than gas-phase molecular vibrations, resulting in lower wavenumber shifts.
- Crystal orientation can be determined from the polarization of scattered light.
- For more complex molecules, Raman/IR activity can be determined using symmetry and group theory, which is beyond the scope of this TLP but has links in the "Going further" section.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"For a mode to be Raman active it must involve a change in the polarisability, α of the molecule"
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Practical Group Theory and Raman Spectroscopy, Part II ---
URL: https://www.spectroscopyonline.com/view/practical-group-theory-and-raman-spectroscopy-part-ii-application-polarization

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific article from Spectroscopy Online (published March 1, 2014) titled "Practical Group Theory and Raman Spectroscopy, Part II: Application of Polarization" by David Tuschel, a Raman applications manager at Horiba Scientific in Edison, New Jersey. It is the second installment of a two-part series applying group theory concepts to polarized Raman spectroscopy across liquids, single crystals, and polycrystalline compounds.

Key content covered:

1. **Water (H2O)**: The article presents polarized Raman spectra of water showing three Raman active modes—two stretching (ν1 totally symmetric A1, polarized; ν3 antisymmetric B2, depolarized) and one bending (ν2, A1, polarized). The bending mode at 1635 cm-1 is weak, leaving the fingerprint region clear, which is why Raman is well-suited for aqueous solutions. OH stretching covers approximately 2900-3700 cm-1 due to H bonding.

2. **Carbon Tetrachloride (CCl4)**: Belongs to point group Td with four Raman active modes (1A1, 1E, 1T1, 1T2). The A1 totally symmetric stretch at 459 cm-1 is polarized (nearly vanishes perpendicular). The E, T1, and T2 bands are depolarized with a perpendicular-to-parallel ratio of 0.75. A combination band at 762 cm-1 is assigned to T2 + A1 (since 314 + 459 = 773 cm-1, and combination bands appear slightly lower in energy). The 459 cm-1 band shows isotopic splitting from natural Cl abundances (~25% 37Cl, 75% 35Cl), with five resolved components (ν1a-ν1e). Only C35Cl4 and C37Cl4 retain true Td symmetry; the mixed isotopic species have lower symmetry (C3v, C2v) but collisional broadening in liquid prevents resolving the degeneracy lifting.

3. **Raman scattering strength of totally symmetric modes**: Totally symmetric modes produce the largest changes in polarizability, giving the strongest Raman signals. Examples include toluene (point group Cs, with polarized A' bands at 521, 786, 1003, 1030, 1210 cm-1 being the most intense) and acetonitrile (point group C3v, with intense polarized bands at 919, 2253, 2943 cm-1). Notably, the CH stretch (2943 cm-1) is as intense as the CN stretch (2253 cm-1) despite the CN triple bond, demonstrating that symmetry species matters as much as functional group character.

4. **Single-crystal LiNbO3**: A ferroelectric crystal in the C3v crystal class with A1 and E modes (both Raman and IR active) and silent A2 modes. Using the X-face with Z-axis laser polarization, the parallel analyzer selects A1 bands (254, 275, 632 cm-1) while the perpendicular configuration selects E modes. Unlike liquids (random molecular orientation), crystals have fixed bond orientations, so not all Raman bands can be detected from one crystal face. Raman polarizability tensor forms are dictated by crystal symmetry.

5. **Polycrystalline rubrene**: A cautionary tale about Raman sampling. Rubrene (orthorhombic, D2h crystal class, 4 molecules/unit cell) grains from the same reagent bottle can produce significantly different spectra (different relative band intensities but same band positions) depending on grain orientation relative to the laser polarization. This can lead to falsely concluding two samples are chemically different when they are identical.

References include prior work by the author in Spectroscopy journal (2012, 2014) and a YouTube demonstration of polarized Raman spectroscopy of LiNbO3.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Although bond order and functional group identity are indeed important and suggestive regarding Raman scattering strength, the nature of the symmetry species to which the vibrational mode belongs can be just as important to Raman signal strength."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: vibrational sum frequency and raman spectroscopic studies ---
URL: https://etd.ohiolink.edu/acprod/odb_etd/ws/send_file/send?accession=osu1204583563&disposition=inline

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is a doctoral dissertation by Man Xu, submitted to The Ohio State University in 2008 (Environmental Science Graduate Program), advised by Professor Heather C. Allen, with committee members Professor James V. Coe and Professor John Lenhart. The dissertation investigates nitrate ions at air-aqueous interfaces and in bulk aqueous solutions using vibrational sum frequency generation (VSFG) spectroscopy as the primary technique, supplemented by Raman and infrared spectroscopies.

Key findings and conclusions include:

1. **Bulk ion pairing studies (Chapter 4):** In divalent metal-nitrate aqueous solutions, ion pairing is concentration- and cation-dependent. Pb²⁺ has the strongest tendency to form ion pairs with nitrate, and contact ion pair formation decreases with increasing cation charge density in the order: Pb²⁺ > Sr²⁺ > Ca²⁺ > Mg²⁺.

2. **Air-aqueous interface studies (Chapters 5-6):** For the first time, the vibrational symmetric stretch mode of nitrate ions at the air-aqueous interface was directly probed by VSFG. For Mg(NO₃)₂ at low bulk concentrations, interfacial nitrate anions are relatively free from Coulombic effects of Mg²⁺ cations, revealing that water solvation significantly affects interfacial ion pairing. The bulk frequency evidence suggests Mg²⁺–nitrate interaction via solvent-shared or solvent-separated ion pairing. The presence of nitrate salts perturbs the interfacial water hydrogen-bonding network, with interfacial depth increasing with cation size: Mg²⁺ < Ca²⁺ < Sr²⁺.

3. **Silica surface acidity study (Chapter 7):** Using ethylenediamine (EDA) as a surface acidity probe molecule, VSFG studies of EDA adsorption onto silica surfaces revealed that adsorption occurs via protonation of an amine group by a silica surface silanol site. The surface acidity of silica was quantified to be in the range of the two pKa values of EDA: 7.56 to 10.71.

The dissertation includes theoretical chapters on VSFG theory, Fresnel factors, Raman depolarization ratios, and Kramers-Kronig relations, plus detailed experimental methodology for scanning VSFG instrumentation (20 Hz and 10 Hz systems), Raman instrumentation, and FTIR instrumentation. The work was funded by the Department of Energy (DOE-BES, DE-FG02-04ER15495).

The dissertation's environmental significance is emphasized: nitrate is ubiquitous in atmospheric aerosols, surface and ground waters, and plays roles in the nitrogen cycle, atmospheric chemistry, eutrophication, and toxicity (nitrite from nitrate reduction is toxic to humans, especially infants). The work also relates to polar snowpack nitrate photolysis and marine sea salt aerosol chemistry.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The spectral features of the nitrate vibrational modes indicate that the ion pairing in the metal-nitrate aqueous solutions are concentration and cation dependent. Pb2+ has a strong tendency to form ion pairs with nitrate anions, and the formation of contact ion pairs decreases with decreasing cation size and increasing cation charge density: Pb2+ > Sr2+ > Ca2+ > Mg2+."

--- SOURCE 7: Theoretical Vibrational Analysis of Bidentate and ... ---
URL: https://www.sid.ir/en/VEWSSID/J_pdf/84320210317.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This research article (Iran. J. Chem. Chem. Eng., Vol. 40, No. 3, 2021, pp. 881-887) by Fatih Ucun and Ahmet Tokatlı from Süleyman Demirel University, Turkey, presents a theoretical vibrational analysis of bidentate and unidentate coordination of carbonate (CO3²⁻), nitrate (NO3⁻), sulfate (SO4²⁻), and perchlorate (ClO4⁻) ions to metal atoms.

**Methodology:** DFT calculations using the B3LYP functional at the DEF2-TZVP basis set level were performed with Gaussian 09 software. Cobalt, nickel, and copper were chosen as the metal centers. Vibrational modes were assigned via Gauss-View 5.0, and calculated frequencies were not scaled as they were sufficiently close to experimental values.

**Key Findings:**
1. Free CO3²⁻ and NO3⁻ ions belong to the D3h point group with four normal modes; the symmetric stretching mode (A1') is IR inactive. Free SO4²⁻ and ClO4⁻ ions belong to the Td point group, where symmetric stretching (A1) and bending (E) modes are only Raman active.
2. Bidentate coordination changes the symmetry to the C2v point group, making all vibrational modes both IR and Raman active except the A2 symmetry mode (Raman active only).
3. Upon coordination, doubly degenerate modes (E1' or E) split into two bands, while triplet degenerate modes (T2) split into three bands.
4. All splitting bands of degenerate modes are nearly center-out (the frequency of the degenerate mode sits at the center of the splitting bands), and the intensity relationship follows proportionally (high-intensity degenerate modes produce high-intensity splitting bands).
5. The M-O stretching vibrational frequency is LOWER in unidentate complexes than in bidentate complexes due to decreased force constant. Example: Co-O stretching was calculated at 457 cm⁻¹ for bidentate CoCO3 vs. 325 cm⁻¹ for unidentate carbonate complexes (force constants of 0.953 and 0.657 mDyne/Å, respectively).
6. Splitting bands of degenerate modes are LARGER in bidentate than in unidentate complexes.
7. The IR-inactive symmetric stretching mode of carbonate/nitrate becomes IR active after coordination, confirming the structure determination utility of infrared spectroscopy.

The paper includes detailed frequency tables for all ions and their metal complexes (Co, Ni, Cu) with symmetry species assignments, and comparisons of calculated vs. experimental frequencies for representative complexes such as Co(NH3)4CO3Cl (bidentate), Co(NH3)5CO3Br (unidentate), Cu(ClO4)2 (bidentate), and Cu(ClO4)2·2H2O (unidentate). The authors conclude that these theoretical results will aid experimental researchers in determining coordination structures of their complexes.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The coordination of the ions to the metal atom lowered the symmetry and so, the splitting of degenerate modes occurred together with the appearance of IR inactive modes."

--- SOURCE 8: Group Theory Part 8: D3h point group problem + IR and Raman stretching solved ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_FNgO_8GSH4

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an educational chemistry video from Aaron's Chem Videos (posted April 6, 2011) that works through a group theory problem for the D3h point group using a trigonal bipyramidal molecule. The video walks through the process of finding a reducible representation and reducing it using the D3h character table.

Key steps covered:
1. The D3h point group contains: E, 2C3, 3C2, one horizontal reflection plane (σh), 2S3, and 3 vertical reflection planes (σv), with H = 12.
2. For the trigonal bipyramidal molecule (6 atoms total), the unshifted atom counts are determined for each symmetry element: E=6, C3=3, C2=2, σh=4, S3=1, σv=4.
3. The contribution per atom values are used: E always = 3, reflection planes always = 1, C3 (2cos120°+1) = 0, C2 (2cos180°+1) = 1, S3 (2cos120°-1) = -2.
4. The reducible representation is calculated by multiplying (number of operations × unshifted atoms × contribution per atom): Γ = 18, 0, 6, 4, -4, 12 (sum = 24, which is a multiple of H=12).
5. The reducible representation is then reduced using the D3h character table:
   - A1' = 2
   - A1'' = 1
   - E' = 2
   - A2' = 0
   - A2'' = 3
6. The video emphasizes checking that all terms sum to multiples of H to verify calculations, and instructs viewers to revisit earlier steps (unshifted atoms and contribution per atom) if errors are found.
7. The video ends with a break before completing the E'' irreducible representation, with the problem to be finished in the next video.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an educational video from RojasLab (published March 18, 2024, with ~10,774 views) on using group theory to predict IR and Raman vibrational modes in molecules, specifically focusing on CO stretching frequencies. The video demonstrates a step-by-step methodology for determining the irreducible representations that make up the reducible representation of CO stretches.

The primary example walks through a manganese carbonyl molecule with four CO bonds and a bromine ligand, which is identified as belonging to the C4v point group. The process involves:
1. Determining the point group by identifying symmetry elements (C4 principal rotation axis, no perpendicular C2 axes, presence of σv mirror planes)
2. Placing vectors on each CO bond and tracking their behavior under each symmetry operation to generate the reducible representation (characters: E=5, C4=1, C2=1, 2σv=3, 2σd=1)
3. Using the reduction formula (1/order × sum of coefficients × characters) to reduce the representation to irreducible representations: 2A1 + 1B1 + 1E
4. Using the character table's linear functions (x, y, z) to determine IR-active modes (A1 and E are IR active; B1 is not) and quadratic functions (x²-y², z², xz, yz) to determine Raman-active modes

The second worked example is a C2v molecule with three CO bonds, a metal center, and two chloride ligands. The reducible representation for CO stretches is (3, 1, 3, 1), which reduces to 2A1 + 1B1, predicting 3 IR peaks and 3 Raman peaks for the CO stretches.

Key pedagogical points include: the order of C4v is 8, the reduction formula must always yield whole numbers (fractions indicate an error), and this method is valuable for structure determination by predicting how many IR and Raman peaks to expect.
