## 2. Organic groups on silica surface

Recent examples of the use of FTIR and FT-Raman spectroscopies in the monitoring of surface reactions between silanol groups and ligands for organic and organometallic compounds. The possibility of distinguishing liquid-like and crystalline configuration for long-chain alkyl groups from the C–H stretching vibrations position.

The organic groups’ presence and interactions are monitored in different types of materials, as the ones discussed above. In terms of corrosion protection coatings, the organosilanes are widely known that due to their efficient properties as coupling agents, representing an interesting and environmentally friendly alternative in the field of surface treatments [[26](#B26)]. One of the employed organosilanes is the glycidyloxypropyltrimethoxysilane (GPS) that when mixed with methyltriethoxysilane can improve coating resistance, charge transfer resistance and present low-frequency impedance parameters. FTIR was employed by Foroozan et al. [[18](#B18)] to investigate the reaction between glycidyl groups of GPS molecules with silanol groups. It was possible to identify bands reflecting the epoxy ring breathing around ~910 and 840 cm−1 and also a new band appeared near 1730 cm−1 for C=O stretching that could be associated with the oxidation of the epoxide ring. The spectra confirmed a strong network reticulation as a result of the reaction between glycidyl groups of GPS molecules with hydrolyzed silanes. However, the complimentary results of water contact angles decreased probably due to higher amount of –CH–OH, produced in the reaction between glycidyl and silanol groups, so they reached an optimum point at which a more reticulated structure overcomes the silane layer hydrophilicity.

Silanol groups are also employed to investigate the grafting of catalytic compounds at the silica surface. Ochędzan-Siodłak et al. describes a catalytic system where metallocenes and postmetallocene compounds are immobilized in an ionic liquid modified silica surface. The modification process could be followed by the Si–OH stretching vibration, at 3700 cm−1, disappearing after the ionic liquid modified silane reaction with the silanol groups ([Figure 2A](#F2)) [[27](#B27)]. This strategy is becoming popular nowadays, where different organosilanes are first used to modify the surface with specific chemical groups with which is possible to graft the catalysts species or precursors itself [[28](#B28), [29](#B29)]. Similarly, the Si–OH vibration can be used to follow direct grafting of catalyst in the silica surface, where the silanol groups can react with a metallic center producing chemical bond between the catalyst compound and the silica surface. Li et al. [[30](#B30)] describes the grafting of a nickel complex in silica and alumina surfaces by following a band at 3745 cm−1, which is assigned to isolated surface hydroxyl groups drops gradually with reaction time and almost completely vanishes after 24 h and correspondingly the absorption bands at 3070–2877 cm−1 related to C–H stretching vibrations of the catalyst allyl groups steadily raise in intensity ([Figure 2B](#F2)). Capel-Sanchez et al. [[31](#B31)] also investigated the grafting by silanol groups and in the development of a single site titanium on an amorphous silica surface, they report that the titanium precursor is preferentially anchored over the silica surface by the bridging hydroxyl groups (broad band around 3500 and 3700 cm−1) over the isolated ones (~3700 cm−1).

By using Raman spectroscopy, there is also the possibility of final conformation studies in the case of hybrid silica with long alkyl chains at the silica surface. Structure and order information about alkane-based systems can be obtained from multiple indicators in their Raman spectra, especially in the ν(C–H) region between 2750 and 3050 cm−1. Also, significant conformational order information exists for alkane systems in the ν(C–C) and δ(C–H) regions between 900 and 1500 cm−1. However, it is necessary some care about fluorescence phenomena interferences in Raman around this region [[32](#B32)]. Using this methodology, Brambilla et al. evaluated the gauche and trans conformation of hybrid silica with different octadecyl groups (octadecylsilane [ODS]) content by Raman spectroscopy. The two bands centered at 1080 and 1062 cm−1 are assigned, respectively, to *ν*(C–C) for *gauche* e *trans* conformation of the ODS alkyl chains. The ratio in intensity of these two bands was evaluated in order to monitor the influence of the TEOS/ODS molar ratio in the organic groups’ behavior. For all ratios, the intensity between the two bands laid above 1, meaning there is a predominance of *trans* conformation in comparison to *gauche* one, indicating therefore an intense molecular organization in the hybrid silica prepared by the sol-gel method. In addition, it was found that the organization degree of alkyl chains decreases with the ODS content increase, with data from 29Si-NMR and FTIR detected in attenuated total reflectance (ATR) mode, corroborating to the findings [[33](#B33)].

## 3. Molecules within bulk silica

The FTIR technique can also be employed to evaluate silica network characteristics such as hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity degree and siloxane ring structure regarding thin film porosity [[34](#B34), [35](#B35)]. In terms of sensors, these features may impact the analyte interaction and access to the encapsulated molecules, known as receptor elements, within the silica matrix. If the encapsulated molecules’ interaction with the silica network occurs through their active sites, it is possible that these active sites are not available to further interact with the analyte. Reduced sensor performance can also occur if the silica network is nonpermeable. In this case, the silica network itself limits the pathways the analyte can travel to reach the encapsulated receptor molecules hindering the reaction. Consequently, both cases could reduce the sensor performance or completely disable it [[36](#B36)].

Silica materials have a prominent band corresponding to the Si–O–Si bond asymmetric stretching in the region from 1300 to 1000 cm−1. Literature reports that the maximum centers and relative intensities of the longitudinal optic (LO) and transversal optic (TO) modes of this bond are shifted with the introduction of chemical groups or organic molecules in the silica network [[35](#B35)]. So, a complete analysis of its components can be conducted, including the deconvolution of the LO and TO modes in their relative main contributions: the four-membered (SiO)4 and six-membered (SiO)6 siloxane rings ([Figure 3A](#F3)), resulting in a total of four components (LO6, LO4, TO6 and TO4) ([Figure 3B](#F3)). Usually, materials with higher content of chemical groups or organic molecules use to present higher formation of less stressed six-membered ring, thereby allowing a better accommodation of the nonreactive organic groups [[37](#B37)]. Furthermore, there is a correlation between the formation of six-membered rings and an increase in the relative degree of crystallinity, as well as with the long-range organization in hybrid silica materials that is normally observed with an increase in the degree of matrix alkylation [[38](#B38)].

![](//cdnintech.com/media/chapter/52212/1512345123/media/fig3.png)

#### Figure 3.

A) Two of the most common cyclical arrangements of SiO4 structural units in xerogels: four-membered siloxane ring (SiO)4 above and six-membered siloxane ring (SiO)6 below. B) Band deconvolution to asymmetric stretching ν(Si–O(–Si)) bond [39].

Using this approach, a series of silica-based acid-base optical sensors prepared by encapsulating pH indicators using three different sol-gel routes was investigated [[36](#B36)]. The employed routes were: nonhydrolytic, acid-catalyzed and base-catalyzed and the pH indicators were alizarin red, brilliant yellow and acridine. The FTIR spectra were performed for all the materials and the peak corresponding to the Si–O–Si asymmetric stretching was deconvoluted and their respective components analyzed and [Figure 4](#F4) assembles the results. For the acidic and nonhydrolytic routes, a positive correlation between the pH indicator content and the increase in (SiO)6 percentage was established, thereby indicating the silica network structure rearrangement in order to accommodate the indicator molecules. Using a basic route, the reached indicator contents were notably low and so this relationship was not observed. In addition, no relationship between the (SiO)6 percentage and the response time could be established in spite of less dense networks, with bigger rings, might render easier the analyte permeation. This behavior may indicate that the analyte probably accessed the receptor elements through the passages between the siloxane rings and not through the siloxane rings themselves [[36](#B36)].

![](//cdnintech.com/media/chapter/52212/1512345123/media/fig4.png)

#### Figure 4.

Comparison of (SiO)6 percentage () and encapsulated indicator content () in each sample [39].

It is remarkable that depending on the sol-gel route, the rate between hydrolysis and condensation reactions will change with the pH medium and can explain the behavior of the basic-catalyzed sensor material. Under basic conditions, the condensation reactions of silanol groups are strongly accelerated, and the particles are rapidly formed. Thus, the probability of rearrangement as a function of the presence of other molecules, as pH indicators for example, during the synthesis decreases, since the tridimensional network is quickly formed. When the condensation reactions are slower, such occurs in acid pH, the network can be more influenced by the addition of molecules to be encapsulated [[39](#B39)].

## 4. Silica molecular imprinting

The molecular imprinting methodology involves a molecular recognition process where the analyte can recognize and preferentially bind to specific sites built by using a template of the target molecule during the matrix network formation. After an extraction process in order to remove the template, the resulting material is bulk silica with cavities that are morphologically and stereochemically compatible with the analyte. Therefore, an option of analytical technique to follow this procedure is FTIR. It is possible to track the template interaction with the silica network by the template bands appearance and/or SiO2 vibrations change.

With this approach, Morais et al. [[40](#B40)] describe the interactions of different drugs such as fluoxetine, gentamicin, lidocaine, morphine, nifedipine, paracetamol and tetracycline with silica matrix during the preparation of molecular imprinting materials. All these drugs present nitrogen atoms as primary, secondary or tertiary amines that can interact with silanol groups. The investigation was performed comparing the vibrations of bare drug with the encapsulated drug, before removal by extraction. The silica spectrum presents intense bands in the region of ~3500 cm−1 assigned to the O–H vibrations of silanol groups and adsorbed water; and in the region of 1200–800 cm−1, where the Si–O stretchings are observed. As a result of these strong bands and the frequently low concentrations of the encapsulated compounds, it is common to observe an overlapping of their signals by the silica ones avoiding this type of evaluation [[36](#B36)].

As an example, [Figure 5A](#F5) illustrates the spectra of lidocaine with its main bands at 1675 cm−1 is assigned to the ν(C=O) of the amide chemical group, 1655 and 1546 cm−1 attributed to δ(C–N–H) of the amine group and the band at 1476 cm−1 to the δ(C–CH3) of the methyl group; and [Figure 5B](#F5) shows the spectra of the lidocaine-silica composite where the main bands of the drug can still be observed. However, the bands assigned to the carbonyl stretching and amino bending modes were shifted to 1683 and 1639 cm−1, respectively, suggesting a potential medicine-silica network interaction through these chemical groups. Similar behavior was observed for the other drugs, considering the machine resolution of 4 cm−1. Most of the pharmaceutical presented infrared band shifts toward higher wave numbers (bathochromic shift) when encapsulated, indicating they are interacting with the silica structure, resulting in a rearrangement of the chemical groups, which was confirmed by the rotational isomerism of the molecule. In addition, some of the bands were shifted for lower wave numbers (hypsochromic shift) reflecting a tension increase in the molecule rotational conformation, since the encapsulation process may incur in difficulty of the functional groups vibrational movements demanding more energy. Most of the nitrogen-related bands, for all samples, had their wave numbers shifted. These results denote possibility of a hydrogen bonding interaction through electron donation between these groups and silica network, as illustrated by [Figure 6](#F6). Among the studied drugs, the exception was tetracycline which presented a shift in the OH group deformation band and so indicating an interaction by this group [[40](#B40)].

In other approaches, hybrid silica networks have been used to improve both the process of molecular imprinting as the following usage of the material as an extraction matrix. Han et al. reports the functionalization of silica with amino groups provided by aminopropyltriethoxysilane to help interaction with the toxic herbicide pentachlorophenol [[41](#B41)]. By using FTIR to monitor this process, they were able to identify the N–H bond around 1560 cm−1 and C–H bond around 2935 cm−1, suggesting the –NH2 grafting onto the activated silica gel surface. In this case, imprinted and nonimprinted sorbents showed similar location and appearance of the major bands, reflecting the already mentioned problem of overlapping bands with the major bands of silica network. Similar behavior was observed by Chrzanowska et al., Ren et al. and Li et al. [[42](#B42)–[44](#B44)]. The first one employed the functionalization of silica nanoparticles surface with aminopropyl groups to promote the encapsulation of biochanin A, producing a selective solid-phase extraction of biochanin A, daidzein and genistein from urine samples [[42](#B42)]. Analogously, Ren et al. employed the same procedure with aminopropyl groups, although the target analyte was bisphenol A [[44](#B44)]. Finally, the later one made use of propylthiocyanate groups to modify the silica surface, creating a selective phase for selective removal of cadmium(II) competing with copper, zinc and lead in aqueous solution [[43](#B43)]. In all the cases, the assisting organic groups’ bands were detected; however, the molecular imprinted and nonimprinted spectra were really similar.

## 5. FTIR and Raman modes

When analyzing hybrid silica materials, sometimes it is necessary to use complementary techniques to better evaluate the materials’ characteristics. The same occurs for vibrational spectroscopy methods. A wide investigation was performed with a series of different hybrid silica prepared with tetraethoxysilane (C0), methyltriethoxysilane (C1), octyltriethoxysilane (C8), octadecyltrimethoxysilane (C18), vinyltrimethoxysilane (Vy), phenyltrimethoxysilane (Ph), mercaptopropyltrimethoxysilane (SHp), isocyanatepropyltriethoxysilane (NCOp), chloropropyltrimethoxysilane (Clp) and glycidoxypropyltrimethoxysilane (Gp) [[45](#B45)]. Using FTIR, the main bands of silica were well determined for all the hybrid silicas and they showed shifts depending on the organic group presenting at the network, although the organic groups’ bands were barely seen. Using Raman spectroscopy, the organic groups were well described and some of the silica network bands were also observed.

The region around 3600–3000 cm−1 is attributed to hydroxyl groups ν(O–H) stretching modes. The shoulder at ~3600 cm−1 matches the OAH vibrations associated with alcohols that are a subproduct of sol-gel reaction, while the maximum at ~3425 cm−1 is related to surface –OH participating of hydrogen bonds. Water is also described here as a shoulder at ~3230 cm−1, which is also observed at ~1630 cm−1. As mentioned before, silica presents a characteristic region of peaks from 1250 to 700 cm−1 that can provide structural characteristics of the network. Specially, when related to the main bands between 1250 and 1000 cm−1 corresponding to the asymmetric ν(Si–O–H) and their deconvolution on LO at ~1130 cm−1 and TO at 1047 cm−1 modes. The Si–O(H) bond stretching appears at slightly different positions in the FTIR (~950 cm−1) and Raman (~980 cm−1) spectra. The symmetric mode of ν(Si–O–Si) band is found at ~791 (FTIR) and ~799 cm−1 (Raman), while the Si–O− rocking mode was observed at ~540 cm−1 (IR). Finally, the Raman spectra also show the siloxane ring breathing mode (with 3 or 4 SiO units) located at ~490 cm−1 [[45](#B45)].

The silica-related bands presented wave number shifts depending on the employed organic group in the different hybrid silicas. For Si–O(–Si) LO mode, the largest shift occurs from the nonhybrid to the hybrid samples. In this case, shifts to lower wave numbers use to be related to the network deformation in order to accommodate the organic groups within the inorganic silica matrix resulting in larger siloxane rings and greater Si–O–Si angles and longer Si–O bond lengths. LO and TO mode shifts occur mainly near the surface of the material, which can be better detected employing attenuated total reflectance (ATR) mode of FTIR spectroscopy. In addition, the organic groups’ introduction can originate from heterogeneous regions that may introduce local deformations in the network resulting in the differences observed for Si–O bond lengths and Si–O–Si angles in the different hybrid materials. Another interesting behavior is reported to Si–O(H) band, considering that, in a general way for this case, the wave number shifts result from hydrogen bond formation with the silanol groups. A significantly higher wave number occurred for C18 while the lower ones occurred for Clp and Gp [[45](#B45)]. The very hydrophobic C18 organic chain can hinder hydrogen bond formation by comparison with the other samples, thus, the Si–O bond length is decreased and the wave number is shifted to higher values. However, the groups Clp and Gp can facilitate hydrogen bond formation with the silanol groups and, as a consequence, the Si–O bond length is increased and the vibrational wave number is decreased [[46](#B46)].

As mentioned before, the characterization of the organic groups of hybrid network is better done using Raman spectroscopy than FTIR. The last one can observe only some bands, while Raman presents a series of them showing the complementarity of both techniques for hybrid materials’ characterization. [Table 1](#tab1) compiles some important assignments regarding the organic groups and their respective wave numbers detected by both techniques, when applicable [[45](#B45)].

The complementary use of FTIR and Raman spectroscopies can be also employed to deeply investigate the processes taking place during sol-gel process and there are other types of detection modes for these vibrational techniques as DRIFTS, PAS, IRES, micro-FTIR and Raman which can help.

DRIFT spectroscopy is primarily used on samples where most of the reflected radiation is diffused. It is important that the specular reflectance is reduced to a minimum because it distorts the DRIFT spectrum and lowers the band intensities [[47](#B47)]. During the last years, it has become the most effective technique for studying the processes taking place at the gas-solid interface [[48](#B48)]. Ivanovski et al. investigated the region of the OH stretching vibrations of silica gel activated at different temperatures for the purpose of checking the availability of the OH groups for further reaction with 3-aminopropyltrimethoxysilane (APTMS) molecules and whether chemisorption was successful, finding evidence whether chemisorption of APTMS involves all available methoxy groups. It is also possible to investigate the conformation of the aminopropyl groups (APS) backbone on the silica gel surface and the possible proton transfer between the NH2 groups of APS and OH from silica gel detected by the formation of NH3+ and SiO− which is spectroscopically detectable through the appearance of the δ(NH3+) vibrations at 1668 cm−1 [[49](#B49)]. In addition, Bukleski et al. developed a direct quantitative method of quantification of maximal chemisorption of 3-aminopropylsilyl groups on silica gel using DRIFT spectroscopy, as (APS) modified silica gel plays an important role as a precursor for further modifications, where APS acts as a spacer or bridging molecule. By integrating the spectra in the frequency range of the *ν*(CH2)/*ν*(CH3) vibrations between 3014 and 2808 cm−1, the mass fraction of APTMS of 19.04% was found to correspond to a maximal concentration of APS on silica gel of 2.23 μmol m−2, which was confirmed by elemental analysis for carbon [[47](#B47)].

| S–H | 2574 R |

### Table 1.

Organic group bands detected by the complementary techniques of FTIR and Raman [[45](#B45)].

\*asym: asymmetric; sym: symmetric; bend: bending; term: terminal; def: deformation; R: Raman; and I: infrared.

The photoacoustic spectroscopy (PAS) FTIR is a broad-applicable mid-infrared solution when samples present opacity problems [[50](#B50)]. It is a unique extension of IR spectroscopy which combines the utility of interferometry with the standard sample-gas microphone of the photothermal technique for depth-profile analysis of materials. Its signal generation processes automatically and reproducibly isolates a layer extending beneath the sample surface which has suitable optical density for analysis without physically altering the sample. PAS involves measurement of acoustic wave (pressure oscillations) in a hermetically sealed cell fitted with a very sensitive microphone. The microphone signal, when plotted as a function of wavelength, contains a spectrum proportional to the absorption spectrum of the sample. The wave generation follows absorption of light, which is modulated at a frequency in the acoustic range, by the sample. Most FTIR instruments provide modulation frequencies between 50 and 500 Hz in the 400–4000 cm−1 wave number span [[51](#B51)]. Therefore, this approach can be employed to evaluate silica samples as described by Gao et al. to widely explore a polyethylene-*co*-Zn-acrylic acid hybrid material prepared by the sol-gel process. They could identify both vibrations for silica and the organic group. By investigating the silica bands it is noted that not only silica but also other forms of silicon groups are formed via the sol-gel reaction, while the existence of the Si–OH group indicates that the condensation reaction was not completely finished. However, analyzing the peaks referring to the organic groups, it was reported that –CH2– and –CH3 positions in the region of 2800–3000 cm−1 remain the same after hybrid material fabrication, indicating no chemical bond between silicon and these two groups forms after the sol-gel reaction. The band at 1700 cm−1 is the C=O stretching mode from the –COOH group was also noticed for both materials. This is due to unneutralized acrylic acid. While the transparency of the hybrid is a result of strong organic-inorganic interaction, and a high degree of mixing, no evidence of hydrogen bonding is observed from the FTIR peak position [[52](#B52)].

Infrared emission spectroscopy (IRES) is a method in which a sample is energized by heating and so on, and the infrared light emitted from the sample is measured to obtain a spectrum. It utilizes the contrast between the sample and the base material with possibility of an improved signal-to-noise ratio compared to absorption spectroscopy. Ideally only photons emitted by the sample are detected (“zero background”), free from the noise produced by the continuum lamp in an absorption experiment. This improvement in sensitivity is particularly useful for the spectroscopy of transient molecules because of their intrinsically low concentrations [[53](#B53)]. In the case of hybrid silicas, this methodology can be successfully employed to evaluate the thermal stability of materials. Brambilla et al., for example, describe the behavior of octadecylsilane (ODS) hybrid silicas prepared by grafting and sol-gel methods with a spectra series from 100 to 900°C between 4000 and 500 cm−1. The decrease of physically adsorbed water band and the surface silanol interactions, leading to an increase in the band at 3747 cm−1, attributed to isolated silanol groups was observed. For temperatures higher than 450°C up to 900°C, the band assigned to isolated silanol groups (3747 cm−1) is reduced due to condensation reactions and structural reorganization with generation of siloxane groups. Concerning the ν(C–H) stretching region, the bands at 2963, 2929 and 2855 cm−1 are reduced in the range of 250–550°C, as a result of the thermal degradation of ODS chains. [Figure 7](#F7) presents the relative band area for this vibration. It was possible to compare the thermal stability of hybrid materials prepared by grafting (GR100) and sol-gel method (SG10A), confirm the higher thermal stability of the first one [[54](#B54)].

![](//cdnintech.com/media/chapter/52212/1512345123/media/fig7.png)

#### Figure 7.

Relative area of ν(C–H) bands versus temperature for grafting prepared (GR100) and sol-gel prepared (SG10) hybrid silicas [54].

Finally, micro-Raman and micro-FTIR modes have less sensibility, however, they are key methods employed when spatial resolution of a few micrometers is necessary. It can be employed, for example, to evaluate radial distribution of the fictive temperature in pure silica optical fibers [[55](#B55)], porous silica supports for individual living cells [[56](#B56)] and phenyl-bridged polysilsesquioxane positive and negative resist for electron beam lithography where the technique helped to propose a description of the tone switching mechanisms [[57](#B57)].

## 6. Final remarks

Observing all the procedures and results described above, it is noticeable that a vibrational spectrum is not collected only to simply evaluate peak positions anymore. Nowadays, it is possible to obtain deep information about materials’ formation, evolution and structure, as well as to acquire spatial resolution spectra or in high-resolution modes with low signal/noise ratios. The reaction chemical processes following methods are getting more and more specific, as collected data are more and more exploited in order to give the maximum results information, bringing fast advance in the materials characterization field.

This is an open-access peer-reviewed chapter published by IntechOpen in the edited volume "Applications of Molecular Spectroscopy to Current Research in the Chemical and Biological Sciences," edited by Mark T. Stauffer. The chapter, titled "Fourier Transform Infrared and Raman Characterization of Silica-Based Materials," was written by Larissa Brentano Capeletti and João Henrique Zimnoch from the Chemistry Institute, Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul, Porto Alegre, Brazil. Submitted December 2, 2015; reviewed June 2, 2016; published October 5, 2016 (DOI: 10.5772/64477). The chapter has 5,324 downloads and 47 citations.

The chapter reviews the use of FTIR and Raman spectroscopies to characterize silica-based and hybrid silica materials. Key applications of silica-based materials discussed include catalysts (e.g., hydrogen production, desulfurization, polymerization), chromatographic phases and sorbents (including molecular imprinting and hybrid silica monoliths for drug extraction from plasma), sensors (optical pH sensors, electrochemical, electrochemiluminescence, biosensors), and protective/surface-functional coatings (corrosion protection, superhydrophobic self-cleaning surfaces, antimicrobial surfaces).

Key technical content organized into sections:
1. Introduction: overview of silica-based materials applications and synthetic routes (sol-gel, grafting, nonhydrolytic sol-gel, molecular imprinting).
2. Organic groups on silica surface: FTIR monitoring of silanol reactions with organosilanes (e.g., GPS coatings, catalyst grafting tracked via Si–OH stretching at ~3700 cm⁻¹ disappearing). Raman spectroscopy used to evaluate gauche vs. trans conformations of octadecyl (ODS) alkyl chains via ν(C–C) bands at 1080 and 1062 cm⁻¹; trans conformation predominates, and organization degree decreases with ODS content.
3. Molecules within bulk silica: Deconvolution of Si–O–Si asymmetric stretching (1300–1000 cm⁻¹) into LO and TO modes with four- and six-membered siloxane rings ((SiO)4 and (SiO)6). Higher organic content favors less-stressed six-membered rings for accommodating organic groups. Study of pH-indicator encapsulation via three sol-gel routes showed positive correlation between indicator content and (SiO)6 percentage for acidic and nonhydrolytic routes; base-catalyzed routes reach low encapsulation due to rapid condensation.
4. Silica molecular imprinting: FTIR tracking of drug interactions (fluoxetine, gentamicin, lidocaine, morphine, nifedipine, paracetamol, tetracycline) with silica networks. Bands shift upon encapsulation indicating hydrogen bonding interactions through nitrogen or OH groups. Silica functionalization with aminopropyl or other groups used to improve imprinting; overlapping bands between imprinted and nonimprinted materials noted as a limitation.
5. FTIR and Raman modes: Complementary techniques for hybrid silicas (with groups including methyl, octyl, octadecyl, vinyl, phenyl, mercaptopropyl, isocyanatopropyl, chloropropyl, glycidoxypropyl). Detailed band assignments provided, including Si–O(H) at ~950 cm⁻¹ (FTIR) and ~980 cm⁻¹ (Raman), symmetric Si–O–Si at ~791/799 cm⁻¹, and siloxane ring breathing at ~490 cm⁻¹. A comprehensive table (Table 1) compiles organic group band assignments for both techniques. Additional detection modes covered: DRIFTS (for gas-solid interface studies, quantification of APS chemisorption on silica gel at 2.23 μmol m⁻²), photoacoustic spectroscopy (PAS) for opaque samples, infrared emission spectroscopy (IRES) for thermal stability evaluation (ODS hybrid silicas from 100–900°C), and micro-Raman/micro-FTIR for micrometer spatial resolution applications (optical fibers, porous silica supports for living cells, lithography resists).

Final remarks note that vibrational spectroscopy has evolved beyond simple peak position evaluation to provide deep information about materials' formation, evolution, structure, and spatial resolution, advancing materials characterization.

<webpage_content>
Bull. Mater. Sci., Vol. 34, No. 2, April 2011, pp. 299–303. c ⃝Indian Academy of Sciences.
IR and Raman spectroscopic studies of sol–gel derived alkaline-earth silicate glasses ANGELOS G KALAMPOUNIAS Department of Chemical Engineering, University of Patras, GR – 26 504, Patras, Greece; and Foundation for Research and Technology Hellas, Institute of Chemical Engineering and High Temperature Chemical Processes, GR – 26 504, Patras, Greece MS received 20 June 2008 Abstract.
IR and Raman spectroscopies have been utilized to study the structure and vibrational modes of sol–gel-derived binary silicate glasses. The present study is motivated by the immense geological signiﬁcance and focuses on the MO–SiO2 (M = Ca, Mg) binary systems in an effort to unveil the role of the CaO and MgO modiﬁers when incorporated to the 3D silica structure. Glasses in the composition range x = 0, 0·1, 0·2, 0·3 and 0·4 prepared by the sol–gel method were compared with the corresponding glasses formed by appropriate mixing of SiO2 and MO powders through melting and fast cooling. The vibrational spectra of the sol–gel-derived glasses have revealed considerable changes in relative intensities as a function of the MO mole fraction. These changes signify structural modiﬁcations on the silica network. The population of the Q3 species was found to increase for both modiﬁed silicate systems. The rate of increase is more pronounced in the CaO–SiO2 glasses. The extent of network depolymerization in the porous glass is higher at the same content of alkaline earth oxide compared to the bulk glass. The results are indicative of a more ‘defective’ nature of the sol–gel glasses compared to the corresponding melt-quenched ones.
Keywords.
Sol–gel silicate glasses; Raman spectroscopy; IR spectroscopy; structure; silicates.
1.
Introduction The present study is motivated by the immense geological signiﬁcance of silica based materials since almost all igneous processes are associated with the presence of a silicate melt phase or magma (Heany 1994). However, since the struc-ture of multi-component glasses can be described in a less straightforward way, the choice of binary systems seems advantageous for undertaking systematic studies (McMillan 1984; McMillan and Wolf 1995). The microscopic structure can be vastly different between two glasses of the same com-position prepared by different routes. In particular, silicate glasses that are derived by the sol–gel process exhibit exten-sive differences compared to bulk, melt quenched glasses, at the microstructure as well as at the morphological or textu-ral properties. Silicate glasses that contain calcium and phos-phorus are known to exhibit bioactive behaviour (Hench et al 2002).
The bioactive silica-based materials present an open struc-ture which enables the accommodation of alkali and/or alka-line earth cations (K+, Na+, Li+, Ca2+, Mg2+, etc). These alkali and/or alkaline earth oxides act as network modi-ﬁers provoking the disruption of the continuity of the glassy network due to the breaking of the Si–O–Si bonds lead-ing to the formation of nonbridging oxygen species (Si–O– NBO) (Scholze 1990). Concerning the bioactive processes, (angelos@chemeng.upatras.gr) this is the key step since the concentration of Si–O–NBO groups monitor the dissolution rate of the silica through the formation of silanol groups at the surface (Kokubo 1990).
Thus, the study of the bonding conﬁguration of glasses and the quantitative estimation of the Si–O–NBO species by analytical techniques contribute to improve the ability to design new bioactive glasses. Raman and infrared spectro-scopies are sensitive techniques to the local structure of sili-cate glasses allowing the determination of changes on the Si–O–Si vibrational modes.
The aim of this study is to verify the bonding conﬁ-guration of silica glasses modiﬁed by alkaline earth oxides (MgO, CaO) prepared by the sol–gel method and to identify the presence of nonbridging silicon–oxygen groups by com-bining the two spectroscopic techniques, viz. Fourier trans-form Raman and infrared spectroscopies. A complete study of glasses with different silica concentrations and type of alkaline earth is presented.
2.
Experimental 2.1 Sample preparation Binary glasses along the joints of xCaO·(1 −x)SiO2 and xMgO·(1 −x)SiO2 with x = 0, 0·1, 0·2, 0·3 and 0·4 were prepared by hydrolysis and polycondensation of tetraethyl orthosilicate (TEOS), tetrahydrated calcium (Ca(NO3)2·4H2O) and hexahydrated magnesium nitrate 299 300 Angelos G Kalampounias (Mg(NO3)2·6H2O). Nitric acid (HNO3, 2 N) was used to cata-lyze the TEOS hydrolysis, using a molar ratio of (HNO3 + H2O/TEOS = 8). After the addition of all reactants, the solu-tion was stirred for 1 h. The sol was cast in containers and kept at room temperature to allow the hydrolysis and poly-condensation reactions, up until the formation of a viscous gel. For aging, the gel was stored in a sealed container and kept at 60◦C for 3 days. The drying of the gel was carried out in three stages by heating the gel at 60◦C, 90◦C and 130◦C for 20, 24 and 40 h, respectively. The stabilization procedure took place in three steps by sintering the samples at 100, 300 and 700◦C for 1, 2 and 5 h, respectively. The temperature increase rate was kept constant at 0·1◦C/min for all heating procedures.
2.2 Instrumentation—Spectroscopic techniques Fourier transform Raman (FT–Raman) measurements were obtained using a Bruker (D) FRA-106/S component attached to an EQUINOX 55 spectrometer. A R510 diode pumped Nd:YAG laser at 1064 nm (with a maximum output power of 500 mW) was used for Raman excitation in a 1808 scatter-ing sample illumination module. An optical ﬁltering reduced the Rayleigh elastic scattering and, in combination with a CaF2 beamsplitter and a high sensitivity liquid N2-cooled Ge-detector, allowed the Raman intensities to be recorded from 50–3300 cm−1 in Stokes-shifted Raman region, all in one spectrum.
For Fourier transform infrared measurements (FTIR) sol– gel derived glasses were crushed with pestle in an agate mor-tar. The crushed material was mixed with potassium bro-mide (Merck IR spectroscopy grade) in 1:100 proportion and dried at 40◦C. The mixture was compressed to a 12 mm semitransparent disk by applying a pressure of 10 tonnes for a few min. The FTIR spectra over the wavelength range 4000–400 cm−1 were recorded using a FTIR spectrometer (UV–vis-NIR spectrophotometer V-570 Jasco).
3.
Results and discussion 3.1 Bulk and porous silica glass In order to facilitate the analysis of the experimental data of the sol–gel-derived glasses, we present in ﬁgures 1(a) and 1(b) the Raman and IR spectra of pure bulk (suprasil) and sol–gel silica glass, respectively. The spectra of the corre-sponding quartz crystal are shown for comparison. In gene-ral, the Raman spectra of silica glasses (bulk and sol–gel) seem to be similar and the differences are focused on the rela-tive intensities of several bands and only one new relatively sharp band appears in the spectrum of sol–gel-derived sili-ca. This band is located near ∼980 cm−1 referred to as Qa.

This scientific paper by Angelos G. Kalampounias (Department of Chemical Engineering, University of Patras, Greece, and FORTH/ICE-HT) published in Bull. Mater. Sci., Vol. 34, No. 2, April 2011, pp. 299–303, presents IR and Raman spectroscopic studies of sol–gel-derived alkaline-earth silicate glasses in the MO–SiO2 (M = Ca, Mg) binary systems.

**Purpose and Motivation:** The study was motivated by the geological significance of silica-based materials and aims to unveil the role of CaO and MgO modifiers when incorporated into the 3D silica structure. It focuses on understanding network depolymerization, which is critical for bioactive glasses since Si–O–NBO (non-bridging oxygen) groups monitor the dissolution rate of silica through silanol group formation at surfaces.

**Methodology:** Glasses in the composition range x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and 0.4 were prepared by the sol–gel method using hydrolysis and polycondensation of tetraethyl orthosilicate (TEOS), Ca(NO3)2·4H2O, and Mg(NO3)2·6H2O. Nitric acid (2 N) catalyzed TEOS hydrolysis (molar ratio HNO3 + H2O/TEOS = 8). The gel was aged at 60°C for 3 days, dried in three stages (60, 90, 130°C for 20, 24, 40 h respectively), and stabilized by sintering at 100, 300, and 700°C (1, 2, and 5 h respectively) with a constant heating rate of 0.1°C/min. FT-Raman measurements used a Bruker FRA-106/S with Nd:YAG laser at 1064 nm; FTIR spectra were recorded over 4000–400 cm−1 using KBr pellet technique.

**Key Findings:**
1. The sol–gel-derived silica showed a new sharp band near ~980 cm−1 (Qa), characteristic of Si–O stretching vibration of (Si–OH) silanol groups, absent in bulk silica.
2. The number of three-membered rings (D2 defect mode at ~606 cm−1) increased in porous silica, while four-membered rings (D1 at ~493 cm−1) showed no significant change.
3. The broad band at ~440 cm−1 decreased in intensity with increasing modifier content, indicating lowering of network dimensionality by breaking Si–O–Si bridges.
4. A new shoulder band appeared near ~680 cm−1 attributed to bending motion of oxygen bonds in "defective" structures.
5. In the high-frequency region, bands at ~980 cm−1 (Q2 species) and ~1050 cm−1 (Q3 species) dominated the spectra for both alkaline earth silicate systems.
6. The population of Q3 species increased systematically with modifier content for both systems, with a more pronounced rate of increase in CaO–SiO2 glasses.
7. The Si–O–NBO(s)/Si–O(s) absorbance intensity ratio showed a monotonous increase with modifier content for both systems, confirming gradual network depolymerization.
8. Depolymerization was more enhanced in CaO-modified silicates compared to MgO-modified ones at the same composition.
9. The extent of network depolymerization in porous (sol–gel) glass was higher than in bulk (melt-quenched) glass at the same alkaline earth oxide content, indicating a more "defective" nature of sol–gel glasses, likely related to the presence of OH groups responsible for network connectivity.

**Conclusions:** The vibrational spectra revealed significant structural modifications of the silica network upon alkaline earth oxide addition. The Q3 species population increased for both modified silicate systems, with CaO being more effective than MgO in promoting depolymerization.

The results are indicative of a more 'defective' nature of the sol–gel glasses compared to the corresponding melt-quenched ones."

<webpage_content>
This article has been accepted for publication and undergone full peer review but has not been through the copyediting, typesetting, pagination and proofreading process, which may lead to differences between this version and the Version of Record. Please cite this article as doi: 10.1111/jace.18206. This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved. Vibrational Spectroscopy Analysis of Silica and Silicate Glass Networks Hongshen Liu,1 Huseyin Kaya,2 Yen-Ting Lin,1 Andrew Ogrinc,1 and Seong H. Kim1,2* 1. Department of Chemical Engineering and Materials Research Institute, Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA 16802 2. Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA 16802 * Corresponding author: shk10@psu.edu Abstract: Vibrational spectroscopy has been widely used to investigate various structural aspects of the glass network and there are a plethora of papers reporting subtle but consistent changes in IR and Raman spectral features of glass upon alterations of glass compositions, thermal histories, mechanical stresses, or surface treatments. However, interpretations of such spectral features are still obscured due to the lack of well-established physical principles accurately describing vibrational modes of the non-crystalline glass network. Due to the non-equilibrium nature of the glass network three dimensionally connected without any long range orders, vibrational spectral features of glass cannot be interpreted using the analogy with those of isolated molecular moieties or crystalline counterparts. This feature article explains why such comparisons are outdated and describes the recent advances made from theoretical calculations of vibrational spectral features of amorphous networks or comparisons of computational results with experimental data. For the interpretation of vibrational spectral features of silica and silicate glasses, the following empirical relationships are suggested: (i) the intensity-weighted peak position of the Si-O-Si stretch mode negatively correlates with the weighted average of the Si-O bond length distribution and (ii) the broad band of the Si-O-Si bending mode negatively correlates with the Si-O-Si bond angle distribution. Selected examples of vibrational spectroscopic imaging of surface defects are discussed to deliberate the implication of these findings in the structure-property relationship of silica and silicate glass materials. Unanswered questions and continuing research challenges are identified. This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved. I. Introduction Along with nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and x-ray and neutron scattering, vibrational spectroscopy is one of the widely used methods for structural characterization of glass materials. Being operated with different physical principles, each method provides structural information that may be complementary to others. NMR is particularly useful for determination of the short-range structure such as connectivity in the first coordination shell, Qn speciation of silicon species (here n is the number of bridging oxygen bonds connected to other silicon atoms), and coordination of boron and aluminum network formers.1-9 X-ray10-13 and neutron scattering14-18 can give intermediate-range structural information beyond the first coordination shell such as radial distributions of atoms in the second, third, and fourth shells. These are static coordinates of atoms that can be readily simulated computationally; thus the agreement of those structures with simulation results can confirm the accuracy of the analysis.19-25 In contrast, vibrational spectroscopy such as infrared (IR) and Raman techniques26-38 probes dynamic responses of electronic polarizations, which are coupled with atomic motions covalently bonded with surrounding atoms. Such responses are much more challenging to calculate or simulate computationally when the subject of study is three-dimensionally connected amorphous networks without any long-range order. Early pioneering works in 1970s and 1980s, which became the foundation of vibrational analysis protocols currently used in glass research, were mostly based on small molecular analogues of short-range structural units of glass and isocompositional crystalline counterparts.39-42 Those models certainly provided much needed insights, because their spectral band positions were close to the ones observed for amorphous glass networks. However, neither small molecule analogues nor crystalline counterparts can fully represent the vibrational modes (band position, shape, and intensity) of glass networks. In those early studies, assumptions or simplifications were made to reduce the complexity originating from the randomness of the glass network and thus enable theoretical calculations or provide conceptual explanations for ‘model’ glass structures.39, 43 Note that conclusions from those studies are meaningful only within the validity of assumptions used, and many of those assumptions ignored the fact that silicate glass networks consist of covalently bonded structural units that are subject to additional constraints that do not exists in isolated molecules and crystalline counterparts. Physical structures of isolated molecules having only weak van der Waals interactions with surroundings or crystalline materials with recurring orders over a long length scale are state This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved. functions; in other words, they are in equilibrium states and thus their properties are mostly determined by their compositions at a given temperature and pressure.44 In contrast, glass is a non-equilibrium solid or a ‘frozen liquid’ with an extremely slow relaxation behavior;45 thus, its structure and properties are a function of not only the present temperature and pressure at which the glass object is exposed, but also the past history that it has gone through (such as cooling rate, annealing, mechanical stress, post-synthesis treatment, etc.).46-51 This is an inevitable complexity of non-equilibrium thermodynamics.46-48 For example, the peak position of the Si-O-Si stretch mode detected in IR was reported to shift when the cooling rate or fictive temperature of a silica glass changed.52, 53 In and around the Vickers indents created on silica and silicate glass surfaces, Raman analyses showed substantial changes in vibrational spectral features.54, 55 Vibrational spectroscopies were also applied in understanding structural modifications induced by compression and laser irradiation.56, 57 A nanoscale IR imaging study showed that even a fully-elastic physical contact, leaving no topographic damage on a silica glass surface, can lead to a red-shift in the local Si-O-Si stretch band of silica.58 All these spectral changes occur without any alteration of glass composition. When a silicate glass surface contacts with water, modifier ions (especially monovalent alkali ions) are leached out and even some network former species can be dissolved.59, 60 This obviously alters the composition of the surface layer of the glass, which is accompanied by changes in spectral features in IR and Raman analyses.61-64 Such history-dependent properties of glasses and their corresponding vibrational spectral features cannot be explained using the properties of equilibrium parallels. The equilibrium materials do not have any memory of non-equilibrium state before reaching equilibrium. Thus, the structural deviation from the equilibrium geometry cannot be accurately predicted by a simple extrapolation of the equilibrium structure. Although this poses a great deal of challenges in spectroscopic analysis of glass networks, it also presents an opportunity to make significant impacts on glass science if such interpretation can be done properly and explain physical or chemical properties of glass materials. Vibrational spectroscopy can be coupled with high resolution imaging techniques, enabling spatially-resolved structural analysis of surface defects that are too small to be probed with NMR or scattering methods.5, 10 This feature article provides a critical review of historic origins of various spectral interpretation models widely used or cited in current vibrational spectroscopy literatures of silica and silicate glasses, discusses their findings and limitations, and summarizes the recent This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved. advances in spectral interpretation as well as the potential implications of these new findings in glass science. II. IR and Raman measurements of glass network vibration The transmission IR measurement produces the absorbance spectrum which can be described with the Beer-Lambert law: 𝐴= −𝑙𝑜𝑔(𝐼𝑡/𝐼𝑜) = 𝑎𝑏𝑐, where 𝐼𝑡 and 𝐼𝑜 are the intensities of the transmitted and incident IR beams, respectively, 𝑎 is the absorptivity or attenuation coefficient, 𝑏 is the optical path length across the sample, and 𝑐 is the concentration of analyte in the sample.65 Here the absorptivity is related to the imaginary part of complex refractive index (𝑛+ 𝑖𝑘) of the sample: 𝑎= 4𝜋𝑘/𝜆 where 𝜆 is the wavelength of IR in resonance with a specific vibrational excitation in the system.65 Although this simple approach works well for organic materials, it does not work well for vibrations of silica and silicate glass networks. While 𝑘 values of most organic functional groups are on the order of 10-3 – 10-2,66, 67 those of the Si-O-Si stretch modes in the 900 – 1200 cm-1 region are close to 1 or even higher.68 Thus, the characteristic attenuation or penetration length (𝑑𝑝) over which the IR intensity decreases to 𝑒−1 (36.8%) of the incident intensity is only on order of 1 m for the Si-O-Si stretch band of most silica and silicate glasses.68-71 This means that, if the sample is thicker than a few microns, transmission across the glass sample is fully attenuated and the signal intensity in the Si-O-Si stretch region drops below the detection limit.68 Even if one uses crushed powders mixed in a KBr (IR-transparent) matrix, transmission IR spectrum may not reflect the bulk spectrum properly. If the powder size is larger than a few microns, transmission IR would selectively probe the ‘skin’ regions of the glass particles. Also, mechanical grinding creates defects in the skin region of the powders, which may have different vibrational features due to altered network structures.72, 73 For this reason, IR measurements of glass samples are typically carried out in reflection modes, such as attenuated total reflection (ATR) or specular reflection (SR) methods, which requires optically flat surfaces.68, 74, 75 The ATR-IR measurement is widely used as a ‘surface-sensitive’ analysis method.76 It uses an internal reflection element (IRE) with a high refractive index (n) that can create total internal reflection and only the evanescent wave penetrates into the sample which is in intimate contact with the IRE surface. Again, due to the high absorptivity of the Si-O-Si stretch mode of silicate glass, this simple principle gets complicated when it comes to the ATR-IR analysis of this mode. Figure 1b plots the ATR-IR spectra theoretically calculated for the soda lime silicate (SLS) glass with the refractive index shown in Figure 1a and a diamond IRE (n = 2.4) at various incidence angles (𝜃𝑖) of the IR beam with respect to the surface normal direction. Note that the maximum position of the Si-O-Si stretch band appears at ~910 cm-1, although its position is at 1030 cm-1 in the 𝑘-spectrum. Because of the strong absorptivity of the Si-O-Si stretch band of SLS, the total internal reflection is fully disrupted at that maximum intensity position of the 𝑘-spectrum. The absence of this band in the ATR-IR spectrum is simply an optical artifact which should not be interpreted as the dissociation of the Si-O-Si network bonds in the surface region.77 In summary, ATR-IR is not suitable for probing the Si-O-Si network vibrations of silica and silicate glass, although it is well suited for detection of subsurface hydrous species in glass by measuring 𝑙𝑜𝑔(1/𝑅) in the ~1640 cm-1 region for the H2O bending mode and the 3000 – 3700 cm-1 region for the OH stretch mode.68, 75, 78 For these reasons, the most widely used method is the SR-IR measurement. The reflectance 𝑅 is enhanced at the resonance absorption band of the sample,68 producing the spectrum that looks similar to the 𝑘-spectrum. At a near-normal incidence (for example, 𝜃𝑖= 20𝑜 in Figure 1c), the 𝑅-spectrum is quite close to the 𝑘-spectrum, but the maximum peak position is gradually blue-shifted to ~1070 cm-1 as the incidence angle (𝜃𝑖) increases. This is because the real part (𝑛) of refractive index of the sample is smaller in the wavenumber region above the absorption band (Figure 1a).79 This convolution effect varies depending on the absorptivity (i.e. intensity) and width of the absorption band. In Figure 1c, a small shoulder at 1180 cm-1 is present in the R-spectrum, which is absent or negligible in the 𝑘-spectrum (Figure 1a); it grows larger as the 𝜃𝑖 increases. This peak, often called a longitudinal optical (LO) mode in many references,80-83 also originates from the involvement of the real part (𝑛) of refractive index in the 𝑅 measurement (see Section III.2). For accurate spectral interpretation, it would be necessary to convert the measured SR-IR spectrum to the true resonance absorption spectrum. The 𝑘-spectrum can be calculated from the 𝑅-spectrum using the Kramers-Kronig (KK) transformation algorithm.84 The KK algorithm can be performed to obtain the k-spectra. However, it should be noted that not all data acquisition software of commercial instruments can do KK conversion properly. It requires IR spectra measured This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved. at near-normal incident angle and with integration performed from -∞ to +∞ in vibrational frequency, which cannot be fulfilled in most cases. Typical reflectance IR spectra are collected at an oblique incidence angle and the low end of spectral window is truncated at 400 cm-1. As a result, the errors of integration can propagate in the KK transform, leading to calculation artifacts, such as negative backgrounds.84 Depending how these are modeled or compensated, the KK algorithm can generate some variances in the produced k-spectra.85-87 Ohta suggested that different results can be produced based on different numerical integration methods in the KK calculation.85 Bonnal showed disagreements among deconvoluted n and k values obtained with the KK algorithm in the literature.86 Note that the KK transformation of the data acquisition software of most commercial IR instruments assumes 𝜃𝑖= 0𝑜 and does not work properly when 𝜃𝑖  10𝑜.84 This limitation can be overcome by measuring 𝑅-spectra at 𝜃𝑖 = 10𝑜 and 45𝑜 and numerically solving the Fresnel coefficient equations.84 The 𝑘-spectra calculated from the measured 𝑅-spectra of selected silica, silicate, borosilicate, boroaluminosilicate glasses are shown in Figure 2. Due to the convolution of 𝑛 in the SR-IR measurement, the maximum peak position in the 𝑅-spectrum is always blue-shifted from that in the 𝑘-spectrum and the degree of such a shift varies depending of the sharpness of the absorption band as well as the incidence angle of IR.84 Alternatively, one can use infrared variable-angle spectroscopic ellipsometry (IR-VASE), which is beyond the scope of this review. Readers can find relevant information from Ref. 88, 89. Unlike SR-IR, the Raman analysis is insensitive to the refractive index dispersion, especially the real part (𝑛) of the complex refractive index of the sample. This is because the excitation is made at a fixed wavelength and Raman scattering is a dissipative process producing absorption bands at different wavelengths.90-92 The Raman intensity is proportional to the polarizability change of the vibrational mode,90-92 which is different from the intensity of the 𝑘-spectrum (= IR absorption) and the reflectance of the SR-IR spectrum. Review of current peak assignments III.1 Vibrational modes in IR and Raman spectra of silica and silicate glass Figure 3 displays the SR-IR and Raman spectra of silica and a series of sodium silicate glasses. Although detailed spectral positions and relative intensities vary, the general shapes of vibrational spectra of other alkali silicate, alkaline-earth silicate, and alkali alkaline-earth silicate glasses (including SLS)68, 98-100 are similar to the ones shown in Figure 3. The dominant band in the high wavenumber region is a broad peak centered around 1070 – 1120 cm-1. In the low wavenumber region, another broad band at 400 – 600 cm-1 is prominent. A small band is also observed at ~800 cm-1. The vibrational peak assignments that are frequently found in the silica and silicate glass literature are summarized in Table 1. Bell and Gaskell showed that the ~1080 cm-1 band arises from the stretching motion of Si-O-Si bond (also called, bridging oxygen (BO)) in the silicate network through theoretical calculations.104, 105 Those early calculations were based on a small structural model in which positions of all atoms were fixed at specific coordinates.106 Discrete force constant values were given to the BO stretching, Si-O-Si bending and O-Si-O bending modes, and normal modes of vibrations were calculated by solving equations of motion (see Section IV).117 The weak band at ~800 cm-1 is also ascribed to the BO stretching vibration. Later, Galeener suggested that the dominant peak at ~1080 cm-1 is the asymmetric BO stretch, and the weak band at 800 cm-1 arises from the symmetric BO stretch.36 The ~480 cm-1 band is attributed to the BO bending.43 These assignment schemes have been adapted in IR spectroscopy studies ever since.32, 108, 118 The small shoulder at ~950 cm-1 in IR spectra of silicate glasses was suggested to be associated with the stretching vibration of Si-OH or Si-O- species.34, 108-110 Since these species break the network connectivity, they are called non-bridging oxygen (NBO). Sanders attributed the band at 950 cm-1 to the vibration of Si-O of NBOs associated with modifier ions based on the correlation of its reflectance intensity with the modifier concentration.30 Other studies also suggested the same origin based on lattice dynamic calculations104 and the IR spectra of neutron damaged vitreous silica glass.119 However, our recent MD study showed that, for a series of sodium silicate glass, the simulated vibrational spectra of the entire glass network are quite similar to those of the BO-only components, suggesting the contributions from NBO-only are quite minute.97 Then, the ~950 cm-1 shoulder could still be the vibrations of the BO network with a red-shift from the ~1080 cm-1 position This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved. due to the disruption of the network connectivity by NBOs, rather than specific to the vibrations of NBO only. This view will be re-visited in Section VI. Like the IR spectra, the Raman spectra of silicate glasses show a dominant band at ~1090 cm-1 in the high frequency region, which is often assigned to the symmetric BO stretch. In the case of vitreous silica, this stretch band is quite small and split into two peaks at ~1060 cm-1 and ~1200 cm-1 (see the fused quartz spectrum in Figure 3b).38, 40 These assignments were based on theoretical calculations for model structures constructed with small molecule clusters,36, 43 disordered networks,104, 106 and quasi-crystalline units.29 The low intensity band at 800 cm-1 is often attributed to the silicon motion symmetric to the bridging oxygen.111 McMillan specifically claimed that it is associated with silicon motion against tetrahedral oxygen cage.112 This is equivalent to the O-Si-O bending.104, 113 In the low frequency region, the broad band at 400-600 cm-1 region was assigned to the bending deformation of the Si-O-Si linkage.110 One study argued that the two peaks at ~500 cm-1 and ~600 cm-1 could be attributed to structural defects in the glass network, such as broken Si-O bonds.120, 121 Other studies related the same bands at ~500 cm-1 and ~600 cm-1 to four- and three-membered rings, respectively.37 However, such assignments may not be fully compatible with modern computational simulation results (see Sections V and VI). III.2 TO-LO modes The shoulder band at 1180~1200 cm-1 in SR-IR spectra of silica and silicate glasses is often called the LO mode.122-125 This band becomes more prominent as the incidence angle (𝜃𝑖) increases (Figure 1c). At a given 𝜃𝑖, it becomes less prominent as the modifier concentration increases (Figure 3a). This section explains that the shoulder band observed at ~1200 cm-1 in the SR-IR spectra is not an intrinsic vibrational mode of glass that can be attributed to the transition from the ground state of a normal mode of a specific structural unit to its vibrationally excited state. It is just an optical effect of the reflection process intrinsically associated with the complex refractive index (𝑛+ 𝑖𝑘) of glass, which is related to the complex dielectric permittivity (𝜀1 + 𝑖𝜀2).126 In an ionic crystal lattice, the oscillatory displacement of atoms at optical frequencies can be described in two modes: transverse optical (TO) mode where the displacement of atoms is perpendicular to the wave vector (i.e., perpendicular to the propagation direction of light) and longitudinal optical (LO) mode in which atomic displacements occur along the wave vector.127, 128 These two modes will have different force constants and thus have different resonance frequencies. Such a TO-LO splitting is defined for phonon modes of crystals with long-range periodic orders,129 but This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved. glass does not have any long-range order. Thus, the same TO-LO splitting concept of ionic crystals cannot be applied to the vibrational mode of noncrystalline glass network. For a dielectric material, the real part (𝜀1) of dielectric permittivity is negative over a certain frequency range above the strong absorption band.65 In this range, the reflectance R is significantly enhanced; this phenomenon is called the Reststrahlen effect.130 The low-frequency boundary of this range is called the transverse excitation frequency (𝜔𝑇𝑂), which is very close to the resonance absorption frequency (𝜔𝑟) of the 𝜀2-spectrum (which is similar to the 𝑘-spectrum) if the damping frequency is negligible compared to 𝜔𝑟. The high-frequency boundary of this range is designated as the frequency of the LO wave (𝜔𝐿𝑂). At this frequency, 𝜀(𝜔) = 0; this means the electric field is longitudinal.65 The Lyddane-Sachs-Teller relation depicts that 𝜔𝐿𝑂 2 /𝜔𝑇𝑂 2 = 𝜀𝑠𝑡/𝜀∞ where 𝜀𝑠𝑡 and 𝜀∞ are the static and high-frequency dielectric constant, respectively.65 Unlike the transverse excitation, the longitudinal excitation is nonradiative for any optical geometry. It means that the sample does not interact with the transverse electric field of IR propagating through the sample. So, a vibrational mode absorbing IR at 𝜔𝐿𝑂 is not expected. Based on the observation of additional blue-shifted band in the p-polarized transmission IR spectra that is absent in the s-polarized spectra (Figure 4a), Lehmann et al. reported the TO-LO splitting for amorphous silica.123, 131, 132 This work became the key experimental evidence justifying the interpretation or presence of the LO mode in glass.133-135 However, it should be noted that this observation was made for silica thin films deposited on a silicon substrate. It is well known that for thin films whose thickness is much smaller than the wavelength () of light, an additional absorption peak is observed at the frequency close to 𝜔𝐿𝑂 in the p-polarized transmission or reflection spectrum.136 The p-polarized radiation at an oblique incidence angle has the electric field components both tangential and normal to the film, while the s-polarized radiation has the surface parallel field only. Thus, in the p-polarized spectrum, an additional band observed near 𝜔𝐿𝑂 originates from the enhancement of macroscopic polarization across the film due to the strong absorption band, and this cannot be seen in the s-polarized spectrum. This phenomenon, known as the Berreman effect,136 is demonstrated in Figure 4b which plots the theoretical s- and p-polarized transmission IR spectra of a silica film on a silicon substrate calculated with the Fresnel coefficient equations using the complex refractive index of amorphous silica. So, the additional band near 𝜔𝐿𝑂 detected only in the p-polarization spectrum is not a new ‘absorption’ band (𝜔𝑟) resonating with a vibrational excitation of a specific structural unit that is absent in the 𝑘-spectrum (Figure 1a). In the This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved. cases shown in Figure 4, it is just an optical effect naturally occurring upon transmission of the p-polarized light through a thin film of a strongly absorbing material at an oblique angle. The mechanism producing the additional peak near 𝜔𝐿𝑂 for the thin film geometry cannot explain the appearance of the additional peak at the higher wavenumber side (~1200 cm-1) of the main ~1070 cm-1 peak observed in the SR-IR spectra of bulk glass (Figures 1c and 3a). If the origin is the same, then only the p-polarized SR-IR spectrum of the bulk sample should show the enhancement of the ~1200 cm-1 shoulder or band, and the s-polarized SR-IR spectrum should not. However, experimental results and theoretical calculations (Figure 5) confirm that the enhancement of the second peak at the higher wavenumber side of the main peak occurs in both s- and p-polarization spectra, indicating that it cannot be explained by the Berreman effect. Then, the most appropriate explanation for this phenomenon is that the real part (𝑛) of refractive index has the minimum value, even smaller than that of air (𝑛𝑎𝑖𝑟= 1), in the higher wavenumber side of the strong absorption band (Figure 1a), so the reflectance is greatly enhanced as 𝜃𝑖 increases (same as the Reststrahlen effect). Note that immediately above this enhancement peak (i.e., around 1280 cm-1 in Figure 5), the reflectance is nearly zero. This happens because the real part (𝑛) of the sample refractive index is close to 𝑛𝑎𝑖𝑟 and the imaginary part (𝑘) is nearly zero (Figure 1a), which means that the surface is optically indistinguishable from the surrounding air and thus it cannot reflect the incident beam at that wavenumber. Many papers attributed the observation of the shoulder peak in SR-IR spectra of bulk glasses to the TO-LO splitting.123, 124, 137, 138 This was mostly based on the fact that this shoulder peak appears near the maximum position of the LO energy loss function, 𝐼𝑚(−1/𝜀).138-140 But, note that this location simply coincides with the high-frequency boundary of the Reststrahlen effect where 𝜀(𝜔) ≈0. This additional band becomes prominent in the high wavenumber side of the strongly absorption peak; this phenomenon is miniscule and not easy to see for the weakly absorbing band (for example, the band at ~800 cm-1 in Figure 4b). So, its appearance is a function of the absorptivity of the main band. In Raman analysis of crystalline materials, the TO and LO phonon modes near the Brillouin zone produce a doublet band.141, 142 Crystalline quartz shows this splitting of Raman bands.80, 82 Based on these observations, two small peaks at ~1060 cm-1 and ~1200 cm-1 of vitreous silica (Figure 3b; also see Figure 6a) were also ascribed to the TO-LO splitting.36, 81 If that interpretation was correct, it would be difficult to explain why similar splitting or doublet is not prominent for the ~1090 cm-1 This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved. band in the Raman spectra of silicate glasses which show a stronger intensity than the amorphous silica (Figure 3b). This experimental trend is opposite to the theoretical prediction that the frequency separation between 𝜔𝑇𝑂 and 𝜔𝐿𝑂 (TO-LO splitting) should be larger for the band with a higher oscillator strength.65 For that reason, it would be difficult to ascribe the doublet at ~1060 cm-1 and ~1200 cm-1 of vitreous silica to the TO-LO splitting. There were some studies presenting vibrational density of state (VDOS) spectra calculated from equations of motion as a supporting evidence for the TO-LO splitting assignments in vibrational spectra of amorphous glasses.131, 143 The presence of specific peaks and their intensities in the IR and Raman spectra are determined by specific interactions with the electric field of the light, while VDOS is determined by the velocity correlations of atoms without considering interactions with the electromagnetic wave. Thus, vibrational spectra obtained through optical measurements are quite different from the VDOS distribution.144-146 Putting all information together, it is highly questionable whether the ~1200 cm-1 shoulder peaks observed in SR-IR and Raman spectra of silica and silicate glasses rigorously meet the full definition of the TO-LO splitting found in the crystalline materials. Without meeting all aspects of the theoretical mechanism, it is inappropriate to attribute the experimentally observed phenomenon in SR-IR spectra of the bulk glass to the TO-LO splitting process. The LO mode is not an observable band in IR. Remember that SR-IR measures the reflectance, 𝑅= 𝐼𝑟(𝑛,𝑘,𝜃𝑖) 𝐼𝑜 , which is different from the absorbance, 𝐴= −𝑙𝑜𝑔( 𝐼𝑡 𝐼𝑜) = 𝑎𝑏𝑐, that is a function of 𝑘 only (see Section II).68 The appearance of a secondary peak at the higher wavenumber side of a strongly absorbing peak is an optical effect in the 𝑅 measurement of the glass surface at an off-normal incidence angle (see Figures 4 and 5). In the absence of the long-range order, it is dubious whether the extremely-weak doublet-like peaks in Raman spectra of the bulk glass can be explained in the manner similar to the TO-LO splitting of the ionic or highly-polar crystalline materials. III.3 Comparison of vibrational bands of glass with those of crystalline materials A frequently adapted approach in vibrational spectroscopy of glass is to compare the vibrational spectral features of glass samples with those of crystalline materials with the same or similar chemical compositions. Since the repeating structural units of crystals can be determined from x-ray diffraction, it is tempting to utilize the same units to describe the vibrational spectral features of glass materials with similar compositions. However, the compositional similarity is not This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved. sufficient to guarantee the spectral similarity because the phonon modes of crystalline networks can be forbidden or allowed depending on the long-range translational symmetry, while the vibrations of the amorphous network are not bound to such symmetry rules.90, 147 In addition, the glass network has broad distributions of bond angles and lengths, while the crystal network has atoms at specific coordinates in the unit cell. Thus, Raman spectra of crystalline materials often have narrow and intense bands, while those of glass materials give very broad bands with different relative intensities and maximum-intensity positions. The comparison of the spectra of crystalline quartz versus those of fused quartz and vitreous silica shown in Figures 3 and 6a manifests such differences. In the high frequency region of the Raman spectrum of amorphous silica (Figure 6a), two weak bands are observed at 1060 cm-1 and 1200 cm-1, which have been called the TO-LO modes of fully-connected Q4 species108, 123, 137 (although its origin is debatable as discussed in Section III.2). These two peaks appear to merge to one at ~1090 cm-1 as soon as the sodium modifier is added to the silica glass (see Figure 3b). This merged peak grows continuously until the sodium modifier concentration increases to Na2O2SiO2; in the same concentration range, a small peak grows at ~950 cm-1 (Figures 6b). As the modifier concentration increases from Na2O2SiO2 to Na2O1.22SiO2, the ~1090 cm-1 peak decreases and the ~950 cm-1 peak grows.32, 148 Based on the stoichiometric model of the glass structure, the Q3 and Q2 species must be dominant species in the glass network with Na2O2SiO2 and Na2OSiO2 compositions, respectively. Then, it could be considered reasonable to assign the 1090 cm-1 and 950 cm-1 modes to the Q3 and Q2 species in the silicate glass network.32, 38 Expanding this approach further, the weak band at ~900 cm-1 and ~850 cm-1 could be attributed to Q1 and Q0, respectively (Figure 6c).32 Recently, the Henderson and Neuville group performed an investigation of the Qn species from Raman spectra for alkali silicate glasses. Peak fittings were performed with innovated Lorentzian dominated lineshapes and linewidths.149-151 Although classical model calculations with small structural moieties39, 43 were used to support this assignment (Section IV), comparison with the IR mode assignment raises some questions that need to be addressed further. For example, the Raman studies attribute the ~1090 cm-1 and ~950 cm-1 bands to the Q3 and Q2 species, separately; for the bands at similar positions, the most papers attribute the ~1080 cm-1 band to the asymmetric stretch of Si-O-Si (BO) bonds and the ~950 cm-1 shoulder to the stretch mode of Si-O- (NBO) bonds without distinguishing Q3 and Q2 species (Table 1). Why are the Raman and IR peaks in the same (almost identical) wavenumber region attributed to different modes? If they are the same mode, why does the Raman band in the This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved. 1050-1100 cm-1 region grow as the Q3 fraction increases, while the same band in IR decreases?97 This question will be re-visited in Section VI. The low frequency bands in the 430~600 cm-1 region have been typically attributed to bending vibrations of (SiO)m rings with different sizes (m) that can be identified in three-dimensionally connected amorphous networks. Sharma attributed two bands centered at 437 cm-1 and 490 cm-1 to six- and four-membered rings, respectively, in vitreous silica glass.41 This assignment was proposed based on the fact that their peak positions are similar to the ones observed in Raman spectra of α-quartz and coesite (Figure 6a). However, it is not obvious if the sharp phonon band defined by the long-range order could be compared with the broad band of the amorphous network without any long-range order. The (SiO)m rings identifiable in -quartz are mostly 8-membered rings and 6-membered rings are a minor fraction.152 The 4-membered rings in coesite are the smallest ring with a minor abundance; larger size rings are more abundant in the coesite crystal structure.153 Also, the peak position of Raman bands of crystalline and fused quartz are different, even though their chemical compositions are identical (Figure 3b). The broadness of Raman spectral features of glass reflects the variance of structural parameters in the glass network, which lacks in the crystalline lattice. Galeener performed a central-force field model calculation assuming the existence of planar rings consisting of corner-shared tetrahedra clusters in vitreous silica, and obtained the calculation result supporting the assignment of the small but sharp peak at 606 cm-1 to the three-membered rings (m = 3).37 He further suggested the assignment relating the 495 cm-1 and 606 cm-1 bands in Raman spectra to four- and three-membered rings, respectively, via a decoupling derivation method.154, 155 It was argued that the sharpness must appear in the Raman spectra when Si-O is strongly bonded within a well-defined ring where Si atoms are completely stationary (no motion) and coupling among vibrational modes is weak. However, Thorpe and colleagues criticized this argument, pointing out that the model was based on uniform identical rings, which were further embedded in a Bethe lattice for calculation.156 If the rings are not identical, e.g. part of rings are distorted, the simulated spectra will be very broad, which cannot explain the relative sharpness of certain bands attributed to specific rings.
