Classical models of solving equations of motion for small clusters The interpretation of vibrational spectra of glass in 1970s and 1980s was made with assistance from theoretical calculations solving differential equations of motion to obtain vibrational frequencies of normal modes for small molecular clusters, e.g. a few connected tetrahedra units, that look identical to the basic structural units composing the glass network.36, 39, 40, 43, 111 Figure 7 displays examples of such structural models.38 Without considering damping of vibrational modes which affects the resonance peak width (Δ𝜔𝑟), the equations of motion of atoms under the harmonic oscillation approximation can be written as:39 𝑚(𝑙) 𝑑2 𝑑𝑡2 𝑋𝛼(𝑛 ⃗ , 𝑙, 𝑡) = ∑ 𝑉 𝛼𝛽 𝛽,𝑛′ ⃗⃗⃗⃗ ,𝑙′ (𝑛 ⃗ , 𝑙|𝑛′ ⃗⃗⃗ , 𝑙′)𝑋𝛽 (𝑛′ ⃗⃗⃗ , 𝑙′, 𝑡) (1) where 𝑙 is the label of atom, m is the mass of atom, 𝑛 ⃗ is the vector in two or three dimensions, X is the displacement, 𝑉 𝛼𝛽 represents the force constant matrix. In many cases, two types of force constants were assumed to be involved in displacements of atoms: central force for Si-O stretching and non-central force for O-Si-O and Si-O-Si deformation or bending.40, 43, 104 The non-central component accounts for the dependence of the Si-O-Si stretch motion on the O-Si-O and/or Si-O-Si bond angles.158-160 Then, the atomic coordinates and force fields are expressed in matrix G and F, respectively, and the eigenvalues of dynamic matrix can be calculated through the Wilson GF method.104, 105, 161 Finally, a certain peak width was assumed arbitrarily to compare with the broad vibrational spectrum of glass. Key limitations of these classical models are as follows. In isolated structural models consisting of small clusters, considering the connections with nearest neighbors would be sufficient since there are no chemical bonds outside those clusters. In glass, however, those clusters are intricately connected to the three-dimensional network without any long-range order. Hence, their vibrations will be influenced by the connectivity with the neighboring and next-neighboring clusters because those will alter the boundary conditions of the differential equations to be solved. In silicate glasses, BO atoms can also interact with nearby modifier ions,162, 163 which may affect their force constants. The force constants used in the equations were chosen to match the experimentally observed peak positions. In these classical models of small clusters, arbitrarily chosen peak widths were introduced to mimic the broad bands of glass in experiments. Would that be sufficient to justify assigning the experimentally observed broad bands of amorphous networks to the modes calculated from isolated clusters? There were calculations for larger-scale disordered networks;104, This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved. 106, 164 but, the methods used to create disordered atomic arrangements were unclear.104, 165 Overall, even though the classical model calculations provide analytical solutions with clear visualization of isolated structural moieties, the accuracy of calculation results is sacrificed by over-simplification of ignoring the broad bond length and angle distributions of structural units and their connectivity in the amorphous network. In order to show the Si-O-Si stretch band position with different ring sizes, the non-central force constant concept was employed.36, 38, 43 In this model, the Si-O stretch force constant was assumed to be a simple function of Si-O-Si bond angle (Figure 8a). It is conceivable that the local Si-O-Si bond angle would be coupled with the local Si-O bond length because both are directly related to the hybridization of atoms in the first-shell SiO4 unit. However, a priori justification for choosing a specific mathematical function was not fully discussed. Certain forms or parameters could have been adapted from crystalline materials and adjusted with scaling factors to enforce the calculation results to be consistent with experimental results.158, 166, 167 Nonetheless, coupling between the Si-O-Si bond angle and the Si-O stretch force constant may not be as simple as the trigonometric function assumed in these non-central force constant models (see Section VI).168-171 If the Si-O-Si bond angle influences the Si-O-Si stretch mode through the non-central force constant, why does it not affect the Si-O-Si bending mode at all? No thorough discussion on this question could be found in the literature. VDOS calculations were often employed to compare with vibrational spectra of glass network.36, 43, 111, 173, 174 An example is shown in Figure 8b. It must be recalled that VDOS is calculated through velocity autocorrelations of all atoms in the model,175, 176 and obtained without considering interactions with the electric field of light.31, 177 Thus, it could be considered as all ‘possible’ vibrational modes; but only few of them can be observed in the vibrational spectrum. The VDOS analysis cannot tell which ones are observable in IR and Raman analysis. Thus, direct one-to-one comparison is not possible. The VDOS is not directly accessible in experiment; the experimental technique that most closely reproduces the local VDOS spectrum is inelastic neutron scattering,178, 179 which is not the same as IR or Raman.179 V. The force constants relevant to specific vibrational modes are calculated from the second derivatives of total energy with respective to atomic coordinates.181-185 Then, the resonant vibrational frequencies are calculated from the force constants obtained from the first principles rather than peak fitting to experimental values.31, 186 Quantum mechanical calculations are computationally expensive and thus the number of atoms that can be modeled is quite limited. For that reason, DFT calculations of glass materials were carried out mostly for small clusters representing basic structural units of the glass network.92, 187-192 For example, orthosilicic acid molecule or disiloxane clusters (Figure 9) are modeled to portray silica glass or other silicate structures. In that sense, early DFT calculations were not much different from classical models other than the optimum structures and force constants were obtained from quantum mechanical calculations. Thus, they could not address the effects of the broad distributions of bond lengths and angles of basic structural units and their random connectivity without any long-range order. Similar to the classical models described in the previous section, the early DFT calculations could provide only line intensities of specific normal modes allowed for the modeled clusters (Figure 9) and could not provide any insights into the band shape or width observed in IR spectra.193, 194 Being a first principles approach, DFT calculations can still be used to understand how vibrational modes of small clusters vary among specific geometries. For example, DFT calculations were used to check if the peak positions of ~490 cm-1 and ~600 cm-1 match with the assignment of four-membered and three-membered rings, respectively.157, 187, 188 However, the minimum energy conformation could vary depending on symmetry constraints or energy normalization factor applied in DFT calculations,187, 194, 195 which will lead to divergence of predicted vibrational characteristics.196, 197 In fact, the calculated Raman spectra are quite different from one study to the other using H6Si2O7 dimer and cyclic H6Si3O9 trimer.197 The calculation results are very sensitive to the bond parameters, such as bond angle of Si-O-Si, optimized differently in each study.187, 196, 198 More recently, Giacomazzi et al. reported comprehensive DFT calculation results for vitreous silica model containing 144 atoms, which corresponds to 48 units of SiO2 (Figure 10).179, 199 Their vibrational spectral analysis included not only VDOS calculations, but also the evaluation of the first and second derivatives of atomic forces with respect to the electric fields. The first derivative term is expressed with the Born effective charge tensor associated with the polarization in response to This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved. electric field; this can be related to the dielectric permittivity (𝜀1 + 𝑖𝜀2). The IR spectrum can be calculated from 𝑛 and 𝑘 which can be derived from 𝜀1 and 𝜀2. The second derivative term is expressed with a derivative of the dielectric polarizability tensor under the Placzek approximation, which determines the Raman susceptibility. In Figure 10, the agreement of the calculation results with the experimental spectra is quite remarkable. Since the 144-atom model has broad distributions of Si-O bond length as well as O-Si-O and Si-O-Si bond angles, the predicted spectrum shows the natural broadening of the bands. By comparing this 144-atom model with two other models containing only 72 atoms and having different Si-O-Si bond-angle distributions and ring statistics, Giacomazzi et al. found interesting correlations between the spectral features and the bond parameter distributions.179 In the VDOS spectrum, the 800 cm-1 peak appears to be sensitive to the average Si-O-Si bond angle distribution, suggesting that it involves the bending vibrations of Si-O-Si bonds. In the IR spectrum, the ~450 cm-1 and ~1080 cm-1 bands reflect differences in the Si-O-Si bond angle and Si-O bond length distributions, respectively. In the Raman spectrum, the band in the 300 – 700 cm-1 region shifts toward higher wavenumbers as the average Si-O-Si bond angle in the model decreases. The small band at ~600 cm-1 is claimed to reflect the population of three-membered ring, even though the relative population of this ring is only minor compared to those of larger rings. The results of this first principles approach did not show the trend assumed in the non-central force constant model (Figure 8a). Caution must be taken when these trends are compared with the experimental data since the 144-atom model used in DFT calculations cannot represent all aspects of the amorphous silica network whose structure will vary depending on the sample history.118, 200 In some literature, the symmetric and asymmetric Si-O-Si stretch modes are attributed to the A1 and T2 symmetry modes, respectively, of the SiO4 moiety in the glass because this smallest topological unit has the tetrahedral (Td) point group.30, 201, 202 The symmetry rule of vibrational spectroscopy dictates that the A1 mode is Raman-active only, and the T2 mode is both Raman-active and IR-active.203 If the broad band in the 1000-1200 cm-1 region the VDOS spectrum obtained from DFT calculations (Figure 10a) is the A1 symmetry mode, it should be strong in Raman, but weak or negligible in IR. If it has the T2 symmetry, it should be strong in both IR and Raman spectra. But, the experimental spectra of amorphous silica are not consistent with these symmetry rules – the Si-O-Si stretch band is very weak or negligible in the Raman spectrum (Figure 3b and Figure 10d) and appears as a strong peak only in IR (Figure 3a and Figure 10b & c; note that the IR intensity is proportional to 4𝜋𝑘/𝜆 where 𝑘 can be calculated from 𝜀1 and 𝜀2). This discrepancy clearly shows This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved. that the vibrational modes of amorphous glass network cannot be adequately described with the analogy to those of small molecular clusters.95 Although the ~1080 cm-1 IR band is often called the asymmetric Si-O-Si stretch and the Raman band in the same region is attributed to the symmetric BO stretch (Table 1), those bands are not the same as (or as simple as) the stretch mode of the isolated SiO4 (Q4) moiety.84 VI. This is a feature article (DOI: 10.1111/jace.18206) by Hongshen Liu, Huseyin Kaya, Yen-Ting Lin, Andrew Ogrinc, and Seong H. Kim from Pennsylvania State University (Department of Chemical Engineering and Materials Research Institute, and Department of Materials Science and Engineering). The article critically reviews the interpretation of IR and Raman vibrational spectra of silica and silicate glass networks.

KEY POINTS:

1. **Core Argument**: Traditional interpretations of glass vibrational spectra based on analogies with isolated molecular moieties or crystalline counterparts are outdated because glass is a non-equilibrium ('frozen liquid') 3D network without long-range order. Glass properties depend not only on composition and temperature/pressure but also on thermal/mechanical history (cooling rate, fictive temperature, annealing, mechanical stress).

2. **Empirical Relationships Proposed**: (i) The intensity-weighted peak position of the Si-O-Si stretch mode negatively correlates with the weighted average of the Si-O bond length distribution; (ii) the broad band of the Si-O-Si bending mode negatively correlates with the Si-O-Si bond angle distribution.

3. **IR Measurement Issues**: Due to very high absorptivity (k values near 1 or higher) of Si-O-Si stretch modes in the 900–1200 cm⁻¹ region, the penetration depth is only ~1 μm, so transmission IR fails for bulk glass. ATR-IR is unsuitable for Si-O-Si network vibrations (the apparent absence of the ~1030 cm⁻¹ band in ATR is an optical artifact, not bond dissociation). Specular reflection (SR-IR) is preferred but requires Kramers-Kronig (KK) transformation to obtain true k-spectra; KK has limitations including oblique incidence angle assumptions and truncation at 400 cm⁻¹.

4. **TO-LO Mode Reinterpretation**: The ~1200 cm⁻¹ shoulder in SR-IR spectra, often attributed to TO-LO splitting, is actually an optical effect (Reststrahlen effect) arising from the real part of the refractive index being below that of air on the high-wavenumber side of the strong absorption band. The Berreman effect explains the p-polarization-only band in thin films but cannot explain the shoulder in bulk glass (present in both s- and p-polarization). The authors argue LO mode is not observable in IR and the TO-LO concept requires long-range order that glass lacks.

5. **Critique of Classical Models**: 1970s-1980s models using small molecular clusters with Wilson GF method and assumed non-central force constants (e.g., Si-O stretch force constant as a trigonometric function of Si-O-Si bond angle) are oversimplified—they ignore broad bond length/angle distributions and network connectivity.

6. **Critique of Ring Assignments**: Assignments of ~490 cm⁻¹ and ~600 cm⁻¹ Raman bands to four- and three-membered rings (Galeener, Sharma) are questioned. Thorpe criticized the uniform-ring assumption; DFT shows rings in silica are not planar; crystalline comparison is inappropriate since quartz phonon bands depend on long-range order.

7. **DFT Calculations**: Giacomazzi et al.'s 144-atom DFT model of vitreous silica shows remarkable agreement with experimental spectra, revealing that the ~450 cm⁻¹ and ~1080 cm⁻¹ IR bands reflect Si-O-Si bond angle and Si-O bond length distributions respectively. The A1/T2 symmetry-based assignments of SiO4 moieties fail to explain experimental observations (the Si-O-Si stretch band is weak in Raman but strong in IR, inconsistent with symmetry rules).

8. **Qn Species Assignment Question**: Raman assigns ~1090 cm⁻¹ and ~950 cm⁻¹ bands to Q3 and Q2 species, while IR assigns the same regions to BO asymmetric stretch and NBO stretch—raising unresolved questions about why Raman and IR peaks in identical wavenumber regions are attributed to different modes.

9. **MD Simulations**: Molecular dynamics with empirical force fields can handle larger models capturing more local variations, making it more suitable for modeling glass structure, but the article notes the section on MD simulations is cut off at the end of the provided content.

You are tasked with summarizing the raw content of a webpage retrieved from a web search. Your goal is to create a summary that preserves the most important information from the original web page. This summary will be used by a downstream research agent, so it's crucial to maintain the key details without losing essential information.

Here is the raw content of the webpage:

<webpage_content>
Vibrational Spectroscopy Analysis of Silica and Silicate Glass Networks 1 Hongshen Liu,1 Huseyin Kaya,2 Yen-Ting Lin,1 Andrew Ogrinc,1 and Seong H. Kim1,2* 2 1. Department of Chemical Engineering and Materials Research Institute, Pennsylvania 3 State University, University Park, PA 16802 4 2. Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Pennsylvania State University, University 5 Park, PA 16802 6 * Corresponding author: shk10@psu.edu 7 Abstract: Vibrational spectroscopy has been widely used to investigate various structural 8 aspects of the glass network and there are a plethora of papers reporting subtle but consistent 9 changes in IR and Raman spectral features of glass upon alterations of glass compositions, 10 thermal histories, mechanical stresses, or surface treatments. However, interpretations of such 11 spectral features are still obscured due to the lack of well-established physical principles 12 accurately describing vibrational modes of the non-crystalline glass network. Due to the non-13 equilibrium nature of the glass network three dimensionally connected without any long range 14 orders, vibrational spectral features of glass cannot be interpreted using the analogy with those of 15 isolated molecular moieties or crystalline counterparts. This feature article explains why such 16 comparisons are inadequate and describes the recent advances made from theoretical calculations 17 of vibrational spectral features of amorphous networks or comparisons of computational results 18 with experimental data. For the interpretation of vibrational spectral features of silica and silicate 19 glasses, the following empirical relationships are suggested: (i) the intensity-weighted peak 20 position of the Si-O-Si stretch mode negatively correlates with the weighted average of the Si-O 21 bond length distribution and (ii) the broad band of the Si-O-Si bending mode negatively 22 correlates with the Si-O-Si bond angle distribution. Selected examples of vibrational 23 spectroscopic imaging of surface defects are discussed to deliberate the implication of these 24 findings in the structure-property relationship of silica and silicate glass materials. Unanswered 25 questions and continuing research challenges are identified. 26 27 2 I. Introduction 28 Along with nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and x-ray and neutron scattering, 29 vibrational spectroscopy is one of the widely used methods for structural characterization of 30 glass materials. Being operated with different physical principles, each method provides 31 structural information that may be complementary to others. NMR is particularly useful for 32 determination of the short-range structure such as connectivity in the first coordination shell, Qn 33 speciation of silicon species (here n is the number of bridging oxygen bonds connected to other 34 silicon atoms), and coordination of boron and aluminum network formers.1-9 X-ray10-13 and 35 neutron scattering14-18 can give intermediate-range structural information beyond the first 36 coordination shell such as radial distributions of atoms in the second, third, and fourth shells. 37 These are static coordinates of atoms that can be readily simulated computationally; thus the 38 agreement of those structures with simulation results can confirm the accuracy of the analysis.19-39 25 In contrast, vibrational spectroscopy such as infrared (IR) and Raman techniques26-38 probes 40 dynamic responses of electrons of covalently-connected atoms to the externally applied 41 electromagnetic fields. Such responses are much more challenging to calculate or simulate 42 computationally when the subject of study is three-dimensionally connected amorphous 43 networks without any long-range order. 44 Early pioneering works in 1970s and 1980s, which became the foundation of vibrational 45 analysis protocols currently used in glass research, were mostly based on small molecular 46 analogues of short-range structural units of glass and isocompositional crystalline counterparts.39-47 42 Those models certainly provided much needed insights, because their spectral band positions 48 were close to the ones observed for amorphous glass networks. However, neither small molecule 49 analogues nor crystalline counterparts can fully represent the vibrational modes (band position, 50 shape, and intensity) of glass networks. In those early studies, assumptions or simplifications 51 were made to reduce the complexity originating from the randomness of the glass network and 52 thus enable theoretical calculations or provide conceptual explanations for ‘model’ glass 53 structures.39, 43 Note that conclusions from those studies are meaningful only within the validity 54 of assumptions used, and many of those assumptions ignored the fact that silicate glass networks 55 consist of covalently bonded structural units that are subject to additional constraints that do not 56 exists in isolated molecules and crystalline counterparts. 57 3 Physical structures of isolated molecules having only weak van der Waals interactions 58 with surroundings or crystalline materials with recurring orders over a long length scale are state 59 functions; in other words, they are in equilibrium states and thus their properties are mostly 60 determined by their compositions at a given temperature and pressure.44 In contrast, glass is a 61 non-equilibrium solid or a ‘frozen liquid’ with an extremely slow relaxation behavior;45 thus, its 62 structure and properties are a function of not only the present temperature and pressure at which 63 the glass object is exposed, but also the past history that it has gone through (such as cooling 64 rate, annealing, mechanical stress, post-synthesis treatment, etc.).46-51 This is an inevitable 65 complexity of non-equilibrium thermodynamics.46-48 66 For example, the peak position of the Si-O-Si stretch mode detected in IR was reported to 67 shift when the cooling rate or fictive temperature of a silica glass changed.52, 53 In and around the 68 Vickers indents created on silica and silicate glass surfaces, Raman analyses showed substantial 69 changes in vibrational spectral features.54, 55 A nanoscale IR imaging study showed that even a 70 fully-elastic physical contact, leaving no topographic damage on a silica glass surface, can lead 71 to a red-shift in the local Si-O-Si stretch band of silica.56 All these spectral changes occur without 72 any alteration of glass composition. When a silicate glass surface contacts with water, modifier 73 ions (especially monovalent alkali ions) are leached out and even some network former species 74 can be dissolved.57, 58 This obviously alters the composition of the surface layer of the glass, 75 which is accompanied by changes in spectral features in IR and Raman analyses.59-62 76 Such history-dependent properties of glasses and their corresponding vibrational spectral 77 features cannot be explained using the properties of equilibrium parallels. The equilibrium 78 materials do not have any memory of non-equilibrium state before reaching equilibrium. Thus, 79 the structural deviation from the equilibrium geometry cannot be accurately predicted by a 80 simple extrapolation of the equilibrium structure. Although this poses a great deal of challenges 81 in spectroscopic analysis of glass networks, it also presents an opportunity to make significant 82 impacts on glass science if such interpretation can be done properly and explain physical or 83 chemical properties of glass materials. Vibrational spectroscopy can be coupled with high 84 resolution imaging techniques, enabling spatially-resolved structural analysis of surface defects 85 that are too small to be probed with NMR or scattering methods.5, 10 This feature article provides 86 a critical review of historic origins of various spectral interpretation models widely used or cited 87 4 in current vibrational spectroscopy literatures of silica and silicate glasses, discusses their 88 findings and limitations, and summarizes the recent advances in spectral interpretation as well as 89 the potential implications of these new findings in glass science. 90 91 II. IR and Raman measurements of glass network vibration 92 The transmission IR measurement produces the absorbance spectrum which can be 93 described with the Beer-Lambert law: 𝐴= −𝑙𝑜𝑔(𝐼𝑡/𝐼𝑜) = 𝑎𝑏𝑐, where 𝐼𝑡 and 𝐼𝑜 are the 94 intensities of the transmitted and incident IR beams, respectively, 𝑎 is the absorptivity or 95 attenuation coefficient, 𝑏 is the optical path length across the sample, and 𝑐 is the concentration 96 of analyte in the sample.63 Here the absorptivity is related to the imaginary part of complex 97 refractive index (𝑛+ 𝑖𝑘) of the sample: 𝑎= 4𝜋𝑘/𝜆 where 𝜆 is the wavelength of IR in 98 resonance with a specific vibrational excitation in the system.63 Although this simple approach 99 works well for organic materials, it does not work well for vibrations of silica and silicate glass 100 networks. While 𝑘 values of most organic functional groups are on the order of 10-3 – 10-2,64, 65 101 those of the Si-O-Si stretch modes in the 900 – 1200 cm-1 region are close to 1 or even higher.66 102 Thus, the characteristic attenuation or penetration length (𝑑𝑝) over which the IR intensity 103 decreases to 𝑒−1 (36.8%) of the incident intensity is only on order of 1 m for the Si-O-Si stretch 104 band of most silica and silicate glasses.66-69 This means that, if the sample is thicker than a few 105 microns, transmission across the glass sample is fully attenuated and the signal intensity in the 106 Si-O-Si stretch region drops below the detection limit.66 Even if one uses crushed powders mixed 107 in a KBr (IR-transparent) matrix, transmission IR spectrum may not reflect the bulk spectrum 108 properly. If the powder size is larger than a few microns, transmission IR would selectively 109 probe the ‘skin’ regions of the glass particles. Also, mechanical grinding creates defects in the 110 skin region of the powders, which may have different vibrational features due to altered network 111 structures.70, 71 112 For this reason, IR measurements of glass samples are typically carried out in reflection 113 modes, such as attenuated total reflection (ATR) or specular reflection (SR) methods, which 114 requires optically flat surfaces.66, 72, 73 The ATR-IR measurement is widely used as a ‘surface-115 sensitive’ analysis method.74 It uses an internal reflection element (IRE) with a high refractive 116 5 index (n) that can create total internal reflection and only the evanescent wave penetrates into the 117 sample which is in intimate contact with the IRE surface. The absorption of the evanescent wave 118 by the sample in the 3𝑑𝑝 range from the surface attenuates total reflectance at the IRE/sample 119 interface and is measured in the form of 𝑙𝑜𝑔(1/𝑅), where 𝑅 = 𝐼𝑟/𝐼𝑜 is the reflectance and 𝐼𝑟 120 and 𝐼𝑜 are the intensities of the reflected and incident IR beams, respectively. Again, due to the 121 high absorptivity of the Si-O-Si stretch mode of silicate glass, this simple principle gets 122 complicated when it comes to the ATR-IR analysis of this mode. Figure 1b plots the ATR-IR 123 spectra theoretically calculated for the SLS glass with the refractive index shown in Figure 1a 124 and a diamond IRE (n = 2.4) at various incidence angles (𝜃𝑖) of the IR beam with respect to the 125 surface normal direction. Note that the maximum position of the Si-O-Si stretch band appears at 126 ~910 cm-1, although its position is at 1030 cm-1 in the 𝑘-spectrum. Because of the strong 127 absorptivity of the Si-O-Si stretch band of SLS, the total internal reflection is fully disrupted at 128 that maximum intensity position of the 𝑘-spectrum. The absence of this band in the ATR-IR 129 spectrum is simply an optical artifact which should not be interpreted as the dissociation of the 130 Si-O-Si network bonds in the surface region.75 In summary, ATR-IR is not suitable for probing 131 the Si-O-Si network vibrations of silica and silicate glass, although it is well suited for detection 132 of subsurface hydrous species in glass by measuring 𝑙𝑜𝑔(1/𝑅) in the ~1640 cm-1 region for the 133 H2O bending mode and the 3000 – 3700 cm-1 region for the OH stretch mode.66, 73, 76 134 For these reasons, the most widely used method is the SR-IR measurement. The 135 reflectance 𝑅 is enhanced at the resonance absorption band of the sample,66 producing the 136 spectrum that looks similar to the 𝑘-spectrum. At a near-normal incidence (for example, 𝜃𝑖= 137 20𝑜 in Figure 1c), the 𝑅-spectrum is quite close to the 𝑘-spectrum, but the maximum peak 138 position is gradually blue-shifted to ~1070 cm-1 as the incidence angle (𝜃𝑖) increases. This is 139 because the real part (𝑛) of refractive index of the sample is smaller in the wavenumber region 140 above the absorption band (Figure 1a).77 This convolution effect varies depending on the 141 absorptivity (i.e. intensity) and width of the absorption band. In Figure 1c, a small shoulder at 142 1180 cm-1 is present in the R-spectrum, which is absent or negligible in the 𝑘-spectrum (Figure 143 1a); it grows larger as the 𝜃𝑖 increases. This peak, often called a longitudinal optical (LO) mode 144 in many references,78-81 also originates from the involvement of the real part (𝑛) of refractive 145 index in the 𝑅 measurement (see Section III.2). 146 6 For accurate spectral interpretation, it would be necessary to convert the measured SR-IR 147 spectrum to the true resonance absorption spectrum. The 𝑘-spectrum can be calculated from the 148 𝑅-spectrum using the Kramers-Kronig (KK) transformation algorithm.82 Note that the KK 149 transformation of the data acquisition software of most commercial IR instruments assumes 𝜃𝑖= 150 0𝑜 and does not work properly when 𝜃𝑖  10𝑜.82 This limitation can be overcome by measuring 151 𝑅-spectra at 𝜃𝑖 = 10𝑜 and 45𝑜 and numerically solving the Fresnel coefficient equations.82 The 152 𝑘-spectra calculated from the measured 𝑅-spectra of selected silica, silicate, borosilicate, 153 boroaluminosilicate glasses are shown in Figure 2. Due to the convolution of 𝑛 in the SR-IR 154 measurement, the maximum peak position in the 𝑅-spectrum is always blue-shifted from that in 155 the 𝑘-spectrum and the degree of such a shift varies depending of the sharpness of the absorption 156 band as well as the incidence angle of IR.82 Alternatively, one can use infrared variable-angle 157 spectroscopic ellipsometry (IR-VASE), which is beyond the scope of this review. Readers can 158 find relevant information from Ref. 83, 84. 159 Unlike SR-IR, the Raman analysis is insensitive to the refractive index dispersion, 160 especially the real part (𝑛) of the complex refractive index of the sample. This is because the 161 excitation is made at a fixed wavelength and Raman scattering is a dissipative process producing 162 absorption bands at different wavelengths.85-87 The Raman intensity is proportional to the 163 polarizability change of the vibrational mode,85-87 which is different from the intensity of the 𝑘-164 spectrum (= IR absorption) and the reflectance of the SR-IR spectrum. In molecular 165 spectroscopy, the Raman bands are often known to be complementary to the IR bands because 166 they follow different selection rules governed by the symmetry of molecule.88, 89 Whether the 167 same symmetry rules could be applied to the vibrational modes of three-dimensionally connected 168 glassy network is questionable.90, 91 169 170 III. Review of current peak assignments 171 III.1 Vibrational modes in IR and Raman spectra of silica and silicate glass 172 Figure 3 displays the SR-IR and Raman spectra of silica and a series of sodium silicate 173 glasses. Although detailed spectral positions and relative intensities vary, the general shapes of 174 vibrational spectra of other alkali silicate, alkaline-earth silicate, and alkali alkaline-earth silicate 175 7 glasses (including SLS)66, 93-95 are similar to the ones shown in Figure 3. The dominant band in 176 the high wavenumber region is a broad peak centered around 1070 – 1120 cm-1. In the low 177 wavenumber region, another broad band at 400 – 600 cm-1 is prominent. A small band is also 178 observed at ~800 cm-1. The vibrational peak assignments that are frequently found in the silica 179 and silicate glass literature are summarized in Table 1. 180 Bell and Gaskell showed that the ~1080 cm-1 band arises from the stretching motion of 181 Si-O-Si bond (also called, bridging oxygen (BO)) in the silicate network through theoretical 182 calculations.99, 100 Those early calculations were based on a small structural model in which 183 positions of all atoms were fixed at specific coordinates.101 Discrete force constant values were 184 given to the BO stretching, Si-O-Si bending and O-Si-O bending modes, and normal modes of 185 vibrations were calculated by solving equations of motion (see Section IV).112 The weak band at 186 ~800 cm-1 is also ascribed to the BO stretching vibration. Later, Galeener suggested that the 187 dominant peak at ~1080 cm-1 is the asymmetric BO stretch, and the weak band at 800 cm-1 arises 188 from the symmetric BO stretch.36 The ~480 cm-1 band is attributed to the BO bending.43 These 189 assignment schemes have been adapted in IR spectroscopy studies ever since.32, 103, 113 190 The small shoulder at ~950 cm-1 in IR spectra of silicate glasses was suggested to be 191 associated with the stretching vibration of Si-OH or Si-O- species.34, 103-105 Since these species 192 break the network connectivity, they are called non-bridging oxygen (NBO). Sanders attributed 193 the band at 950 cm-1 to the vibration of Si-O of NBOs associated with modifier ions based on the 194 correlation of its reflectance intensity with the modifier concentration.30 Other studies also 195 suggested the same origin based on lattice dynamic calculations99 and the IR spectra of neutron 196 damaged vitreous silica glass.114 However, our recent MD study showed that, for a series of 197 sodium silicate glass, the simulated vibrational spectra of the entire glass network are quite 198 similar to those of the BO-only components, suggesting the contributions from NBO-only are 199 quite minute.92 Then, the ~950 cm-1 shoulder could still be the vibrations of the BO network with 200 a red-shift from the ~1080 cm-1 position due to the disruption of the network connectivity by 201 NBOs, rather than specific to the vibrations of NBO only. This view will be re-visited in Section 202 VI. 203 Like the IR spectra, the Raman spectra of silicate glasses show a dominant band at ~1090 204 cm-1 in the high frequency region, which is often assigned to the symmetric BO stretch. At a given 𝜃𝑖, it becomes less prominent as the modifier concentration 222 increases (Figure 3a). This section explains that the shoulder band at ~1200 cm-1 is not an 223 intrinsic vibrational mode of glass that can be attributed to a specific structural unit responsible 224 for electronic transition from the ground state to the vibrationally excited state upon IR 225 absorption. It is just an optical effect of the reflection process intrinsically associated with the 226 complex refractive index (𝑛+ 𝑖𝑘) of glass, which is related to the complex dielectric permittivity 227 (𝜀1 + 𝑖𝜀2).121 228 In an ionic crystal lattice, the oscillatory displacement of atoms at optical frequencies can 229 be described in two modes: transverse optical (TO) mode where the displacement of atoms is 230 perpendicular to the wave vector (i.e., perpendicular to the propagation direction of light) and 231 longitudinal optical (LO) mode in which atomic displacements occur along the wave vector.122, 232 123 These two modes will have different force constants and thus have different resonance 233 frequencies. Such a TO-LO splitting is defined for phonon modes of crystals with long-range 234 periodic orders,124 but glass does not have any long-range order. Thus, the same TO-LO splitting 235 9 concept of ionic crystals cannot be applied to the vibrational mode of noncrystalline glass 236 network. 237 For a dielectric material, the real part (𝜀1) of dielectric permittivity is negative over a 238 certain frequency range above the strong absorption band.63 In this range, the reflectance R is 239 significantly enhanced; this phenomenon is called the Reststrahlen effect.125 The low-frequency 240 boundary of this range is called the transverse excitation frequency (𝜔𝑇𝑂), which is very close to 241 the resonance absorption frequency (𝜔𝑟) of the 𝜀2-spectrum (which is similar to the 𝑘-spectrum) 242 if the damping frequency is negligible compared to 𝜔𝑟. The high-frequency boundary of this 243 range is designated as the frequency of the LO wave (𝜔𝐿𝑂). At this frequency, 𝜀(𝜔) = 0; this 244 means the electric field is longitudinal.63 The Lyddane-Sachs-Teller relation depicts that 245 𝜔𝐿𝑂 2 /𝜔𝑇𝑂 2 = 𝜀𝑠𝑡/𝜀∞ where 𝜀𝑠𝑡 and 𝜀∞ are the static and high-frequency dielectric constant, 246 respectively.63 Unlike the transverse excitation, the longitudinal excitation is nonradiative for any 247 optical geometry. It means that the sample does not interact with the transverse electric field of 248 IR propagating through the sample. So, a vibrational mode absorbing IR at 𝜔𝐿𝑂 is not expected. 249 Based on the observation of additional blue-shifted band in the p-polarized transmission 250 IR spectra that is absent in the s-polarized spectra (Figure 4a), Lehmann et al. reported the TO-251 LO splitting for amorphous silica.118, 126, 127 This work became the key experimental evidence 252 justifying the interpretation or presence of the LO mode in glass.128-130 However, it should be 253 noted that this observation was made for silica thin films deposited on a silicon substrate. It is 254 well known that for thin films whose thickness is much smaller than the wavelength () of light, 255 an additional absorption peak is observed at the frequency close to 𝜔𝐿𝑂 in the p-polarized 256 transmission or reflection spectrum.131 The p-polarized radiation at an oblique incidence angle 257 has the electric field components both tangential and normal to the film, while the s-polarized 258 radiation has the surface parallel field only. Thus, in the p-polarized spectrum, an additional band 259 observed near 𝜔𝐿𝑂 originates from the enhancement of macroscopic polarization across the film 260 due to the strong absorption band, and this cannot be seen in the s-polarized spectrum. This 261 phenomenon, known as the Berreman effect,131 is demonstrated in Figure 4b which plots the 262 theoretical s- and p-polarized transmission IR spectra of a silica film on a silicon substrate 263 calculated with the Fresnel coefficient equations using the complex refractive index of 264 amorphous silica. So, the additional band near 𝜔𝐿𝑂 detected only in the p-polarization spectrum 265 10 is not a new ‘absorption’ band (𝜔𝑟) resonating with a vibrational excitation of a specific 266 structural unit that is absent in the 𝑘-spectrum (Figure 1a). In the cases shown in Figure 4, it is 267 just an optical effect naturally occurring upon transmission of the p-polarized light through a thin 268 film of a strongly absorbing material at an oblique angle. 269 The mechanism producing the additional peak near 𝜔𝐿𝑂 for the thin film geometry cannot 270 explain the appearance of the additional peak at the higher wavenumber side (~1200 cm-1) of the 271 main ~1070 cm-1 peak observed in the SR-IR spectra of bulk glass (Figures 1c and 3a). If the 272 origin is the same, then only the p-polarized SR-IR spectrum of the bulk sample should show the 273 enhancement of the ~1200 cm-1 shoulder or band, and the s-polarized SR-IR spectrum should 274 not. However, experimental results and theoretical calculations (Figure 5) confirm that the 275 enhancement of the second peak at the higher wavenumber side of the main peak occurs in both 276 s- and p-polarization spectra, indicating that it cannot be explained by the Berreman effect. 277 Then, the most appropriate explanation for this phenomenon is that the real part (𝑛) of 278 refractive index has the minimum value, even smaller than that of air (𝑛𝑎𝑖𝑟= 1), in the higher 279 wavenumber side of the strong absorption band (Figure 1a), so the reflectance is greatly 280 enhanced as 𝜃𝑖 increases (same as the Reststrahlen effect). Note that immediately above this 281 enhancement peak (i.e., around 1280 cm-1 in Figure 5), the reflectance is nearly zero. This 282 happens because the real part (𝑛) of the sample refractive index is close to 𝑛𝑎𝑖𝑟 and the 283 imaginary part (𝑘) is nearly zero (Figure 1a), which means that the surface is optically 284 indistinguishable from the surrounding air and thus it cannot reflect the incident beam at that 285 wavenumber. 286 Many papers attributed the observation of the shoulder peak in SR-IR spectra of bulk 287 glasses to the TO-LO splitting.118, 119, 132, 133 This was mostly based on the fact that this shoulder 288 peak appears near the maximum position of the LO energy loss function, 𝐼𝑚(−1/𝜀).133-135 But, 289 note that this location simply coincides with the high-frequency boundary of the Reststrahlen 290 effect where 𝜀(𝜔) ≈0. This additional band becomes prominent in the high wavenumber side of 291 the strongly absorption peak; this phenomenon is miniscule and not easy to see for the weakly 292 absorbing band (for example, the band at ~800 cm-1 in Figure 4b). So, its appearance is a 293 function of the absorptivity of the main band. 294 11 In Raman analysis of crystalline materials, the TO and LO phonon modes near the 295 Brillouin zone produce a doublet band.136, 137 Crystalline quartz shows this splitting of Raman 296 bands.78, 80 Based on these observations, two small peaks at ~1060 cm-1 and ~1200 cm-1 of 297 vitreous silica (Figure 3b; also see Figure 6a) were also ascribed to the TO-LO splitting.36, 79 If 298 that interpretation was correct, it would be difficult to explain why similar splitting or doublet is 299 not prominent for the ~1090 cm-1 band in the Raman spectra of silicate glasses which show a 300 stronger intensity than the amorphous silica (Figure 3b). This experimental trend is opposite to 301 the theoretical prediction that the frequency separation between 𝜔𝑇𝑂 and 𝜔𝐿𝑂 (TO-LO splitting) 302 should be larger for the band with a higher oscillator strength.63 For that reason, it would be 303 difficult to ascribe the doublet at ~1060 cm-1 and ~1200 cm-1 of vitreous silica to the TO-LO 304 splitting. 305 There were some studies presenting vibrational density of state (VDOS) spectra 306 calculated from equations of motion as a supporting evidence for the TO-LO splitting 307 assignments in vibrational spectra of amorphous glasses.126, 138 The presence of specific peaks 308 and their intensities in the IR and Raman spectra are determined by specific interactions with the 309 electric field of the light, while VDOS is determined by the velocity correlations of atoms 310 without considering interactions with the electromagnetic wave. Thus, vibrational spectra 311 obtained through optical measurements are quite different from the VDOS distribution.139-141 312 Putting all information together, it is highly questionable whether the ~1200 cm-1 313 shoulder peaks observed in SR-IR and Raman spectra of silica and silicate glasses rigorously 314 meet the full definition of the TO-LO splitting found in the crystalline materials. Without 315 meeting all aspects of the theoretical mechanism, it is inappropriate to attribute the 316 experimentally observed phenomenon in SR-IR spectra of the bulk glass to the TO-LO splitting 317 process defined for the ionic or highly polar crystals or the polarization of thin films. Remember 318 that SR-IR measures the reflectance, 𝑅= 𝐼𝑟(𝑛,𝑘,𝜃𝑖) 𝐼𝑜 , which is different from the absorbance, 𝐴= 319 −𝑙𝑜𝑔( 𝐼𝑡 𝐼𝑜) = 𝑎𝑏𝑐, that is a function of 𝑘 only (see Section II).66 The appearance of a secondary 320 peak at the higher wavenumber side of a strongly absorbing peak is an optical effect in the 𝑅 321 measurement of the glass surface at an off-normal incidence angle. In the absence of the long-322 range order, it is dubious whether the extremely-weak doublet-like peaks in Raman spectra of the 323 12 bulk glass can be explained in the manner similar to the TO-LO splitting of the crystalline 324 material. 325 III.3 Comparison of vibrational bands of glass with those of crystalline materials 326 A frequently adapted approach in vibrational spectroscopy of glass is to compare the 327 vibrational spectral features of glass samples with those of crystalline materials with the same or 328 similar chemical compositions. Since the repeating structural units of crystals can be determined 329 from x-ray diffraction, it is tempting to utilize the same units to describe the vibrational spectral 330 features of glass materials with similar compositions. However, the compositional similarity is 331 not sufficient to guarantee the spectral similarity because the phonon modes of crystalline 332 networks can be forbidden or allowed depending on the long-range translational symmetry, 333 while the vibrations of the amorphous network are not bound to such symmetry rules.85, 142 In 334 addition, the glass network has broad distributions of bond angles and lengths, while the crystal 335 network has atoms at specific coordinates in the unit cell. Thus, Raman spectra of crystalline 336 materials often have narrow and intense bands, while those of glass materials give very broad 337 bands with different relative intensities and maximum-intensity positions. The comparison of the 338 spectra of crystalline quartz versus those of fused quartz and vitreous silica shown in Figures 3 339 and 6a manifests such differences. 340 In the high frequency region of the Raman spectrum of amorphous silica (Figure 6a), two 341 weak bands are observed at 1060 cm-1 and 1200 cm-1, which have been called the TO-LO modes 342 of fully-connected Q4 species103, 118, 132 (although its origin is debatable as discussed in Section 343 III.2). These two peaks appear to merge to one at ~1090 cm-1 as soon as the sodium modifier is 344 added to the silica glass (see Figure 3b). This merged peak grows continuously until the sodium 345 modifier concentration increases to Na2O2SiO2; in the same concentration range, a small peak 346 grows at ~950 cm-1 (Figures 6b). As the modifier concentration increases from Na2O2SiO2 to 347 Na2O1.22SiO2, the ~1090 cm-1 peak decreases and the ~950 cm-1 peak grows.32, 143 Based on the 348 stoichiometric model of the glass structure, the Q3 and Q2 species must be dominant species in 349 the glass network with Na2O2SiO2 and Na2OSiO2 compositions, respectively. Then, it could be 350 considered reasonable to assign the 1090 cm-1 and 950 cm-1 modes to the Q3 and Q2 species in 351 the silicate glass network.32, 38 Expanding this approach further, the weak band at ~900 cm-1 and 352 ~850 cm-1 could be attributed to Q1 and Q0, respectively (Figure 6c).32 353 13 Although classical model calculations with small structural moieties39, 43 were used to 354 support this assignment (Section IV), comparison with the IR mode assignment raises some 355 questions that need to be addressed further. For example, the Raman studies attribute the ~1090 356 cm-1 and ~950 cm-1 bands to the Q3 and Q2 species, separately; for the bands at similar positions, 357 the IR community attributes the ~1080 cm-1 band to the asymmetric stretch of Si-O-Si (BO) 358 bonds and the ~950 cm-1 shoulder to the stretch mode of Si-O- (NBO) bonds without 359 distinguishing Q3 and Q2 species (Table 1). Why are the Raman and IR peaks in the same 360 (almost identical) wavenumber region attributed to different modes? If they are the same mode, 361 why does the Raman band in the 1050-1100 cm-1 region grow as the Q3 fraction increases, while 362 the same band in IR decreases?92 This question will be re-visited in Section VI. 363 The low frequency bands in the 430~600 cm-1 region have been typically attributed to 364 bending vibrations of (SiO)m rings with different sizes (m) that can be identified in three-365 dimensionally connected amorphous networks. Sharma attributed two bands centered at 437 cm-1 366 and 490 cm-1 to six- and four-membered rings, respectively, in vitreous silica glass.41 This 367 assignment was proposed based on the fact that their peak positions are similar to the ones 368 observed in Raman spectra of α-quartz and coesite (Figure 6a). However, it is not obvious if the 369 sharp phonon band defined by the long-range order could be compared with the broad band of 370 the amorphous network without any long-range order. The (SiO)m rings identifiable in -quartz 371 are mostly 8-membered rings and 6-membered rings are a minor fraction.144 The 4-membered 372 rings in coesite are the smallest ring with a minor abundance; larger size rings are more abundant 373 in the coesite crystal structure.145 Also, the peak position of Raman bands of crystalline and 374 fused quartz are different, even though their chemical compositions are identical (Figure 3b). 375 The broadness of Raman spectral features of glass reflects the variance of structural parameters 376 in the glass network, which lacks in the crystalline lattice. 377 Galeener performed a central-force field model calculation assuming the existence of 378 planar rings consisting of corner-shared tetrahedra clusters in vitreous silica, and obtained the 379 calculation result supporting the assignment of the small but sharp peak at 606 cm-1 to the three-380 membered rings (m = 3).37 He further suggested the assignment relating the 495 cm-1 and 606 381 cm-1 bands in Raman spectra to four- and three-membered rings, respectively, via a decoupling 382 derivation method.146, 147 It was argued that the sharpness must appear in the Raman spectra 383 14 when Si-O is strongly bonded within a well-defined ring where Si atoms are completely 384 stationary (no motion) and coupling among vibrational modes is weak. However, Thorpe and 385 colleagues criticized this argument, pointing out that the model was based on uniform identical 386 rings, which were further embedded in a Bethe lattice for calculation.148 If the rings are not 387 identical, e.g. part of rings are distorted, the simulated spectra will be very broad, which cannot 388 explain the relative sharpness of certain bands attributed to specific rings. Also, DFT calculations 389 showed that the rings in silica glass are not planar.149 More discussion on this subject will be 390 provided in Sections V and VI. 391 392 IV. Classical models of solving equations of motion for small clusters 393 The interpretation of vibrational spectra of glass in 1970s and 1980s was made with 394 assistance from theoretical calculations solving differential equations of motion to obtain 395 vibrational frequencies of normal modes for small molecular clusters, e.g. a few connected 396 tetrahedra units, that look identical to the basic structural units composing the glass network.36, 39, 397 40, 43, 106 Figure 7 displays examples of such structural models.38 Without considering damping of 398 vibrational modes which affects the resonance peak width (Δ𝜔𝑟), the equations of motion of 399 atoms under the harmonic oscillation approximation can be written as:39 400 𝑚(𝑙) 𝑑2 𝑑𝑡2 𝑋𝛼(𝑛 ⃗ , 𝑙, 𝑡) = ∑ 𝑉 𝛼𝛽 𝛽,𝑛′ ⃗⃗⃗⃗ ,𝑙′ (𝑛 ⃗ , 𝑙|𝑛′ ⃗⃗⃗ , 𝑙′)𝑋𝛽 (𝑛′ ⃗⃗⃗ , 𝑙′, 𝑡) (1) 401 where 𝑙 is the label of atom, m is the mass of atom, 𝑛 ⃗ is the vector in two or three dimensions, X 402 is the displacement, 𝑉 𝛼𝛽 represents the force constant matrix. In many cases, two types of force 403 constants were assumed to be involved in displacements of atoms: central force for Si-O 404 stretching and non-central force for O-Si-O and Si-O-Si deformation or bending.40, 43, 99 The non-405 central component accounts for the dependence of the Si-O-Si stretch motion on the O-Si-O 406 and/or Si-O-Si bond angles.150-152 Then, the atomic coordinates and force fields are expressed in 407 matrix G and F, respectively, and the eigenvalues of dynamic matrix can be calculated through 408 the Wilson GF method.99, 100, 153 Finally, a certain peak width was assumed arbitrarily to compare 409 with the broad vibrational spectrum of glass. 410 15 Key limitations of these classical models are as follows. In isolated structural models 411 consisting of small clusters, considering the connections with nearest neighbors would be 412 sufficient since there are no chemical bonds outside those clusters. In glass, however, those 413 clusters are intricately connected to the three-dimensional network without any long-range order. 414 Hence, their vibrations will be influenced by the connectivity with the neighboring and next-415 neighboring clusters because those will alter the boundary conditions of the differential equations 416 to be solved. In silicate glasses, BO atoms can also interact with nearby modifier ions,154, 155 417 which may affect their force constants. The force constants used in the equations were chosen to 418 match the experimentally observed peak positions. In these classical models of small clusters, 419 arbitrarily chosen peak widths were introduced to mimic the broad bands of glass in experiments. 420 Would that be sufficient to justify assigning the experimentally observed broad bands of 421 amorphous networks to the modes calculated from isolated clusters? There were calculations for 422 larger-scale disordered networks;99, 101, 156 but, the methods used to create disordered atomic 423 arrangements were unclear.99, 157 Overall, even though the classical model calculations provide 424 analytical solutions with clear visualization of isolated structural moieties, the accuracy of 425 calculation results is sacrificed by over-simplification of ignoring the broad bond length and 426 angle distributions of structural units and their connectivity in the amorphous network. 427 In order to show the Si-O-Si stretch band position with different ring sizes, the non-428 central force constant concept was employed.36, 38, 43 In this model, the Si-O stretch force 429 constant was assumed to be a simple function of Si-O-Si bond angle (Figure 8a). It is 430 conceivable that the local Si-O-Si bond angle would be coupled with the local Si-O bond length 431 because both are directly related to the hybridization of atoms in the first-shell SiO4 unit. 432 However, a priori justification for choosing a specific mathematical function was not fully 433 discussed. Certain forms or parameters could have been adapted from crystalline materials and 434 adjusted with scaling factors to enforce the calculation results to be consistent with experimental 435 results.150, 158, 159 Nonetheless, coupling between the Si-O-Si bond angle and the Si-O stretch 436 force constant may not be as simple as the trigonometric function assumed in these non-central 437 force constant models (see Section VI).160-163 If the Si-O-Si bond angle influences the Si-O-Si 438 stretch mode through the non-central force constant, why does it not affect the Si-O-Si bending 439 mode at all? No thorough discussion on this question could be found in the literature. 440 16 441 VDOS calculations were often employed to compare with vibrational spectra of glass 442 network.36, 43, 106, 165, 166 An example is shown in Figure 8b. It must be recalled that VDOS is 443 calculated through velocity autocorrelations of all atoms in the model,167, 168 and obtained 444 without considering interactions with the electric field of light.31, 169 Thus, it could be considered 445 as all ‘possible’ vibrational modes; but only few of them can be observed in the vibrational 446 spectrum. The VDOS analysis cannot tell which ones are observable in IR and Raman analysis. 447 Thus, direct one-to-one comparison is not possible. The VDOS is not directly accessible in 448 experiment; the experimental technique that most closely reproduces the local VDOS spectrum is 449 inelastic neutron scattering,170, 171 which is not the same as IR or Raman.171 450 451 V. DFT calculations of vibrational spectra of glass 452 Density functional theory (DFT) calculations deliver an approximate solution to the 453 Schrödinger equation of a many-body system.182172 The optimized configuration of a given 454 molecule or crystalline solid is found by minimizing total energy of the system upon adjusting 455 bond lengths and angles within possible structures. The force constants relevant to specific 456 vibrational modes are calculated from the second derivatives of total energy with respective to 457 atomic coordinates.173-177 Then, the resonant vibrational frequencies are calculated from the force 458 constants obtained from the first principles rather than peak fitting to experimental values.31, 178 459 Quantum mechanical calculations are computationally expensive and thus the number of 460 atoms that can be modeled is quite limited. For that reason, DFT calculations of glass materials 461 were carried out mostly for small clusters representing basic structural units of the glass 462 network.87, 179-184 For example, orthosilicic acid molecule or disiloxane clusters (Figure 9) are 463 modeled to portray silica glass or other silicate structures. In that sense, early DFT calculations 464 were not much different from classical models other than the optimum structures and force 465 constants were obtained from quantum mechanical calculations. Thus, they could not address the 466 effects of the broad distributions of bond lengths and angles of basic structural units and their 467 random connectivity without any long-range order. Similar to the classical models described in 468 the previous section, the early DFT calculations could provide only line intensities of specific 469 17 normal modes allowed for the modeled clusters (Figure 9) and could not provide any insights 470 into the band shape or width observed in IR spectra.185, 186 471 Being a first principles approach, DFT calculations can still be used to understand how 472 vibrational modes of small clusters vary among specific geometries. For example, DFT 473 calculations were used to check if the peak positions of ~490 cm-1 and ~600 cm-1 match with the 474 assignment of four-membered and three-membered rings, respectively.149, 179, 180 However, the 475 minimum energy conformation could vary depending on symmetry constraints or energy 476 normalization factor applied in DFT calculations,179, 186, 187 which will lead to divergence of 477 predicted vibrational characteristics.188, 189 In fact, the calculated Raman spectra are quite 478 different from one study to the other using H6Si2O7 dimer and cyclic H6Si3O9 trimer.189 The 479 calculation results are very sensitive to the bond parameters, such as bond angle of Si-O-Si, 480 optimized differently in each study.179, 188, 190 481 More recently, Giacomazzi et al. reported comprehensive DFT calculation results for 482 vitreous silica model containing 144 atoms, which corresponds to 48 units of SiO2 (Figure 483 10).171, 191 Their vibrational spectral analysis included not only VDOS calculations, but also the 484 evaluation of the first and second derivatives of atomic forces with respect to the electric fields. 485 The first derivative term is expressed with the Born effective charge tensor associated with the 486 polarization in response to electric field; this can be related to the dielectric permittivity (𝜀1 + 487 𝑖𝜀2). The IR spectrum can be calculated from 𝑛 and 𝑘 which can be derived from 𝜀1 and 𝜀2. The 488 second derivative term is expressed with a derivative of the dielectric polarizability tensor under 489 the Placzek approximation, which determines the Raman susceptibility. In Figure 10, the 490 agreement of the calculation results with the experimental spectra is quite remarkable. Since the 491 144-atom model has broad distributions of Si-O bond length as well as O-Si-O and Si-O-Si bond 492 angles, the predicted spectrum shows the natural broadening of the bands. 493 By comparing this 144-atom model with two other models containing only 72 atoms and 494 having different Si-O-Si bond-angle distributions and ring statistics, Giacomazzi et al. found 495 interesting correlations between the spectral features and the bond parameter distributions.171 In 496 the VDOS spectrum, the 800 cm-1 peak appears to be sensitive to the average Si-O-Si bond angle 497 distribution, suggesting that it involves the bending vibrations of Si-O-Si bonds. In the IR 498 spectrum, the ~450 cm-1 and ~1080 cm-1 bands reflect differences in the Si-O-Si bond angle and 499 18 Si-O bond length distributions, respectively. In the Raman spectrum, the band in the 300 – 700 500 cm-1 region shifts toward higher wavenumbers as the average Si-O-Si bond angle in the model 501 decreases. The small band at ~600 cm-1 is claimed to reflect the population of three-membered 502 ring, even though the relative population of this ring is only minor compared to those of larger 503 rings. The results of this first principles approach did not show the trend assumed in the non-504 central force constant model (Figure 8a). Caution must be taken when these trends are compared 505 with the experimental data since the 144-atom model used in DFT calculations cannot represent 506 all aspects of the amorphous silica network whose structure will vary depending on the sample 507 history.113, 192 508 In some literature, the symmetric and asymmetric Si-O-Si stretch modes are attributed to 509 the A1 and T2 symmetry modes, respectively, of the SiO4 moiety in the glass because this 510 smallest topological unit has the tetrahedral (Td) point group.30, 193, 194 The symmetry rule of 511 vibrational spectroscopy dictates that the A1 mode is Raman-active only, and the T2 mode is both 512 Raman-active and IR-active.195 If the broad band in the 1000-1200 cm-1 region the VDOS 513 spectrum obtained from DFT calculations (Figure 10a) is the A1 symmetry mode, it should be 514 strong in Raman, but weak or negligible in IR. If it has the T2 symmetry, it should be strong in 515 both IR and Raman spectra. But, the experimental spectra of amorphous silica are not consistent 516 with these symmetry rules – the Si-O-Si stretch band is very weak or negligible in the Raman 517 spectrum (Figure 3b and Figure 10d) and appears as a strong peak only in IR (Figure 3a and 518 Figure 10b & c; note that the IR intensity is proportional to 4𝜋𝑘/𝜆 where 𝑘 can be calculated 519 from 𝜀1 and 𝜀2). This discrepancy clearly shows that the vibrational modes of amorphous glass 520 network cannot be adequately described with the analogy to those of small molecular clusters.90 521 Although the ~1080 cm-1 IR band is often called the asymmetric Si-O-Si stretch and the Raman 522 band in the same region is attributed to the symmetric BO stretch (Table 1), those bands are not 523 the same as (or as simple as) the stretch mode of the isolated SiO4 (Q4) moiety.82 524 525 VI. args.summary:
This feature article by Hongshen Liu, Huseyan Kaya, Yen-Ting Lin, Andrew Ogrinc, and Seong H. Kim (Pennsylvania State University) critically reviews the use of vibrational spectroscopy (IR and Raman) for structural analysis of silica and silicate glass networks. The paper argues that traditional interpretations of glass vibrational spectra—based on analogies with isolated molecules or crystalline counterparts—are inadequate because glass is a non-equilibrium, three-dimensionally connected amorphous network without long-range order. Its structure and properties depend not only on present temperature and pressure but also on thermal history (cooling rate, annealing, mechanical stress, surface treatments).

Key technical points include: (1) transmission IR is unsuitable for Si-O-Si stretch bands (900–1200 cm⁻¹) due to extremely high absorptivity (k ≈ 1), so specular reflection IR (SR-IR) is the standard method, though it requires Kramers-Kronig transformation for accurate k-spectra; (2) ATR-IR is not suitable for probing Si-O-Si network vibrations but works for subsurface hydrous species; (3) the ~1200 cm⁻¹ shoulder band in SR-IR spectra, often attributed to TO-LO splitting, is argued to be an optical artifact (Reststrahlen effect) related to the complex refractive index, not an intrinsic vibrational mode—the Berreman effect explains the apparent LO mode in thin films but cannot explain the bulk glass phenomenon; (4) comparisons between glass and crystalline spectra are problematic because phonon symmetry rules based on long-range translational symmetry do not apply to amorphous networks.

The paper reviews historical interpretation models: classical force-field calculations on small clusters (Bell & Gaskell, Galeener) assigned the ~1080 cm⁻¹ band to asymmetric Si-O-Si (BO) stretch, ~800 cm⁻¹ to symmetric BO stretch, ~480 cm⁻¹ to BO bending, and ~950 cm⁻¹ to NBO-related modes. The authors challenge these assignments, noting contradictions between IR and Raman attributions of the same spectral regions (Q3/Q2 vs. BO/NBO). Modern DFT calculations (e.g., Giacomazzi et al.'s 144-atom vitreous silica model) show good agreement with experimental spectra and reveal that the ~1080 cm⁻¹ IR band reflects Si-O bond length distributions while the ~450 cm⁻¹ band reflects Si-O-Si bond angle distributions. MD simulations computing IR spectra from dipole moment autocorrelation functions support these findings.

The authors propose two empirical relationships for interpreting silica/silicate glass spectra: (i) the intensity-weighted peak position of the Si-O-Si stretch mode negatively correlates with the weighted average of the Si-O bond length distribution, and (ii) the broad band of the Si-O-Si bending mode negatively correlates with the Si-O-Si bond angle distribution. Selected examples of vibrational spectroscopic imaging of surface defects (e.g., Vickers indents, elastic contact) are discussed to show implications for structure-property relationships. The paper identifies unanswered questions and continuing challenges in glass vibrational spectroscopy research.
args.key_excerpts: "Glass is a non-equilibrium solid or a 'frozen liquid' with an extremely slow relaxation behavior; thus, its structure and properties are a function of not only the present temperature and pressure at which the glass object is exposed, but also the past history that it has gone through (such as cooling rate, annealing, mechanical stress, post-synthesis treatment, etc.).", "For the interpretation of vibrational spectral features of silica and silicate glasses, the following empirical relationships are suggested: (i) the intensity-weighted peak position of the Si-O-Si stretch mode negatively correlates with the weighted average of the Si-O bond length distribution and (ii) the broad band of the Si-O-Si bending mode negatively correlates with the Si-O-Si bond angle distribution.", "The absence of this band in the ATR-IR spectrum is simply an optical artifact which should not be interpreted as the dissociation of the Si-O-Si network bonds in the surface region.", "Putting all information together, it is highly questionable whether the ~1200 cm-1 shoulder peaks observed in SR-IR and Raman spectra of silica and silicate glasses rigorously meet the full definition of the TO-LO splitting found in the crystalline materials.", "The vibrational modes of amorphous glass network cannot be adequately described with the analogy to those of small molecular clusters."

## Abstract

This study aims to compare photoacoustic (FTIR–PAS), diffuse reflectance (DRIFT), and attenuated total reflection (ATR) FTIR modalities in the wide wavenumber range from NIR (7500 cm−1) to FIR (150 cm−1) for the same silicate soil samples under the same conditions. The possibilities of non-destructive rapid qualitative analysis of soils by these modalities without comprehensive data treatment were compared. The assignment of more than 100 bands for the chernozem and sod-podzolic as common types of silicate types of soil was made. The following groups of bands of organic matter and inorganic matrix were reliably found in spectra of all or at least two modalities: 3690–3680 cm−1 (hydrogen-bonded SiO–H…H2O stretch, not ATR), 2930–2910 cm−1 and 2860–2850 cm−1 (methylene stretch), 1390–1380 cm−1, (symmetric stretch carboxylate, DRIFT and FTIR–PAS); 2000–1990 cm−1, 1885 cm−1, and 1790–1783 cm−1 (SiO2 overtones, DRIFT and FTIR–PAS), 1163–1153 cm−1, SiO2 lattice (not FTIR–PAS), 1037 cm−1 (Si–O or Al–O stretch), 796 cm−1 (lattice symmetrical Si–O–Si stretch); 697 cm−1, SiO2; and 256 cm−1 (not FTIR–PAS). Amide I, II, and III bands appear in DRIFT and FTIR–PAS spectra while not in ATR. Except for methylene and carboxylate groups, CH vibrations (3100–2900 cm−1) are not seen in ATR. Bands at 1640–1630 cm−1, 1620–1610 cm−1, 1600–1598 cm−1 (primary water bands and probably carboxylate) appear in the spectra of all three modalities but are unresolved and require data treatment. It is preferable to use all three modalities to characterize both soil organic matter and mineral composition. DRIFT provides the maximum number of bands in all three modalities and should be selected as a primary technique in the NIR and 4000–2000 cm−1 regions for hydrogen-bonding bands, CHX groups, and the silicate matrix. ATR–FTIR complements DRIFT and provides a good sensitivity for soil water and the matrix in 2000–400 cm−1. FTIR–PAS in 4000–1500 cm−1 reveals more bands than DRIFT and shows the highest sensitivity for absorption bands that do not appear in DRIFT or ATR-IR spectra. Thus, FTIR–PAS is expedient for supporting either DRIFT or ATR–FTIR. This modality comparison can be a basis for methodological support of IR spectroscopy of soils and similar organomineral complexes.
